The most common etchants used for FS poly-silicon removal are KOH and TMAH aqueous solutions. TMAH is the most popular because of its relatively low toxicity and high etch selectivity of silicon to oxide  [7] . However, TMAH and KOH have several demerits, namely, higher etch rate for n-doped polysilicon over p-doped, strong etch rate dependence on dopant type and doping level  [8] , and a strong effect of small amounts of contaminants on the etch rate  [9] ,  [10] . The latter property results in additional requirements to sample preparation prior to the etching. Etch rate similarity for n-and p-doped silicon is essential for CMOS FA applications, especially for SRAM, where gate oxide under both ndoped and p-doped poly should be exposed for further inspection.


In the present investigation we use a 50% wt. choline hydroxide aqueous solution for FS polysilicon etching. This choice is determined mainly by unique silicon to oxide etching selectivity. Choline hydroxide is an organic etchant, which develops strong oxidizing properties. The oxidizing agents are OH -ions.


In the first part of the paper, a set of experiments, which investigates the general etching characteristics of silicon and SiO 2 in choline hydroxide, such as etch rate, selectivity, and surface quality of silicon, is described.


The second part of the paper is devoted to the failure analysis applications of the obtained results. In this set of experiments FS poly-silicon etch for gate oxide exposure was performed. The goal was to find the best etching conditions, which enable exposure of gate oxide under both: the n-poly and the p-poly simultaneously, and to develop a reliable and robust procedure for gate oxide exposure for subsequent SEM analysis.


# Experimental Method


Experimental Method


The etch rate of silicon and SiO 2 in choline hydroxide , Si/SiO 2 selectivity, and the etch influence on silicon surface morphology were investigated. Silicon substrate specimens 3 mm x 10 mm x 0.75 mm with (100) orientation, p-type doped to 5-10 milliohms-cm were used. Two sets of specimens were prepared. The first one had unpolished surfaces with overall average roughness of 850 Å. In the second set, mirror-face polished silicon specimens with initial average roughness of 70 Å were used. A part of each specimen was covered by 1 micron of SiO 2 , grown by PECVD. This oxide was used as an etch mask for the silicon. SiO 2 etching experiments were carried out on 700 nm thick oxide films, grown by PECVD on mirror-face polished silicon specimens.


Etching experiments were performed in 50% wt. choline hydroxide aqueous solution, heated to temperatures ranging from 20°C to 92°C. Etching was carried out in a glass vessel thermostated with a water bath on a laboratory hot plate. The temperature variation was less than +/-1.5ºC. The solution was slowly stirred during the etching. The specimens were kept in a teflon strainer. A reflux condenser was used to reduce concentration change during the etching. The silicon specimens were dipped for 15 seconds in 2% hydrofluoric acid prior to the etching to remove the native oxide layer. The etch rate for Si (100) was calculated by dividing the etch depth by the etching time. The silicon etch depth was measured by focusing an optical microscope on the grown SiO 2 film and then on the etched silicon surface, and subtracting the respective heights, giving the result with an accuracy of ~+/-1 µm. In addition, the silicon etch depth was measured using an electronic micrometer. The last method gives the data that match within 1 µm with the data obtained by optical microscope. SiO 2 film thickness before and after the etching was measured using a spectrophotometer. SiO 2 etch rate was calculated by dividing the film thickness difference by the etching time.


Silicon surface roughness was measured using an alpha-step profilometer, by performing four 2-mm length scans for each specimen with a sampling rate of 1 point/micron, and averaging the results over four scans. Silicon surface morphology was examined using an optical microscope and SEM.


The second part of the work was devoted to the application of silicon and SiO 2 etch data obtained in the first part, to gate oxide failure analysis. In these experiments, FS poly-silicon selective etching for gate oxide exposure was performed. CMOS 0.13 µm technology SRAM specimens were used for the experiments. The sample preparation preceding the etching includes FS polishing of dies down to the poly-silicon layer, optical and SEM inspection, and final polishing targeted to remove any salicide residuals and SEM-related carbon built-up, which can interfere with the etching process. The setup of this experiment was the same as for the first set. The variables were etch temperature and etching time. The etching results were documented using SEM micrographs at 40,000X magnification.


The high viscosity of choline hydroxide creates problems in rinsing and cleanling. This makes the post-etching cleaning procedure essential for enabling the consequent SEM inspection of a specimen. It is standard practice to allow the specimen to soak in DI water for several minutes after the etching. This procedure was followed by the treatment in hot solvents accordingly to the following scheme:


-boiling acetone for 8 minutes, and then ultrasonic bath in acetone for 2 minutes; -boiling methyl alcohol for 6 minutes, and then ultrasonic bath in methanol for 2 minutes; -ultrasonic bath in isopropyl alcohol for 2 minutes at room temperature. This procedure completely removes all choline residues from the specimens providing the clarity of the SEM micrographs.


# Results and Discussion


# Etch Rate and Si/SiO 2 Selectivity


Etch Rate and Si/SiO 2 Selectivity


Figure  1  represents a graph of the logarithm of the etch rate of silicon and SiO 2 vs. inverse absolute temperature. One can see from the graph, that silicon and SiO 2 etch in choline hydroxide is a thermallyactivated process which obeys the Arrhenius Law:


V =Aexp( -E a /kT),  (1)  where V is the etch rate, T is absolute temperature, E a is the activation energy, k is the Bolzman coefficient, and A is a constant. The calculated values of activated energy are: 0.51 eV for unpolished silicon specimens, 0.61 eV for mirrorface polished silicon specimens, and 0.72 eV for SiO 2 .


The etch rate for mirror-face polished p-doped silicon ranges from ~4 nm/min at room temperature to ~360 nm/min at 90°C. This etch rate is sufficient for poly-gate etching applications, taking into account that poly gate thickness is typically several hundreds of nanometers for modern technologies, and assuming that poly-silicon etch rate should be close to monocrystalline silicon etch rate. The etch rate for unpolished silicon specimens is higher than for mirror-face polished ones, reaching 430 nm/min at 90°C. The simple explanation for this fact is, that the rougher surface provides more total contact area with the reactive agent during the etching.


Table  1  represents Si and SiO 2 etch rates at various temperatures and shows the dependence of Si to SiO 2 etching selectivity on temperature. One can see that the selectivity of silicon to oxide is superior and reaches 10000:1 at room temperature. The selectivity decreases slowly to ~5000 with the temperature increase up to 93°C. This high silicon to SiO 2 selectivity provides a good basis for the gate oxide failure analysis application. If the standard polysilicon gate thickness is ~10 -7 m, and the gate oxide thickness is ~10 -9 m, we still have enough selectivity reserve for a robust process which is tolerant to etching condition variability.


# Silicon Surface Morphology


Silicon Surface Morphology


Surface morphology dependence on etching temperature, etch time, and initial surface roughness was investigated.


Figures 2(a)-3(f) show surface relief development during etching in choline hydroxide for unpolished silicon specimens etched at varying temperatures. One can see that the etching yields surfaces that are texturized, i.e. covered with pyramids, whose sizes and shapes depend on etching temperature. Sizes range from several microns (at 20°C) to 100 micron (at 90°C). Table  2  represents an average background roughness of the specimens shown in Figure  2 . The roughness of the specimens increases considerably with etch temperature. The surface of mirror-face polished specimens after choline hydroxide etch differs considerably from the surface of unpolished specimens. As can be seen in Figure  3 , a similar overall surface finish has been obtained in two cases: after 50 hours etching at room temperature, and after 3 hours etching at 90°C. The surface remains smooth, although a distribution of varying sized square-shaped pyramids (hillocks) appears on both samples. It has been found, that for mirror-face polished specimens, the surface quality depends on etch time, rather than on the etch temperature. Roughness data for mirror-face polished specimens, represented in Table  3 , confirm this assumption.


Figure  4  shows an example of small square-based {111}-bounded pyramid-shaped hillocks, which appears on the mirror-face polished surface after choline etch. Silicon surface roughness and morphology are essential for micromachining applications, which require a mirror-like quality. In general, the nature of surface morphology formation in aqueous hydroxide solutions (as KOH or TMAH) is a competition between the rate of dissolution of silicon and the local passivation of the surface by the accumulation of masking species. Hydrogen bubbles  [11] , reaction by-products  [12] , and foreign impurities  [9] , while adsorbing to the silicon surface, can act as nucleation points for relief formations. As reported, surface roughness also depends on such factors as OH -ion concentration  [12]  and silicon etch anisotropy in different crystallographic directions  [13] . In the current study we didn't investigate the influence of the above-mentioned factors on the surface quality. However, by comparison of our results with the data presented in literature for KOH and TMAH, we can conclude that silicon etching in choline hydroxide yields a surface good enough for MEMS applications.


# Poly-Silicon Etching and Gate Oxide Exposure


Poly-Silicon Etching and Gate Oxide Exposure


On the basis of the data obtained in the first part of this investigation, the method for gate oxide exposure by selective poly-silicon gate etching has been elaborated. The goal is to find the best etch conditions, which enable exposure of gate oxide under both the n-poly and the p-poly simultaneously, and to develop a reliable and robust procedure for gate oxide exposure.


Figure  5  presents a SEM micrograph of SRAM memory cells at ILD0/contacts/poly level with completely exposed (and free of salicide) poly-gates. This is an example of a specimen that is ready for choline etching. The remaining poly thickness is estimated as ~100-120 nm. Etch temperatures 34°C, 55°C, and 92°C have been tried. Accordingly to the data obtained from p-doped bulk silicon etching, the etch rates for these temperatures should be ~10 nm/min, ~50 nm/min, and ~400 nm/min, respectively. The best etching results were found at 55°C. At 34°C, the etching is too slow. Alternatively, heating the choline hydroxide aqueous solution above 90°C results in a change in choline concentration: it looses water and intensively consumes CO 2 from the atmosphere. The process becomes too fast and uncontrollable under these conditions. In additional, etching selectivity decreases with the etch temperature increase. These considerations have resulted in the etch temperature choice of 55°C.


Figures  6 through 9  show the etching results at temperature 55°C for 2, 4, 6, and 8 minutes of etching, respectively. One can see that the poly gate is completely etched and the gate oxide is exposed under both n-doped and p-doped poly, when etching lasts 4, 6, or 8 minutes. Taking into account silicon to SiO 2 selectivity data, the upper time limit can be estimated as ~12 minutes. It's important to note, that the etching doesn't introduce artifacts and yields to the clearly exposed gate oxide. As can be seen in Figure  6 , etching during two minutes results in gate oxide exposure only under n-doped poly. This means that some etch selectivity between n-doped and pdoped poly exists. The author's estimations give ~70-80 nm/min for n-poly etch rate, 30-35 nm/min for ppoly etch rate, which results in factor of 2 for n-poly to p-poly selectivity. The poly-silicon etch rate at 55°C in these experiments is found to be lower than that obtained from bulk silicon etching. This can be explained by the heavy doping level of poly-gates, which can degrade the etch rate. In addition, the gate width to gate thickness ratio can also be responsible for the etch rate decrease.


The etching conditions thus proposed by the author are: etching during 4-8 minutes at 55°C. This provides complete and artifact-free poly-gate etching for both n-and p-regions with a high selectivity to gate oxide. Etch rate for gate oxide has been estimated to be  < 0.01nm/min. This ensures a high tolerance of the suggested method to the etching conditions (etch time and temperature) variations.


# Conclusion


Conclusion


This paper presents the novel technique for FS gate oxide exposure using choline hydroxide. The technique is based on the extremely high silicon to SiO 2 etch selectivity of choline hydroxide. The Si:SiO 2 selectivity reaches 10,000 at room temperature, and decreases gradually to 5000 with the temperature increase to 92°C.


Etching in choline hydroxide considerably degrades the Si surface quality, if applied to initially rough and unpolished surface. However, the etching causes minimal degradation to previously polished Si surfaces. This fact, together with the superior Si/SiO2 selectivity, and good process controllability, makes choline hydroxide a promising process for MEMS production.


Etching conditions, which allow the simultaneous etching of n-doped and p-doped poly-silicon and reliable gate oxide exposure, fit for subsequent SEM inspection have been found.


The regime of post-etching specimens cleaning which enables the subsequent SEM inspection has been elaborated.


The method has been successfully used for failure analysis of Intel's integrated circuit components. Figure  10  shows a SEM micrograph of a real gate oxide defect in a CMOS component, which was exposed using the proposed technique.


# Introduction


Introduction


Decapsulation of a device still mounted to a printed circuit board (PCB), while maintaining functionality of both the device and the PCB, can be of great advantage in some situations. For instance, the additional heat cycle needed to reflow the solder for device removal can confound assembly related problems, such as broken bond wires due to suspected package delamination.


Other failure mechanisms, such as trapped charge, can be adversely affected by the heat necessary to remove a part from a PCB. Additionally, when a part requires mounting to a circuit board for active microprobing, the ability to decapsulate the part in situ eliminates the need to remove the part, decapsulate it, and resolder it to the board. This paper will describe techniques developed to decapsulate devices while still mounted to a printed circuit board, maintaining both the functionality and integrity of the circuit board. These techniques incorporate materials that are readily available and easily customized to specific applications.


# Technique


Technique


The primary decapsulation tool used in our laboratory is the B & G International Dual Decap system. 1 The In situ technique uses the rubber template gaskets typically used with this system, plus a piece of ~ 4.1 mm (0.16") thick polyethylene foam to protect the PCB from the decapsulation chemicals.


The polyethylene foam sheet is a readily available packaging/shipping material. It has a maximum operating temperature of 80° to 100°C, is easily cut to any shape, and offers good sealing characteristics. 2  It is also relatively resistant to attack from the 5:1 mixture of fuming nitric acid and sulfuric acid, heated to 80°C, which is typically used for decapsulation in our facility. Figure  1  illustrates a board being prepared for in situ decapsulation, along with the necessary gasket materials. Referring to the photograph of Figure  1 , the decapsulation gasket scheme (in order of assembly) consists of the following: Immediately below the PCB is the rubber gasket that is typically used to define the decapsulation hole for the device when decapped on a stand-alone basis. The polyethylene foam sheet is below this gasket. The sheet has been cut to match the size of the PCB, and a hole has been cut into the sheet at the center of the device location. The hole is approximately the same size as that in the rubber decap gasket. A number of methods can be used to cut the hole in the foam, including an X-acto knife, or miniature scissors. Metal tubing can be used to punch a hole in the foam, and is available in many different diameters. The rubber gasket below the polyethylene sheet is simply a spacer. Since the heated decapsulation etch head is recessed below the main surface of the decap chamber, and components on the PCB further raise the board above the level of the etch head, this spacer is needed to ensure a good seal between the stack of gasket material and the etch head. The gasket components are assembled to one another using double-sided adhesive tape to maintain alignment. Single-sided tape, rather than doublesided, can be used to affix the rubber decap hole definition gasket (next to the device) to the polyethylene foam. Care should be taken to place the tape at the periphery of the rubber gaskets, well away from the center opening and the flow of acid. This gasket assembly is then placed on the PCB so that the holes in the gaskets are directly over the center of the part.


Single-sided tape is used to attach the polyethylene sheet to the board to hold it in place. The drawing of Figure  2  illustrates a side view of the arrangement of gasket materials assembled onto a printed circuit board that is ready for in situ decapsulation. The PCB and gasket assembly is then placed in the decap system as shown in Figure  4 . Since the device to be decapsulated is on the underside of the board, and the board covers the etch head, alignment must be accomplished using features or marks on both the back of the board and in the decapsulation chamber.


In our Dual Decap system, there are four holes located 90° apart around the decapsulation head in the chamber floor, and these are used to center the device over the etch head. A permanent marker can be used to mark the edges of the PCB at points, which if connected, would intersect over the center of the device to be decapsulated. These marks, in turn, can be aligned to the holes in the chamber floor. If the device to be decapsulated uses an exposed paddle type package style, often there will be through holes on the circuit board directly beneath the exposed paddle. These through holes are very helpful when performing the alignment to the etch head.


# Figure 4. PCB and Gasket Assembly in Decap System


Figure 4. PCB and Gasket Assembly in Decap System


Once the PCB is correctly positioned, decapsulation can begin. Because of the greater distance between the unit and the decapsulation etch head, the acid spray is not as focused, and etch times must be extended by a few seconds. After the decapsulation is complete, the gasket stack should be removed and the device rinsed with water, acetone, or isopropyl alcohol. Acetone is typically the most effective at removing decapsulation residue. The individual pieces of the gasket stack should be separated and rinsed well in water. The polyethylene foam sheet can be used several times before needing to be replaced. Figure  5  shows the device and PCB after the in situ decapsulation, while Figure  6  is a micrograph of the device itself, in this case a 32 lead TQFP package. This technique works well with boards that are exclusively built with surface mount components.


For boards with taller components, such as SMA coaxial connecters, trimming potentiometers, etc., this particular technique does not provide enough vertical clearance to accommodate these components.


To overcome this problem, a riser was designed and constructed using Teflon to effectively raise the etch head by 8.9 mm (0.35 inches). The riser was designed to emulate the silicon carbide etch head of the Dual Decap system, with a center hole for fresh acid flow and two holes on either side for the waste drains. The diameter of the top portion of the riser was reduced from that of the Dual Decap etch head to provide more flexibility for use on PCB's with tall components in close proximity to the device of interest. Figure  7  is a top view photograph of the completed riser, while Figure  8  shows the underside of the riser. The riser eliminates the need for additional rubber gaskets to be used as spacers to raise the height of the PCB. Polyethylene foam can be used alone as the decapsulation gasket in these cases. Figure  9  shows a PCB that has been prepared for in situ decapsulation by affixing a piece of poly foam over the device, and surrounding area, using adhesive tape.


# Additional Applications of In Situ Decapsulation


Additional Applications of In Situ Decapsulation


The use of polyethylene foam has been useful in the decapsulation of other package styles and assembly technologies.


192 Pin 25 X 25 mm SBGA Package


The SBGA package style is challenging to decapsulate, as both the package body, as well as the solder balls, can be adversely affected by the decapsulation chemicals. By using polyethylene foam to make a custom gasket, these packages can be successfully decapsulated. The gasket is created by heating a sacrificial package to about 100°C, and then placing the package into polyethylene foam, solder balls down. The elevated temperature of the package will cause the polyethylene foam to melt, making a perfect impression of the package. Slight and even downward pressure should be applied to the package during this process to form a good impression into the foam. Be sure to note the pin 1 location, in case the package is keyed or the solder ball placement is not symmetrical. An X-acto knife can be used to cut the etch window into the gasket to define the area to be decapsulated. This technique does not require any of the standard rubber gaskets; only the poly foam is required. Figure  11  shows the poly foam gasket and the final decapsulation results of the package. Because of the extended etch time of 180 seconds to remove the "glob-top" type compound used to fill the package cavity, and the elevated temperature of the etch head (80°C), the 4.1 mm poly foam was only capable of decapsulating 2 units before becoming permanently compressed and no longer providing a good seal.


# Chip-on-Board


Chip-on-Board


The "glob-top" used to encapsulate die on chip-onboard assemblies can also be removed using the aforementioned techniques. Figure  12  shows a chipon-board module, a piece of polyethylene foam cut to match the size of the PCB, and a rubber gasket which was used as a spacer to raise the PCB sufficiently above the base of the decap system. As with the other examples, a small hole was placed in the polyethylene foam, and all of the gasket materials were taped together and to the PCB to maintain alignment.


Figure  12 . Chip-on-Board Module With Gasket Materials


The domed shape of the "glob-top" and its smooth texture make it difficult to achieve a good seal to the polyethylene foam. Thus in some cases damage can occur to the PCB. However, the technique still allows controlled exposure of the die itself, including the wire bonding. Figure  13  is a micrograph that shows the result of the in situ decapsulation performed on this device.


# Post Decapsulation Cleaning


Post Decapsulation Cleaning


After a unit has been successfully decapsulated, it is often necessary to clean the unit much more thoroughly than what is achieved by the initial rinsing to remove residual acid. This is particularly true if FIB circuit modifications or probe points will be required. A dirty die surface can hamper both accurate identification of the desired features to be worked on, and the success of the FIB work itself. Three different methods have been used to remove residual decapsulation debris from the die surface without harming the PCB or surrounding components. The first and preferred method uses Microstrip 2001 positive resist developer. 3 This product has been found to work extremely well to remove the decapsulation residue left on the die. In order to avoid damage to the PCB, an eye dropper is used to place the Microstrip into the cavity created by the decapsulation. If the decapsulation cavity is centered, a well will be formed in the package that prevents the Microstrip from coming into contact with the PCB material. Allow the Microstrip to remain in the cavity for several minutes, and rinse the entire PCB in water. Repeating this process with some fresh Microstrip typically results in a cleaner die, as the small amount of solution in the decap well quickly becomes dirty and looses effectiveness. This same technique can be performed using Nanostrip, a stabilized formulation of Sulfuric acid and Hydrogen Peroxide compounds. 4 The Nanostrip is a more aggressive cleaner than the Microstrip, but also can cause more damage to the PCB if it should come in contact with it. The third technique places the entire PCB into a surfactant + isopropyl alcohol solution, and enough Buehler Transoptic Powder to completely cover the board. 5  With ultrasonic agitation, the Transoptic Powder spheres act as a mild abrasive and are quite effective at removing decapsulation residue. A few minutes of agitation is all that is necessary, and the whole board is cleaned by rinsing in water. Surprisingly, circuit boards containing trimming potentiometers and quartz crystals were still functional after this cleaning technique.


# Risks and Trade-Offs of In situ Decapsulation


Risks and Trade-Offs of In situ Decapsulation


There are some risks that need to be taken into account before performing an in situ decapsulation. The primary risk is a misalignment of the gasket material which can cause an off center decapsulation, or even worse, damage to the PCB. Great care must be taken to ensure the gasket materials are securely taped to the PCB. A self aligning decap gasket, used in conjunction with the polyethylene foam, might be a good approach to reduce this risk. 6 The other consideration is the time involved to make the polyethylene foam gasket, and the additional time required to perform the decapsulation itself compared to performing a stand alone decapsulation. One obvious limitation of this technique is the size of the circuit board that can be accommodated by the decapsulation system chamber. For the investigation of packaging problems, and even some electrical issues, the circuit board can be physically cut around the device of interest so that it will fit into the decap system chamber.


# Summary and Conclusions


Summary and Conclusions


Techniques for decapsulating devices while still mounted to a PCB were described. The techniques all utilize polyethylene foam as a gasket material. The standard rubber decapsulation gaskets can also be used in conjunction with the polyethylene foam as spacers to provide more clearance for components mounted on the PCB. To accommodate boards with taller components, a custom decapsulation riser was fabricated from Teflon. The techniques described were extended to other unique packaging technologies, such as SBGA packages and chip-onboard. Techniques for cleaning the decapsulated devices were also described. Performed carefully, these cleaning techniques will not harm a PCB, and will leave the die surface clean enough for in depth analysis. These cleaning techniques can also be applied to devices decapsulated on a stand alone basis.


# Outlook for Analysis


Outlook for Analysis


Once the bulk silicon has been removed from the sample, subsequent deprocessing is possible using a variety of delayering techniques. For SOI samples, the remaining BOX (buried oxide) can be easily removed with wet etch, parallel polish or reactive ion etch due to the planar nature of the BOX (Figure  17 ). The underlying active areas and isolation oxides can then be removed with parallel polish leaving behind a wire harness. The term wire harness refers to the remaining metal layers and electrical connections that interface the circuit to the outside world. This is only for packaged samples. The remaining wire harness can be removed either chemically using a chemical/reactive ion etch combination or with parallel polish. A combination of the above may also be used. For flip chip packages, care must be taken during the parallel polish to avoid nonuniformities in the remaining thickness due to the warpage of the wire harness in the vicinity of the bumps. For bulk silicon samples, the process is similar; however, planarization is more difficult due to the topology of the surface after the removal of the silicon (FIG. 18. ).


Care must be taken to replanarize the surface and to use etches specific to the material being removed. If at all possible, a planarizing layer such as a SOG oxide may be applied prior to further deprocessing. FIB cross sectional analysis and traditional scanning electron microscope analysis may be utilized throughout the entire delayering process.

Figure  18 : Backside delayering challenges of the bulks silicon device after complete removal of the backside silicon. Note the topology of the shallow trench isolation and the difficulty it presents for further deprocessing.


In conclusion, the TMAH/IPA technique has proven to be an efficient method of sample deprocessing from the backside. The technique opens the door to further backside deprocessing once the silicon has been removed. The technique provides a safe alternative to thin die removal for frontside deprocessing. This is particularly important when performing analysis on flip chip packaged devices that have been back thinned. Finally, the technique provides additional deprocessing flexibility as the analyst can examine the salicide and preserve the overlying metal interconnect for additional deprocessing and FIB cross section. Through continuous adaptation and optimization this process will become an important FA tool for all types of integrated circuits.


The trend in the semiconductor technology is to increase component density and reduce device minimum dimensions, such as channel length and gate oxide thickness. These changes make devices more susceptible to gate oxide related failures, such as shorts or leakage due to gate oxide holes or soft gate oxide breakdown. From the failure analysis point of view, micro-miniaturization introduces additional challenges to device de-layering, particularly to gate oxide exposure targeted for SEM inspection. It's important to note, that some gate oxide related defects, such as soft gate oxide breakdown, cannot be visualized using standard analytical tools. In recent years, Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) and AFM based tunneling techniques have been reported  [1]  as potential methods for gate oxide leakage mapping. AFM also requires gate oxide exposure to enable the analysis. This makes gate oxide exposure a key sample preparation step for root cause analysis of gate oxide related failures.


Two approaches exist in gate oxide exposure techniques. The first approach uses planar polishing and selective poly-silicon wet etch to expose the gate oxide from the front side (FS)  [2] . The second includes silicon bulk grinding followed by wet silicon etching for gate oxide exposure from the back side (BS)  [3] . The present work is devoted mainly to the first of the above-mentioned methods, and describes a robust procedure for selective to SiO 2 poly-silicon wet etch using choline hydroxide. An investigation of some general silicon etching characteristics of choline hydroxide, such as etch rate, silicon to SiO 2 selectivity, surface roughness, and hillocks formation has been also carried out. Previously, many etchants have been proposed for selective to SiO 2 silicon etching, including the inorganic aqueous solutions KOH, NaOH, CsOH, NH 4 OH  [4] , as well as organic solutions containing tetramethyl ammonium hydroxide (TMAH), ethylenediamine-pyrocatechol-water (EDP) and hydrazine-water (N 2 H 4 ) n solutions  [5] . As reported in  [3] ,  [6] , choline hydroxide [(CH 3 ) 3 N(CH 2 CH 2 OH)OH] has been used for silicon etching from the BS that leaves the underlying gate oxide untouched.

# Sample preparation for vertical transistors in DRAM


Sample preparation for vertical transistors in DRAM


## Authors


- ## Keywords


interconnection strength, shear test, area array package, solder joint, pad surface finish


## Abstract


This paper describes a newly developed preparation technique for vertical transistors in DRAM. The recently developed concept of DRAM cells combining a deep trench storage capacitor and a vertical access transistor promises a significant reduction in cell size. In the vertical transistor concept two gates are used to access one storage cell, which creates a challenge for the analysis of gate oxide fails. A gate oxide breakdown is determined and localized in the memory array by electrical probing and photoemission microscopy. The preparation technique combines focused ion beam (FIB) milling and selective wet chemical etching to expose both gates of the transistor simultaneously. Gate oxide pinholes are decorated by the wet etch to allow efficient inspection in a secondary electron microscope (SEM).


The rapid development of new technologies for DRAM presents a constant challenge for physical failure analysis (PFA). In order to guarantee sophisticated and reliable analysis new preparation techniques have to be developed constantly. One example given in this paper is the newly introduced concept of vertical transistors in DRAMs. The vertical transistor is used as access transistor to a deep trench storage cell  [1] [2] [3] . This new concept promises a smaller cell size in combination with an easier-to-optimize access transistor. The advantages are based on the fact that this transistor is formed in a separate processing step independent of forming the support devices of the DRAM. The vertical layout also allows a dual-gate transistor design for increased pass current to and from the storage capacitors. PFA on this new transistor structure demands new preparation methods especially for gate oxide investigations. The simple, 2-dimensional gate given in planar transistors is replaced by a 3-dimensional structure given by two gates of the vertical transistor  [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] . Figure  1  shows the schematic cross-section of the vertical transistor in use. Connection of the storage cell to the bit line is established by the two back-to-back transistors with a shared gate contact connected to the word line. The two transistors thus cannot be electrically separated or individually measured, which has to be considered for PFA.

Reliability of the newly developed vertical gate oxide was investigated via some DRAM like array structures. Failure samples from these stress experiments were also used to develop a sample preparation technique for PFA of actual gate oxide failures. # New sample preparation technique for gate oxide investigation on vertical transistors


New sample preparation technique for gate oxide investigation on vertical transistors


The developed sample preparation technique was intended for inspecting the oxide breakdown from both of the vertical transistors simultaneously. This is necessary since it is not possible to electrically isolate the two gate structure.


Existing preparation approaches were evaluated to determine the best approach:


(1) Cross section (2) Back side preparation A simple cross section, using mechanical polishing or FIB, has the advantage that the technique is well established but the significant drawback is that only one gate is accessible. Therefore at least 50% of the failure cases will have the failure site irrecoverablly destroyed. For this reason, the above method was not used here. The second preparation approach allows access to both gates as well as multiple cells.


Backside preparation was also used very successful in the past for vertical gate oxide test structures  [5] . However, the deep trenches of real product, if not removed, will block the view of the gates completely. Since there is no known reliable technique for removing trenches without damaging the gate oxide, the backside preparation method is also not used. A double cross sectioning technique, which accesses both gates and multiple cells along one wordline, is thus developed at Infineon to expose both gates for inspections. This new preparation approach takes advantage of the experience in basic sample cross sectioning and therefore does not face any major new challenges. The complete process flow of the double cross-section preparation method is described in full details below.


The stress leakage current data does not provide any location information of the failing transistors. The PFA flow has to start with localization of the gate oxide breakdown site. The widely used photoemission microscopy is used here along with electrical probing to narrow down the failure site within some  (3) (4) (5)  transistors along one word line.


Figure  5  shows a photoemission image example. The sample preparation starts from delayering the array to the bit line level using mechanical polishing and etching. Reactive ion etching (RIE) is then used to remove the dielectric between the bit lines. RIE etching is necessary here in order to make the word lines visible in the FIB tool. Alternatively the sample can be delayered to the word line level, but the area of interest must be capped with metal to avoid any damage of the polysilicon within the gate during the following wet etch. With the limited number of samples that were processed so far the second approach resulted in better quality SEM images. The next step is to remove materials on both sides of the word line connecting the failing cell through FIB milling.


Figure  6 : Cross-section of vertical access transistor in DRAM array A Micrion 9000 FIB was used to perform two crosssections on both sides of the wordline, as shown in Figure  6 . The figure shows a cross-sectional view of a vertical transistor cell. This cross section is not part of the here described preparation flow for the vertical transistor. It illustrates were the cross-sections which are used for the vertical transistor remove material (hatched areas) in order to access the vertical gate oxide. Figure  6  shows also the range where the actual cross section can be located (arrow). This range is about three times as wide as the minimum feature size since it is only necessary to cut in between two vertical gates. The remaining silicon is removed by a wet etch. The material removal was performed with a step mill followed by a single pass mill, both using a 100pA beam current. The milling box size was in the range of 3µm by 3µm. Since the space between two trenches is 3 times the minimum feature size (range of successful cross-section), this cross-section operation is believed to be applicable down to 110nm minimum feature size without problems. The final stage of the preparation is to remove the silicon surrounding the trenches so that the gate oxide is exposed for SEM examination. Chemical solution HNO3:HF (100:1) wet etch was used. Typical etch time is between 5 and 20 seconds depending on the location of the FIB cuts. The etch process can be done in iterations with SEM inspection to find the exact etch time. The exposed oxide surfaces were shown to be able to sustain several seconds of overetching without any visible damages. Past experience with this etch proofed to be selective enough and very reliable to expose thin oxides from Silicon  [1] . Figure  7  shows the sample after wet etching. The vertical transistors along one wordline are completely exposed. Since multiple transistors along one wordline can easily be exposed, an exact prelocalization of the failing transistor is not required in this direction. Perpendicular to the wordline the location information is crucial for the success of the described preparation technique since adjacent word lines are removed. Figure  8  and Figure  9  show a pinhole in the vertical gate oxide exposed after the described sample preparation. The gate oxide breakdown spot is not correlated to any interfaces, which provides important information for further process improvements.

Range for successful crosssection . The dark decoration of the failing gate oxide is caused by an etch-out effect. The HNO3:HF (100:1) wet etch reached the gate poly-silicon through the pinhole and etched out some of the poly-silicon around the pinhole within the gate -leaving a cavity there. This cavity reduced the secondary electron emission rate and thus caused the darker appearance of the failing gate. This is a typical result as expected for intrinsic gate oxide fails.


# Summary


Summary


A new sample preparation technique was developed for the vertical access transistor used in DRAM chips. The technique combines FIB cross-section and wet silicon etch in order to expose gate oxide of both gates of the dual-gate vertical transistor for a complete inspection. The preparation technique was used for the first time to analyze gate oxide stress fails on product like DRAM cell array structures. The paper shows the successful application of the developed preparation technique. The whole analysis of the gate oxide stress fails showed that a significant number of fails were caused by voids filled with poly silicon in thick oxide layers under passing word lines. The remaining thin oxide in these areas showed similar breakdown behavior as the gate oxide breakdowns. The observed gate oxide breakdowns were found to be in the gate oxide area, clearly separated from all interfaces. The PFA on the observed stress fail directed process improvements to the STI voiding problem and showed that the reliability of the gate oxide itself was significantly better than previously expected based on the fail numbers. Using the newly developed sample preparation technique it could be shown that a gate oxide reliability  (1)  was significantly better than indicated by the stress results  (2)  further improvement has to be focused on the intrinsic oxide properties rather than on interfaces and (3) that the test structure had an STI voiding problem.


As IC processing migrates to the deep sub-micron technology nodes, structural analysis will rely even more heavily on TEM. Sub-nanometer level resolution is necessary for the inspection of IC devices, features such as gate oxide integrity, thickness of barrier layers, micro defect/material analysis, and interface inspection all require TEM examination. It is very difficult to find enough information without the support of high resolution TEM. In recent years, the combination of STEM and EELS  [2]  has made materials analysis more precise and user friendly.


Before the development of FIB, the most common procedure for TEM specimen preparation was by manual polishing.


Especially for Si based semiconductors, polishing combined with Ar ion milling might have been the only way to prepare specimens less than 100 nm in thickness  [3] .


Compared with manual polishing, FIB has the benefit of high precision, high throughput, and high success rate in TEM specimen preparation. Furthermore, the time required to train a user to become familiar with FIB sample preparation is shorter than that required for manual polishing. Even automated procedures for sample preparation are now available  [4] . The main weakness of preparing TEM samples by FIB is the damage induced to the sample by the high momentum ion beam  [5, 6] .


Therefore, how to reduce the damaged layer induced by the FIB is key to produce high quality specimens. This paper will describe how we measure the damaged layer induced by FIB, and how to reduce the damage to the specimen through low energy ion beam milling as well as special operating attention. This procedure can reduce the damages caused by the FIB to the same level as that created by manual polishing followed by ion milling.


# Experiment


Experiment


In order to measure the thickness of the material damaged by the ion beam, we prepared TEM samples perpendicular to the side walls of a trench dug with the FIB, i.e.; we prepared TEM cross-sections of SEM cross-sections.


# [Step]


[Step]


1. An 8 inch/P-doped Si wafer was selected as our test vehicle. 2. A protection oxide layer was deposited onto the wafer surface to prevent it from oxidation and contamination during subsequent steps. 3. The wafer was then mounted on a FIB tool, A segment of Pt  (15 X 15 um^2 ) was then FIB deposited on the wafer surface 4. Using the same FIB tool, square trench of 15 um x 6 um x 6 um(X x Y x Z) was milled out using various ion beam control settings (Table -1  &  2). 5. The wafer was then filled with Spin-on Glass (SOG) to protect the surfaces of the holes.


The SOG was then cured for 24 hrs. 6. Another Pt layer was again FIB deposited on top of the SOG filled holes. A well along the X-direction was then milled out to expose half of the SOG filled holes, After this, another well from a different side of those holed were also prepared. . As the wall thickness of the filled holes approached 1 um, we follow the standard procedure of TEM specimen preparation, final thickness of the wall are reduced to around 0.1 um.(Fig. 1 ). 7. The specimen was picked up using a micromanipulator, and placed on a Carbon grid.


# Results


[Damage model] Generally, the damaged layer consists of two layers: an inner layer which is the stopping region of Ga ions and an outer damaged layer shell which is the ion bombardment damaged layer. From simulation results obtained using "SRIM"(Stopping and Range of Ions in Matter)  [7] , a 30keV-ion beam would generate a 40 nm-damage layer. While a 5 keV-ion beam would produce only a 10 nm-damage layer. From the experimental data, we found that if we fixed the beam energy at 30keV and increased the beam current from 150pA to 10000pA, the thickness of the damaged layer would not increase but remained around 40 nm. This result matches the simulation results. The only difference is the reduced processing time due to the higher beam currents.

# Table-2: Damaged layer induced by different beam energy


Table-2: Damaged layer induced by different beam energy


Equipment/Ion FIB/Ga FIB/Ga FIB/Ga  Miller  We then applied different beam energies and found that lowering the energy of the ion beam would reduce the damaged layer depth. Therefore, using a 10 keV beam can reduce the damaged layer thickness down to around 14 nm. However, the sample preparation time would increase from 45 min to 120 min. Incidentally, if the beam energy was reduced to 5 keV and below, the processing time would increase to an unacceptable level. Beam stability would also become a serious problem. The net result was that the amount of ion beam damage actually increased. A good compromise between efficiency and quality is therefore to use higher beam energies for initial coarse milling followed by fine milling at lower energies. This method has shown good results in reducing the damaged layer thickness. For example, operating the FIB initially at 30keV followed by a 10keV "touch-up" can reduce the damaged layer down to 18 nm. The operation time will just increase around 10 min. However, if we start at 30keV and reduce the ion beam energy to 5keV while tilting the sample by a small angle during the final milling, the damaged layer can be further reduced to 10 nm, The latter, is comparable to the quality of samples prepared by mechanical polishing followed by Ar ion-milling.


A good TEM specimen with a minimum amount of damage is very important in material interface identification, crystalline orientation/defect diagnosis and EELS spectrum/mapping analysis.


The methodology presented in this work satisfies the need for high precision, rapid turnaround time and good quality.


Deprocessing silicon CMOS devices for failure analysis has become a critical part of semiconductor product development. Many chip manufacturers rely on deprocessing data to help improve their devices. Whether the goal is a faster transistor, longer reliability, or improved production cost, there are many reasons that failure analysis plays a key role in this industry.


Recently, there has been a trend in the industry toward backside deprocessing for silicon analysis. Backside deprocessing has become a desirable technique due to the fact that many manufacturers are mounting their devices on packages with the circuit facing down. This technique, also known as flip-chip packaging, leaves only the backside of the die exposed, which is usually a thick layer of bulk silicon.


Many techniques for backside analysis have been developed such as light emission microscopy, Laser Induced Voltage Alteration (LIVA), and Thermal Induced Voltage Alteration (TIVA). These techniques require a sample to be prepared with backside polishing for electrical fault isolation. Once a problem in the silicon is isolated, deprocessing is in general necessary for inspection of physical damage, measurement of critical transistor dimensions, and analysis of process defects. Usually at this point in the analysis the die is too thin to be removed without the risk of damage. Backside deprocessing provides an excellent method of physical defect analysis without having to remove the die.


The preparation technique described here uses a solution of TMAH and IPA (Isopropyl Alcohol) to evenly etch the remaining layer of silicon from the back of the die after mechanical polishing. IPA is added to the TMAH to improve anisotropic etching and lower the boiling point. Upon removal of the silicon the circuitry remains intact for analysis.


# Backside Deprocessing Procedure


Backside Deprocessing Procedure


The entire procedure consists of only a few steps. The technique for initial preparation is dependant upon the type of sample being deprocessed.


# Polishing and Initial Preparation


Polishing and Initial Preparation


Both packaged and unpacked die may be deprocessed with the TMAH process. The initial sample preparation is different depending upon whether the die is packaged or unpackaged. When deprocessing an unpackaged die it must be mounted to a glass microscope slide for polishing 1 . An epoxy glue 2 is used to attach the die to the glass. Before mounting the die to avoid damage once the circuit is deprocessed, a smooth surface is desirable on the circuit side of the die. The bumps are chemically removed from the front side of the die to provide a more uniform interface for the epoxy to bond with between the glass slide and the die. The die is then clamped to minimize epoxy thickness while the epoxy is cured in an oven. Once the sample is mounted and the epoxy is cured, the die is polished. A diagram for a glass slide mounted sample is shown in Figure  1 . The die can also be deprocessed while still packaged. The package can be cut away from around the die or left in tact. Cutting away the package provides a smaller sample size, which is advantageous for SEM analysis. A small sample will minimize focal distance and allow better tilting. Deprocessing the sample with the entire package is sometimes desirable when time is critical. The backside deprocessing technique will work for either option, which gives the analyst flexibility in sample size. Cutting away the package is not recommend after the sample is deprocessed because there is a possibility that the circuit will fracture from the stress. When the sample is left in package for organic package types, there is an extra preparation step that is required due to chemical interference. This is discussed in the next sub heading.


The sample die should be polished as close to the circuitry as possible without causing damage to the die. The samples are typically polished on a polish wheel with diamond lapping film. Much care should be taken to ensure that the samples are level during polish. The die is polished until approximately 25µm or less of backside silicon remains above the active circuitry. The total die thickness is measured during the polishing. The thickness is determined in reference to the package or glass slide surface. For packaged samples the bump thickness is taken into consideration. Care must be taken during polish to avoid exposing the circuitry during polish, particularly when thinning organic packaged devices. Organic packaged devices are particularly prone to developing a concave topology that often results from parallel polish for silicon thinning. The chemical etch time to remove the bulk silicon with the TMAH / IPA solution is substantially reduced if the starting silicon thickness is 25µm or less.


In an instance such as localized deprocessing a selective polish on the die is desirable. When a small area of interest is known that area can be polished thinner by mounting the sample at a slight angle. The mounting angle should put the region of interest closest towards the polishing surface. Because of the anisotropic etch characteristics of the TMAH -IPA solution the thinnest area of silicon will be removed first, thus reducing unnecessary over exposure of the circuitry to the TMAH solution. Reducing the exposure of the sample to the TMAH will prevent damage to the package underfill and epoxy which is known to etch away after long exposure in TMAH, (i.e. more than 45 min.) thus causing edge damage to the die. Even though TMAH is a very selective etch it does etch oxides at a very slow rate ( < 0.1nm/min) 1 , this becomes an issue for newer technologies that implement extremely thin gate oxide. Once the oxide is etched the poly silicon is then susceptible to etching.


# Package Issues


Package Issues


Some package types increase the risk of damaging the die by the described preparation technique. The die is mounted to the package with an epoxy-based underfill. The underfill is etched by the TMAH. Once the underfill is etched away from the edges of the die, the circuit and any remaining silicon will lift and fracture around the edges. For devices in organic type packages, this is a significant problem. However, the underfill used on ceramic packages can withstand the TMAH long enough to remove the silicon without damage.


For a successful preparation it is essential on one hand to thin the silicon enough to avoid over etching of the under fill, but on the other hand to leave the silicon thick enough to avoid mechanical damage the circuitry. For all samples a good thickness of remaining silicon is between 20um to 30um.


A special preparation method is used, after polishing, to protect the underfill from etching. The method uses a wax 3 seal to cover the underfill. The wax is applied by using a hot glue gun to melt the wax into a rubber mold. The die side of the sample is pressed into the mold to create a thin layer of wax that completely covers the surface of the die and most of the package. Once the wax is cooled it is cut out along the edges of the underfill and then peeled off the surface of the die. The edges are reflowed using a heat gun to ensure that a good seal is formed over the underfill. The wax will withstand the TMAH long enough to remove the bulk silicon without causing any edge damage to


# Chemical Preparation and Deprocessing


Chemical Preparation and Deprocessing


An important point to remember is proper PPE (personal protective equipment) should be worn when handling chemicals. All experiments should be conducted in an acid hood while wearing an acid gown, gloves and safety glasses.


The chemical bath is prepared in a glass beaker that is large enough to allow the sample to remain submerged.


A solution of 60 ml tetremethylammoniumhydroxide (25% wt.) and 20 ml isopropyl alcohol (100%) is prepared. The temperature is monitored using an immersible thermometer. The solution is heated to a boil. The temperature stabilizes around 83 degrees Celsius. A cover slip placed over the beaker reduces the evaporation rate of the IPA by allowing it to condense back into the solution.


Once the solution temperature has stabilized the sample die is dipped into a buffered oxide etch of 40:1 HF (hydrofluoric acid) with surfactant, in order to remove any native oxide that may have formed on the silicon. Immediately after the BOE dip, the sample is rinsed with DI water, blown dry with a compressed nitrogen flow and immediately placed into the solution of TMAH/IPA.


A good indication of a successful etch process are small gas bubbles rising from the silicon surface. The sample should be visually monitored with the naked eye or with a low powered optical microscope until the silicon is completely removed or the area of interest is exposed. If after ten minutes there is no evidence of chemical reaction, the sample is removed and examined under the optical microscope. A good etch will show small square geometries indicative of etching along the silicon lattice planes. This is shown below in Figure  4 .


# No-Etch Issues


No-Etch Issues


Certain factors can prevent the silicon from being etched. Ensuring that no contaminants remain on the sample is important. Native oxide formation is often the cause of a no-etch sample. If no etching is observed, another BOE dip is recommended. After the second BOE dip, it is important to avoid exposure to the atmosphere so that a native oxide cannot reform. In addition to the BOE dip, polishing to roughen the surface of the silicon may stimulate etching. This method is used as a precaution to oxide formation.


# Etch Rate Characterization


Etch Rate Characterization


The etch rate that was published by Frank Zachiriasse 1 is 0.35um/min for silicon. A study was done to determine the etch rate of the samples used in this paper. The results of the experiments showed that the etch rate of the silicon in the TMAH/IPA solution is 0.5 um/min, at 83 degrees Celsius. The etch rate was calculated with a controlled experiment on un-mounted die samples. One sample was etched in a TMAH / IPA solution and the other in TMAH only solution. Incremental measurements were taken and used for rate calculations. Increased temperature will provide a slight increase in etch rate. The etch-rate of TMAH Circuitry without IPA for the same type silicon is approximately 0.79 um/min at 83 degrees Celsius. This etch-rate then increases to 1.1 um/min at 93 degrees Celsius. Adding IPA to TMAH slows the etch rate of silicon, but provides a valuable trade off for a lower boiling point and an even etch rate in all directions.


# TMAH Etch Selectivity Cross -Section Analysis


TMAH Etch Selectivity Cross -Section Analysis


A cross-sectioned sample was etched for varying time intervals to determine the TMAH selectiveness for salicide. The sample was initially examined in a SEM (figure  5  and 6 ) to observe preetch appearance of cross-section. The sample was then etched for 1 minute in a 60:20 TMAH:IPA solution. The sample was then re-examined in the SEM (figure  7 ). The etch process was repeated two additional times, for 3 minutes, and again for 6 minutes. Results of these 2 etches can be seen in figures  [13] [14] [15] [16] . After all 3 etch processes, salicide was still visible on the cross-section. There was also evidence of silicon etch-back and polysilicon etch, thus indicating that the TMAH/IPA solution was in fact removing the silicon material, but leaving the salicide material intact.


# Applications in Failure Analysis


Applications in Failure Analysis


The backside deprocessing technique is being developed while working with actual failure analysis cases. The technique is now being used for follow-up analysis on known device failures and is also used in root cause FA. Prior analysis is used to correlate damage characteristics from the backside with similar front side features.


# Salicide Formation Process Investigation


Salicide Formation Process Investigation


While developing a new salicide for a CMOS manufacturing process, this technique proved to be helpful in solving some initial yield problems.


Front-side analysis was difficult because floating away the metal layers with HF often destroyed the salicide before it could be inspected. The backside technique, however, allowed selective removal of the bulk silicon without compromising the layer of salicide. Once the bulk silicon was removed, islands of shallow trench isolation (STI) remained.


The layers of salicide and the gate oxides located between the STI layers remained intact. The selectivity of the TMAH left the salicide undamaged as seen in Figures 12 through 14 below.
