Figure  13 : Backside of transistor with poor salicide coverage.


Figure  14 : Non-uniform salicide grain formation from the backside.


The salicide grains can be seen clearly. The large grain formation did not provide complete coverage over the active areas. Backside deprocessing was used throughout the development of this salicide step for this process.


# ESD Failure Analysis


ESD Failure Analysis


The technique was also used as follow-up analysis to a root cause failure analysis where known damage was found from the front side. The devices under analysis were ESD stress tested and damage was found in the I/O protection circuitry. From the topside, the damage can be seen in the poly gate as shown in Figure  15  below. Once the bulk silicon was removed using the TMAH-IPA technique and the same structures were examined from the backside, the damage was seen from a completely different perspective. Due to high current, the salicide actually re-flowed under the gate shorting the source and the drain of the power clamp transistors. Seeing this damage which was not as obvious from the front side, led to the discovery of a design inadequacy in the channel width of the transistor. The backside of the damaged transistor is shown below in Figure  16 .


and so on. Each of these implications describes a cause-effect relationship; each possible effect provides something to measure.


After each measurement, an interpretation of the results indicates whether the predicted effect exists. As the list of observed effects grows, with no unsuccessful tests, the strength of the correlation grows with it, until the analyst can conclude that the common cause exists. After a sufficient number of measurements, each verifying a predicted effect, we consider the cause proven. This process is called proof by induction. (In actual analyses, we would be very specific about exactly what common cause-gate oxide leakage on the input of an and-or-invert block, threshhold voltage shifts in the region of a failing register, or poor transmission-gate design electrically close to the Vdd node-we wish to demonstrate.) Inductive proof-enough successful tests with no failuresrepresents a powerful tool for the analyst, in spite of its subjectivity.


Should we find on the other hand that a predicted effect of our possible prior cause is clearly and definitively absent, we conclude that the cause is absent. This needs to happen in principle only once, not repeatedly as with inductive proof. The logical principle by which we disprove such a prior cause is the contrapositive test. This test's principle states that if any cause positively implies a given effect, the real absence of that effect immediately disproves the existence of the cause. To reiterate, while it typically takes multiple iterations of measurement and interpretation to prove a correlation and its prior cause, in principle it takes the absence of only one predicted and sure effect to disprove a correlation or possible prior cause.


But our use of logic tools runs throughout the engine. On the other side of the decision engine loop are the Correlation List and Selection steps (Figure  4 .)


Where the Measurement and Interpretation steps prove or disprove whether our possible prior cause is real, the Correlation List and Selection steps identify those PPCs in order to prove or disprove them. Logical principles applied at this step include, among others, logical implication, axioms of independent and dependent causes, and causation checking (identifying possible prior causes).


# Avoiding False Paths


Avoiding False Paths


Logical implication, inductive proof, and contrapositive testing are among at least twelve logical principles applicable at one or more steps in the decision engine loop. Space limitations prevent a full description in this paper, but others govern the logic of interactions, identifying failure characteristics by looking for patterns, handling multiple possible causes of a given effect, and justifying destructive steps. Each of these logical principles helps to identify false analysis paths and avoid all but brief trips down these paths. In the process, analyses succeed more often.


For example, inductive proof directs the analyst to test repeatedly, not just once, for a possible prior cause. Many effects such as photon emission and local temperature excursions have multiple possible prior causes, of course. These must be distinguished from one another during analysis by looking for their other effects, as we described above in our discussion of the Interpretation step. To make a mistake in connection with this process means an unknowing trip down a false path. Inductive proof leads the analyst to look for these false paths by finding the one prior cause whose effects all appear. In the process, the other possible (but not actual) prior causes are rejected. For example, suppose a particular signal never makes it from one block's output to the next block's input. A clear voltage contrast change on either side of the lone contact on the failing metal line (Figure  5 ) leads immediately to the initial suspicion that the contact is open or high resistance. If inductive proof is not used, the suspicion may easily become a conclusion without further testing, which is a logically-incorrect, and risk-laden, approach. Alternatively, use of inductive proof would lead to more careful scrutiny of the downstream voltage contrast to look for harder-to-find evidence of the output signal, mechanical microprobing to test for DC current flow across the contact, and even photon emission tests to examine the behavior of the input stage to which the trace connects. If any evidence of low-frequency, low-amplitude post-contact signal exists, or photon emission in the input stage correlates with the failing condition, or especially if current flows normally through the contact, the analyst is immediately led away from the open contact prior cause, which is clearly in those cases a false path.
 A low-value short at the downstream input stage, creating a resistor divider with the contact, as illustrated in Figure  6 , may conceivably turn out to be more likely based on inductive proof's additional results.


But what might have happened if we followed events in the pursuit of the incorrect open contact prior cause? A natural next step to evaluate an open contact would be a focused-ion-beam cross-section, clearly a destructive step. Other possible steps would produce a similar result. In fact, whatever the sequence of analysis operations chosen, the path eventually will include a destructive step. Therefore pursuit of the false path would sooner or later result in a destructive step performed prematurely and at the wrong location. This illustrates the point that destructive steps are generally not the cause, in and of themselves, of unsuccessful analyses. Some analyses, in fact, are composed almost entirely of destructive steps, with extremely successful results due in large part to proper and logical methodology 4 . Analyses fail rather because a false path is mistaken for the true path, and premature or misplaced destructive steps remove essential evidence for the actual causeeffect chain. The root anomaly then remains undiscovered in spite of all further analytical efforts. Good use of inferential logic within the metaprocess thus avoids improper destructive steps and increases the analysis success rate.


# Analysis Speed


Analysis Speed


Execution speed may be the first concern that an analyst (or a lab manager) has with a scientific-methodbased approach. This methodology addresses that concern first by efficiency. Unrecognized false paths waste more analysis time than any other time sink, not to mention the disastrous results if the analyst performs a destructive step. The remedy, testing for multiple effects of a PPC, costs far less in time than an unrecognized false path. Secondly, the method provides a level of organization that permits multiple decision engine cycles to operate in parallel without confusion, as described above. This means that the analyst can investigate several PPC's at a time and still keep track of the analysis easily. Finally, methodological insights into cause-effect versus effecteffect correlations and other characteristics of the main cause-effect chain enable the analyst to choose the fastest among several possible analytical routes to the root anomaly.


# Uniform Analysis Representation


Uniform Analysis Representation


While providing the above benefits to analysis execution, speed and success, the metaprocess described here also generates a uniform, informative and compact way to represent an entire analysis flow. When each loop's Answer and Correlation List contents are written down, the analysis path revealing the main cause-effect chain, and also each investigated but disproven prior cause, appear in graphical form. A generic example of such a summary appears in Figure  7 .


Failure analysis is one of the key competencies to enable high volume manufacturing. According to Moore's law, transistor count doubles every 18 months. This is achieved through advancement in semiconductor fabrication processes that enables smaller feature size. Moreover, the microprocessor architecture has changed from a simple superscalar pipeline to a multi-threading, dynamic Out-Of-Order execution with hyper pipeline. Packaging technology has advanced to the flip-chip package. Traditional FA approaches have relied heavily on equipment to identify the defect location such as Laser Voltage Probe, Emission Microscopy, etc. However, due to resolution limit and sample preparation risk, FA success rate and analysis time have been impacted. A breakthrough approach in which no probing is required was developed to overcome this.


# FA in a glance


FA in a glance


FA is a critical function in the modern semiconductor manufacturing process. It is important for ensuring the high quality and reliability of the product by continuously finding defect mechanisms that are associated with the manufacturing process. The root causes for the defects can then be fixed to ensure higher yield, better quality and reliability. FA evolved from a traditional brute force method to a modern method with advanced equipment. Traditional FA was characterized by the use of thermal and emission methods to detect the defect location. Modern FA approaches the defect location through the use of a probing method not only to identify the defect location but also to study the behavior of the circuitry.


# Thermal and Emission approach


Thermal and Emission approach


The thermal approach relies heavily on the physical behavior of the defect. A shorted material may radiate heat when current flows through it. A traditional method like liquid crystal can be used to detect the heat generated by a defect when comparing a good and bad component under the same condition. A modern approach has replaced the liquid crystal method with equipment that is able to detect infrared (IR) emissions. Light emission can be detected from a defect where abnormal electron-hole pair recombination takes place.


# Probing approach


Probing approach


The probing approach uses physical contact to actually measure the electrical characteristics of the component to detect an open or short within the device. Electrical excitation can be applied to a transistor to confirm the electrical behavior. An electron beam has been used as a physical means of acquiring the internal state of the device. It works like a normal tungsten microprobe except with a better resolution and faster response in terms of AC timing measurement. With the probing approach, the electrical behavior of the defect and it's effect on the circuit can be further understood.


# FA challenge


FA challenge


After 30 years of research and development, semiconductor device geometries have evolved Proceedings from the 28 th International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis, 3-7 November, 2002, Phoenix, Arizona from very large size (microns) to very small size (nanometers). Functionality of the component has changed from a simple logic gate built in a chip to a microprocessor that consists of millions of transistors. Packaging design has also changed from a simple package with a low pin count to a package that has hundreds of pins. All of these add to the complexity of the failure analysis process.


# Device complexity


Device complexity


Microprocessor design has changed from a 4-bit to a 64-bit data and address bus. Its microarchitecture has changed from a simple pipeline design to a hyper-pipeline, multi-threading, dynamic Out-Of-Order execution superscalar design. Huge integrated cache has been added to the design to increase performance. All of these design changes require a huge increment in terms of transistor count. A simple assembly instruction will be translated into microinstructions and each microinstruction will activate millions of transistors within the chip. Therefore, localization of a failing transistor among millions of transistors is no longer a simple and straightforward task.


# Semiconductor fabrication


Semiconductor fabrication


Semiconductor fabrication has advanced from one metal layer interconnect to six or more metal layers of interconnect. The feature size is as small as 130nm in current technology. Therefore, it is no longer easy to use front-side emission microscopy to localize a defect. The probing approach also faces its limitation as it is more difficult to access the lower level metal layer to acquire the logic state of the signal due to the higher metal density.


# Packaging technology


Packaging technology


Packaging technology has evolved from a simple dual-in-line-package (DIP) to an advanced flipchip design. The flip-chip design inhibits the use of electron beam probing to isolate the failing location without backside sample thinning and FIB editing as silicon is a physical barrier to the electron beam. This extra step increases the chance of sample being destroyed during analysis.


# Recent advancement in FA techniques


Recent advancement in FA techniques


With increasing complexity in microprocessor design, semiconductor fabrication processes and packaging technology, a few new methods have been used to help the failure analysis process.


A laser of suitable wavelength can penetrate the silicon substrate and can be used to replace electron beam probing. LVP was developed to work similar to electron beam probing to acquire the AC behavior of the device.


The Infrared Emission Microscope (IREM) was developed to detect the infrared radiation emitted by the defect when the device is excited under normal operation.


# Limitations


Limitations


Even though many new and advanced analysis tools have been developed to help the failure analyst, there are still limitations associated with using them in the FA process.


# Resolution limit


Resolution limit


Resolution limit is one of the main issues with any of the advanced defect localization equipment. Due to smaller feature size, the equipment has difficulty in telling exactly where the emission comes from. CAD overlay helps to correlate an emission spot to the actual layout of the microprocessor but did not to help to improve the resolution of the equipment.


# Secondary versus primary emission


Secondary versus primary emission


The emission is a characteristic of a failing circuit. Most of the time, a defect site will emit (primary emission). However, not all defects emit. Many defects only cause an emission in a down stream transistor due to a nondeterministic input value to the transistor (secondary emission). Therefore, the analyst will need to differentiate whether an emission spot is primary versus secondary emission. This could potentially lead the analyst to concentrate on the wrong area and lead to a stage of "failure cause not found".


to be damaged. Even with very good care, the sample preparation process is a manual/physical operation and as such the results are often not consistent.


# Probeless FA


Probeless FA


A new failure analysis technique was developed to bridge the gap. This technique heavily relies on microprocessor architecture knowledge, design simulation and Design For Testability (DFT) tools.


# Architecture knowledge


Architecture knowledge


Architecture of the microprocessor is a key factor in ensuring the success of probeless FA. The architecture of a microprocessor is broken down into macro and micro architectures. Macro-architecture describe the behavior of the microprocessor in the system level such as instruction set, bus protocol, user visible register, etc. Micro-architecture describes how the functionality of the microprocessor being implemented internally to support the macro level architecture.


# Design Simulation


Design Simulation


Every microprocessor has their model built using hardware description language (HDL). This model enables the use of stimulus-response behavior of the model to compare to the behavior of the actual microprocessor. The simulation will also allow the engineer visibility to the internal operations of the microprocessor through the use of a simulation engine.


# DFT


DFT


The DFT feature is a built in design feature that allows an engineer to have control and to observe the operation of the microprocessor.


With the DFT programs developed on a tester or a personal computer, an internal signal can be read out or modified to help the FA process.


# Process


Process


The basic flow of this new probeless FA approach is shown in Figure  1 . The whole failure analysis process can be broken down into 6 major steps.


In step a, the unit will go through failure verification. This step is important to make sure that the failing signature is consistent with what is reported from the production tester. Other critical information that is gathered during this step is failing behavior due to temperature, speed and voltage sensitivity. That information is required to make a first cut hypothesis as to the behavior of the defect. In step b, the macro-level fault isolation is carried out. During this step, the failing assembly code will be identified. This is done by checking the bus activities of the tester. Every test pattern has its expected bus activities on the I/O pins captured by the tester. By comparing the expected and acquired bus activities, an engineer will have high-level information on which block of code is failing. Through the use of DFT program to read out the instruction pointer, the actual failing instruction can be obtained. The information about the failing instruction can be input into the simulation engine and the logic block that is responsible for handling the failing instruction can be known.


While not totally risk free, in situ decapsulation has been shown to be an effective method to decapsulate devices without altering or confounding the failure mechanism because of heat applied during the desoldering operation.


In the large volume of semiconductor Failure Analysis technical publications, the subject of the analysis process flow 1-3 is an occasional theme among a relatively small fraction of articles. While many or most Failure Analysis departments make the definition and application of specific process flows a significant priority, the subject remains a minor one in the literature. This paper presents a fully-general analysis formalization intended to make the analysis process efficient, rigorous and uniform from analysis to analysis and from failure to failure. It amounts to a practical form of scientific method, customized for the failure analysis discipline, and enabling faster analysis to satisfy business constraints.


The analysis decision-making methodology, or decision engine, consists of six steps arranged in a cycle or loop, shown in Figure  1 . This paper attempts to show that these operations in this order form a metaprocess, that is, a process whose function is to create another process. Applied to semiconductor failure analysis, this general decision engine metaprocess creates a specific analysis flow for a specific failure based on the facts about the failure, the results of analysis operations, the body of knowledge about physical causes and their effects and, finally, inferential logic. This metaprocess is intended to work properly-that is, generate a correct unique failure analysis flow-for any failure analysis of a manufactured product coming from any of the semiconductor wafer and packaging processes predominant today. Using the approach described in this paper, the analyst of any experience level should become able to make analysis choices in ways that reflect mature failure analysis skills. This approach can therefore accelerate the maturity of beginning analysts once they have enough experience to use the metaprocess effectively. Some benefits of this methodology will be described in detail a little later in the paper. All examples of any kind in this paper are hypothetical but possible.


# Six Metaprocess Steps


Six Metaprocess Steps


The generality of this approach does not lessen its ability to create correct practical analysis flows. To show this, we start with some clear definitions of basic terms and then proceed to explain the six steps.


Every phenomenon we observe is an effect of some cause-that is, it does not create itself. When we have directly measured or observed an effect, we can call it a known effect. Any candidate for a cause of our known effect is a possible prior cause, or PPC. Other (initially unverified) effects of our PPC will be secondary effects in relation to the (primary) known effect. The first cause of failure in an electronic device will be called the root anomaly. The cause of the root anomaly within the manufacturing process will be termed the process cause. It should be observed that we do not use the term 'root cause,' since it does not adequately distinguish between the first cause within the semiconductor device and the first cause within the manufacturing process.


# ECC Question


ECC Question


We can begin now to see whether the approach described in Figure  1  does a good job of constructing an analysis flow for us. Suppose we have found (Fig.  2a ), through earlier analysis, a voltage contrast anomaly (that is, our failure differs from a good part in this way.) The anomalous contrast could be a re-sult of any of a number of possible prior causes, but let's select one (Fig.  2b ): a conductive path between the metal trace showing the contrast and some other nearby metal trace. (The resulting short would change the trace's voltage, and therefore its contrast.) Our possible prior cause, then, is an intermetal conductive path, and the ECC Question step would lead us to construct this question: "Does an intermetal conductive path exist, correlate with our observed voltage contrast anomaly, and cause it?"


# Measurement


This second step uses analysis tools, observation, and even simply logical reasoning to look for an effect of the possible prior cause-the intermetal conductive path-other than our known effect. In other words, what else would an intermetal conductive path do besides create our observed contrast anomaly? When we come up with such secondary effects, we measure them at this second step. We might, for example, measure I(V) current to adjacent lines and look for a linear relationship as an effect of an intermetal path (Fig.  2c ). Such an ohmic I(V) characteristic between adjacent lines is a second, different effect of our possible prior cause.


# Interpretation


Interpretation


We next interpret our measurement results and determine what answer they give to our ECC Question. If we find the ohmic or linear I(V) trace we just mentioned (Fig.  2d ), we can keep our possible prior cause-intermetal conduction-as a candidate for the actual cause. We cannot yet conclude, however, that we have found the actual cause, since there are still other possible prior causes, which could explain both our observed contrast and also ohmic I(V) simultaneously. At this point, then, we loop back to the measurement step (see Figure  1 ) and look for yet another secondary effect of the PPC (Fig.  2e ). We may look for other effects such as Liquid Crystal phase changes, current local to the output block or to the phase change (Fig.  2f ), and so on, as we continue to loop. When we actually find enough of our predicted effects (Fig.  2g ), we can conclude that their common cause, intermetal conduction, exists.


If on the other hand the linear I(V) trace is absent, then we immediately rule out an intermetal short (Fig.  2h ), in accordance with a logic guideline called the Contrapositive Test, also discussed below.


# ECC Answer


ECC Answer


After interpreting our measurement results and finding enough evidence for our prior cause, we formulate an answer that corresponds exactly in form to the question we posed. If and when results support it, we a) conclude that the linear I(V) exists, b) demonstrate that the I(V) trace correlates with the node's leakage anomaly, and c) show by appropriate physical laws that the I(V) causes the leakage. We may find that our possible prior cause doesn't exist, or we may find that it exists but that it doesn't correlate with our known anomaly, or we may find existence and correlation but not find that our PPC causes the known anomaly. Or (Fig.  2i ) we may find all three, existence, correlation and causation. In this case, for our example we would answer, "An intermetal conductive path exists, correlates with our observed voltage contrast behavior, and causes it." This IM conduction now becomes our new known effect, since we have proven its existence and shown where it lies in the failure's cause-effect chain.


# Correlation List


Correlation List


Now that we have a new known effect, we next create a brainstorm list of PPC's of the intermetal short (Fig.  2j .) We might include lateral or vertical dielectric cracking, intermetal particles, oxide pinholes, electromigration-induced metal extrusions, metal overheating, and so forth. We also-and this is very important-generate an exhaustive list of other secondary effects of each of these possible prior causes. For example, along with our metal extrusion item we add to the Correlation List expected secondary effects including local liquid crystal phase change, further local voltage changes, visible metal anomaly, fragility with temperature, fragility with high current, along with any other such effects we can think of (Fig.  2k ). One thing to note is that visual evidence of an anomaly has no special place in this methodology: it falls equal in importance to any other equallyattested effect. A well-built correlation list will include at least ten secondary effects of each PPC. If it proves difficult to come up with many secondary effects, this indicates, among other things, the need for analysts to strengthen their understanding of the physics of device failure. Our measurement step above, however, shows how important these secondary effects are to a successful analysis.


# Selection


Selection


In the final step of our loop we select one of the Correlation List items and use it to begin a new Decision Engine cycle. We make the selection based in part on factors such as whether our choice must be investigated destructively, whether investigation of the PPC or effect is easy or difficult, and how likely the item is. In our example, we might select (Fig.  2l ) local liquid crystal phase change as our effect, since it is likely, relatively easy to measure, and nondestructive. We are free to choose more than one list item, each starting its own new Decision Engine cycle. This methodology enables us to increase our productivity in this way while giving us a tool to keep track of where we are in each analysis direction.


# ECC Question (next loop iteration)


ECC Question (next loop iteration)


At this point we prepare our next ECC Question about this selection: "Does local liquid crystal phase change exist, correlate with the observed intermetal conduction, and cause it?" The Engine cycle begins again with this step. But what has happened during these six steps plus one? We have moved from one known anomaly, a difference in voltage contrast between a good part and our failure, to the actual prior cause for that anomaly, an instance of anomalous intermetal conduction. Our single loop has taken us down one link in the unique chain of cause-and-effect that the failure contains.


# Moving from Mode to Root Anomaly


Moving from Mode to Root Anomaly


This pattern of steps, then, demonstrably creates an analysis flow, which proceeds efficiently back down the cause-effect chain by which the root anomaly creates the failure mode (Fig.  2m ). If we simply apply the Decision Engine loop, our analysis flow unfolds, and the failure's cause-effect chain relationships are revealed link by link. From the initial failure mode (question, "Does a failure mode exist on this new design and correlate with the complaint?) and its verification (answer, "the mode exists and correlates with the complaint") through intermediate questions (e.g., "do hillocks exist, correlate with the observed intermetal conduction, and cause the conduction?") and their answers, to the root anomaly ("does incomplete CMP exist in the region of the conduction, correlate with the observed conduction, and cause it?"), this metaprocess creates the analysis flow which leads the analyst from the mode, or the first detected effect of the failure cause, back through intermediate cause-effect relationships to the root anomaly. In this way the metaprocess reveals the entire cause-effect chain from root anomaly to failure mode.


# Analysis Flow Characteristics


Analysis Flow Characteristics


Rather than delivering a prepackaged analysis flow, which may or may not apply well to the failure at hand, this metaprocess produces the analysis flow one step at a time based on actual failure characteristics. This makes the unfolding analysis flow very responsive to the most current information about the failure. The metaprocess also directs the analyst to explore applicable cause-effect relationships at each point, and points to needed measurement equipment and techniques, whether available to the analyst or not.


These characteristics provide two benefits. First, they prioritize the analyst's focus correctly, placing greater importance on an understanding of good and failing device behavior than on technique or tool operation expertise. Second, they encourage the development of an analytical lab infrastructure, which serves the objective of finding causes of failure, rather than the other way around. Many labs unwittingly make the toolset primary. The analysis process then becomes in large part a way of 'grading' failures to determine whether or not they will reveal their secrets to a lab's existing analysis tool and technique set. Failures, which do not yield, to existing analysis capability often merely land in the "Cause unknown" bin rather than driving the lab's capability forward until their causes are found. The metaprocess described here makes the need for missing techniques both evident and quantifiable, enabling labs to improve their equipment set with confidence in the value of the techniques developed or purchased.


Second, the flow's characteristics make the formal use of inferential logic easier, so as to help avoid analysis pitfalls and improve success. It does so by breaking the analysis process down into segments small enough that their relationship to formal logic principles becomes clear. The following section explains this for three of the most important logic concepts: logical inference, proof by induction and disproof by contrapositive testing.


# Applying Formal Logic


Applying Formal Logic


Figure  3  shows a segment of the full six-step loop. This segment relates to how we prove and disprove possible correlations in the course of a failure analysis. For example, if we have a functional failure mode which only occurs at positive supply voltages above 2.5V, we must look for possible prior causes that imply this specific voltage dependence. These may not be easy to identify. The apparent nonlinear relationship with supply voltage may suggest, as one possibility, that our failure mechanism involves active devices, and therefore may correlate with photon emission.


To investigate this possible correlation we identify implied characteristics of a common cause for the failure and the photon emission, then look for those characteristics. Simple but important logical implications-if-then statements-used here begin with the clause:


# "If a common cause creates the functional failure mode and photon emission, then..."


and end with clauses such as,


# "any observed photon emission will show an intensity change at 2.5V"; "temperaturedependent shifts in the failure onset will correlate with observed photon intensity change"; "emission pattern will correlate with the failing vector(s)"; "good devices will not show the observed correlations"


"any observed photon emission will show an intensity change at 2.5V"; "temperaturedependent shifts in the failure onset will correlate with observed photon intensity change"; "emission pattern will correlate with the failing vector(s)"; "good devices will not show the observed correlations"


The results of the drop tests on the 289 ball CSP are presented in Figure  13  in the form of a twoparameter Weibull plot. The for the non-underfilled assemblies indicate two distinct distributions with different slopes, namely, a much steeper slope for failures after 50 drops and a more gradual slope for those failures between 8 and 40 drops. This can be explained in terms stresses experienced by packages at different locations on the board. The initial failures  are experienced were from packages located in the center of the board, that undergo greater deflection during drop test. On the other hand, packages located near the edges of the board under go a relatively smaller deflection and hence may survive more drops. These are represented by the points on the steeper section of the plot.


The underfilled assemblies, however, appear to be insensitive to the location on the board. It is hypothesized that the underfill constrains the board and the package to deform at the same curvature, which makes the assemblies experience the same stresses irrespective of their location on the board.


## Comparing the results for underfill of different


Comparing the results for underfill of different


No underfill 100% underfill Figure  12 : Crack opening stress contour plot of critical corner solder joint moduli, it is seen that the there is a small but noticeable improvement in reliability with decreasing underfill modulus. Compared to the non-underfilled case, however, the presence of any underfill improves the reliability more significantly. Therefore, the most improvement in reliability was observed for the underfill with modulus of 2 MPa.


These results are best explained in terms of the stresses induced during the drop test, which are a combination of board bending induced stresses and inertial dynamic stresses. It is hypothesized that these two effects may compete with each other to dominate failure of the CSP. One possible explanation for the improved reliability of low modulus underfills is that their dynamic shock damping capabilities may dominate any smaller degradation due to a more compliant underfill material that increases the stress due to bending. From the limited tests performed, it is not clear what the optimum combination of underfill properties should be to minimize bending as well as maximize shock protection. It is more evident from the data that a lack of underfill significantly degrades the reliability of a CSP subjected to drop impact stresses. Thus, even if only the corner joint is not encapsulated by underfill, the reliability of the CSP would approach that of a non-underfilled CSP unless the corner ball is functionally redundant.


## Conclusions


Conclusions


Both experimental data and finite element stress analysis results suggest that the reliability of underfilled CSPs can be expected to be superior to that of non-underfilled assemblies subject to mechanical stresses such as drop and bending. This improvement in reliability in drop testing is inversely proportional to the modulus of the underfill. More importantly, the presence of even a small corner underfill void that exposes the corner solder joint of the CSP can degrade the reliability significantly, potentially to that of a non-underfilled assembly. Therefore, considering the additional cost and process complexity involved in the underfill process, any decision to underfill a CSP must also place critical importance on process optimisation and monitoring for eliminating corner voids in the underfill.


## Introduction


Leakage detection has been an important subject in fault diagnosis and defect isolation for integrated devices. It has become increasingly challenging and time consuming to effectively isolate the internal nets with marginal resistive or non-resistive leakage at device operating modes in advanced integrated devices (e.g. some complex mixed-signal devices) by curve tracer testing or Iddq testing  [1] [2] [3] [4] .


Sometimes the amount of the leakage from an internal net is marginal and is less than the spec limit of total operating current for an integrated device. The leakage is difficult to be detected and screened effectively from the external pins of the device.


In some cases, such a marginal internal leakage may only cause some functional failures of an integrated device instead of failing direct leakage testing.


The defect diagnosis and isolation may become even more difficult for a mixed-signal device if a small leaky net is located inside a digital circuitry which is surrounded by large analog circuit blocks. The failed net may not be easily accessible from the external pins of the mixed-signal device by curve tracer testing.


Sometimes it may also be time consuming to find the marginally leaky pins for a complex mixed-signal device in order to run emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing.


For example, all the digital and analog power pins of a mixed-signal device have to be powered up in proper sequence in order to avoid the leakage from undesired latching conditions from some internal parasitic transistors in the device  [5] .


## System Evaluation Board


System Evaluation Board


A system evaluation board (SEB), which was designed to test an integrated device at system level, was used in this experiment to isolate defects at the internal nets with small resistive or non-resistive leakage at operating modes for some mixed-signal devices.


All the power pins for the digital circuit blocks of the mixed-signal devices were connected to a VDD power supply and all the power pins for the analog circuit blocks of the devices were connected to a separate VDD power supply.


The SEB is portable and can be used for emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing.


A portion of the SEB is shown in Figure  1 . In this experiment, an FBGA socket was mounted on the SEB for testing some mixed-signal devices with internal leakage.


Figure  1  A portion of a system evaluation board (SEB) mounted with an FBGA socket for loading a decapsulated device. The FBGA socket has a square-shaped opening on its top plate for emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing. The device was powered up and put into a desired operating mode using the SEB to activate its internal leaky nets for emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing.


After loading a device under test (DUT) into the FBGA socket, the device was pressed down using the top plate by tightening the four screws at each corner of the top plate to make good contact between the solder balls of the device and the pins in the socket.


Figure  2  shows a side view of the FBGA socket and a top plate.


Figure  2  A side view of the FBGA socket and the top plate with a square-shaped opening for emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing of a decapsulated integrated device with internal leakage.


The top plate has a square-shaped opening and the device was decapsulated to expose the silicon surface so that emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing can be performed for the device.


Both the digital and analog VDD power pins of a mixed signal device were powered up with proper timing using the SEB to avoid the leakage from undesired parasitic latching conditions. For example, a phone board for testing a modem chip can be used as an SEB for the device.


The device was put into a desired operating mode by the SEB so that the internal leaky nets can be activated and then be detected using emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing. In some cases, the SEB may also be used to exercise different functional circuit blocks of an integrated device through a JTAG debugger in order to activate certain internal net at various testing conditions.


Two experiments were designed and performed using the SEB for failure diagnosis and leakage isolation of failed mixed-signal devices.


The first experiment was to isolate a large leaky net of a mixed-signal device at its operating mode by using an SEB. Then the observed leaky site was verified using a curve tracer to isolate the leaky pins of the failed mixed-signal device.


In this case, the leakage from the mixed-signal device was large enough to be detected by direct curve tracer measurement and the leaky site could be verified using conventional leakage isolation methodologies.


The purpose of this experiment is to verify this SEB technique and to show the quickness in leakage isolation using the SEB without finding the leaky pins first.


In the second experiment, the internal leakage from a mixed-signal device was so small that the device only failed some functional automatic test equipment (ATE) testing instead of direct leakage testing.


In this case, it was difficult and time consuming to find the marginally leaky pins by curve tracer testing in order to run emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing.


This technique was found to be very quick and effective in isolating such small internal leakage in complex mixed-signal devices.


## Experiment I


Experiment I


## Isolation of Internal Leakage for a Mixed-Signal Device with Unknown Leaky Pins


Isolation of Internal Leakage for a Mixed-Signal Device with Unknown Leaky Pins


A mixed-signal device (Device A) with unknown leaky pins was studied in this experiment using the SEB technique.


After the device was decapsulated using a hot fuming acid mixture and loaded into the FBGA socket on the SEB, both digital and analog power pins were powered up by the SEB and the device was put into its operating mode.


Emission microscope testing was then performed for the device at its operating mode without isolating its leaky pins first. An emission spot was observed (as shown in Figure  3 ) from an internal net of the mixedsignal device.


This emission spot was then verified using curve tracer testing to find the leaky pins for the device first and then run emission microscope testing to verify the emission site.


In this case, the leakage was large enough to be detected by direct curve tracer measurement through the external pins of the mixed-signal device so that the leaky net could also be isolated and verified by using conventional leakage isolation methodologies.


## Experiment II


Experiment II


## Isolation of Small Internal Leakage at Operating mode Using SEB and Emission Microscope


Isolation of Small Internal Leakage at Operating mode Using SEB and Emission Microscope


Another mixed-signal device (called device B) was also studied by using the SEB. ATE testing results from this device only showed some functional failures instead of showing direct leakage failures. No anomalous high leakage was detected from this device by either curve tracer testing or ATE testing through its external pins.


The internal leakage from this device was believed to be marginal and the amount of the leakage might be small comparing to the spec limit for total operating current of the device in order to be detected effectively from the external pins of the device.


In this case, it would be difficult and time consuming to find the marginally leaky pins for the device by since the device only failed some functional testing instead of failing direct leakage testing.


It would also be difficult to activate such a small internal leaky net in this mixed-signal device using a curve tracer for emission microscope testing or liquid crystal testing.


The device was then studied by the SEB technique.


All the digital and analog power pins of the device were powered up using the SEB and the device was put into its operating mode by the SEB.


A highly sensitive Hamamatsu infrared detector with an effective wavelength range from 2 to 5µm was used in this experiment to isolate possible infrared emission site due to the suspected small internal leakage from the mixed-signal device at its operating mode.


An infrared emission spot was found at an internal net of the device (as shown in Figure  4 ) using the infrared emission microscope.


Figure  4  An emission spot was observed at an internal net (as pointed by an arrow) of device B with marginal internal leakage at a device operating mode using the SEB and a highly sensitive infrared detector.


Figure  5  is a closer look of the infrared emission spot from this device (as pointed by the arrow). The sharpness of the infrared image is usually less than that of the optical images from optical microscopes.


Figure  5  An infrared image with a higher magnification shows the emission spot (as pointed by an arrow) of device B.


After finding the emission spot using the SEB, optical inspection was performed on device B around the emission spot. A defect of less than 0.5 µm was found at the emission site using a high-resolution optical microscope (see Figure  6 ).


Figure  6  A process defect of less than 0.5 um was found at the emission site for device B (as pointed by an arrow), which was believed to cause the observed marginal leakage in the mixed signal device.


There was no sign of electrical overstress or other damages at the nearby area around the small defect. It was believed that this defect was likely a wafer process-induced defect.


As a comparison to device B, the same area was inspected on a known good decapsulated device. No similar defect was found from this known good device (as shown in Figure  7 ).


Figure  7  As a comparison to device B, the same area was shown (as pointed by an arrow) from a known good device (without the process defect as observed in device B).


The good device showed no similar emission spot as observed in device B after it was powered up and put into its operating mode using the SEB under the same testing condition. It was believed that the observed ATE functional failures were related to this marginal leakage at the internal net.


The process defect at the emission site in device B was then inspected using a Hitachi S-4700 field emission scanning electron microscope.


A top view SEM image of the process defect is shown in Figure  8 . This SEM image was rotated by 90 degree comparing to the microscopic image as shown in Figure  6 .


Figure  8  SEM photo of the process defect (as pointed by an arrow) at the emission site for device B). This SEM photo was rotated by 90 degree comparing to the microscopic image (in Figure  6 ).


Figure  9  A closer look of the process defect at the emission site for device B (as pointed by an arrow), which was located between the two narrowly spaced metal lines.


Figure  9  is a higher magnification SEM image of device B around the small process defect, which was located between two narrowly spaced metal lines (as pointed by an arrow).


Some anomalous and circular surface topology around the small process defect in device B was also observed (as shown in the SEM images). The 3-D oblique image also showed some anomalous and circular surface topology around the process defect, which was located between the two adjacent metal lines. As a comparison, a regular FESEM image of the same area is also shown in Figure  10  (at lower right corner).


Figure  11  is a SEM image of focused ion beam (FIB) cross-section at the observed process defect between the two adjacent metal lines.


The SEM image revealed a thin Ti/TiN barrier metal residue (stringer) over the right side of the two adjacent metal lines (as pointed by an arrow).


As FIB cross-sectioning was continued towards the process defect, the Ti/TiN metal stringer was found to extend from the metal line at the right side (as shown in Figure  11 ) to the adjacent metal line on the left (as shown in Figure  12 ).


Figure  11  SEM image of the FIB cross-section at the small process defect between the two adjacent metal lines revealed a thin Ti/TiN barrier metal stringer over the two narrowly spaced metal lines and a void in aluminum metal under the Ti/TiN layer (as pointed by the arrows).


Figure  12  The Ti/TiN metal stringer was found to extend over to the adjacent metal line on the left side (as pointed by an arrow) as further FIB crosssectioning was performed across the small process defect.


Beside the Ti/TiN stringer across the two adjacent metal lines, a void was also observed in the aluminum metal line on the right side under the Ti/TiN barrier metal layer (as shown in Figure  11  and 12 ).


The adhesion between the barrier metal and the aluminum metal might have been degraded due to the formation of the void, which might explain the differences in the passive voltage contrast between the Ti/TiN barrier metal and the aluminum metal layers (as shown in Figure  11  and 12 ).


## Discussions


Discussions


From the FIB cross-section images, the process defect found at the internal net of device B was mostly likely associated to the observed Ti/TiN barrier metal stringer as shown in Figure  11  and 12.


The thin Ti/TiN metal stringer might overlap somewhere between the two FIB locations as shown in Figure  11  and 12 and therefore lead to the near resistive bridging between the two narrowly spaced metal lines.


The Ti/TiN stringer is likely a metal etch residue associated to the observed anomalous surface topology at this process defect between the two adjacent metal lines.


The void in the aluminum metal under the Ti/TiN barrier metal layer might be caused by electromigration from electrical thermal stress in the aluminum metal line  [6] .


The observed infrared emission spot in the mixedsignal device B was believed to be caused by the marginal and near-resistive leakage (in sub-µA range) from the bridging of the metal lines due to the observed thin Ti/TiN barrier metal stringer across the two narrowly spaced metal lines.


Therefore, the ATE functional failures of the mixedsignal device B were most likely originated from the marginal internal leakage due to this tiny Ti/TiN metal residue.


It would be difficult to find such a small process defect without isolating the internal leaky net at the operating mode of the mixed-signal device using this SEB technique. The SEB is useful in fault isolation when there is a marginal leakage from the internal nets of an integrated device.


This technique is especially useful in failure diagnosis and defect isolation for a complex mixed-signal device when its internal leakage is marginal and small comparing to its total operating current or when the device fails only some functional testing instead of failing direct leakage testing.


By using this technique, it is not necessary to isolate the leaky pins for the failed device before running emission microscope testing.


It is a quick way to power up both the digital and analog power pins of a mixed-signal device and put the device into a desired operating mode using the SEB for emission or liquid crystal testing. The SEB is portable and may be modified to run backside emission microscope testing or be used for e-beam probing  [6] .


## INTRODUCTION


One of the primary factors controlling the reliability of an electronic product subjected to adverse thermal and/or mechanical exposure is the robustness of the solder joints. Solder joint shear strength, along with pull strength, is especially critical to the reliable operation of chip scale packages (CSP), ball grid array packages (BGA), flip chips and other fine pitch leadless surface mount components, because of small feature sizes. Shear strength defines failure from thermal excursions while pull strength of the solder joints influences failure in mechanical drop or bending.


In a package mounted on a board and subjected to shear forces, failure can occur at one of three locations: a) in the solder, b) at the pad/solder interface of the component or the board, and c) under the pad. Interconnection failure is defined by the failure that is most likely among the three failures. Therefore, the weakest of the three strengths will dominate the definition of the interconnection strength. The test method to evaluate the Package to Board Interconnection Shear Strength (PBISS) described in this paper was developed to measure this interconnection strength for functional products and not just laboratory samples. Instead of forcing failure to occur at one of the three locations, the test allows failure to occur naturally and dictated only by the relative ranking of the three strengths.


The ability to measure the interconnection shear strength can potentially be used a) for production and supplier quality assessment, b) for materials/process selection in the development phase, c) as a cost effective and scientific test method complementary to thermal fatigue tests and mechanical shock tests in research.


A candidate test method needs to meet the following requirements to be useful in a high volume, manufacturing environment:


1. These measurements should be possible on actual products from a production line 2. Speed of testing and ease of interpretation should be accompanied by good sensitivity to factors affecting reliability


## BACKGROUND


BACKGROUND


## Pad Surface Finish


Pad Surface Finish


The nature and quality of the surface finish on the pad determines how well the solder bonds to the pad via the intermetallic layer. ENIG (Electroless Nickel/Immersion Gold) is a metal finish on PWB that has emerged as an alternative to hot-air solder levelling (HASL)  [4]  because of the surface flatness necessary for fine pitch components. Although this finish has been successfully used for many electronic products, brittle interfacial fracture of solder joints, at the interface between solder ball and Ni surface on Cu pad has been reported  [5, 6] . It appears that poor solderability or blackpad problem is caused by undesirable process variations, with variations in quality between and within lots. Alternatively, organic solderability preservatives (OSPs) have also been used in the PWB industry as a replacement for HASL  [7] . However, whether these finishes can withstand multiple thermal cycles, and whether solder wettability and shelf life are acceptable, are concerns that need to be addressed. Thus, both OSP and ENIG surface finish are capable of producing good solder joints, but the ENIG process has inherent quality problems that could produce larger variation in the quality of the solder joint.


## PWB build-up layer


PWB build-up layer


Another factor determining the solder joint strength of components in products is the build-up layer under the pad because of its effect on the peel strength. Aramid  and resin coated copper (RCC) on FR-4 are currently widely used for the build-up layer. Chopped, short Aramid fiber reinforcement is used due to its unique advantage of low in-plane coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE), excellent dimensional stability, highspeed laser and plasma processability, and low dielectric constant. Although Aramid reinforcement is an excellent choice for low CTE  [8]  and micro via technology applications, potential disadvantages include susceptibility to moisture and weak fiber-matrix interface. An example of cracking in the Aramid layer due to weak interfacial bond between the Aramid fiber and the epoxy matrix after PWB exposure to mechanical impact is shown in Figure  1a . Such cracking in the build-up layer can cause electrical failure when the crack surfaces outside the pad and severs the trace as shown in Figure  1b . Therefore, the shear strength of  Aramid is the trade mark of Dupont Corp.


Aramid build-up samples is compared to an alternative, resin coated copper (RCC).


## CSP design


CSP design


The height, diameter, and number of bumps along with package construction are also expected to have a significant impact on the shear strength of a CSP. The primary features of C1 and C2 from a package perspective are listed in Table  2 . It should be noted that the CSP C1 has a polyimide interposer while CSP C2 has an interposer of BT reinforced with woven glass fibers. In the test method proposed, the motion of crosshead is translated into a shear load at the component solder joints via a fixture  [9]  that was designed to ensure pure shear loading at the solder joint by minimizing bending moments. The basic configuration of the component shear test is shown schematically in Figure  3 .


The goal of this study is to evaluate the sensitivity of the component level shear test method to variations in a) pad finish (ENIG vs. OSP), and b) build up layer on boards (RCC/FR4 vs. Aramid/FR4) for two different packages: 1) 144 ball BGA with polyimide interposer and 2) 168 ball BGA with BT laminate interposer.


## EXPERIMENTAL


EXPERIMENTAL


## Shear Test Procedure


Shear Test Procedure


The CSPs (C1 and C2) were cut from each board with a diamond saw such that the cut was at least 1 mm from the edge of the CSP. Next, each CSP was cleaned with methanol in an ultrasonic cleaner to prepare the surface for adhesion. Then it was bonded to the fixture using 401 Super Bond 1 . The shear tests were conducted with a crosshead speed of 0.2 mm/min (0.0033 mm/sec). In comparison to ball shear tests reported in literature, the strain rate used here is approximately 10 -100 times slower, and this can be expected to favour solder failures more than failures at other locations. Since solder strength characterization is the primary goal, the strain rates used are appropriate. The ram height was 1 Trademark of Loctite Corporation controlled to be less than 0.05 mm above the solder mask on PWB using metal shims. A 10 Newton (N) preload was applied to samples to minimize the effect of any slack in the load train. Shear tests were terminated when the load fell to 20 percent of maximum load. The shear strength was calculated by dividing the shear force by the area of pad.


During the shear test, the orientation of different samples with respect to the applied shear loading was identical to minimize any variability due to asymmetry of traces. The parallelism of shear ram and leading edge of CSP was ensured to better than 1°. Via holes were first filled with non-adhesive fluid such as correction liquid to ensure that solder balls were not covered by the glue. The data from tests where the solder balls were reinforced by the glue are not included in the analysis. To ensure that the protruding polyimide interposer in C1 did not cause anomalies in the loaddisplacement curves, the excess poyimide was ground off with a dremel tool before the shear test, taking care C1 C2  to exert minimal force during grinding.


## Failure Location analysis


Failure Location analysis


Dye penetrant testing was used to detect hidden cracks in the solder joints, especially at the interface between pad and solder ball. A red dye was applied to the suspected area and allowed to penetrate into the defect. This method was useful for early stage inspection to discern the failure locations. Magnaflux  SKL-SP penetrant was mixed with isopropyl alcohol (IPA) in ratio of 1 to 5 by weight to perform this test Fracture surface analysis method was used to inspect failures of solder joints to measure the distribution and nature of failures. After shear tests, an optical microscope was utilized to count and characterize the nature of failures, assuming three possible failure locations as depicted schematically in Figure  4 . The numbers of the three different failure locations were recorded for each shear-tested specimen to quantify damage and the nature of failures. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used for high magnification microstructural analysis of fractured solder joints.

## SHEAR STRENGTH


SHEAR STRENGTH


The shear strengths for C1 from S1, S2, and S3 sample sets are plotted in Figure  5 . Considering that ENIG samples had known blackpad issues, solder/pad brittle interfacial cracking can be expected to dominate the results. A comparison of the maximum value of shear strength in S1 and S2 indicates that ENIG surface finish can yield as high strength as OSP with optimal board quality. However, the minimum strength value is significantly lower due to poor solderability. Figure  6  shows the cross section view of solder joints on C1/S1 sample that had not been stressed. The hypercorrosion of the Ni-P layer, brittle interfacial cracking between the intermetallic layer and the Ni-P pad and cracks in the Ni-P layer are apparent. Solder joints such as this can be expected to exhibit very low strengths and this is reflected in the low strength values measured for S1 sample set.


# Sample preparation


Sample preparation


Sample preparation is another area that poses challenges to the failure analysis process. The device needs to be prepared and maintain its functionality so the analyst can operate the device in the desired state. The sample preparation process can easily cause the device Figure  2  : Area of interest after macro level fault isolation


In step c, the micro-level fault isolation is carried out. In Complex Instruction Set Computer (CISC) microprocessor, a macroinstruction will be decoded into a few micro-operations (uOp). By knowing which uOp is failing, the failing region can be further reduced to the functional block that is handling the uOp. To accomplish this task, another DFT feature will be invoked to read out the value of a certain signal. With that information, the actual behavior of the microprocessor can be understood, without using any probing equipment. To verify whether a sub-functional block is failing, experiments can be carried out. This is done by exercising the failing block in a different manner and looking at the response.


Figure  3  shows the physical connection of the Dispatch, Integer Addition Unit, Integer Multiplication Unit and the Result Write-back block. If the failing instruction is integer addition, a modification can be made to the assembly code to test out the integer multiplication and can be used to determine if the common path (Dispatch and Result Writeback) contains the failing location. This can further reduce the area of interest (Figure  4 ). In step d, the actual time the uOp fails will need to be identified because the uOp actually flows through several circuit blocks. In order to further understand exactly which sub-functional block the fault actually locates. These steps require a very good understanding of the microprocessor architecture. Together with some fault injection tools to simulate the behavior of a failing signal, the exact region where the fault is located can be determine (Figure  5 ). This thus narrows down the region where the instruction flows through and the potential failing area (Figure  2 ). Step e, involves a circuit and a layout study. The schematic diagram will be inspected to determine the implementation of the circuit. A circuit simulation program is used to simulate the behavior of the circuit and comparing it to the actual behavior observed. This provides a hypothesis of what the fault is. A layout study is carried out to look for the most likely defect mechanism that can cause the behavior taking into consideration the defect characteristics gathered during the defect verification stage. This reduces the area of interest to a transistor or a single node. (Figure  6 ) In step f, physical failure analysis is carried out to actually locate the defect. This step is carried out in junction with some level of defect localization like passive voltage contrast technique. However, unlike the conventional method, physical failure analysis will be carried out without any probing.
