Manufacturing of any new microelectronic device usually has a yield ramp-up period at the initial stage. This period may have several yield learning cycles as shown in Fig.  1 . A yield learning cycle may include several steps such as manufacturing a test lot, wafer sort, failure analysis and proposed corrective actions. Among all the steps, failure analysis is the most important one because the corrective actions implemented in the next test lot are based on the root cause identification of the low yield wafers with careful failure analysis. A critical failure analysis step is fault isolation. Conventionally, electrical faults are usually captured during wafer sort or final test. Then the electrical faults are isolated by emission microscopy  [1] , liquid crystal  [2] , LIVA/TIVA  [3, 4] , and ORBIRCH  [5]  etc. techniques. All these techniques are performed with the failing device powered properly to stimulate the failure. Sometimes certain failures even need to be excited by a test pattern by a tester. This requires the failure analyst to know the device and the failure very well. As microelectronic devices are becoming more complicated and with multiple metal layers, a single yield learning cycle could take at least one and a half months to complete. Moreover, the high integration and complexity of the microelectronic devices pose more challenges on fault isolation than before. These challenges are even tougher in wafer foundries because there, little device information is available. This makes yield ramp-up take longer time. Recently, the inception of in-line E-beam inspection equipment greatly improves the situation.


# In-line E-beam Inspection


In-line E-beam Inspection


In-line E-beam inspection is analogous to KLA inspection. In-line E-beam inspection makes use of secondary electron imaging by rastering a focused primary E-beam over a wafer surface. With an electrostatic field (could be extraction field or retarding field) set up by an intermediate electrode in the E-beam column, its sensitivity and signal-noise ratio can be adjusted so as to reduce false alarm or missing capture. Because of high resolution, in-line E-beam inspection can find very tiny defects on the wafer surface, which cannot be detected by KLA. On the other hand, when different types of structures, such as grounded and floating structures, are exposed to E-beam radiation, they will be at different potentials (voltages) because of charging-up effect. The inspection results are well recorded in a file for post-inspection review. This file is compatible with most navigation software and provides all the information required for following defect characterization. In-line E-beam inspection can be easily applied in any critical layer in wafer fabrication so that the yield-limiting defects can be captured at the source layer rather than after wafer Fab-out, and corrective actions can be implemented in time.


# Case studies


Case studies


The following three cases demonstrate the application of in-line E-beam inspection on different layers for different types of devices. After an electrical fault is captured, the physical defect can be characterized by Focused Ion Beam (FIB) crosssection or further Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) analysis.


# Gate-oxide Issue


Gate-oxide Issue


In this case, in-line E-beam inspection was performed after poly spacer formation in array mode for a memory device. It was found that some poly showed abnormally dark contrast compared with other poly as shown in Fig.  2 . These abnormally dark poly were cross-sectioned by FIB and subsequent XTEM analysis was performed. It was found that the gate oxide underneath these dark poly was 130-200 A, much thicker than normal gate oxide (65A) (see XTEM picture shown in Fig.  3 ). This was because the presence of water residue caused the gate-oxide to grow faster at that area. The water residue was introduced during the pre-clean step before gate-oxide growth.


# Contact Issue


Contact Issue


Fig.  4  is the image of in-line E-beam inspection performed after contact W CMP in array mode for another memory device. It showed that some PMOS contacts had dark contrast, compared with other PMOS contacts. Fig.  5  is the XTEM picture of a dark contact and Si wormhole found underneath the contact. This was because misalignment made the contact partially land on STI, leading to a hump at the bottom of the contact (as pointed to by an arrow). At the hump site, barrier metal coverage was thin.


Fig.  4  In-line E-beam inspection found abnormally dark PMOS contact.


During the following W deposition, Tungsten hexafluoride (WF6) penetrated through the barrier metal at the weak point and reacted with the Si substrate to form a Si wormhole according to formula  (1) . The by-product of W was left in the resultant Si wormhole.


2WF6 + 3Si = 3SiF4 + 2W (1) Fig.  5  XTEM picture showing Si wormhole underneath a contact.


# Interconnect Issue


Interconnect Issue


Besides performing at poly and contact levels, it is also feasible to perform in random mode at any via level for any logic device. Fig.  6  and 7 are two typical examples performed at via2 level for a logic device. From Fig.  6 , it was found that one via2 showed bright contrast, while the same via2 showed dark contrast in an adjacent die. After FIB crosssectioning, it was found that a via1, which was connected with the abnormally bright via2 by a short metal, was empty (see Fig.  8 ). The empty via1 was believed to be due to a particle blocking the via1 hole before barrier metal and/or W deposition.


Fig.  6  In-line E-beam inspection found abnormally bright via (left die). From Fig.  7 , it was found that one via2 showed dark contrast, while the same via2 showed bright contrast in an adjacent die. Subsequent XTEM analysis revealed that the via2 was bridged to an adjacent metal2 by W extrusion (see Fig.  9 ). This issue was due to two problems, gap-fill void at narrow spacing metal and misalignment. Because of misalignment, via2 etch touched the gap-fill hole formed during FSG deposition, and thus W extruded into the gap-fill hole and bridged to the adjacent metal2 during the following W deposition.


In-line E-beam inspection is a very useful technique for accelerating yield improvement in a wafer Fab.


Incorporation of E-beam inspection in a manufacturing line at critical layers can capture electrical faults at the source layer in-line, rather than after wafer Fab-out, leading to a short yield learning cycle.


Portable electronic products are subject to severe mechanical stresses in addition to thermally induced stresses in the normal end use environment. These mechanical stresses could arise from such occurrences as dropping and bending the product, or even from relatively routine keypad strokes. For nonleaded packages, such as flip chips, chip scale packages (CSPs) and ball grid array packages (BGA),


underfilling the package with an epoxy-based encapsulant has been found to provide significant improvement in life for both thermally  [1, 2]  and mechanically induced stresses  [3, 4] . The improvement in reliability is achieved at additional cost in terms of process steps and reworkability. Several alternatives have been proposed to address the above limitations of underfilling in recent years, such as no-flow processes  [5]  and reworkable underfills  [6] . However, irrespective of the underfill materials employed and processes followed, the probability of underfill defects, such as voids, delaminations, improper fillets, etc., occurring in a manufacturing environment are significant enough to warrant an understanding of the reliability risk.


In recent years, several studies have focused on understanding the deleterious effects due to underfill flaws on the performance of flip chips. For example, Rzepka et al.  [7]  studied the effect of void size and delaminations on the solder joint stresses for the case of thermal cycling between 25 C and 125 C. They concluded that voids that occurred near the perimeter were much more harmful than interior voids away from the perimeter. Schubert et al.  [8]  studied the effect of particle settling, size of voids, degree of solder mask misregistration, fillet geometry and Figure  1 . Finite element model of a) 144 I/0 CSP mounted on FR4 board subjected to four-point bend, b) constructional details of the package. Solder joints were modeled as a viscoplastic material (Anand's model) while the PWB was modeled as an orthotropic material. All other materials in the model were modeled as linear elastic, isotropic materials. material characteristics on the thermal cycling performance in the range -55 C to 125 C (AATC air to air thermal cycling). They also found that large voids ranked higher in terms of reliability impact than small voids. Similar studies for packages on printed wiring boards (PWBs) subjected to mechanical stresses, either static, bending of dynamic impact, have not received much attention.


The performance of underfilled assemblies in adverse mechanical environment such as mechanical impact (drop) and bending has been receiving increasing attention with the rising popularity of mobile communication and hand held computing devices  [4] . One of the primary contributors to failure in both drop and bend stress excursions is the bending of the board. Inertial and other dynamic stresses only make the drop test more damaging than just bending alone. For the case of BGAs and CSPs, although several studies have been published documenting the benefits of underfilling  [1, 9] , the role of underfill defects is not clearly understood.


The goal of this study is to better understand the effect of void size on the stress state in the solder joint of an underfilled CSP under mechanical loading.


The following experiments were conducted to understand the mechanics of failure and quantify the degree of risk in improper underfilling:


1. Test vehicles with a 144 ball, 0.8 mm pitch CSP, with varying corner void content (0 to 75%), were subjected to simulated end use environment followed by failure analysis. These experimental results are explained with the aid of a finite element model.


# Effect of Process issues on Underfill Voiding


Effect of Process issues on Underfill Voiding


Ideally, the underfill process must completely fill the space between the package and board touching adjacent components. The primary process variables that affect quality of underfill are described below.


# Dispense Pattern


Dispense Pattern


For the capillary flow underfill process, tight control over the amount of the material and the speed of the dispenser are critical factors in order to get consistent results. Because fluid characteristics vary from one underfill to another, the dispensing process must be carefully tailored for each application. Some examples of dispense patterns are: a) L-shaped dispense pattern, b) Single pass -single line pattern, c) Underfill through a shield, and d) Underfill through a hole in the PWB. Achieving high flow rates and assuring complete filling of the package-board gap are critical for throughput.


In this operation, linear positive displacement pumps are preferred because of their ability to have high flow rates with consistently precise volumes  [10]  in comparison to time pressure pumps and screw driven pumps. Linear positive displacement pumps use servo driven pistons, which can dispense precise amounts of underfill from the fluid chamber, thus achieving consistent dispensing of   From a process cycle time point of view L-patterns are attractive. When designing the dispensing pattern for a CSP component, it is essential to find a pattern that minimizes the risk of voids. For example, with an L-pattern it is important not to start or stop dispensing at a corner to prevent voids.


# Substrate Temperature


Substrate Temperature


The PWB temperature also plays an important role as it influences the flow characteristics of the dispensed underfill. The PWB is heated to 80-120°C and is maintained at that temperature throughout the process. Higher temperatures reduce the viscosity of the underfill, and help the underfill flow under the CSP and adhere better to the balls, die and the PWB. Also heating the PWB helps reduce the voiding. In some materials, needle heaters can also be used to lower the viscosity of the underfill, thus reducing stringing at the needle tip and ensures a clean fluid break at the end of the dispense cycle.


# Proximity of Needle to the Edge of the Package


Proximity of Needle to the Edge of the Package


The dispensing needle is positioned 3-5 mils (75-125µm) away from the edge of the package. Underfill material is then dispensed on two adjacent sides of the device and is allowed to flow toward the center of the package. Some of the benefits and limitations of different dispense pattern are listed in Table  1 .


Process defects can be a result of a) insufficient volume of material dispensed, b) adjacent components removing material from the intended area, c) incorrect or out-of-control dispense pattern, d) significant chang in viscosity of the material from optimal value, or e) poor process monitoring and control.


# Experimental


Experimental


## 144 ball CSP test vehicles subjected to simulated end use


144 ball CSP test vehicles subjected to simulated end use


The L-shaped dispense pattern was selected for this study based on cycle time considerations. As a consequence of the process optimization, CSPs with varying degrees of underfill voiding were obtained. Test vehicles representing various degrees of underfill voiding along with those that had completely underfilled CSPs were subjected to simulated end-use environment consisting of a combination of bending, drop and temperature excursions. Detailed nondestructive and microstructural analysis was performed on 25 failed test vehicles along with 5


## 289 ball CSP test boards subjected to drop testing


289 ball CSP test boards subjected to drop testing


For the second set of tests, daisy-chained Tape Interposer CSPs were used (10 mm x 10 mm, 151 I/O, 0.5 mm ball pitch and 13 mm x 13 mm, 289 I/O, 0.5mm ball pitch). A 0.9 mm thick, FR-4 glass epoxy laminate board with electroless Ni/ Immersion Au (ENIG) pad surface finish was used. All boards were subjected to 12 hours of drying at 125°C in nitrogen prior to assembly. Components were received in vacuum-sealed desiccated packaging. After opening the packages, all components were baked for 24 hours at 125°C. Both PWBs and the components were stored in a dry nitrogen box prior to use.


Four boards/modules (12 -13 mm x 13 mm, 289 I/O) were tested for each material group in a board level tester and dropped face down from 2 meters onto a smooth concrete base. The board was held in place using a vacuum suction cup and was released by releasing the vacuum prior to hitting the base. The electrical resistance was measured after every three drops and a 7.5% change in resistance was considered to represent failure. The data were plotted assuming a 2-parameter Weibull distribution.


## Finite Element Analysis


Finite Element Analysis


During dynamic drops, the flexure of the board is the primary contributor to failure of the solder interconnects. Other factors are inertial forces and dynamic stresses. For the sake of simplicity, however, only static bending loads are considered for the parametric study. It is assumed that the static bending approximation adopted in this study negatively impacts only the absolute stress values without significantly influencing the relative stress values.


Since only relative values of stress are considered in this study, the static approximation is appropriate and adequate.


## Model Description


Model Description


The geometry model of a 144 I/O CSP mounted on FR4 PWB is shown in Figure  1a , and the mesh of the package is shown in Figure  1b . The boundary conditions are also indicated on the meshed geometry. Figures  2 (a  incompletely filled underfill layouts used in the parametric simulations. Underfill voids resulted from L-shaped dispensing operations were assumed for the simulation studies. Accordingly six cases were analysed: No underfill, 100%, 75%, 50%, 25% underfill and corner void where the corner solder joint was left without underfill. The supporting span of the four-point bend load was fixed at 100mm and the loading span was fixed at 80mm. A displacement load of 1mm was applied for all the simulation cases.


## Results and Discussion


## Failure Analysis Of 144 Ball Csp


Failure Analysis Of 144 Ball Csp


In this study, low magnification optical microscopy was used to screen samples that had underfill defects at the periphery of the CSP. Figures  3(a ) through 3(c) shows examples of various degrees of underfill quality. Since visual inspection was incapable of estimating the extent of voiding in the underfill, and acoustic microscopy was used for more detailed analysis after X-ray techniques proved inconclusive.


Acoustic microscopy has become the preferred nondestructive technique to study delaminations and voids because of its sensitivity to air gaps. However, the current application of investigating CSP underfill voids can be considered to be non-routine because of the attenuation suffered by the acoustic beam in passing through the molding compound and the interposer. A second difficulty arises from the multitude of interfaces in the package that makes it difficult to choose the particular reflection from the void in the underfill. While acoustic microscopy of flip chip underfill defects has become a mainstream application  [10] , successful inspection of underfill quality in CSP is dependent on package construction and molding compound materials as evidenced by reports in literature citing difficulties in acoustic microscopy  [3, 11] .


The 144-ball CSP inspected in this study used a polyimide interposer, which facilitated the inspection of underfill voids. If the interposer had been a thicker and more attenuative material such as epoxy or BT reinforced with glass fiber, underfill void imaging would have been more challenging. Focused transducers in the range of 30 MHz to 50 MHz were suitable for imaging voids in the underfill in this package. The challenge was in gating on the correct pulse in the A-scan. Calibration specimens with known defects solved this problem.


The acoustic images of a properly underfilled CSP above and below the interposer are shown in Figure  4a  and b, respectively. From the image above the interposer, the die and the copper pads on top of the interposer are clearly visible, and from the image of the interposer/underfill interface, the absence of voids in the underfill is indicated by a uniformly dark, low reflection amplitude image.


The acoustic images of samples with varying degrees of underfill voids, where the voided area is pseudocolored in red for ease of analysis. In the acoustic image of the sample with a large corner void, shown in Figure  5a , a significant portion of the interposer has a void under it, as indicated the by the area in red or yellow. The reflection from the interposer/underfill interface is very small because of the similarity of their acoustic impedances but the reflection from the interposer/void interface is strongly negative because the acoustic impedance of air is 0.


In the acoustic image, however, the voided area also contains black squares representative of the copper pads on top of the interposer (Figure  4a ). This is unavoidable because the relatively high acoustic impedance of Cu (approximately 45), causes strong shadows of the Cu pads in any acoustic image of the underfill. The Q-BAM image shown in Figure  5b  indicates that the void is clearly below the interposer.


A second example of void under the interposer caused by non-optimal underfill process parameters is shown in Figure  6  along with A-scan plots proving that the reflection from the red area is negative and deeper in the sample than the reflections from the Cu pad over the interposer. In contrast, the reflections from the die surface and the Cu pads are positive and occur earlier in time (and thickness). The use of A- scan data is critical in facilitating interpretation of the acoustic image when the inspection application is not straightforward and involves several layers of materials.


## Microstructural Analysis


Microstructural Analysis


For the BGA whose image is shown in Figure  6  every ball that did not have underfill around it in the row sectioned was cracked as shown in Figure  7 . In other samples, damage appeared to start near the corner and progress inward. Cracks more often occurred on the board side, above the Cu pad. In some cases, cracks were observed below the pad in the build-up layer and also at the component side of the solder joint. Little damage was observed within the solder joint itself.


Several but not all the solder balls in the underfill voids were observed to have cracks in them. Although most of the corner solder balls were cracked no underfill was present, not all the inner solder balls were cracked. Among those that were damaged, the cracks appeared to originate at locations where the solder mask created stress concentration close to the pad surface. A representative image is shown in Figure  8 . In some of these balls, the cracks occurred below the intermetallic layer and between the solder/pad interface. Evidence characterizing the hypercorrosion of the Ni layer on the Cu pad was not extensive but it appears that at least some of the samples studied suffered from poor solderability or blackpad. An example of such a failure is shown in Figure  9 . It is possible that fewer solder balls could have suffered damage in the absence of underfill if the solder/pad bond strength was better. For example, if organic socalled solderability preservative (OSP) were used, the poorly underfilled samples might not have suffered as many failures.


## Stress Analysis


Stress Analysis


The finite element analysis is focused on the stresses primarily in the solder, so the mesh size was adjusted for convergence only in the solder volume. This adjustment is still valid for getting a confidence in relative parametric analysis while keeping the computational time low.


The deformed geometry when the model is subjected to a four-point bend is shown in Figure  10a , while the first principal stress contours are shown in Figure  10b . It is seen that the first principal stresses are highest in the outer rows, as anticipated. The stresses along the row indicated by the dotted line in Figure  10b  are of primary interest because the row spans both the anticipated high and low stress regions due to corner voids. This row was used to monitor the distribution of the maximum peel stresses, which are the mode I crack opening stresses 'σ y ', in the solder joint. It was found that these out-of-plane stresses, followed the same trend as the first principal stresses but differed in value.


The calculated stresses (σ y ) were normalized with the maximum stress calculated for the case with no underfill and plotted in Figure  11as  a function of the solder joints (along the dotted line in Figure  10b ). The baseline data are for the completely underfilled case. Comparing the cases with no underfill and complete underfill, data indicate that the underfill serves to reduce the stresses by the greatest degree in the corner joints and by smallest extent in the central joints. Attention is drawn to the solder joint-void coverage indicated in Figure  2 . It is trivial fact that for the completely underfilled and non-underfilled cases, respectively, 0 and 13 solder joints are exposed (along line A-A in Figure  10b ). For the single solder joint corner void, 75% corner void, 50% corner void, 25% corner void models, respectively, 1, 6.5, 9.5 and 11.5 joints along line A-A (Figure  10b ) are exposed to very high stresses. Solder joint# 1 is always surrounded with underfill in all cases (Figure  2 ).


Indeed, even if only the corner joint is not protected by a small corner void, the stresses in the solder are almost half that of the non-underfilled case (Solder joint #13 in Figure  11 ). For other partially underfilled cases, the stresses approach the stresses calculated for the non-underfilled CSP very quickly. As it can be seen from Figure  11 , the stresses beyond solder joint # 1 starts to approach the no-underfilled stress values as the amount of underfill missing is increased. Thus, even if a single corner solder joint is surrounded by a void, the stress level in the CSP approaches that of a non-underfilled CSP. In other words, there is no benefit in underfilling a CSP if even a single corner joint is missed. These results are similar to that obtained by Rzepka et al. for simulation of flip chips subjected to thermal excursions  [7] . concentrations can be seen at the two diagonally opposite corners of the solder joint. For all cases except the 100% underfill case, the stress pattern looks identical to that on the case with no-underfill.

Drop Test Reliability of 289 Ball Csp


The use of OSP with Aramid/FR-4 board eliminated the problem of strength reduction due to blackpad but did not improve the shear strength of C1 in S2 although the spread in the data decreased (Figure  5 ). This can be attributed to the weak peel strength of Cu pad and Aramid build-up layer becoming prominent in controlling failure. However, when RCC-FR4 was used as build-up layer along with OSP, the strength of C1 increased significantly (40%) as shown in the case of C1/S3 (OSP and RCC/FR4). The 30% increase in strength from S1 to S2 is surprisingly high considering that there was no improvement in the mean strength for the same pad finish change for C1 CSP. However, the significantly higher improvement between S1 and S3 is comparable to that observed for the C1 CSP. ## FRACTURE LOCATION ANALYSIS


The fracture location data for C1 are plotted in Figure  9a . S1 (ENIG/Aramid) has 30% higher incidence of failures at the pad-solder interface compared to those of S2 and S3 (OSP). This is due to the presence of blackpad observed in the ENIG samples. Replacing ENIG with OSP, one finds a significantly reduced incidence of failure at the pad/solder interface in S2 and S3 due to the strong bonding between solder and pad.


That the relative proportion of failures under the pad in the case of S2 is comparable that observed in S3 is surprising. After all, since RCC-FR4 was known to have higher peel strength than Aramid-FR4, one would expect a lower incidence of failures under the pad in S3 as compared to S2. This apparent contradiction can be explained in terms of the ranking of failure mechanisms. Although the peel strength of the build-up layer is improved in RCC, it still ranks higher than the solder strength or solder-pad interfacial strength in terms of the preferred failure location, and therefore, there is no appreciable difference in the fracture location data between S2 and S3 samples. A more accurate picture of the solder joint strength is obtained only when the fracture location data is examined along with the strength data, where the effect of the higher peel strength of the S3 is evident in addition to the effect of pad surface finish.


The relative distribution of fracture locations in C2 is shown in Figure  9b . The fraction of fractures at the solder/pad interface decreased when OSP was used (S2) as pad surface finish, which is understandably due to the improved adhesion between solder and the pad. It is interesting to note that, for C2/S3 samples, virtually all the failures occurred in the solder, unlike in C1/S3 samples that had approximately 50% of the failures under the pad. Indeed, the number of solder failures is higher for C2 than for C1 samples for the other two sample sets (S1 and S2) although the difference is smaller. Further, results of dye penetrant testing performed on some of the C2/S1 samples in conjunction with shear testing indicate that percentage of cracked pads are lower in C2/S1 than in C1/S1. A representative image from C1/S1 samples is shown in Figure  10 . Thus, irrespective of the solder/pad bond strength and the board peel strength, C2 CSP is characterized by a greater predisposition for solder cracks than in C1, which points to the possible influence of package construction related issues. The fractography of the same phenomenon is described in the next section.


## Fractography


A closer look at some of the solder balls in the row closest to the shear ram revealed that the ram is close to the PWB (Figure  11 ). This validates the precautions taken during the test to ensure that the shear ram was closer than 50 µm to the PWB. Low magnification fractographs are shown in Figure  12a  and b , respectively, for C1/S3 and C2/S3 to illustrate the differences in failure mechanism between C1 and C2. In C1, which has an unreinforced polyimide interposer, the damage appears to occur both at the component side and at the board side during the shear test. This is reflected in the partially lifted pads in spite of final fractures at the top of the solder ball in the vicinity of the component pad. In C2, however, which has a fiberglass reinforced BT interposer, the fractures occurred in bulk solder in the vicinity of the interposer solder mask away from the PWB and the component pad. Concomitant damage under the pad at the PWB side of the solder ball was much less prevalent in C2 shear tests. At a global level, however, solder balls in both C1 and C2 show evidence of the shearing forces that caused fracture.


The local stress field immediately preceding fracture can sometimes be deduced by examining the fracture surface morphology. The morphology of the fracture surfaces of a solder ball in a C1/S3 sample is shown in Figure  13a    Equiaxed dimples characteristic of ductile fracture in a tensile stress field and an elongated intermetallic compound particle with very little solder adhering to it can be seen in Figure  13a . It appears that ductile failure started at cracked or debonded intermetallic inclusions, progressed by void growth and ended by microvoid coalescence immediately prior to fracture. Examination of the mating component side reveals a surface predominantly composed of intermetallics with very little adhering solder. Therefore, it appears the fracture occurred in the solder along the interface between solder and intermetallic layer.


The presence of equiaxed dimples on both fracture surfaces (Figure  13 ) coupled with the evidence of shear forces exerted on the solder balls and the partial lifting of the pads on the PWB (Figure  12a ) indicates that although failure started under a global shear stress field, it culminated in ductile failure in the solder by microvoid coalescence under a locally tensile stress field. It is hypothesized that the global shear stress field was transformed into a tensile stress field at the microscopic level due to solder ball rotation evident in Figure  12a . Thus, partial pad lifting at lower load levels in the test could have transformed the applied shear stress into a stress field that is essentially tensile at the interface between the solder and component side intermetallic compound layer.


In contrast, the fracture surfaces of C2/S3 appear to be dominated by ductile shear failure as evidenced by elongated dimples representing microvoid coalescence under shear stresses. Void nucleation probably occurred at the interfaces between the lead and tin phases in the microstructure. In a characteristic fashion, the dimples are elongated in the direction of the shear stresses and point in opposite directions on the two matching surfaces. Since fracture occurs in the vicinity of the solder mask where intermetallic inclusions are not abundant, microvoids nucleate between the tin and lead phases in the microstructure due to relatively severe strain incompatibilities. Subsequently, failure occurs by coalescence of these microvoids under a shear stress field giving rise to the features observed in the fracture surfaces in Figure  14 . Since little partial or complete pad peeling failures occurred (Figure  12b ), the microscopic stress field at the failure plane remains predominantly shear in character, giving rise to the elongated dimples on the fracture surface. It is hypothesized that the glass fiber reinforced BT substrate, shown in Figure  2 , lends additional stiffness to C2 as compared to the polyimide layer in C1. This higher stiffness of the component results in more highly localized stresses in the solder resulting in a higher incidence of solder fractures. A rigorous approach that includes the effect of package construction details such as finite element analysis would be necessary to verify this hypothesis. The fracture locations and fracture mechanisms are dictated not only by the global shear stress field but also by the local stress fields. Therefore, results from the component shear test method can be sensitive to relatively subtle package construction details such as interposer stiffness.


## CONCLUSIONS


CONCLUSIONS


A new measure of characterizing system level interconnection reliability, the Package to Board


Increasing leakage currents in MOSFETs is, possibly, the most important effect that hinders device scaling. This effect stems from two sources. First, as threshold voltages lower, the OFF-state current in MOSFET increases. For high performance devices, the OFFstate current is in the range of ∼10 pA/µm for 0.25 µm, 2.5V technology as compared with ∼1-100 nA/µm for 0.09 µm, 1.2V one 1 . Second, as gate dielectrics get thinner, the tunneling current through the insulator increases as well.


Combined, these currents increase the standby power dissipation and deteriorate circuit operating margins. Numerous techniques are being developed to circumvent detrimental consequences of the leakage current, including multiple V t CMOS 2 , reverse body biasing 3 , and circuit optimizations. 4   In the IC test area, increasing leakage current is traditionally considered as bad news. One of the most common arguments: it impacts the utility of I ddq and other current based test methods 5 . As it happens, there is another point of view...


The increasing leakage currents significantly improve the usefulness of Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM), and, specifically, its time-resolved variant -Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) 6,7


## Transient Logic State Detection


Transient Logic State Detection


The first technique allows one to observe in optical domain the sequence of logic states of a CMOS circuit during its operation. Figure  1  illustrates the idea for the case of a simple CMOS inverter. When the input V in is low, nFET N1 is OFF, pFET P1 is ON, and V dd drops across N1. The OFF-state leakage current through N1 causes the light emission L N . The light from P1, L P , is absent since there is not any significant voltage drop across this device. When the input V in changes to high, N1 closes and discharges output node. It spends a fraction of the fall time in saturation and produces, during this time, a narrow peak on L N , which is a traditional object of interest for PICA. After the inverter completes the transition, the situation is reversed. P1 is OFF, and drops most of V dd . The leakage light from P1 (L P ) becomes noticeable, while L N disappears. An important difference between the two states is that L P  < <  L N . The technique can easily be generalized for an arbitrary CMOS gate. Moreover, for stacks of FETs it potentially can pinpoint all devices in OFF-state, and, consequently, the state of inputs to the circuit.


We illustrate it using an example of PICA analysis of the basic compression tree of 54 bit IEEE multiplier of 64 bit POWER4 GHz microprocessor 10 . The microprocessor was implemented using 0.18 µm CMOS SOI dual-V t technology with seven layers of Cu metallization. Time-resolved optical emission measurements were performed from the backside of a flip-chip mounted microprocessor thinned to 50 µm.


The acquisition time was 60 hours at power supply voltage V dd =1.6 V; the operating frequency was set to 100 MHz -the maximum frequency the chip could run at without a heat sink. The microprocessor was executing a 10 clock cycles long loop of floating point multiply instructions out of on-chip L1 cache. The loop has 6 cycles of valid data (arranged as a checkerboard) and 4 pipeline bubbles (empty slots in pipeline occurring when the processor can not schedule an instruction to fit in that slot). The practical goal of our analysis was to measure the signal propagation delay between two nMOSFETs (boxes SRC and DEST). Figure  3  shows timeresolved light emission (or, simply, optical waveforms) from these transistors and the local clock buffer. The presence of unrelated numerous peaks (transitions from different signal paths; coupling from neighbor devices) and relatively high noise background make the interpretation of optical waveforms SRC, DEST difficult. The leakage light (dashed circles) is handy in solving this problem. The knowledge of circuit logical states helped us to match the optical waveforms with the test pattern and distinguish valid clock cycles from pipeline bubbles. This, in turn, allowed easy identification of peaks for our standard timing analysis   An immediate use of the technique, as we have shown, is to simplify the interpretation of PICA datathe knowledge of circuit logic states makes the identification of transition peaks straightforward. The technique can also be used to debug circuits with limited electric test capabilities such as non-scanable designs or memory structures.


It is important to notice that if the circuit under test allows stopping the clock at an arbitrary cycle, then the technique does not require time-resolved photon counting capability and can be performed on simple CCD camera based PEM tools.


## Power Supply Noise Analysis


The previously introduced technique relies only on the presence or absence of L OFF . More elaborate techniques are possible that measure the details of the transient behavior of L OFF . They are based on the fact that I DOFF (and, consequently, L OFF ) strongly depends on such parameters as V GS , V DS , device temperature, etc. 12 Assuming that the relationship between L OFF and these parameters is known (either theoretically or experimentally) valuable quantitative information about the internal IC operation can be extracted from the time-resolved measurements of L OFF .


One practically important application for such an approach is the analysis of microprocessor power distribution network voltage drops caused by circuit switching activity. In this case we use the dependence of L OFF on V DS , which for I DOFF in short channel MOSFETs is known as drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL). For a CMOS inverter with its nFET in OFF state, V DS ≈V dd , and the time dependence of V dd can be extracted from L OFF .


We illustrate this technique using the same hardware as in the previous section. This time the microprocessor is operated in such a mode that only one phase of the clock (C2) is running. As a result, the LSSD latches do not change their state and there are no switching transistors except those in the clock distribution tree. The clock frequency F=50 MHz is set close to the power grid resonance frequency in order to increase the amplitude of V dd variations, and, consequently, make it easier to measure. Figure  4  shows time-integrated PICA image of the same area as on Fig.  2 , corresponding to 50 hours of data acquisition.


Figure  4 : Time-integrated emission from OFF-state leakage current.


The only switching devices within the field of view are located the box "CLOCK BUFFER". Figure  5  compares time-resolved leakage light from low-V t devices L OFF (box "LOW V T DEVICES" on Fig.  4 ) with that from the clock buffer (L CLK ). The later signal integrates the light emission from all inverters in the buffer so that the large peaks correspond to the falling edges of the C2 clock, the smaller ones -to the rising edges. There is a clear correlation between L OFF and L CLK -the minima of L OFF correspond to the clock edges. It can be easily explained by taking into account that current drawn by switching clock buffers causes V dd (and, consequently L OFF ) to decrease. Presented results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed technique. Low signal-to-noise ratio of L OFF and insufficient knowledge of relationship between L OFF and V DS make it difficult to obtain quantitative results at present time.


An immediate use of the proposed technique is the debug of power noise related problems (e.g. clock skew caused by V dd variations), and the experimental verification of computational models used for power supply noise estimations 13 .


The dependence of L OFF on parameters other then V DS makes possible a number of similar techniques. For example, the dependence of L OFF on V GS would, in principal, allow optical characterization of VLSI signal integrity. Similarly, the dependence of L OFF on device temperature opens a possibility to optically measure this important parameter. The most straightforward implementation of this technique is the comparison of L OFF when the clock is running with that when the clock is stopped.


The amount of light emitted by OFF-state leakage currents in advanced CMOS technologies becomes comparable to that coming from switching MOSFETs. The analysis of this light provides valuable insights into the operation of CMOS circuits.


In this paper we suggested the use of leakage light to detect transient logic states of CMOS circuits and experimentally demonstrated this technique for 0.18 µm technology generation. Next we suggested to exploit the dependence of leakage light on V DS to measure power supply noise and experimentally demonstrated the feasibility of this approach. Finally we proposed the use of leakage light to optically measure signal integrity and device temperature distribution on a chip.


Scanning SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device) microscopy has been well documented for two-dimensional current density imaging in microelectronic devices  [1] -  [3] . A number of publications describe its specific use for IC packaging failures  [4] -  [8] . Of added interest is the utility of SSM for isolation of short circuit defects within the silicon die itself. Publications having specific mention of die level SSM are limited in detail  [9] -  [11] .


Two attributes of SSM make it attractive for die level imaging of current density. The first is the nature of magnetic flux to pass through non-ferrous materials undisturbed (notwithstanding the decrease in field strength with distance), enabling non-destructive measurement at die surfaces with minimal sample preparation. Intervening package materials, interconnect wiring, or silicon substrates that may obstruct signals with other PFI methods are not an impediment.


The second is the wide dynamic range and low-end sensitivity of the SQUID. This allows imaging in situations where other techniques may be limitedspecifically large area defects with very low resistance. Here low power density and large heat diffusion may obviate thermal analysis. Such samples are also difficult to bias at energies sufficient to effect photon emission.


The results of four separate analyses follow. All SSM data were taken using a high-temperature superconductor (HTS) scanning SQUID microscope with a Z-oriented (i.e., planar to the sample surface) SQUID operating at 70-73K. SQUID-to-sample separation was in the range of just under 100 to about 600 microns. Devices were stimulated using a sinusoidal AC voltage at 9.5 kHz, with a DC offset of one-half of the peak-topeak voltage to maintain a positive bias. The frequency was chosen arbitrarily to be in the approximate center of the SQUID electronics bandwidth. Bias was applied in two-point mode from V DD to ground with all other pins floating. The peak voltage was selected to provide enough current for a reasonable signal-to-noise ratio without exceeding specified operating voltage limits.


A lock-in amplifier synchronized with the stimulus frequency was used to minimize the influence of background flux caused by ferrous materials and other DC fields, and asynchronous currents. Typical scan times were 45 minutes, not including setup and data analysis. Raw magnetic flux gradients were automatically transformed to current density using a fast-Fourier transform (FFT) inversion  [12] . Data were further postprocessed using commercial image analysis software to highlight gradients with false-color mapping, to overlay current density with optical and CAD layout images, and to produce threedimensional surface plots.

A B F D C E V DD GND


Optical examination of the frontside of the chip, after removal from the substrate, identified a defect located at the center of the four-lobed peak highlighted by SSM, and also between the two lobes of the STM signal therein, as seen in Figure  10  (after the images were aligned and scaled using CAD data having features common to all three). ## Microprocessor Yield Failure


Microprocessor Yield Failure


A power supply short in a 16 x 19 mm, seven level metal, 0.14 micron L-drawn SOI microprocessor was analyzed with SSM from the frontside of the die (frontside liquid crystal had failed to localize a site). The purpose was to examine the spatial resolution attainable from the front side of a device, whereby the SQUID-to-current path distance could be reduced significantly versus scanning from the backside. Power and ground were supplied by two orbital microprobes with a bias of 50 mVAC pp at 1.3 mA (P avg = 31.8 W).


Figure  12  shows the current density and optical overlay with a suspect short circuit location highlighted. Although no defect was found at the site, the surface plot in Figure  13  shows the greater detail gained by frontside (vs. backside) SSM, where scanning distance can be reduced to under 100-microns. Current in the vertical top-metal power busses feeding the defect is clearly visible in both images. More importantly, horizontal paths are also seen, indicating current in a lower interconnect level. Two distinct signatures are also evident in the data. The single strong peak and surrounding 'fingers' in Fig.  6 , for example, are consistent with current converging to and diverging from a point between two conductors. The size scale and orientation of the signature is also in agreement with the circuit layout shown in Fig,  6a . A second signature, the four-lobed signal in Fig.'s 7, 9, and 10, is also consistent qualitatively and dimensionally with current converging and diverging on orthogonal paths. The polarity of the magnetic flux in Fig,  9  was used to determine the direction of current. The flux concentration in this case is caused by the superposition of the gradients associated with the four current segments. Contributing to the fourlobed nature of the signature is the physically vertical component of the path seen in Fig,  11 . A magnetically 'silent' area exists directly over such vertical segments because their corresponding magnetic flux is parallel to the horizontal SQUID, and therefore not detected by it.


The ultimate precision and accuracy with which current density can be localized by SSM is determined primarily by SQUID spatial resolution, and to a lesser extent by optical image resolution, and overlay accuracy. SQUID spatial resolution is in turn dependent on separation distance, step size, current, and magnetic field noise  [13] . Fig,  4b , for example, shows how a peak can be thresholded to one pixel of 20 x 25 microns, limited in this case by the step size chosen. This dimension is also in the range of the limiting SQUID resolution, governed by its size of approximately 30 microns square. As SQUID-to-sample scanning distance is such a strong determinant of resolution, scanning devices from the frontside surface, where possible, is superior as demonstrated by the increased detail shown in Fig,  13 , where scanning distance was less than 100 microns.


In comparison with alternative fault isolation techniques, the data show that SSM is qualitatively in good agreement with LC, PEM, STM, and TIVA. While SSM currently suffers in relative spatial resolution it does possess three major advantages. The first is its high sensitivity to current-induced magnetic flux, independent of voltage bias. This enables imaging particularly of very low resistance short circuits often manifested as large area defects. Such failures cause little Joule-heating, may be difficult to heat sufficiently with a laser (e.g., for TIVA), and are difficult to bias at levels sufficient to produce photon emission.


Secondly, the SSM's wide dynamic range allows simultaneous imaging at both relatively low and high current densities. In some cases this rich dataset is an advantage over the more typical highly localized signals often produced by other PFI methods. Finally, the ability to measure magnetic flux through the non-ferrous materials commonly used in ICs, especially in packaging,  broadens the applicability of SSM considerably and enables truly non-destructive analysis.

## Trigger Algorithms and Defect Identification


Trigger Algorithms and Defect Identification


## Method I. Stuck at Fault Vector


Method I. Stuck at Fault Vector


This method uses a function generator as a system clock with 1 MHz input to do the dynamic testing, stopping at the failed address reported from auto test equipment. The leakage current of the core power is monitored to see if it goes up. If not, the input state is changed until leakage occurs so that emissions can be detected. This algorithm is effective on closed loop circuits like those represented in Fig.  1  which shows a high-R defect connected not only to a CMOS gate (Cg) but also to an active region contact just like a latch cell in case 1. Or another possibility in case 2 in Fig.  1  which shows a high R bridge to adjacent bus line from another inverter output. Once the CMOS of the failing address was stuck at "0", the loaded devices will be charged up in a transient time. That should have no DC current flowing after circuit reaches to steady state. However, due to the voltage drop on high-R defect, the latch cell in case 1 cannot be latched so that a small DC current appears from VDD, PMOS, high-R defect then goes into the active region contact of the latch cell. A solid emission from high-R interconnect of a single via was detected, as shown in figure  2 , associated with emissions from Cg1 and the latch cell. Emissions from Cg1 and the latch cell were known as the floating gates leakage due to the high-R voltage drop. TEM analysis for the problematic single via profile revealed oxide rich layer and roughing via top surface as shown in Fig.  3 . In case 2, two CMOS output bus lines were shorted by a bridge defect.


Once both CMOS devices of the failing address were stuck at different state, "0" and "1" respectively, and then the monitored core Idd goes up, a DC current flows through the bridge defect. A solid emission can be detected right at the high-R bridge at metal spacing.


The subsequent deprocess and SEM inspection revealed metal TiN (AES analysis) residue bridging to adjacent bus line which was connected to another inverter's output, shown in Fig.  4 .


## Method II. AC Cycling of the Failing Address


Method II. AC Cycling of the Failing Address


In this method dynamic testing of the failing address is done in the same manner as in method I, then AC cycling the input state of the CMOS as shown in Figs.  5  and 6 . The loaded device that represented by capacitor Cg will be charged from Vdd and Qp as input goes "0", then discharges to Qn and Vss as input goes "1". This method is effective for most CMOS circuits, even if the defect is located in an open loop, for example connected only to CMOS gates (loaded by capacitors only). The charging and discharging current gives rise to dynamic power dissipation in Qn, Qp and the high-R defect. This method was successfully used to detect emissions at a high-R via reported to be a high frequency function failure. TEM of the via showed that slurry residue caused by tungsten CMP over polishing of an isolated via-3 was the cause of the failure (Figs.  7  and 8 ). In order to get more efficient emission acquisition, the dynamic frequency should be well selected to let more dynamic power dissipation on the defect. In this case a frequency that is higher than its maximum workable frequency was applied and showed the result of faster getting solid emission at high-R defect than lower frequency.


## Method III. Stuck at fault followed with AC power


Method III. Stuck at fault followed with AC power


Again, here the same dynamic testing approach as method II is used. Keeping "0" at the input state of the CMOS as shown in Fig.  9 . The loaded device modeled by capacitor Cg will be charged to VDD, and then dynamic varying VDD from about 10~20 % higher and lower VDD like Fig.  10 . The variation range can be extended as maximum as the product's VDD operation range for more dynamic power dissipation. Dynamic Varying VDD will cause Cg to be repeatedly charged or discharged. Meanwhile, the high-R defect would be "heated". Two different high-R failures of metal voids (Fig.  11 ) and high-R via (Fig.  12 ) had been accurately detected emissions by this method. This method is easy to be applied because it just is only necessary to vary VDD after stopping at the failing address. FIB circuit repair and E-beam probing were used to confirm the consistency of the isolated high-R defect site shown in Fig.  13 .   Figure  13 . FIB circuit repaired and e-beam for internal circuit probing was applied to confirm the frequency dependent failures. From the waveform detected by e-beam, Via-4 was isolated to be the high-R defect site. A consistent localization with method III.


## Comparison of Traditional and Presented Methods


Comparison of Traditional and Presented Methods


In traditional method of DC bias like standby or Iddq usually cannot toggle the failing device in core circuit. There should be no current flows along problematic path so that no emission could be detected. Another method of randomly dynamic running all devices cannot provide higher toggle rate to get sufficient emissions for CCD detection. Moreover, it would always lead to many noisy emissions to disturb the image inspection. The presented trigger algorithms provide the methods to toggle the failing devices making it possible of emission from interconnects. A brief comparison among traditional method and presented three methods is shown below.


Device modifications using a focused ion beam (FIB) tool now approach the inevitable barriers of high aspect ratios and very dense multi-layered metal circuitry. These barriers, along with flip-chip packaging, no longer make it feasible to successfully perform modifications from the front, or circuit-side of a device. Back-side FIB is the only recourse that allows direct access to today's circuit and packaging technology and can achieve results quickly and consistently  [1] .


With the scaling of transistor technologies, it becomes increasingly important to develop processes by which modifications can be performed below metal-1. For this reason, keeping the contact size to a minimum is a high priority. As a result, electrical contacts have been successfully created through the backside of a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) device to silicon active regions and polysilicon gate in an attempt to successfully modify a test circuit. The entire procedure is discussed, including sections on sample preparation, the actual FIB modification procedure used, and the test procedure of the modified devices.


## Background


Background


SOI devices consist of transistors built above a layer of silicon dioxide that insulates the active silicon from the bulk silicon. In order to access the circuitry from the backside of the die, there are several sample preparation options available. The approach taken, for this experiment, is referred to as the globally thinned method. It involves removing all of the bulk silicon from the backside. First, the die is mechanically thinned to remove the majority of the silicon.


A subsequent chemical etch, Tetramethylammonium Hydroxide (TMAH), is used to remove the remaining silicon because of its high silicon selectivity to oxide.


A Micrion 9800 Flip-Chip FIB tool was used for the device modification. To prevent charging effects, a electron flood gun was used to neutralize the charge on the buried oxide (BOX) layer from the ion beam. The device modifications were done using appropriate mill recipes and all contacts were backfilled with FIB-deposited tungsten.


## Characterization of FIB contacts


Characterization of FIB contacts


Successful circuit modifications require characterization of FIB contacts to n-active, p-active and polysilicon regions. Various size contacts to active silicon have been designed to evaluate the contact resistance (R con .) Contact resistance for contact sizes ranging from 0.25µm to 0.75µm were explored.


Identical contacts, as shown in Figures  1a  and 1b , were made in large blocks of n-active, p-active and polysilicon which were pinned out to external package pins. The contacts were then milled into the active region and filled with tungsten. A 5.0µm x 5.0µm tungsten probe pad was deposited above each contact for microprobing. A scanning electron microscope (SEM) micrograph of the structure is shown in Figure  2 . A test procedure was devised using an HP-4156 Parametric Analyzer to find an approximate value of contact resistance. Current was forced into contact 1 through the active region and out the external pin (see Figure  1a .) The voltage drop was measured and used to calculate R tot (the resistance of the contact, active area and pin.) Next, current was forced into contact 1, but the voltage drop was measured at contact 2 (see Figure  1b .) Since no current flowed through contact 2, the voltage drop was across the active region and pin. This method was used to calculate the active resistance, R act . Subsequently, R con was found by subtracting R act from the total resistance, R tot . However, R con is only an approximation and not a true contact resistance measurement because the resistance of the probe and the probe-tip pad interface are not taken into account. The measured contact resistances of contacts 0.25µm x 0.25µm or greater sizes had resistances less than 50Ω (see Table  1 .) Furthermore, it was also found that contact depth into the active region had very little effect on R con . On occasion, a diode-like curve was observed instead of a standard resistive curve. This effect might be attributed to the fact that "semiconductor surfaces have a large number of defect states (from broken bonds, impurities, etc.)"  [2] . However, further study of this phenomenon is necessary and will not be discussed in this paper. Contact reliability and tungsten adhesion were also studied. Contacts were subjected to current densities in excess of 800µA/um 2 with no reliability issues. Subsequent cross-sections showed both acceptable fill and adhesion (see Figure  2 .) Figure  2 . Cross section of contact to active area for R con measurement.


## Edits Procedure


Edits Procedure


Having proven that acceptable ohmic contact can be achieved to active silicon regions and polysilicon, the same technique was implemented in the modification of a ring oscillator circuit. To demonstrate the device modification capabilities, two inverters were bypassed in a 53-stage ring oscillator circuit (Figure  3 .) The first step in the circuit edit was to contact the source/drain output of the first inverter and the poly gate input of the fourth inverter in the 53-stage ring oscillator chain. Tungsten was deposited to fill the contacts and obtain a contact to the region of interest. After making contact, a deposited tungsten trace connected the two points. The second and third inverters were completely removed by milling away the active areas. Finally, the active areas were covered with a FIB-deposited oxide to protect the remaining circuit from damage. Top-view photos of the modification at various stages are shown in Figures  4(a


## Test Procedure


Test Procedure


The ring oscillator frequency was measured to test the success of the circuit modification. In addition to a baseline measurement, oscillator frequency was measured at various stages of the device modification process: post sample preparation and post circuit modification. The supply voltage V dd was varied from 1.4 to 1.6 Volts in 0.1V increments. All waveform measurements were done with an Agilent Infiniium 1GHz 4 GSa/s Oscilloscope.


Measured oscillator frequency remained close throughout the modification steps. There was a slight increase in measured oscillator frequency after backside Si removal and a slight decrease after device modification.


A detailed investigation into the cause of the increase in measured oscillator frequency after backside Si removal is beyond the scope of this paper. The observed frequency increase could be caused by a number of factors including possibly the slight decrease in parasitic capacitances caused by the removal of the silicon. The measured oscillator frequency decreased between 1.2 -2.5 % as shown in Figure  7  following device modification. The decrease may be understood by weighing the effects of the reduction of the number of stages (i.e. from 53 to 51) which is expected to decrease the oscillator period T osc , and the effects of the interconnect delay associated with the inclusion of the tungsten metal trace which is expected to increase T osc (see Appendix.) This result is somewhat counterintuitive to what one would expect, if one were to explain the results solely on the reduction of the number of stages. As a matter of fact, the oscillator frequency of a 51-stage ring oscillator with similar propagation delays would be expected to be 3.7% greater than a 53-stage ring oscillator. Another possible explanation for the measured oscillator frequency decrease could be due to shifts in transistor parametrics caused by charging effects or Ga implantation by the FIB beam  [4] . Although these effects are known to exist, they have not been examined in sufficient detail to apply the results to our study.


## Conclusion


Minimum sized contacts were created to active silicon regions and polysilicon with acceptable contact resistance. Similar contacts were then implemented in a successful device modification.


Based on the results of the experiments, we are confident that further modifications can be made on similar devices in the future with minimal performance degradation. (after) the FIB modification in terms of the individual gate delays before ( )
