The coaxial photon-ion beam column (Figure  1 ) was developed to address the problem of FIB editing circuitry that was invisible to the FIB due to overlying layers of silicon  [3] . The challenge of 'through-silicon' navigation is identical to that of navigation 'through' planarized passivationcharged particles reveal nothing about what is below the surface because there is no surface contrast information from the buried features  [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] . The optical beam provides information on what is buried under the silicon.


Optical imaging is optimized when an anti-reflective (AR) coating is applied to the silicon  [9] . Because an anti-reflective coating is always a dielectric, the coating can also serve to electrically isolate traces added during editing. A photon-ion column enables in-situ field-of view, with simultaneous optical and ion imaging, and providing the necessary feedback for accurate edit placement (Figure  2 ). In many cases visual alignment alone is sufficient, with the CAD information overlaid to the optical image providing added accuracy. The schematic drawing of Figure  1  depicts how the photon and ion beams are made coaxially coincident, enabling simultaneous and independent operation through software control. The mirrors, labeled M1 and M2, are spherical. Mirror M1 directs the incoming light to M2, which then focuses the light onto the IC. The electrode to the right of M1 in Figure  1  is glass, coated with indium-tin oxide providing both transparency for the photons and a ground plane as the final electrode of the ion objective Einzel lens.


## Coaxial Photon-Ion Column


Coaxial Photon-Ion Column


## Photon-Ion Beam Coincidence


Photon-Ion Beam Coincidence


The requirement for edit placement to be as accurate as possible is influenced by cumulative errors in CAD alignment, ion beam field distortion, and in the case of insitu optical-FIB imaging systems, opticalto-ion beam coincidence and magnification matching. Sub-20nm coincidence agreement between the coaxial photon-ion optics has been accomplished by employing a stepper alignment technique  [10] . This technique performs crosscorrelation between the optical and FIB images viewing an auto-generated FIB fiducial mark or reference feature. The calculated difference is used to apply a static ion beam deflection offset for a given beam current (Figure  3 ). This technique removes any "human eye" error in this alignment, which has been shown to introduce over 100% error of the targeted 100nm placement accuracy when performed manually.


## Figure 3: Based on a region of interest (ROI) in the optical image window, the cross-correlation algorithm calculates and applies the ion beam offset relative to the optical image providing sub-20nm x,y delta between points of coincidence.


Figure 3: Based on a region of interest (ROI) in the optical image window, the cross-correlation algorithm calculates and applies the ion beam offset relative to the optical image providing sub-20nm x,y delta between points of coincidence.


This same cross-correlation algorithm is applied to the optical image, front side or back side, to the CAD layout. With coaxial ion and photon beams now coincident to the CAD, edits can be placed with sub-100nm precision, removing the requirement of seeker holes. Through visual recognition of a circuit feature in the optical image aligned to the corresponding CAD data, the cross-correlation algorithm determines the offset between images and then applies this offset to the CAD display, placing the CAD image with sub-100nm precision (Figure  4 ) to the FIB image. The algorithm is able to perform the calculation and place the CAD data with sub-pixel resolution, even if the optical image is digitally magnified on a discrete feature to the point of loss of optical resolution. Once this calculation is applied, the edit placement precision is applicable to the entire optical field of view.


Verification of placement agreement can be seen in the cross section shown in Figure  5 . In this case a 150nm access hole was milled with the FIB from the backside after performing the OPTI-FIB® alignment first, then performing the Fine CAD Alignment. The measured placement was approximately 30nm from exact center.


## Back Side Applications


Back Side Applications


Flip chips are the obvious devices requiring throughsilicon editing. In addition, the increasing number of metal layers in current generations of wire-bonded devices makes some edits to lower metal layers impossible unless done through silicon, i.e., backside.


Because of this and the increased metalization levels as per the ITRS  [12] , the need for through-silicon editing will increase. The wavelength at which silicon is transparent lies in the infrared (IR) spectral range, at about 1µm (Figure  6 ).


(Note: wavelengths usable for throughpassivation imaging can be half of this.) With the advent of delicate low-k dielectrics,  [11]  the coincident-beam alignment of the coaxial column enables optical mode navigation across planarized passivation. This greatly reduces exposure of the device to 30keV gallium ions and minimizes charging effects. Optical mode navigation is also beneficial for sensitive SOI devices.


Dummy metal, which generally remains invisible in the FIB even when exposed, may prove useful to navigation as it is readily seen optically and can therefore be used for alignment when its CAD information is properly integrated into the CAD databases (Figure  7 ).


One challenge of through-silicon editing is the necessary reduction of silicon thickness in order to better access the edit sites. This can be done globally or locally. Partial global thinning of the die is almost always required to reduce the thickness to  < 100µm, followed by either global ultra-thinning  [13]  or localized removal ('Si trenching') to reach a remaining silicon thickness  < 5µm  [5] . The single advantage of global thinning to less than 10 microns, is the ability to access nodes through this thickness of silicon without requiring local trenching. Additionally, use of a variable wavelength light for an illumination source is necessary to optimize the resolution for the material through which circuitry is being viewed, e.g., passivation/dielectric or silicon. In the case of silicon, the thickness of the layer must also be considered when selecting an appropriate wavelength. A thinned silicon value of 5 microns or less is the most favorable for accurate edit placement, reducing the overall aspect ratio of the node access geometry. This can be accomplished through global thinning, but is more readily realized through local trenching.


## Local Silicon Thinning


Local Silicon Thinning


Local silicon thinning or trenching is where silicon is excavated with very fine control over the specific region where the modification is to occur. Trenching is often preferred and can be done within the FIB  [5] . Optical capability has already been shown to ease the process of FIB trenching  [14] . Furthermore, when the optical capability is real-time and simultaneous to ion beam milling, the remaining silicon thickness can be determined independently of metal or transistor density in the area being thinned  [15] , (Figure  8 ).


The separation and contrast between the fringes, correlate to the thickness of the remaining silicon, i.e., is a measurement of how much substrate silicon material exists before active regions become exposed. Theoretical and experimental data exist that can provide Look Up Table (LUT) capability which can enable endpoint automation. Having in-situ real-time optics allow the user to visually navigate using only IR imaging to the area of interest.


A square trench is typically defined between 100 and 400 microns per side. Having the CAD reference locked is not required at this point, but precision CAD navigation is used upon completion of the trench. A "global lock" when performed, is where the CAD is registered to the IR image on fiducial markers in the die corners, can be easily accomplished with the simultaneous optical imaging system, eliminating the requirement to excavate fiducial markers to be seen by the FIB.


To begin a trench, the physical x-y location on the die needs to be known. Once the specific location of the trench is identified, the milling operation can be performed. The AR coating is sputtered away exposing the silicon, and a surface-normalizing mill is performed to minimize most surface anomalies introduced from the mechanical thinning process. With the trench site optically in focus using 850nm wavelength illumination, the xenon di-fluoride gas is delivered to the region to be milled. The milling is typically performed using a 12nA beam. Optical endpoint is monitored and the milling is terminated when less than 5 microns of remaining silicon is obtained.


Once the local trench is completed, a dielectric deposition is needed on the floor of this trench. The deposited insulator isolates any future traces that might be needed for editing and also masks the etching of silicon during fine milling operation into the interconnect regions. If this insulator is an antireflective coating, then the optical resolution is also improved (Figures  9 10 11 ).


Once the trench is protected by this deposited dielectric, either through FIB or external deposition system, an edit to a specific node can then be performed. Copper interconnects have become the norm for baseline processes for leading-edge technologies. Gaining access to these interconnects through the backside requires some process modifications to the baseline process previously established for aluminum interconnects.


Gas chemistries presently used for milling with focused ion beam systems, are unchanged, with the exception of formulations suitable for etching copper with adequate selectivity over dielectrics at nominal beam densities.


Chemistries such as xenon difluoride (XeF 2 ) are typically used for enhanced milling of dielectrics on front side applications and bulk silicon removal. XeF 2 can also be used for backside applications, e.g., enhanced milling of dielectrics, once inside the inter-level dielectric (ILD) stack.


It is common practice to perform bulk silicon removal such that the mill floor is terminated within 2 to 4 microns of the active regions of the device. It should also be understood that the fluorine component of the XeF 2 chemistry would spontaneously etch silicon and silicon-containing films without the presence of the ion beam. Protecting any exposed silicon surface is a good practice, in particular, in backside applications. Unprotected surfaces that become etched by XeF 2 change the optical transmission properties of the silicon when viewed with near-IR. It is for this reason that mill floor should be passivated with FIBdeposited dielectric, with sufficient thickness to protect the surface, as well as provide an anti reflective coating for optical imaging.


Lateral undercutting of the silicon immediately beneath the protective passivation can also occur due to the nature of the XeF 2 chemistry.


IR imaging through the trench floor after the insulator deposition can be seen in Figure  11 . The circuitry layout matches the same pattern as seen during the optical endpoint, as seen in the fringe pattern of Figure  8 .


## Backside Edit Process


Backside Edit Process


Once the trench has been passivated, the CAD position of the area of interest can be verified optically. By overlaying the CAD data to the optical image, good edit placement can be confirmed. The FIB image will only provide imaging of the backside surface of the silicon. The advantage of having realtime optics during this alignment process is tremendous. Without this capability, placement accuracy would rely exclusively on stage precision aided by CAD, or local fiducials or seeker holes would have to be excavated. Prior to demarcation of the site for edit access, an OPTI-FIB Alignment is performed to be certain that the ion and optical beams are exactly coincident. Once the optical and FIB alignment is complete, and the CAD alignment is in agreement with the optical overlay, the Fine CAD Alignment can be performed. A recognizable feature in the optical image and its corresponding CAD image is used to perform this alignment (Figure  12 ) as previously discussed in the Photon-Ion Beam Coincidence section. This alignment technique provides sub-100nm edit placement accuracy through optical correlation. A mill box is created within the previously created trench, centered on the node to be exposed and is typically 1-2 microns is size. This will be the initial 'micro-trench' cut through the floor of the larger trench. This milling is assisted with iodine-based chemistry, which provides excellent definition in silicon and is performed at a typical beam current of 10pA. The mill is monitored both visually in the FIB display as well as the Secondary Electron End-Point monitor (Figure  13 ). Visual correlation of any change of material during milling is readily detectable. Viewing the end-point plot, the initial peak that occurs during the milling is the removal of the deposited trench floor insulator, which exposes the bulk silicon. Continuing with the milling, the slope of the trace is indicative of the beam burrowing through the silicon with the interface at the siliconto-ILD layer is easily observed as a discontinuity in the slope of the trace. The change in slope in the final mill trace is the contrast change observed in the ion image of ILD material. The milling is terminated when the trace begins to flatten, as the silicon is fully removed.


As observed in the cross sectional drawing of Figure  14 , once the ILD is exposed, a sidewall conformal FIB-deposited insulator is grown. The primary reason for depositing the insulator is to eliminate any electrical leakage through the bulk silicon. By fully encapsulating the silicon with FIB deposited insulator, the subsequent xenon di-fluoride chemistry will not undermine the mill site. With this insulator being conformal, the entire mill site does not need to be plugged and then re-opened, as typical FIB processes have required.


The next step of this edit process is to redefine the FIB box dimension to the final edit size. Final dimensions vary in size based on technology and clearance between diffusions in which to make contact. Access points below 100nm are achievable with this technique. In this case a 150nm mill box was defined in the center of the previously created, insulated, deposited site. A beam current of 2pA and XeF 2 gas chemistry is used to re-expose the ILD and then used to enhance the final material removal. The secondary electron graphical end-point display is monitored through this process. Stopping on metal can be readily accomplished (Figure  15 ). Upon exposing the node, FIB-deposited platinum makes an ohmic contact to the metal line and brings that contact up to the floor of the trench and may be routed to another edit site or is accessible for mechanical probing (Figure  16 ).


The FIB cross-sectional micrographs of Figure  17  show two edit sites contacting metal layer 2, 250nm and 150nm contact areas, accomplished using this technique through silicon. The sidewall insulator and the physically tapered platinum filled holes can be easily seen. The benefit of having excellent sensitivity and resolution in the endpoint detection methodology is that very low ion beam currents can be used successfully. The added value of this sensitivity is recognized, in particular, when performing backside edits to metal layers 2 and 3, where endpoints are accurately detected. The completed five-step process can be applied when exposing multiple nodes. In this case, each node could be completed one at a time or in parallel. The primary concern is to avoid the introduction of any FIB chemistry that may be harmful to any previously exposed feature in a different site located within the same trench. Iodine, chlorine, and bromine all cause corrosion on copper lines  [16] . Being certain that any exposed copper is passivated is important. Similarly, XeF 2 spontaneously attacks exposed silicon, so being certain that each node is fully protected during subsequent processes is important.


A novel technology employing an in-situ real-time, coaxial photon-ion column providing simultaneous imaging and functionality was discussed.


The applications for this technology, in particular for navigating solely using the optical image on front side and backside devices were discussed. The advantage of the coaxial system, in particular over non-simultaneous imaging systems, is the ability to virtually eliminate any ion implantation, surface damage and surface ablation normally observed when navigating with a FIB where the light optics are not available. With both the photon and ion beams being exactly coincident, typically within 20nm, firstorder navigation to a site is accomplished for most applications with the aid of wavelength specific filters. Furthermore, with the ability to recognize a metal node optically, the FIB beam can mill and expose that node without the CAD-assisted navigation as a requirement.


With present technologies being fully planarized, in-situ optical navigation is highly complementary to edit processes for front side devices, and enables the ability to view circuitry through the thinned bulk silicon using IR illumination for backside applications. Automated algorithms for beam coincidence and CAD-assisted edit placement were proven to be highly successful for edit yield.

In recent years, legislative pressures (particularly in Japan and Europe) have forced the electronics industry to consider methods of eliminating Pb from their end products and manufacturing processes, even though there are many benefits derived from the use of tin-lead (Sn/Pb) alloy finishes, such as excellent corrosion protection to many lead materials used in electronic components, enhanced solderability, highdegree of preclusion to tin whisker formation, good electrical conductivity, and non-susceptibility to "gray tin" conversion at low temperatures. The legislative regulations being developed are in response to potential environmental and health hazards that may result from the manufacturing and disposal of consumer products bearing Pb and other hazardous materials  [3] . In fact, it has been reported that Japan's computer makers will start charging fees from consumers for future recycling/disposal of these products.


The U.S. electronics industry's response to these initiatives is to consider alternative solders and coating systems in order to remain competitive in the world market. For many U.S. manufacturers, the simplest and most cost effective alternative to SnPbbased systems  [4]  is pure tin, because the conversion is easy and it is compatible with existing manufacturing and assembly methods. Many passive and active device manufacturers have for years now been supplying commercial (and in some cases high reliability) products with a standard pure tin finish, while others are just exploring the use of pure tin for the very first time.


## Concern Over Tin whiskers


Concern Over Tin whiskers


Despite the attraction of pure tin as a Pb-free alternative, there is one major concern to its acrossthe-board adoption and user acceptance: many pure tin coatings develop tin whiskers. This possibility, in combination with the lack of accepted methods for testing whisker growth susceptibility, gives rise to major reliability concerns. First is direct electrical shorting. Whiskers can grow between adjacent conductors of different potential and cause either a transient short, as the whisker is burned open, or a permanent short in low-voltage high impedance applications. Second, in high voltage circuits, when whiskers fuse open in low-pressure environments, a sustained plasma arc can be generated that carries tens, if not hundreds of amperes of current which can destroy or affect the performance of other components. Finally, whiskers can be broken loose from their substrate and, as debris, cause mechanical problems with slip rings, optical devices, microelectromechanical devices (MEMS) and similar components.


## Components that Have Grown Tin Whiskers


Components that Have Grown Tin Whiskers


Arnold offers an excellent overview of several component applications where whisker problems have occurred  [5] . Arnold's review, and more recent problem reports, show that whisker formation is not restricted to any particular family of electronic devices. Among the pure tin plated components that have exhibited extensive tin whisker formations are electromagnetic relays, IC leadframes, transistor and diode packages, hybrid microcircuit lids, connector shells, terminal lugs, metal washers, printed wiring board traces and plated through holes and very recently ceramic chip capacitors. The lack of established tests to demonstrate immunity to whisker formation creates even more of a concern for pure tin plated chip-style parts because of their very small physical dimensions. Figure  1  provides a few examples from the last few years that the present authors were made aware of.


Only a few papers directly discuss whisker growth in passive components, such as surface mount resistors and ceramic capacitors  [32, 30, 31, 44, 51] . To date these papers have generally proclaimed these device types to be relatively immune to whisker formation based on a number of apparent beneficial characteristics of their termination structure such as the use of a nickel barrier to minimize diffusion, tin grain size and shape factors and post-plating annealing practices].


In 1997, Endo (Murata) reported 18 years worth of whisker-free observation of multilayer ceramic chip capacitors (MLCC) stored at 50°C  [31] . However, the authors of this paper have recently observed moss-like whisker growths on MLCCs as long as 0.25 mm (see Figure  1 ) after thermal cycling. Such apparent contradictions are evidence that proclamations of whisker "immunity" are extremely difficult to validate given the vast array of user application conditions and the absence of industry-accepted test methods to judge whisker propensity. In addition, tin whiskers have been observed growing from "tin-rich" areas of the end metallization (90% tin) on military-grade polycarbonate capacitors  [50] . These whiskers caused electrical shorting on production lots from which spacers designed to help improve vibration capability were inadvertently left out in one case, and purposely eliminated for a wholly different reason in another.


## Ceramic


Ceramic


## 2. Transient short circuits


2. Transient short circuits


Under normal atmospheric conditions, if the available current exceeds the fusing current of the whisker (normally less than 30 mA, but perhaps as high as 75 mA  [35] ), the circuit may only experience a transient glitch as the whisker fuses open.


Schetty  [18]  and others have demonstrated experimentally that the use of substrate materials and/or underplatings that are diffusion resistant (such as nickel) can serve to significantly reduce whisker growth as described by the Lee model. However, other researchers still observed significant whisker formation on specimens thought to be diffusion and IMC formation resistant. For example, Dunn  [21]  observed 2 mm long whiskers growing on a matte tin plated steel (low diffusivity) electronics box, Lal  [36]  has shown that both matte and bright tin finishes over nickel (diffusion barrier) on phosphor bronze are prone to whisker formation, and the present authors have evidence of whiskers approaching 0.25 mm long on tin plated nickel-barrier layer ceramic chip capacitor terminations (see Figure  1 ).


Generally speaking, the whisker growth process may be characterized by 3 distinct stages: incubation (or nucleation), period of growth at a fairly constant rate, followed by transition to growth at a much-reduced rate (or apparent cessation of growth). Perhaps the most insidious trait of tin whiskers is the unpredictable nature of their growth initiation. Several researchers have reported incubation periods as short as a few days from the time of electroplating.


Others have observed incubation periods of many years in duration  [14, 19] . This attribute of whisker growth is particularly challenging because meaningful experiments to determine the propensity of a particular process to form whiskers may need to span very long periods of time, especially in the absence of proven industry-accepted test methods to accelerate the growth mechanism.


Once the initiation period has been completed and growth begins, average growth rates up to 0.8 mm/year have been reported for a bright tin finish on brass  [7] . Growth rate is highly variable and is likely to be determined by a complex relationship of factors including plating chemistry, plating thickness, substrate materials, grain size and structure, and environmental storage conditions  [14] .


In one extreme case  [42]  in the presence of high levels of external pressure, a 1mm long whisker was observed to grow within 16 minutes! Some have suggested that the whisker growth period may only last for a period of a few hundred days from the initiation of growth  [14] . However, such reports are difficult to confirm, as they require extremely long-term experiments and careful monitoring. The apparent failures of 3 commercial on-orbit satellites due to tin whisker shorting events  [25, 26] , at intervals between 6 to 8 years after launch, are suggestive that either the growth or initiation periods could have been much longer in duration than a single year. Some of the commonly reported attributes of tin whiskers are summarized in Table  4 .


## Table 4: Common Tin Whisker Attributes


Table 4: Common Tin Whisker Attributes


## Attribute Description


Attribute Description


Shapes  &  Surface Features (Figure  2 ):


• Many different shapes have been reported including very short irregularly shaped nodules or pyramidal eruptions (typically no more than a few tens of microns in size).


The more concerning longer needle-like structures may be straight or kinked with discrete bends along their length. Such whiskers often appear to emanate from nodules, although nodule formation is not a prerequisite for needle like growth.


## •


•


Some are reported to be hollow  [8] , though such claims are not generally accepted (see Figure  2 ).


Close inspection of their surfaces reveals that most whiskers are striated (grooved) along lines parallel to their longitudinal axis giving the appearance of having been "extruded" as if drawn through an irregularly shaped die. [7, 9]


## Growth Rate


Growth Rate


Growth rates ranging from 0.03 to 9 mm/year have been reported  [38]


## Whisker Length:


Whisker Length:


Whiskers a few millimeters long are the most commonly reported, with some experimenters observing whiskers as long as 10 mm (400 mils)  [1, 11, 12] . Ultimate lengths are dependent on many variables, including the amount of time allowed for growth to occur.


## Whisker Diameter:


Whisker Diameter:


Typical diameters range from 1 -4 •m with some reports as high as 10 •m and as low as 0.006 •m  [14] . In many instances the diameter of the whisker may be larger than the tin grain size as well as larger than the nominal thickness of the electroplate. [15]


## Density of Growths:


Density of Growths:


Whisker densities up to 10 4 /cm 2 have been observed  [15] . There are other cases that showed very sparse growth densities. The less dense growth specimens have sometimes been attributed to unique conditions of highly localized stress in the tin layer such as may result from corrosion of the substrate (i.e., steel)  [27] , or due to residual substrate stresses resulting from operations such as stamping, cutting or bending  [12] .


## Current Carrying Capacity:


Current Carrying Capacity:


• Current carrying capacities as high as 75 mA before fusing (melting) have been reported for whiskers of 4 •m diameter  [35] . Other experiments showed capacity up to 32 mA  [14]  under normal atmospheric conditions.


More astounding are the documented cases in vacuum applications where tin whisker shorts may cause the whisker to vaporize, forming a plasma of tin ions that may sustain currents of several HUNDREDS of AMPERES!  [43] . Such catastrophic events have been reported as the root cause of complete failure of at least 3 on-orbit commercial satellites  [25, 26] . Similar plasma arcing phenomenon has also been reported for zinc whisker shorts during vacuum testing. [28]


## Mechanical Strength:


Mechanical Strength:


Tin whiskers are reported to possess very high mechanical strength in the axial direction due to their near perfect crystalline structure. Experiments using mechanical shock and vibration spectra have shown whiskers to be highly resistant to detachment from such dynamic forces  [13] . However, other researchers have observed component failures resulting from detached whiskers that lodged in areas creating critical short circuits  [5, 29] . Shear strengths, especially in long whiskers, have been reported as low.


## Factors Affecting Whisker Formation


Factors Affecting Whisker Formation


The following paragraphs discuss factors reported to contribute to whisker initiation/growth propensity. Noted differing views are also cited.


Substrate Effects: Whisker growth has been observed on any number of different substrate materials commonly used in the electronics industry. Most agree that brass substrates are most prone to whisker formation (due to zinc and copper diffusion from the brass and copper/tin intermetallic formation). Copper and copper-based alloys (phosphor bronze, alloy 194) are considered to be the next most sensitive. Whisker formation has also been observed for substrates considered to have low diffusivity into tin such as steel  [21]  and alloy 42 (iron/nickel alloy)  [33] . Despite the diffusion barrier properties of nickel, whiskers have also been observed on passive components utilizing a nickel barrier layer construction such as those used in MLCCs and connectors (see Figure  2  and  [36] ). Others, however, have observed a general beneficial effect of nickel barriers with respect to retarding whisker growth  [18] .


Classic "needle-like" whisker Kinks and striations Pyramidal shaped whiskers Nodules (note how it appears to originate from a very fine surface scratch) Nodules originating along a mechanically induced surface scratch Whisker growing from a nodule Irregular shaped whisker tip Focused Ion Beam "cross section" of a tin whisker. Note the solid (not hollow) structure and striations.


Whisker nodules beneath conformal coat (growing preferentially along the line of a surface defect) Plating Thickness: Most researchers suspect there are threshold thicknesses for tin plating above and below which whisker formation may not be supported. Glazunova reported that thicknesses below 0.5 •m and above 20 •m were less prone to whisker formation while 2 •m -10 •m thicknesses showed maximum growth rates for tin on steel and tin on brass  [40] . Zhang and Schetty have suggested thicknesses over 8 •m tend to be in the "safer" region. [18, 22] . Unfortunately, very thin plating thicknesses may reduce the effectiveness of other characteristics of the plating such as corrosion resistance. Thicker platings are not as commonly used probably for cost reasons. It has been hypothesized that thicker coatings tend to distribute the stresses more evenly, especially those originating at the substrate/plating interface  [9] .


Grain Size and Shape: Kakeshita  [39]  reported that the grain size and shape play significant roles in whisker propensity. In particular they have proposed that "well polygonized" grains in the range of 1 •m to 3 •m (possibly as large as 8 •m) in size will greatly inhibit whisker formation. Grain sizes of only a few tenths of a micron were found to be much more prone to whisker formation. [39, 30] . Although there are no industry accepted definitions, tin finishes with smaller grains (~ 1 um and less) are commonly termed "bright" because they produce a very shiny, reflective surface, while those with larger grains (over 1 •m) are often termed "matte" because of their somewhat dull gray appearance.


Relatively speaking, "bright" finishes are considered to be more prone to whisker formation than "matte". However, it must be noted that many examples of whisker growths have been reported from finishes advertised as "matte".


Temperature: Most experimenters report that ambient temperatures of approximately 50°C  [22]  are optimal for whisker formation, while others observe that equivalent specimens maintained at room temperature (22°C to 25°C) have grown whiskers faster  [7] . Reportedly, whisker growth ceases at temperatures above 150°C  [37] . Some researchers have observed that whisker growth can still occur at temperatures as low as negative 40°C.


Barometric Pressure: Whiskers will grow in vacuum as well as under atmospheric conditions  [6] . Observations of whisker growth under vacuum conditions tend to rule out oxidation as a necessary condition for formation, although prior surface oxide formation may be a contributor.


Moisture: Some experimenters observe that whiskers form more readily in high humidity (85% -95% RH). Still others have seen no apparent effect of moisture  [37, 41] .


Thermal Cycling: Some experimenters report that thermal cycling may increase the growth rate of whiskers, but others report no apparent effect. Experiments have commonly utilized temperatures in the range of -40°C to +90°C  [41] . Results with ceramic capacitors reported in this paper do indicate that thermal cycling rapidly accelerates nucleation and/or early growth rates.


Externally Applied Mechanical Stresses: See Table  3  for discussion of this factor. In addition, some experiments have observed that surface defects in the substrate (minor scratches) that were present prior to plating appear to be preferential sites for whisker formation  [7]  (see also Figure  2 ). Electric Field: Whiskers grow spontaneously without requiring an applied electric field to encourage their growth. However, NASA-GSFC has demonstrated that whiskers can bend due to the forces of electrostatic attraction; thus, increasing the likelihood of tin whisker induced shorts  [7] .


## Lack of Whisker Test Methods


Lack of Whisker Test Methods


Unfortunately, there are no industry-accepted test methods to measure the propensity of a given product/process to form whiskers. Various industry consortia in both the U.S and Japan have initiated studies to define and then validate through experimental evidence, the exact mechanism(s) by which whiskers form.


Many of these same organizations are simultaneously working to devise accelerated test methods to determine the whisker formation propensity of a given product/process  [41] .


Ideally, any whisker test that is developed should enable a product manufacturer or user to determine (within a practical period of time) the inherent risk of whisker formation for a given specimen or process. In addition, development of such tests should include studies that correlate an "acceleration factor" of the test condition to some baseline application environment


## Control of Tin Plating Processes to Minimize Whisker Formation Potential


Control of Tin Plating Processes to Minimize Whisker Formation Potential


Plating baths. Responsible part manufacturers who supply discrete components with tin-coated terminations are aware of the potential for tin whisker formation, and are active in controlling their electroplating baths to minimize the possibility. A user should query the manufacturer about the controls in place and the baths being used. A "matte" tin bath, or one that produces a relatively dull [non-bright] finish is preferred, because it minimizes the use of additives that are mainly intended to improve leveling and brightness. A matte bath, in turn, can produce tin without excessive metallic or carbon contaminants; thus, minimizing internal plating stresses that can lead to whisker growth  [18] .


Plating baths require process controls to ensure that contamination buildup is minimized, and frequent chemical replacement (not simply replenishment) should be part of these controls. Other plating parameters should also be optimized and controlled in a manner that achieves minimum internal stresses; time, temperature, current density and gradients are critical process parameters. Generally speaking, electroplating process parameters that achieve the fastest tin deposition tend to be more prone to whisker formation.


Underplating/substrate. Tin should be applied only over a specific substrate, nickel being much preferred to copper or brass. The chemistry, thickness, surface finish, grain size, and surface cleanliness and internal stress of the substrate are all important. tin layer.


Similarly, the substrate nickel grain size may also affect the tin grain size. While part users may not be able to determine what is optimal, ensuring that the manufacturer controls the nickel plating process closely to produce a consistent electroplate is important.


Hot-tin dipped coating. Hot-tin dipped parts should also come from controlled production lines. While the very process of applying a molten layer minimizes internal stresses, coating application will not be uniform in thickness. Regardless, these parts are still prone to abrasion and contact during subsequent automatic feeding and processing which may reintroduce surface compressive stresses, likely the most dangerous type.


Fusing, annealing and handling. Ideally, tin-plated parts should be subjected to a fusing or reflow process to relieve existing stresses after the parts go through manufacturing and testing.. Annealing where the tin coating is held at temperatures below the melting point of tin for a short duration may also have beneficial effects because such practices tend to relieve inherent stress and encourage grain growth (intuitively expected but not observed in recent experiments with MLCCs. [48] ).


Part Handling. Part contact with probes, vacuum chuck pickup heads, tweezers, and anything but lowpressure bars should be minimized or eliminated.


## Part User Mitigation Guidelines


The following items are generally considered to minimize whisker formation. In applications where tin whisker formation cannot be tolerated, users may wish to consider employing as many of the following guidelines as practical for their application. However, even when two or more of the following guidelines are used in concert, their use has NOT been shown to completely prevent whisker formation.


Conformal coating. OEMs should consider the use of conformal coating wherever possible. Coating all electrically active surfaces is recommended. While a whisker may penetrate a layer of conformal coating over its originating surface  [7] **, a whisker is very unlikely to penetrate two layers of coating. The layer over the surface of a different potential will be reached only when a whisker is very long [and relatively flexible], so that it is likely to impact that second layer at an angle and slide to one side or buckle rather than penetrate it. To our knowledge, there are no documented cases of a whisker penetrating two separated layers of conformal coating.


** Conformal coating or foam encapsulation over the whisker prone surface appears to be beneficial but the limitations are not completely understood. NASA GSFC experiments  [7]  suggest that use of polyurethane conformal coat can provide some benefit by reducing the growth rate, but tin whiskers can grow through the coating, and once exposed can then short to other tin whiskers or other exposed surfaces, or break off and lodge in areas where they can cause short circuits. It has also been demonstrated experimentally that conformal coating can sufficiently restrict the availability of tin to prevent plasma formation (a particular concern for space applications)  [38] . However, such factors as the minimum thickness of coating necessary to prevent whisker growth or plasma formation have not been determined. Similarly, it has been shown that foam can prevent sustained arcing but the effects of foam type, foam density, pore size etc. have not been reported.


Physical Barriers. Interposition of non-conductive washers, ceramic spacers, staking compound materials, etc. as a physical barrier is a very simple and powerful method of preventing whisker shorting.


Solder Dipping. Users may consider hot solder dipping of tin plated leads (surfaces) using a SnPbbased solder. This process will help reduce whisker formation by relieving stress in the tin layer through both reflow and the addition of an alloying element (Pb). If the leads were fused before solder coating and then carefully conformal-coated after connections were made, possibilities of detrimental tin whisker growth would be greatly reduced.


The effectiveness of hot solder dipping is limited to those surfaces that can be safely subjected to a hot dipping process without introducing thermal damage. For this reason, solder dipping is frequently limited to areas no closer than 0.010 to 0.050 inch from the component body. Devices where the leads pass through glass-to-metal seals are particularly susceptible to cracking of the seal if the dipping process is not carefully controlled. In addition, the portion of the lead that is internal to the device will not be afforded the whisker-reducing benefits of the dipping process.


## Tin surface reflow.


Tin surface reflow.


Reflowing the tin surface coating as a last step or next-to-last step in an assembly process both removes the internal stresses and may largely redissolve the surface tin oxide; thus, reducing whisker initiation stresses.


The only stresses that would contribute to whisker growth would be those at the substrate interface, due to IMC growth, and those imposed with any subsequent probing, bending or scratching of the new tin surface.


Minimizing elevated temperature exposure. The major theory of tin whisker growth is that it is a means of relieving the compressive stress of the plated tin layer. A major source of that stress is the tin oxide that forms on top of the layer and the tin intermetallic compounds formed at the interface of the tin and its substrate.


Reducing elevated temperature exposures may serve to reduce, but not eliminate, such stresses.


## Performing burn-in in an inert environment.


Performing burn-in in an inert environment.


Minimizing the growth of surface tin oxide by performing burn-in in an inert atmosphere may help reduce the compressive stress on the tin.


## Minimizing thermal cycling. Recent experiments at


The Aerospace Corporation of USA manufactured commercial-grade ceramic capacitors  [49]  that have pure-tin plated terminations show many whiskers (some as long as 30 microns) forming after 554 thermal cycles of -40 o C to 90 o C (5-minute rise time, 5-minute-dwell, 20-minute cool down). A similar experiment was conducted on pure tin plated military-grade capacitors, which grew whiskers as early as after 100 cycles.


Additional cycling was done to determine the whisker growth rate. Periodic examination of four whiskers on four individual parts was done during the cycling process. This began at 100 cycles and continued up to 400 cycles. The additional cycling failed to show an obvious increase in length of the selected whiskers. However, an increase in the quantity of whiskers was observed.


In an attempt to determine if whiskers could appear even earlier than 100 cycles, further testing was done on commercial-grade ceramic capacitors. Whiskers began to appear at 40 cycles and continued to increase in abundance, though not in length, as the number of cycles increased. In these experiments, excess moisture in the thermal chamber was removed by dessicants. Note that all the capacitors tested have nickel underplating that is at least 5 microns thick over silver and under a slightly (10+ microns tin layer).


## Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Examination


Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Examination


Attempts were also made to determine if the root cause of whisker formation and growth were related to unresolved mechanical stresses in the vicinity of whiskers growing at grain boundaries. Several attempts were made to expose subsurface anomalies that would give rise to such mechanical stresses. Using Focused Ion Beam (FIB) cutting techniques, whisker sites were ion milled away to reveal the tin plating and other metallization layers underneath the whisker formation site. However, this technique proved problematic. First, FIB cuts took excessively long times to expose sufficient subsurface area. Second, such areas proved difficult to analyze due to: (a) problems with revealing and resolving grain boundaries in the FIB trench; (b) difficulties with trench geometry that did not readily allow elemental analysis for possible contaminants; and (c) poor resolution of existing spectroscopic equipment onsite resulting in data that lacked the spatial resolution and detail needed to make conclusive arguments about the origin of the mechanical stresses. Consequently, further investigative efforts along these lines were abandoned until more suitable equipment become available.


In summary, the whisker mitigation steps mentioned previously, even when used in concert with two or more of them, have not been shown to completely prevent whisker formation.


## Discussion


Discussion


It is dangerous to simply rely on the manufacturer's certification that pure tin plating was not used in the production of the part supplied. In several cases, including the FDA pacemaker recall and the aforementioned satellite failures, it was found that the procurement specifications required that no pure tin should be allowed as a plating finish. The authors are aware of many instances where pure tin was prohibited, yet the product supplied was later determined to be coated with pure tin. In some of these instances, tin whisker growths were discovered. Users are advised to analyze directly the plating composition of the products received as an independent verification.


The continuing reports of tin whisker induced failures (especially the commercial satellite failures) coupled with the lack of an industry-accepted understanding of tin whisker growth factors and/or test methods to identify whisker-prone products has made a blanket acceptance of pure tin plating a risky proposition for high reliability systems. This is particularly true in the military, aerospace, and telecommunication industries whose products frequently have reliability requirements extending over five years (sometimes over fifteen years). In these instances, especially if deployed in challenging environments of high moisture, high temperature, or near vacuum, the use of tin, as well as cadmium and zinc, as structural materials or surface finishes should be completely avoided.


There is a general class of concerns where a tin-rich area is formed in an alloyed tin matrix that on the average is free from the potential of tin whisker formation, where the tin-rich area is so enhanced in tin that it has the potential for local whisker formation. Local tin-rich areas can be formed through recrystallization and grain growth, selective oxidation, diffusion, and other mechanisms.


A majority of the so-called mitigation factors whose use manufacturers believe may free them from worry are simply rules-of-thumb that have been gathered.


Many have not been adequately verified in the literature or through practice. Other factors, such as use of two conformal coating barriers, one over the tin coatings and one over adjacent conductors, and conductor spacings greater than 0.5 inch, appear to have a documented, experimental basis for their validity, but these approaches may not be practical in all conditions. Specific application reviews are essential in each instance where tin coated hardware is found.


Although the authors of this paper are focusing on whiskers from tin electroplates, it must be noted that other metal electroplates may also be prone to whisker formation (most notably zinc and cadmium).


## Published Works On Tin Whiskers


Published Works On Tin Whiskers


The authors of this present work have encountered nearly 200 references available in the public domain that are related to whisker growth from tin and other common metal electroplates. The majority of these reports describe whisker growth from pure tin electroplates, including both "bright" and "matte" finishes.


A few reports describe whisker formation from some tin-lead alloys (i.e., 90/10)  [4, 10, 18] . Most of these other observations, however, seem to be confined to sparse populations of very small nodular growths that rarely exceed 10 •m or were observed under conditions of high levels of externally applied stress (i.e., compression from torque of nut/bolt). These reports are of major import because one factor believed to dramatically reduce tin whisker formation is to alloy the tin with three percent or more of a metallic element. The amount of alloying material necessary to prevent whisker growth from tin alloys depends upon both the specific alloying metal and the environmental stresses to which the coatings are subsequently exposed. If the compressive stress theory of initiation and growth are valid, then the alloying metals may absorb or reduce compressive stress within the plating. If external stresses are severe, such as a deep surface groove caused by an electrical probe, then whisker nucleation and growth could still occur in such alloyed coatings. Understanding the stress conditions under which whisker formation from such alloyed surfaces may occur should be of high priority.


Viewed collectively the available literature describes a wide range of observations and factors (often contradictory) that affect whisker formation. An extensive listing of whisker-related literature references is provided on the NASA Goddard Tin Whisker www site: http://nepp.nasa.gov/whisker Conclusions 1. Tin whisker formation and the associated risk for catastrophic electrical shorting continues to be a potential problem and must be seriously considered as the discrete component industry moves to greater use of pure tin and other Pbfree surface finishes.


2. Even when prohibited by system requirements, tin-coated finishes continue to appear in electrical equipment.


The authors have participated in several major review teams attempting to determine whether major OEMs have successfully eliminated tin-coated surfaces. In all cases, some instances of components or small mechanical items with pure tin-coated surfaces have been found.


Abstract


A method to detect defects affecting laser diode radiation has been devised by imaging the induced luminescence resulting from a scanning electron beam.


Electron Beam Induced Luminescence (EBIL) involves imaging the current from a sensor diode as the SEM electron beam scans across the laser diode surface. Defects preventing laser diode radiation will be shown as contrast variations in the EBIL image. This technique is similar to electron beam induced current (EBIC), reference 1, in which the electron beam provides the capability for measuring subsurface electrical and physical parameters that effect device electrical performance. However in the case of EBIL, laser diode radiation is utilized as the imaging parameter providing direct correlation between the semiconductor active layer and the resultant diode luminescence output.


Alternative techniques such as Cathode Luminescence (CL), reference 2 and 5, in the scanning electron microscope (SEM) have been used for examination of semiconductor laser diodes for defects preventing radiation. However CL SEM analysis requires costly accessories, including at least an ellipsoidal mirror and a cooled photomultiplier tube sensitive to the particular laser diode output frequency. In addition the laser diode must be at the focal point of an ellipsoidal mirror, making CL SEM examination of a packaged laser diode difficult or impossible.


Light-emitting devices provides a unique problem to the failure analyst in that the resulting output response to an electrical input is light in either the visible or non-visible spectra. Figure  1  illustrates a typical edge-emitting device where bias potential is applied between a top-level contact and the substrate, reference 3.


Common techniques of fault isolation performed by the application of electrical stimulus while monitoring the expected electrical output response are not suitable for locating non-visible defects that affect light output. Total light output or spectral data can be monitored however small or buried spot defects can not be located using such a process. A technique is needed so that the luminescent output can be monitored while selectively exciting portions of the PN junction to provide direct correlation of light output to the location of the excitation beam current.


Electron Beam Induced Current (EBIC) is an established technique to display the external current resulting from the electron hole pairs generated from the interaction of the electron beam with the PN junction, reference 4. This technique uses the electron beam induced current to modulate the z-axis beam intensity of a standard scanning electron microscope. Overlaying this image onto the standard secondary emission image provides direct imaging of the beam-induced current, refer to Figure  2 . Application of this technique in analyzing LED's failures would not provide data on the light output as it relates to location of the scanned beam. An alternative technique has been devised that utilizes a light sensitive diode to monitor the luminescence for modulation of the beam intensity z-axis as is done in the EBIC technique. With this technique the relation between the electron beam location and the resultant induced LED luminescent output can be displayed.


Electron Beam Induced Luminescence (EBIL) involves imaging the laser diode luminescence in the scanning electron microscope, so that damage areas in the diode junction are observed in the luminescent image. Instead of using CL to detect the laser diode luminescence, the current output from a sensor diode is used. If a sensor diode is in the laser diode package, it is used. If not, a photo detector diode can be placed opposite the end of the optical fiber coming out of the laser diode package.


The sensor diode current is connected to the current amplifier of the backscatter detector using the backscatter detector leads and feedthru. A multi-pin feed-thru for voltage contrast can also be used to get the current from the sensor diode to an external current amplifier. Thus the sensor diode current is amplified by the backscatter amplifier, and modulates the brightness of the SEM CRT. One would use the same backscatter leads, feed-thru, and amplifier as is used for EBIC.


The laser diode package lid is first removed. In order to obtain secondary electron images of the damage areas on the semiconductor diode surface, any solder and lead to the top of the laser diode as well as all of the top electrode layers are removed by appropriate etching procedures. Next the SEM accelerating voltage is increased until the electron beam reaches the diode junction and an EBIL image is obtained. Then dark spots in the EBIL image can be correlated with SEM images of damage to the diode top surface.


For optimum EBIL lateral spatial resolution, the lowest possible SEM voltage that allows the electron beam to reach the diode junction should be used. Monte Carlo simulations and EDS analysis in the SEM are also useful in deciding on the SEM accelerating voltage to use in EBIL examination.


EBIL analysis can also be carried out if only some of the top metalization layers are removed from the diode. However one will not obtain secondary electron images of damage sites on the semiconductor surface -one will only see the location of damaged areas. Also EBIL spatial resolution will be reduced because higher SEM accelerating voltages will be necessary.


EBIC can also be used to locate damage areas in the semiconductor diode. However at least one metalization layer must remain on the diode surface for electrical contact to both sides of the diode junction. Thus with EBIC, damaged areas on the diode surface cannot be observed and examined in secondary electron images. Also EBIC spatial resolution will not be as precise as EBIL spatial resolution due to the higher SEM accelerating voltage needed to reach the diode junction.


While CL can also be used to image laser diode luminescence, EBIL has several advantages over CL for locating defects in the laser diode, reference 3. First, the costly CL SEM accessory is eliminated by use of the simple EBIL experimental setup. Second, with CL, a photomultiplier with near infrared spectral response matching that of the type of laser diode is required. Thus EBIL avoids the necessity of having several costly photomultipliers for versatile failure analysis of different laser diode materials. Third, CL uses an ellipsoidal mirror for efficient light collection. The focal length of the mirror is very short, 1-2 mm, so a diode recessed in a package could not be brought close enough to the mirror without cutting off the sides of the package, a dangerous procedure. Moreover, for horizontally emitting laser diodes, vertical light collection by the CL ellipsoidal mirror is very inefficient vs. nearly complete light collection by the EBIL sensor diode.


If the investigation needs to establish that failure is caused by a particular type of defect in the laser diode junction region, then cathodoluminescence would be a valuable follow-on analysis technique after EBIL has located the failure areas in the laser diode. Examples of possible defects in the diode junction region are stacking faults and deep recombination centers.


## Experimental Method


The basic approach to EBIL is to scan the lightemitting device with an electron beam while monitoring the photoemission with an appropriate sensing diode. The variations in the external current generated from the interaction of the electron beam with the PN junction is used to alter the brightness (z-axis) of the raster scan image thus providing an emission map that would correlate to the light-emitting device. The device under test requires either an internal sense diode be available in the device package or be externally provided as part of the test setup. Spectral and power characteristics need to be considered to insure emission detection, however the device in this example contained a built in power monitoring diode.


Electrical measurement of the reverse bias saturation current of the sense diode for various luminescence power levels is shown in Figure  3  which illustrates a direct relationship between the light output and diode saturation current. In order to expose the active area of the light emitting diode scanned by the electron beam, wet chemical techniques were used to etch away top layer solder and metalizations to expose the surface of the die, refer to Figure  4 .


A standard EBIC setup was adapted such that the sense diode provided the modulation signal for the z-axis amplifier commonly available in most scanning electron microscopes, refer to Figure  5 . The scanning electron beam provides the energy for photon generation within the light-emitting device resulting in an electron beam induced luminescence of the LED. Depending on the efficiency of the LED, Photons will be emitting from the active channel and be received by the sense diode.


The EBIL technique is similar to standard electron beam induced current except that induced luminescence rather than junction current was used to enhance the image intensity.


Variations in the saturation current of a sense diode was used to monitor the light output of the LED. The sense diode current modulates the brightness of the SEM CRT showing the locations of low light emissions on the LED.


References:


1. "Practical Scanning Electron Microscopy," J.I.


The development of optically pumped modules for light amplification in photonic communications run by far faster than their qualification procedures. For passive elements, rules like Bellcore 1221 1 embrace several tests, but up to now disregard the role of the high optical power, piped along the optical paths, that may achieve such extreme levels as to became by itself a reliability concern. Raman amplifiers currently represent the very ultimate limit in that field, driving power levels exceeding one Watt into optical fibers, through such other passive elements as filters, couplers, connectors.


It is not surprising that the state-of-the-art of reliability lives its infant age in that new stress domain, and that the violation of those fundamental and not yet completely assessed hygienic rules, as cleanliness and proper handling, may be the cause of catastrophic early failures. The role of moisture and particles is known as sources of optical degradations and catastrophic failures, and the use of sealed packages and controlled internal environment became a must for the most part of optical modules. Optical connectors, on the other hand, remain the sole devices for which such a solution is intrinsically not applicable. Empiric rules have then been developed for limiting the incidence of moisture and particles, which introduces the cleaning procedure as a further variable in the reliability evaluation process. A comprehensive test framework should then embrace high power optical stress, insertion/extraction cycles and also cleaning methods.


The paper reports on a first systematic approach for testing optical connectors at high optical power.

## Results


Failures occurred during the tests, at different values of the optical power. Table  III  and IV summarize the results. The indicated power levels refer to devices failed at the highest optical stress. The other failures occurred at lower power levels.


In each case, the failure was catastrophic, that means that the measured output dropped dramatically for failed devices. No evidence for progressive degradation or for long term sudden events has been achieved for the passed devices. Despite some evidence, as the very good performances of type B devices, and the inference that their mixed use with A devices is weakened by the latter ones, some direct inspection of the failed devices is advisable. The following details have been observed:


## A devices


A devices


Type A connectors are very sensitive to the cleaning conditions and to the "extraction/insertion" operation into the adapter when the power source is on. Results can be summarized as:


• the optimal cleaning, both using absolute ethanol or the appropriate cleaning tape, is sufficient to prevent degradation, even if high power is involved; when absolute ethanol is employed, connector must be wiped.


• the extraction and/or insertion of the connector into the adapter when the power source is "on" causes the degradation of the connector. To extract or insert the connector into the adapter the source must be "off".


## B devices


B devices


SC connectors show a very good behaviour in all the considered experimental set up. Nevertheless the "extraction" procedure appears very tricky: after this operation the connector must be cleaned before the new insertion into the adapter; the


## C S devices


C S devices


Several aspects of C S connector behavior can be deduced from experimental results:


• independently from the cleaning procedure, the C S connector degrades when the power source is "on" and the connector is out off its adapter; degradation is probably due to the light reflection effects, that are caused by the connector cover.


• if the connector is well cleaned (both using absolute ethanol or the appropriate cleaning tape) and inserted into the adapter, no degradation phenomena occur.


• the "extraction/insertion" operation, when the power source is "on", is the crucial problem responsible for degradation phenomena; during the "face to face" test, when the external C S connector is repeatedly extracted and inserted no damage is observed; on the contrary, when the internal C S connector is repeatedly extracted and inserted both the connectors in the adapter degrade. In this last case, the degradation of the internal connector is due to light reflection effects caused by the connector cover; the degradation of the external connector is induced by dusty particles deposited on the ferrules of the internal ones, being the two ferrules in contact, after the "insertion" operation. Notice that the laser beam perforates the cover of the internal connector during "extraction/insertion" operation, at power source of the order of 1 W.


## C E devices


C E devices


the connectors C E show a much more reliable behavior when compared with the connectors C S ; in fact:


• the degradation of the connector is not observed during the "insertion/extraction" operation, if an appropriated cleaning procedure is adopted


• independently from the cleaning procedure, the E2000HP connector degrades when the source is "on", the light power is greater than 1W and the connector is out off its adapter. In this case, the degradation is due to thermo-mechanical damage of the connector package: the output light heats the connector cover causing its detachment from the package. After the cover detachment, the ferrule is not damaged (as we can observe by an optical microscope)


## AB and BA FTF tests


AB and BA FTF tests


Both the connectors FC and SC, independently from their position with respect the power source, degrade during the "insertion/extraction" operation. Comparing this result with the previous one we can conclude that degradation of A connector induces the degradation of BC connector. This is possibly due to the contact of the two ferrules into the adapter.


## Microscopic Observations


Microscopic Observations


Direct observation of the failed elements supported


The more critical operation is the cleaning procedure and the "insertion/extraction" into the adapter (metallic sleeve) when the power source is on. In both of cases the connector ferrules appear burned when observed with the optical microscope (Fig.  3  and 4 ). Notice that when the ferrule is cleaned but non-wiped, alcohol halos are present at the ferrule surface; they can be removed by subsequently ferrule cleaning, nevertheless the burning of the fiber remains .


This type of connectors shows degradation only in the test FTF AB and BA. In this case, the failure analysis shows degradation of A connector due to the burning of dusty particles deposited on its ferrule. Dusty particle deposition is probably due to the contact, into the adapter, with the damaged ferrule of FC connector.


The performed tests point out two critical operations: connector with power on, but without adapter, and "insertion/extraction" operation. In both cases the degradation is due to light reflection effects caused by the connector cover: laser light "evaporates" dusty particles from the internal surface of the cover; dusty particles precipitate on to the connector ferrule. In other of cases, failure analysis shows a perforation of the connector cover due to the incident laser light collimated into a small (about 10µm) spot (fig. 5 ).


During high power tests, with the exception of ferrule burning due to non-accurate procedure of connector cleaning, no ferrule damage is observed. Problems appear when the connector is out of the adapter and the power is greater than 1W: in this case the heating of the metal-plated cover propagates until the plastic package of the connector inducing the detaching of the cover; nevertheless, in this case also, the ferrule is not damaged.


## Discussion and Conclusions


Discussion and Conclusions


Summarizing the results of the whole test framework, it can be stated that the more critical issues are:


• the cleaning procedure: independently from the connector type, the connector must be cleaned (with alcohol or with the appropriate cleaning tape), wiped and observed with the appropriate visor to assess that no dusty particles are present on the ferrule surface.


• the insertion/extraction from the adapter with optical power on: this operation is critical when the adapter has not a guide that favours the insertion/extraction (e.g. in the A connection) or the connector has a cover which shuts during the connector extraction from the adapter (e.g. C connectors).


• (Specific for C types) power on when the connector is not into its adapter: degradation of the ferrule connector appears both for C S and C E connectors when power is on with the connector cover closed.


There is no evidence in tests, done up to now, of long term related failure under high power. All failures give origin to early degradation, which leads to catastrophic failure. The longest test done lasted 1 hour, and the failure mechanisms observed are not likely to be present on longer time. This is mainly due to the fact that failures observed are related to presence of dusty particles that 'immediately' burn.


The obvious conclusion may be drawn that failures of the detected kind could be avoided by observing the simple rules of 1) properly cleaning connectors before plugging them and 2) switching off the optical power before any plug/unplug operation.

## 3. Metal vapor (Plasma) arcing in vacuum


3. Metal vapor (Plasma) arcing in vacuum


In vacuum (reduced atmospheric pressure) a much more destructive short circuit phenomenon can occur. If currents of above a few amps are available and the supply voltage is above approximately 18V, the tin whisker may vaporize creating a plasma of tin ions that can conduct hundreds of Amperes. An adequate supply of tin from the surrounding plated surface can help to sustain the arc until the available tin is consumed or the supply current is interrupted such as occurs when a protective fuse or circuit breaker interrupts the current flow  [43] . This phenomenon is reported to have occurred on at least three on-orbit commercial satellites since 1998 resulting in blown fuses that have rendered the spacecraft nonoperational  [26] .


## 4. Debris/Contamination


4. Debris/Contamination


Mechanical shock, vibration or handling may cause whiskers to break loose from the plated surface. Once free to move about, these conductive particles may then interfere with sensitive optical surfaces or the movement of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). In addition, the debris may also bridge isolated conductors resulting in short circuits (see 1-3 above)  [29] .


## Failure Mechanisms and Field Problems Associated with Tin Whiskers


Failure Mechanisms and Field Problems Associated with Tin Whiskers


Tin whiskers pose a serious reliability risk to electronic assemblies. The most likely hazard is an "electrical short", which can be permanent or momentary. It is tempting to expect that these tiny conductive filaments will fuse open at the instant of shorting, creating perhaps an unnoticeable "glitch" to the circuit performance. However, the miniaturization of electronics and advances in low power, low voltage circuitry demonstrate that such "momentary shorts" can have catastrophic events or even become permanent. Table  1  defines some common failure modes attributed to tin whiskers.


Several instances have been publicly reported where tin whiskers have caused system failures in both earth and space-based applications affecting the military, medical and telecommunications industries. Table  2  presents a few such incidents to emphasize the significance of the inherent risks of tin whiskers. Tin whisker growing from pure tin plated TO-3 transistor can shorts collector to case. ## Nuclear Regulatory Commission


Nuclear Regulatory Commission


Tin whiskers from pure tin plated relays  [34]  What are tin whiskers?


Tin whiskers are hair-like growths of near-perfect single crystalline structures of tin that grow from some electroplated tin surfaces. Tin whiskers are believed to grow in order to relieve mechanical stresses acting within the tin layer. Over time (days or months to years), some whiskers have reached lengths capable of creating electrical short circuits between closely spaced conductors (see Table  1 ).


Whisker growths are frequently defined as "spontaneous", to distinguish them from a completely different phenomenon known as "dendrites" which require the presence of moisture, an ionic species and an electric field in order to form. On the contrary, whiskers require none of these conditions to form. Indeed, they have been observed to grow in inert atmospheres and in vacuum with or without the presence of an electric field  [5] . Almost all research conducted to date agrees that electric field has little to no effect on initiation of tin whisker growth. However, NASA Goddard has demonstrated the ability of whiskers to "bend" in response to forces of electrostatic attraction  [7] . Such behavior is significant, when considering the probability of a whisker-shorting scenario where whiskers growing from a surface at one electrical potential will bend towards a surface at a different potential, especially if those whiskers are relatively long.


## Whisker Growth Mechanism


Whisker Growth Mechanism


Experts in the electronics and electroplating industry have not reached a consensus upon a single accepted explanation of the mechanism(s) that drives whisker formation. However, there are some commonly accepted factors involved in tin whisker formation.


There is general agreement that whisker growth occurs from the base of the whisker (not the tip)  [17]  and that some form of long-range diffusion of tin atoms supports the growth. Long-range diffusion theories are supported by the lack of material depletion in the immediate vicinity of the whisker base  [21] .


Today most experts also agree that a process of stress relief within the tin layer drives whisker nucleation and growth. More precisely, many researchers postulate that the development of "compressive" stresses within the tin layer provides the fundamental driving force for whisker growth  [2, 9, 18] .


Of the more recent studies of whisker growth mechanism(s), Lee and Lee  [9]  have described one model for whisker growth that is heavily reliant upon the processes of diffusion and intermetallic compound (IMC) formation occurring between the tin layer and the underlying substrate. In this model atoms with high diffusivity in tin (i.e., copper, zinc) migrate from the substrate material (phosphor bronze in their study) into the tin layer, preferentially along the tin grain boundaries. These diffusing elements and the resulting IMCs (Cu 6 Sn 5 ), produce a compressive stress in the tin layer. The stress that builds over time can shear the surface tin oxide layer approximately along the boundaries of grains having orientations different from the majority. Once the oxide layer has ruptured, tin grains (whiskers) may then be extruded in a continuous fashion through the oxide layer as a means of relaxing compressive stresses. As growth proceeds, the resultant localized compressive stress tends to reduce until the stress level is no longer sufficient to support further growth (equilibrium). One implication of this is that whisker nucleation is not needed, as pre-existing grains are whisker nuclei, and that growth occurs after there is sufficient stress to overcome the obstacles of pinning the boundaries of a particular grain, which then becomes a whisker. Recent studies have shown that additional stresses, such as those arising from thermal cycling, can initiate the growth of tin whiskers  [49] , which continues even after removal of such stresses. [12]  Mechanical processes used in preparation of the substrate such as cold rolling, swaging, piercing, stamping can leave the substrate in a highly stressed state prior to plating Diffusion of substrate elements into tin layer:  [9]  Elements from the substrate, such as zinc (from brass) or copper, may readily diffuse into tin. Diffusion may occur preferentially along grain boundaries of the tin layer causing compressive stress. Intermetallic Formation:  [9, 22]  Formation of intermetallic compounds (such as Cu 6 Sn 5 ) may alter the lattice spacing in the tin plating. Externally Applied Mechanical Stress:  [5, 12, 42]  •


Compressive stresses such as those introduced by torquing of a nut/bolt assembly. Interestingly, controlled experiments by Dunn  [14]  failed to show any correlation between applied external stress and whisker growth.


Bending or stretching of the surface after plating such as lead forming or crimping • Scratches, gouges in the plating and/or the substrate material introduced by handling, probing, etc. Environmental Stresses:  [37]  • Storage temperature: 50°C reportedly is optimal for growth, but independent researchers have shown higher growth potential at 25°C compared to 50°C  [7] . Higher temperatures may introduce competing effects by increasing rate of diffusion while simultaneously relieving stress through annealing/recrystallization of tin grain structure.
