LCD displays were composed of a liquid crystal matrix surrounded by an array of flip chip drivers linked to the matrix by an anisotropic conductive film (ACF). All the assembly was mounted in a metallic frame. Figure  1  shows the display without the frame. Four failed units (F1 to F4) were received for analysis. The displays were activated and the defective columns were marked on the border of the frame. A good display from older lots was also tested for reference. During this marking a slight pressure on the lower or upper border of the frame produced new failures or withdrew existing failures. About 10% of the failing columns failed intermittently; the failing columns marked by the manufacturer did not match those observed at CenPRA, with new failing columns appearing and others disappearing. There is a tendency toward defects at the end contacts of the driver modules. Row defects were not observed on those four samples. The manufacturer says that row defects are seldom found. With the display operating (without backlight), the region where the ITO (indium-tin-oxide) film and driver module contact occurs was pressed carefully on the failing columns sites. This caused some of the failing columns to operate. Next, a moderate pressure was exerted on one complete driver module contact row by means of a metal bar and this bar was simultaneously heated, causing some failing columns to work, but not all. After releasing the pressure, most of these columns returned to the failing state. A short bake at 70 °C eliminated 10% of the defects of the worst display. Observations led us to conclude that the failure was of an intermittent type and centered at the contacts between the drivers and the ITO preferentially at the borders of the polymer tape. These contacts are made by the ACF. Aspects of the application of ACF at the connection of LCD drivers can be found in the literature 1-5 . Some possible causes of this kind of failure are oxidation of the ACF particles, poor adhesion strength, interruption of ITO and/or flip chip tracks and oxidation of the copper contacts of the flip chip 6-8 .


## Visual Inspection


Visual Inspection


The marked failure contact sites were inspected with an optical microscope. Bonding between the driver module contacts and the ITO film tracks on the glass were inspected without detecting any anomaly such  as a possible adhesive delamination or air bubble, as can be seen in Figure  2 .


The ACF was inspected in a failed display (F2) and compared with that of the good unit. The results are shown in Table  1 . We couldn't find significant differences between the displays. The conductive spheres from ACF in the good display and in the failed one were crushed, as shown in Figures  3  and 4 . This observation showed that there was not an evident process deviation in assembling of the ACF and drivers.


## Electrical Testing


Electrical Testing


The resistances between the ITO tracks and the driver modules contacts were measured and compared with those from the good display. The plastic layer that covers the metallic tracks that The measurements were made in two column drivers in F2: one with various lines failed in the LCD (driver 1) and other with few failures (driver 2). One track in each of these was found open (R=∞). The average resistance in the remaining contacts of driver 1 was 270 Ω and 380 Ω in driver 2. The average resistance in the contact of the column drivers in a good display was 200 Ω. In contrast, the average contact resistance of line drivers of defective and good displays was much lower, 120 Ω and 110 Ω respectively.


The contacts in the good and defective displays, whose resistances were measured, were submitted to a slight pressure and the displays were baked at 70 °C and 85 % of relative humidity for 16 hours.


Resistances of the defective drivers decreased by half, while almost no change was observed for the good devices. Tables  2  and 3  summarize the results. The displays were operated and the signals in the outputs of the column drivers and at ITO contacts were monitored in good and failed lines. It was observed that signals in the ITO contacts of failed lines were degraded when compared with the same signals at the outputs of the column drivers. The signals at ITO contacts in the failed lines showed capacitive coupling to the outputs of the drivers due to loss of contact with the metallic spheres in the flexible film from the drivers. Typical waveforms are illustrated in Figures  5  and 6 .


The results of electrical tests confirmed that the problem is concentrated in the contacts between the flip chip driver and the ITO film tracks. Changes in the resistance values after the bake indicated that this problem is probably related to the ACF curing process. Previous work 7 indicated that variations in the contact resistance are due mainly to incorrect (excessively high or low) bonding pressure. Concentration of the failures in the column drivers is attributed to geometrical aspects of the structure that supports the column drivers; material at this location is thinner and more fragile than that of the row drivers, which makes the bonding process more critical.


The problem of poor contact is exacerbated by the fact that the conductive spheres are in their inelastic state. This hinders maintaining contact when there is some lack of adhesion of the ACF caused by expansion of the spheres, and this emphasizes the importance of correct bonding process.


Although oxidation in the flip chip contacts or spheres can not be discarded as the cause of conduction loss, it is less probable due to the fact that the contacts in the row drivers rarely fail. The same reason explains the low probability of failures due to environmental factors.


## Summary and Conclusion


Summary and Conclusion


LCDs used by a Brazilian manufacturer of computer based products presented failures characterized as dark columns. Visual inspection of the contacts between the ITO lines of the display and the copper lines of the flip chip did not show significant differences between a sample from a defective lot and sample from a non defective lot. Electrical tests showed different contact resistances for a good display and a defective one. This behavior worsts at the contact of column drivers, whose resistance values changed after a bake, probably indicating a modification in the curing of the ACF. Monitoring of waveforms at good and failed lines showed a capacitive coupling to the drivers outputs. Those facts led us to conclude that the probable root cause is an ACF bonding process deviation.


## Process Development 1. Component isolation and probing from back side:


Process Development 1. Component isolation and probing from back side:


In addition to the extreme sensitivity of the PCB substrate to nitric or sulfuric acid, compact design of the module with sharp contrast between the profiles of the components make it extremely difficult if not impossible to expose the components by conventional acid or mechanical decapsulation. Jet-etch with nitric acid, sulfuric acid and their combination proved to be incapable of achieving the desired decapsulation result even with pre-milling. Therefore, experiments were performed using a backside approach. The DUT is molded in epoxy and lapped from its backside. This simple backside lapping method has been quite satisfactory in the exposure of each layer of the PCB copper traces and plated through holes, allowing optical examination and subsequent electrical probing. Figures 6-7  Continued backside lapping can expose the silicon die for backside photo emission microscopic analysis (Figure  7 ). The lapping is then fine tuned such that the bond wires of the FETs, Schottky diodes are cut open while those of the IC is intact, i.e. buried in the mold plastic (Figure  10 ), thanks to the difference in bond wire loop height between the IC and the FETs / diodes. This lapping maneuver yields two results: (a) The FETs and diodes are isolated from the circuitry, thus can be probed using the exposed wires (i.e. the crosssectioned bond wires). (b) Since the IC is isolated from the rest of the devices while maintaining its connection to the substrate, it can be probed from the copper traces from the backside. It makes the otherwise tedious IC probing an easy task with a few probes as shown in Figure  6 .


## 3. De-capsulation after components isolation and un-disturbed fault location:


3. De-capsulation after components isolation and un-disturbed fault location:


Once the failed device is identified, the DUT is continuously lapped down from the top side to reach the point that the bond wire section areas are substantially enlarged, i.e. to minimize the thickness of mold compound for the subsequent precision de-capsulation. Finally, the DUT is manually de-capsulated in sulfuric acid at about 190 0 C in 1.5 minutes (if the mold plastic was carbonized due to local heating of a device failure, de-capsulation time increases accordingly). The result is very satisfactory (Figure  10 ). All the devices are exposed and un-disturbed.

### Conclusion:


Conclusion:


This FA process flow combines front and back side parallel lapping, followed by sulfuric acid de-capsulation. It has been effectively employed in various type of plastic BGA modules' failure analysis. It can isolate the faulty device among the otherwise interconnected active and passive components. Thus allow the identification of the failure mechanism(s) to be precisely executed in multiple components BGA modules.


### Introduction


The Atomic Force Microscope is a unique platform among microscopes in that a sharp probe is scanned across a surface and its contact point generates a topographic map. The probe may be connected to circuits or instruments to be used simultaneously to measure other properties in conjunction with the surface image. This allows the user to compare the surface map with a map of the other measured quantity.


### Nanoscale properties and problems


Nanoscale properties and problems


### Scanning Capacitance


Scanning Capacitance


Since the invention of the AFM is late 1980's, researchers have coupled any measurement that could be devised onto this useful platform. Of those measurements, scanning capacitance has probably been the most useful to failure analysts. 1 With this technique and its ability to image doping concentration and type, many formerly intractable issues stemming from silicon impurity defects are instantly recognizable. 2,3 This technique is spearheading the entrance of AFM techniques into FA. Tunneling AFM Another technique, which the author believes deserves far more attention from the serious analyst, is that of tunneling AFM. 4 Most gate oxide defects including charge loss, high leakage, and low breakdown voltage have been analyzed with a combination of electrical characterization (I-V) and destructive physical analysis primarily with Transmission Electron Microscopy, (TEM). However, neither gate level I-V nor TEM give a complete view of the dielectric properties. Though nothing has higher resolution than zone TEM, the sample is still a 1D slice of the device the image of which is averaged over the thickness of the section sample ( < 1000A).


Moreover, with gate I-V characterization, leakage may occur over a very small percentage of the gate. Figure  2  provides an example of dielectric thickness map with nanometer resolution over the entire gate dielectric. The gate leakage current from this device would be an integration over the entire image of all the local high current  High K and ultra-thin dielectrics In the case of extremely thin dielectrics the presence of charge traps are theoretically detectable. Moreover, for novel or exotic dielectrics currently under study as SiO 2 replacements, tunneling current maps are an ideal characterization method.


Because of the exponential dependence of measured current on dielectric thickness, the technique will become more accurate as Moore's Law continues..


### Probes are often the Limitation


Probes are often the Limitation


As users of AFM will be acutely aware, the conductive probes required for SCM and Tunneling AFM are the limiting factor for repeatability. These probes are primarily made from micromachined, single crystal silicon and therefore, are quite fragile. In order to make them conductive for electrical measurements, coatings of various types are applied to the silicon  Probe tip and coating variations create an uncertainty in electrical measurements. Tip to tip variation is often the dominant factor when comparing data for different samples. Moreover, as the probe is scanned across a sample and images acquired, the probe may change due to coating wear or breakage. This is especially true in the case of contact mode techniques and where the sample contains extremely rough/hard materials, which abrade the probe coating. Often over the course of a measurement or sequence of measurements, the probe may shear or wear, leaving a metal semiconductor junction at the probe tip. The probe coating may even wear such that no metal remains in contact with the surface and the signal deteriorates. If these probes are used to make electrical contact to the structures the contact resistance will be unstable.


### Solid metal probes


Solid metal probes


For many applications, a solid metal probe should be the ideal solution. In the cases of SCM and Tunneling AFM, both would benefit from the lack of metal semiconductor junctions. Moreover, the probes should not wear due to the high hardness (tungsten is about a 7 on the mineral scale relative to nickel about 5). The same probe can be expected to last through multiple experiments allowing the user to compare multiple samples with the same probe.


Tungsten probe wires etched to a point have been used for many years in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy STM and contact probing. These wires are etched down to a point that approaches that of current metal-coated silicon probes. These probe wires are used for contacting circuit nodes on FA probe stations and adapting them to AFM for electrical applications is a natural extension. Atomic Force Probing Another application to which the AFM is expected to make a serious contribution to FA is deep submicron probing. AFM's excel at imaging and contacting ultra-small features. It is an obvious extension of the technology is to use an image to position the probe to make contact to subdiffraction limit structures. The image not only allows the user to identify nodes invisible optically, but the scanned probe contact point generates the image guaranteeing probe registration. The electrical probe is also the imaging probe. Early attempts at this task demonstrate both promise and limitation.


The same issues which arise in electrical measurements such as SCM, Tunneling AFM and nano-SRP become hypercritical in the goal of locating and making ohmic contact to metal lines, poly silicon, silicide, and even diffusions. The structures contacted will generally be much more robust than the materials used to coat silicon tips such as Nickel or Chromium. Even if the coating is very durable such as TiN, the coating must be thin ( < 100A) to allow for sharp tip radius, and is therefore easily worn. One line scan over a tungsten plug field will convince the user that such a tip is seriously degraded in the operation. The rough tungsten surface quickly abrades the coating and the electrical signal becomes intermittent.


For contact probing both sample and probe must be deformed to form low resistance contacts. The probe therefore, must be of uniform material for multiple contacts to be made. The sample to be contacted will often form a native oxide, which must be deformed before ohmic contact can be achieved.


### AFP Design


AFP Design


Certain criteria need to be met when designing an instrument of this type. The most important is the ability to place probe tips with extreme precision. For the single node case, it may be possible to get by with low precision placement, probably as large as half the feature size. If multiple probe tips must be placed in close proximity, the margin for error is greatly reduced as is shown in figure  5 . If the sample to be contacted has minimum feature size W and the pitch is P and the probe radius is R then:


Space Between Probes = (W/2)-R+(P/2) (1)


The error in placement should be an order of magnitude less than this number to allow maximum space between probes. Table  1  below shows that at the 130nm node, placement accuracy is required to be under 10nm. It is also required that probe radius be reduced to 50nm for the 90nm node. The AFM image quality is far higher resolution given the sharper probe tip (~20nm). Moreover, the noise level is about 10X higher in the AFP image. The increased noise is primarily due to the cantilevered mass configuration found on a probe station. It can be seen when comparing the AFP and AFM images, that the probe radius adds to the apparent feature size and decreases the apparent feature spacing. Given the high aspect ratio features often found on IC's and after FIB and RIE deprocessing, the system must be able to identify features at multiple heights. In order to image such features without damage, the AFM feedback must be active in Z. Without active feedback, the probe will be scratching the top metal layer or will not reach the metal lines below. The applications discussed here were tunneling current imaging for oxide study, scanning capacitance for dopant imaging, and atomic force probing. These techniques are the most widely used, and are becoming indispensable tools to those serious analysts. A limiting factor in the use of these tools is tip wear. Solid metal probe wires were proposed as a solution to this issue and their use in probing applications was reported. Probe geometry effects in regards to imaging and placement were discussed, as were the stringent requirements for an AFP tool in order to extend to the limits of the semiconductor roadmap.


Mechanical microprobing of circuits has to address several issues such as circuit imaging, controlled placement of probe on region of interest, controlled contact force of the tip over the circuit node, meeting electrical performance targets for stimulation and probing of circuits. Microprobing on deep submicron circuits offer challenges in all these aspects of probing.


Conventional microprobing using whisker or etched needle probe tips mounted on manipulators or micropositioners and probe stations are commonly used for failure analysis and Integrated Circuit (IC) characterization. This is a very mature technology with a variety of options for the material and physical dimensions of the probe tip. The probe can be used for stimulating the device as well as for measuring electrical signals. The circuit loading is reduced using active probe tips and different designs of the active circuit provide varying bandwidth for electrical measurement. Optical microscopes are commonly employed to guide the placement of probes on the circuit. However, the placement of the probe accurately and reproducibly on sub-micron features is difficult because of the optical resolution of the microscope and placement resolution of the probes.


A microprobing system  [1]  using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) for increasing the image resolution as required to guide placement of probes mechanically on sub-micron features has been reported. A system using multiple probes and an SEM has been described in the product literature  [1] . Because of the use of SEM, the microprobing needs to be performed in vacuum. The probes are navigated to the desired location using motor driven stages under computer control.


Microprobing using multiple probe tips is an option on Focused Ion Beam (FIB) systems from NP Test , Inc. (Schlumberger Probe Systems)  [2] . The large depth of field for circuit imaging available with the ion beam is an advantage over the one using a SEM in this application. However, potential for circuit damage exists because of charging of the insulators and implantation of ions in the circuit of interest. The probes are positioned in vacuum using motor driven stages and can be positioned using the image.


Recently, microprobing  [3] [4] [5] [6]  making use of the very high spatial resolution capability of an Atomic Force Microscope (AFM) has been reported. In this methodology the scanning tip of an AFM is used for probing as well as for imaging. Piezo stages with nanometer positioning resolution are used for scanning and for probe placement. The probe tips are very sharp with a radius of curvature of less than 25 nm, thus making very high spatial resolution possible for imaging the topography of a surface. Because of the high resolution for probe placement and the ability to probe on sub-micron features with this technology, we will refer to this probing as nanoprobing.


Krieg et al.  [3]  have reported AFM based nanoprobing using a single contact probe head. They also have reported achieving an image resolution below 0.1 µm and having been able to resolve 0.5 µm thick metal lines and spaces. Electrical characterization of the probe tips with passive voltage divider circuits as well as low bandwidth ( <  300 MHz) active probes has been reported. Kane et al.  [6]  have reported dual probe heads using AFM based technology to probe on CMOS circuits built in Silicon on Insulator (SOI) technology.


Copper interconnects and low k interlevel dielectric films are particularly sensitive to mechanical stresses of conventional probe tips. Use of AFM based nanoprobing has been reported to be possible and advantageous to probing on sub-micron features without damaging the surface. This paper describes application of a single probe head using an AFM based tool  [3] [4] [5] .


The commercially available nanoprobing AFM from SUSS MicroTec is used to probe on a variety of packaged parts.


Electrical characteristics and probing capabilities of this technique in a variety of applications are presented.


### AFM Based Probing


AFM Based Probing


In AFM based nanoprobing a metal coated or metallic sharp tip akin to a phonograph needle of less than 25 nm tip radius of curvature at the end of a silicon or silicon nitride cantilever beam is scanned over the chip surface for imaging. The tip is scanned over the surface in contact mode. The deflection of the cantilever is detected using an optical lever technique  [3]  where a laser beam is bounced off the cantilever beam and the reflected beam is detected using a split photodiode. The tip is scanned over the surface using a piezo XY stage and the deflection is measured to image the topography of the surface. In this mode of scanning the contact force by the tip to the surface is not a constant.


The spatial resolution in the topographic image of the surface in contact mode scanning is essentially governed by the radius of curvature of the probe tip. A tip radius of less than 25 nm is obtainable. The cantilever is designed so that a probe tip contact force of 1-50 nanonewtons can be applied to the surface. The tip force can be varied during scanning by control of the z-piezo stage to achieve good contrast. The low contact force of the probe ensures that the chip surface is not damaged.


The scanned area of the surface can be as large as ~ 40 µm x 40 µm and any location within the scanned area can be probed under computer control.


Higher resolution images within this area can also be made, if required. After positioning of the probe, the contact force of the tip can be controllably increased to make contact to the circuit to be probed.


The scanning tip is metallized or made from a metal in order to make electrical contact to locations on the chip for measurements. The probe tip, cantilever, and any electrical interface circuits are built into a replaceable cartridge. Further, there is a lens built into the cartridge for deflection measurement using an optical means. Probe cartridges with straight electrical connections are used for stimulation of the circuit or for direct probing. Alternatively, different resistance divider circuits are incorporated for voltage probing with different input resistance to the probe tip. Cartridges with an active circuit using a FET to increase the input resistance are available to decrease probe loading. Various types of filters are used in the circuit to achieve different bandwidths or Signal to Noise ratios for voltage probing.


The cartridge plugs into a probe head (Figure  1 ) that is placed on an Alessi probe station from Cascade Microtech equipped with an optical microscope. A DUT card with a socketed device is typically mounted to the platen to stimulate the device. Voltage at desired nodes is probed with the single probe head. The probe head has coarse x, y, z-slides and a piezo driven XYZ stage for positioning of the probe tip. The XY stage is also used for scanning to acquire the image. The probe head is computer controlled with a Graphical User Interface (GUI) for imaging and placement of the tip for electrical probing. Notice that manual coarse positioning of the tip using a linear slide and micrometer screws can be made.


### Frontside Probing on a Test Chip


Frontside Probing on a Test Chip


A test chip made of a patterned single metal layer was used to evaluate the bandwidth (BW) of the probe and for assessing probe placement accuracy. The test structures consisted of metal lines of various widths and spaces as well as controlled impedance transmission lines (Figure  2 ) but it did not have any active circuits. The die is packaged in a 40 pin DIP package and signals can be applied to the metal lines externally. A 200 MHz signal was applied to a controlled impedance transmission line (Figure  3 ) and the signal was probed on a 5 µm wide line. An Active probe tip of high BW was used to probe the line. An HP Infinium scope with 1.5 GHz BW was used to capture the signal. From the rise time of the signal the BW was estimated to be greater than 1 GHz.


### Frontside Probing of RO


Frontside Probing of RO


In a second application, nanoprobing was carried out on a 101-stage Ring Oscillator (RO) circuit with an on-chip three-stage buffer.


The circuit was fabricated using a 3-metal layer CMOS process and the die was wire bonded to a 48-pin DIP package. The input to the three-stage buffer was probed (Figure  4 ) at different VDD levels. This showed that probing on 0.25 µm lines could be carried out using this method. The probing was performed by milling a window in the passivation layer centered about the probing location. The milling was done using a default mill operation using a FIB.


The FIB box was advantageously used in placing the probe. A second device was de-passivated using a Reactive Ion Etch (RIE) process. The location of a three stage buffer was imaged using the AFM probe (Figure  5 ) to show the resolution achievable with the tool. Please note that the polysilicon gates are in a layer below the metal layer that is imaged. Figure  5 : AFM image of a three stage buffer area obtained using the tool. The image resolution is sufficient to probe on 0.25 µm lines. Note that this buffer is on the output of a RO that is adjacent to the one probed.


The electrical output from the ring oscillator before the buffer stage is measured using a 1.5 GHz BW HP Infinium scope. Results are presented in Figure  6 .


### Backside Probing of a Delay Chain


Backside Probing of a Delay Chain


In a third application, we probed a flip-chip packaged die in a 321 pin ceramic PGA package. The output of a delay chain consisting of a series of inverters is probed from the backside by contacting to a 0.5 µm x 0.5 µm tungsten plug made using a FIB. The probe tip is connected to a FET mounted on the cartridge (AP3 cartridge, from SUSS MicroTec) and has a fairly high input impedance and greater than 1 GHz bandwidth. The results from the measurement using a 50 GHz sampling scope (HP Infinium 86100A) are shown in Figure  7 . The output of the delay chain is probed by contacting to a 0.5 µm x 0.5 µm probe point made using a FIB. Bandwidth of greater than 1 GHz has been observed.


A periodic signal of approximately 80 MHz, 50% duty cycle signal was applied to the delay chain for this measurement. This method allows for voltage probing with high bandwidth on an array of closely spaced probe points that are made of any conducting material such as tungsten.


### Summary


Atomic Force Microscope based nanoprobing provides all the advantages of microprobing such as flexibility and ease of use. Furthermore it makes use of readily available laboratory test equipment. The SUSS MicroTec single probe system is used on a regular probing system to acquire electrical signals on a variety of samples. Passive and active probe tips of low and high bandwidth probe cartridges have been used. From the rise time of measured signals, this type of probing is shown to provide a bandwidth of ~1 GHz in normal use of a DUT board and socket.


The image resolution of the scanned surface topography is sufficient to navigate on the die and to probe 0.25 µm wide lines. The probe contact force for imaging and probing does not cause any damage to the circuit, but it has been observed that probe erosion and collection of debris can occur after some scanning and probing. This change of the tip condition makes electrical contact more difficult. However, with good condition of the tip, the probe contact resistance is not found to be a problem on the circuits probed.


Information about the implant distribution at a failing site can provide root-cause and/or help to isolate the source of a failure to specific production steps. For example an image of an errant implant distribution showing mis-registration or punch-through can be direct evidence of a failure. In other instances the presence (or absence) of an implant at a defect site can help isolate which process steps are responsible. The ability to obtain information about a specific structure or device is critical for investigating localized failures, especially on production material. Techniques optimized for two-dimensional teststructures are not necessarily well suited for failure analysis. 1,2 Qualitative images are often sufficient for a failure analysis diagnosis since images of a failing location can be compared to a passing location to identify differences. 3,4 The criteria for SCM to be a successful FA technique is therefore determined by its ability to analyze specific sites as well as its spatial and implant resolution.


There are several two-dimensional implant profiling techniques which can be used to help diagnose failures. 1,2,5 One common approach is to decorate cross-sections using Acetic:Nitric:HF mixtures to reveal implant profiles. 2,5  Unfortunately the threshold for chemical decoration is high (1e17 atoms/cm 3 ) which can make troubleshooting gradient or well-implant related problems difficult. Implant imaging techniques based on scanning probe microscopy (SPM) have also been applied to diagnose failures. 3,4  SCM can provide twodimensional implant profiles with spatial resolution on the order of 10-15 nm and a dynamic range of 1e15 to 1e20 atoms/cm 3 . 1 Unfortunately, both decoration etches and scanning probe methods are very sensitive to techniques used to prepare the cross-section. Cross-sections can be prepared using a combination of cleave, polish and ion-beam techniques. For FA the choice of sample preparation technique is often dictated by the extent to which the failure is localized. Cleave and polish techniques are used to prepare cross-section samples with nearly damage free surfaces, well suited for SCM and decoration etches. 6 Unfortunately this approach is not ideal for diagnosing site-specific failures since optical microscopy is used during the polish for targeting. FIBs equipped with navigation capability can readily cross-section individual failing bits and are therefore widely used for site specific FA. When combined with SEM technology to create dual-beam (DB) systems, these tools provide the powerful capability to 'slice and view' failing sites in search of a defect. Navigation software allows cross-sections to be placed to within 0.5 um of the failing site. The slice and view technique can further target to within less than 0.01 um of the suspected failure.
 Unfortunately the ion scattering which occurs during the FIB machining produces a 20-35 nm thick amorphous damage layer at the surface of the samples. 7,8 This damage layer inhibits decoration etches and can interfere with imaging techniques. The amorphous layer limits high resolution TEM by scattering the electron beam. 7,8 While the electrical properties of this damage layer have not been extensively characterized, the loss of crystal structure guarantees that these properties do not match that of the original sample. For devices, the electronic structure of the Si is effectively shielded by this damage layer. Attempts to image FIB prepared samples with SPM techniques have shown that the damage layer reduces the implant signal to below the level of detection (discussed below). To enable high resolution TEM, ion mills can be used to further thin samples and produce slivers with low-surface damage (less than 2 nm) for transmission electron microscopy. Several studies have shown that ion mill induced surface damage is minimized by reducing the energy and incident angle of the ions. 7,8 In this work, polish is explored as an approach for removing the damage from a FIB prepared cross-section to allow for site specific SCM analysis.


### The Technique


The Technique


SCM samples are generally prepared by cleaving and polishing to a target location. 1,3,4 The final polish conditions and oxide growth are critical determinants of the technique's implant sensitivity and resolution. The final polish step is thought to result in an almost damage free surface with a thin (approximately 1 nm) native oxide. Reports of final polish conditions vary, but generally favor using a colloidal silica slurry and a felt pad. Next a thin (2-3 nm) layer of oxide is grown at low temperature (300 C) under UV illumination to provide the dielectric required for SCM imaging. In this work the final steps of conventional SCM sample preparation were applied to FIB generated cross-section samples. Figure  1  depicts the integrated FIB and polish sample preparation flow. After the location of the failure has been isolated, the location is cross-sectioned using standard FIB techniques. In this case a commercial DB system with navigation capability was used to mark the location of interest. 9 The wafers were first depassivated to the top layer metal to allow for improved imaging and navigation. After marking the failing location, a 15x5x1 um thick platinum cap is deposited and a 25x15x6 um trench is sputtered (using a 6600 pA, 35 keV Ga + beam). The standard slice and view approach is then used to position the cross-section face approximately 30 nm in front of the desired imaging location (using a 35 keV 350 pA, or smaller beam). This is accomplished by using other structures also visible in the cross-section and layout information to guide the final slices.


Once the failing site has been FIB marked and crosssectioned, the samples are prepared for polish. First the sample is cleaved to a smaller size to be more suitable both for polishing and SPM imaging. The desired result is a roughly 5x5 mm wafer piece with the cleave on one side intersecting the FIB trench, as shown in Figure  1(c ). Today's auto-cleavers can easily target to within 5 um. Manual cleave followed by coarse polish has also been used successfully, but is considerably more time consuming. Depending upon the contact density in the region of interest, the samples can then be etched for 5 minutes in a 1:3 solution of NH 4 OH:H 2 0 2 to remove the W contacts.


There are two principal reasons for removing the W contacts.


Their presence results in undesirable topography on the cross-section face after polish, which can interfere with SPM imaging. The W contacts also provide a locally conductive surface, which can interfere with the capacitance sensor, used during SCM imaging. The polish step is intended to remove most of the FIB induced surface damage layer. The 5x5 mm sample is mounted on to a tripod polisher with the cross-section face positioned on the trailing edge relative to the polish platen, as shown in Figure  1(e) . The sample is then polished for 25 seconds using 0.02 um colloidal Silica and a felt pad. 10,11 The geometric parameters which determine the polish removal rate from the FIB cross-section face are shown in Figure  2 . Good results have been obtained with recess depths ranging from 4 to 8 um and crosssection depths of 6 to 10 um. A 200 mm wheel spinning at 75 rpm was used while the weight of the tripod polisher and the radial distance were kept roughly constant.


A polish removal rate of approximately 1 nm/sec was observed under these conditions. After the polish, a thorough rinse and clean ensures that the remaining silica is removed from the cross-section face. The samples are then heated at 300 C under UV illumination for 20 minutes to produce a 2 to 3 nm thick oxide. 1,3,4 Finally, the samples are mounted to metal SPM stubs, see Figure  1 (g), using hot glue followed by silver paint. The silver paint provides a conductive path for applying a bias to the wafer backside. From start to finish this sample preparation cycle required roughly 4 hours per sample and was completed successfully for 80% of the samples submitted. The SCM imaging conditions used for this work are comparable to those cited in the literature. 1,3,4 A commercially available SCM equipped with Pt-Ir coated Si probes was used. 12 DC biases near zero (+-0.5 V) and AC biases ranging from 0.1 to 2 V were found to work well. Image acquisition times ranged from 2 to 8 minutes per frame.


### Examples and Discussion


Examples and Discussion


FIB assisted SCM has been used both to determine the root cause of failures as well as to isolate the production line source of failures on Intel's flash memory products.


Failing sites were identified using electrical testing and standard fault isolation techniques. Samples were then prepared with the integrated FIB and polish flow (described above) so that SCM analysis of these sites could be performed. The differences between SCM images of good and bad material have been successfully used to draw conclusions about mis-processing and the redistribution of particles.


### Root Cause Example


Root Cause Example


Leakage failures are a common source of yield loss. These failures can be caused by any mis-processing


### Cross-section depth


Cross-section depth


### Recess depth


Recess depth


### Damage Layer


Damage Layer


Failing Site which introduces unwanted conductive paths. Figure  3  demonstrates a case in which FIB assisted SCM was used to determine that a mis-registered well implant was the root cause of a leakage failure. The SCM image shown in Figure  3 (b) was obtained in a location, which was identified as a potential leakage site using emission microscopy. The SCM image shown in Figure  3 (a) was obtained in the same location on a die functioning within specifications. In both images the dC/dV signal is recorded to show n-type material as dark, p-type as light and the intermediate gray is a null-signal indicating few (or infinite) carriers. 1 A schematic representation of implant structure as specified by design is shown in Figure  3 (c). While Figure  3 (a) closely resembles the intended design, the suspected leakage location, Figure  3 (b), does not. This image shows that the nwell is shifted to the left, providing a direct leakage path underneath the oxide trench isolation to the neighboring source implant. This image identified the root-cause of this failure mode, and illustrates the advantages offered by the dynamic range of SCM.


### Example: Isolating a Defect


Example: Isolating a Defect


Particles introduced and distributed during processing are a common cause of failures at test. DB cross-sections can quickly yield information about which layers are disturbed in order to isolate when, during the processing, the defect occurred. In some cases the disruption of physical layers does not sufficiently resolve which process steps were impacted. In these cases the presence or absence of an implant at a defect site can provide additional information. A DB image of a silicon particle causing a single-bit contact to gate short is shown in Figure  4(a) . From this image it is apparent that these defects were present after the gates were patterned and before the spacer was deposited. However there are still several dozen processing steps to consider between these two operations. The SCM image of the same silicon particle is shown in Figure  4(b) . In this case the failing bit can be compared to the neighboring good bits in the same image. As in Figure  3  the n-type material is dark, ptype is light and the intermediate gray is a null-signal indicating few carriers. Note that the W contacts were not removed from this cross-section prior to imaging, resulting in local disruptions to the SCM signal. The obvious difference in the drain implant between good and bad clearly indicates that this particle was present prior to this implant. A similar image was obtained for another particle positioned above a source. Together these SCM images of single-bit failures were used to narrow the search for these defects from 100 down to less than 8 process steps. This example illustrates how FIB assisted SCM can be used to isolate the source of single bit failures.


### Discussion


The integrated FIB and polish sample preparation technique appears to remove enough of the FIB induced surface damage layer to allow for SCM analysis. In preliminary studies, image quality was found to vary with polish time, eventually reaching a steady state after 25 seconds. SCM images of FIB samples (without any polish) were uniformly poor indicating that the FIB damage layer reduces the sample's capacitance signal to below the reasonable level of detection. Samples polished for 25 seconds or more yielded acceptable SCM images. Based on SEM observations of the samples before and after polish, and the product layout, the amount of material removed by the polish was estimated to be 20 to 30 nm. Spatial imaging resolution for these samples appears to be limited by the probe shape as is common for SPM techniques. 1,3,4 For the data presented here the spatial resolution of the implant signal is estimated to be better than 0.1 um. This is insufficient for resolving the detailed structure of device channels on production material. Fortunately successful FA diagnosis only required comparing images of good and bad material. Implant sensitivity was sufficient to resolve both well and source/drain type implants.


Work is now underway to vary the FIB and polish conditions to study their impact on the SCM resolution and sensitivity. Ion milling techniques are also being explored as an alternative for reducing the FIB induced damage layer.


### Conclusions


FIB assisted SCM has been demonstrated as a tool for site specific two-dimensional implant imaging. If an implant problem is suspected, the qualitative implant distribution associated with a particular structure can be obtained. If a defect is found while cross-sectioning, the sample can be converted for SCM imaging. While the sample preparation does require approximately four hours of time per sample it was found to be reliable, controllable and repeatable. Site-specific images of the source/drain and well implants have been used to diagnose and isolate failures on Intel's flash memory products.


The technique provides an unparalleled ability to target failing locations for implant analysis.

With the rapid development of semiconductor manufacturing process and technology, the feature size of integrated circuits is shrinking rapidly. Features that are not designed specifically for testing purposes at specifically designated locations are gradually shrinking beyond the optical resolution. At the same time, the operating frequencies of these circuits are increasing rapidly with significantly reduced signal amplitude. Such systems have less tolerance to noise sources and may exhibit different behaviors due to minor disturbances. This poses great challenges to any instruments designed for online testing, characterization, and failure analysis of such circuits. The instrument must have sufficient spatial resolution to locate features invisible by optical means and measure the signal characteristics with minimum disturbance to the normal operation of the circuits with sufficient temporal resolution. With the miniaturization of the circuitry, the tolerance to disturbance introduced by the testing process is increasingly stringent. Even though special test points and/or buffer circuits may be added to alleviate this problem, they need relatively longer support cycle, use more resources, and may cause unintentional disturbance to circuit characteristics. For high-speed circuits, contact of a probe tip and the associated measurement circuitry, either passive or active, to the live operating circuitry may change the characteristics of circuitry partially or completely due to parasitic loading. This renders any such tests less helpful and even useless in many cases. The higher the operating frequency and the lower the operating voltage, the worse the problems are.


Internal IC probing techniques available to the test engineer include electro-optic probing  [1] , electronbeam probing  [2] , photo-conductive sampling  [3] , infrared laser backside probing  [4] , time-resolved photo-emission probing  [5] , and scanning probe microscopy (SPM) based techniques  [6, 7, 8] . SPM probing tools that are based on a contact mode of operation during electrical measurement, similar to needle probes, but with deep sub-micron imaging and placement ability have been developed  [9] . As with any contact probe method, however, the loading effects of the probe can disturb the circuits operation at higher frequencies. Electrostatic force microscopy (EFM) is an SPM technique that operates in a noncontact mode and dramatically reduces the loading effects of the probe  [10] . EFMs are able to measure internal IC voltage signals by utilizing the localized Coulomb force interaction between a non-contacting micromachined probe and the circuit test point. EFMs are commonly used for voltage contrast imaging at DC  [11] . Techniques for using the EFM for high frequency measurements have also been developed  [12, 13, 14] . These EFMs can provide high temporal and spatial resolution, perform measurements non-invasively, and do this in ambient conditions permitting direct interface with standard test equipment. EFM based probes have measured signals from ICs operating at over 3 Gbit/s  [15] , from passivated circuits  [16] , from sub-micrometer structures  [17]  and from the backside of the die  [18] . They can also provide quantitative voltage results  [19]  and have been used for stroboscopic voltage contrast and logic state mapping  [20] .
 EFMs introduce a loading on the order of only 1 fF to the circuit in test point  [15, 21]  and thus have the potential to provide noninvasive measurements to very high frequencies.


All the EFM methods described above use a repetitive sampling approach. For high-frequency digital signal measurements a single narrow sampling pulse is applied to the probe tip and either frequency modulation  [12]  or amplitude modulation  [13]  is used to provide an equivalent time representation of the desired signal. Since the electrostatic coupling between the probe tip and the circuit is very small, the EFM has an inherent low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) limitation. Thus, when a high temporal resolution (narrow pulse) is desired along with a long test pattern vector length, the method suffers from a very long acquisition time. This is a huge barrier for many practical applications of the EFM technique such as microprocessor test.


A new multi-pulse approach is proposed in this paper to improve the SNR of the sampled EFM technique. Instead of using a single sampling pulse for signal recovery, a set of or several sets of carefully designed pulses are applied to the probe tip for signal measurement and recovery.


Even though the interaction between a single sampling pulse and the circuit may be too small to be measured by the EFM, the effect of a group of pulses can more easily be measured. With a specially designed set of pulses, the original signal can be reconstructed uniquely and accurately. The proposed approach can easily provide an order of magnitude SNR improvement when compared to the single pulse approach. The details of the new approach and the experiment results are presented in this paper.


### Pulse Sampled EFM: Single Pulse Approach


Pulse Sampled EFM: Single Pulse Approach


As shown in Figure  1 , the single pulse sampled EFM waveform measurement system consists of a micromachined cantilever that is located above the point in the circuit where the voltage signal ) , , ( t y x v c is to be measured. As discussed in  [21] , the capacitance coupling between the operating circuit and the probe tip causes an electrostatic force on the probe tip that is described by: is a periodic signal. A sampling pulse is applied to the tip with the same period but with a predefined delay, τ . As shown in Figure  1 , the voltage applied to the probe tip is amplitude modulated as described in  [13]  such that it excites a mechanical vibration of the probe tip at the resonant frequency of the probe cantilever. It can be shown that, for narrow sampling pulses with a delay τ , the magnitude of the vibration of the probe tip can be approximated by  [21]  ∆z

From (2), the amplitude of the probe tip vibration when the sampling pulse has a delay τ is given by:

Assuming the probe tip maintains a constant height and the deflection amplitude is much smaller than the height of the tip above the circuit surface, it follows that both ∆z and β are constants. Therefore, by measuring the vibration amplitude of the probe cantilever at a particular temporal point, by controlling the delay of the sampling pulse, the waveform of the signal can be recovered.

From equation (3), it is evident that monitoring the vibration amplitude of the cantilever is sufficient to recover the relative amplitude of waveform of the signal c v .


The signal recovery process for the single pulse EFM system can be implemented as illustrated in Figure  1 . The test pattern generator, which could be a standard tester, generates a periodic signal on the circuit and also provides a synchronization signal for the test controller to generate the delayed sampling pulse. The waveform of the signal is recovered through a motion detection and signal recovery process.


### EFM SNR


Among the noise sources in the EFM system are shot and laser intensity noise in the cantilever deflection detection mechanism, electrical noise in the detection electronics, and thermal noise. Thermal noise is the fundamental noise source due to the random mechanical vibration of the cantilever when in thermal equilibrium with the finite temperature environment. At higher frequencies, thermal noise is typically the dominant noise source in SPM systems with an rms deflection at r ω given by  [15]  ∆z


N = 4Qk B T a B kω r (5)


where T a is the ambient temperature, k B is Boltzmann's constant and B is the measurement bandwidth. Using (  5 ) and the amplitude of the signal as given in (  4 ), the SNR of the single pulse EFM system is


B a T B kk r Q K T z C res v SNR 8 ω δ ∂ ∂ = (6)


where v res is the required voltage resolution. It is evident from (6) that the following methods and their combinations may be used to improve the SNR of the system:


Increase the effective amplitude, K, of the sampling pulse Increase the width, δ , of the sampling pulse and/or decrease the period, T, of the test pattern Decease the distance between the tip and the circuit so that z


C ∂ ∂ increases


Improve tip design to optimize Q, k, and r ω


Operate the system at a low temperature and/or in a vacuum


The temporal resolution of the system is determined by the width of the sampling pulse and is thus specified by the required measurement bandwidth.


Increasing the amplitude of the sampling pulse has practical limits as the amplitude of the sampling pulse must be designed such that an accidental contact of the probe tip to the circuit does not cause damage. New cantilever design may improve the signal-to-noise ratio to some extent but is limited as there is a tradeoff between stiffness and resonant frequency. Operation in a vacuum or at a reduced temperature makes the system inflexible for use on a standard probe station. Identifying T/ δ in (6) as the duty cycle shows that the SNR is inversely proportional to the duty cycle. Unfortunately, for the sampled EFM system to be of practical use in many test applications, it must support sufficiently long duty cycles in order to analyze reasonably long test vectors. In summary, the performance of a pulse sampled EFM system is characterized by the following parameters:


• Temporal resolution • Voltage resolution • Duty cycle • Acquisition time


The key for all above parameters is to improve the SNR. With the sampling pulse width fixed by the required temporal resolution, the duty cycle is the major factor in determining the SNR of the EFM system.


### Multi-pulse Approach


Multi-pulse Approach


As discussed in the last section, the potential to improve the SNR performance of the single pulse sampled EFM system is limited. As with all repetitive sampling based methods this limits its usefulness for many practical applications requiring a large duty cycle.


For a typical waveform measurement procedure, a set of N sampled data points in a window within the period T is acquired. The N points are usually acquired one point at a time as the sampling pulse is swept through the window. This means that the total waveform acquisition time is N times the single point acquisition time for a specified SNR as given by Equation (  6 ). An alternative to applying a single sampling pulse is to apply a group of pulses (pulse vector) to the probe tip during a single measurement. The impetus for doing this is that the detected probe vibration due to the interaction of a group of pulses will be much larger than that from a single pulse and thus the SNR of a single measurement will be improved. We will show that, with a properly designed set of pulse vectors, the original signal can be recovered.


Assume we are measuring a signal on a circuit within a specified sampling window and desire to collect a total of N samples within that window. Ignoring the constant offset term z ∆ in equation (3), which does not contribute to the relative amplitude of the signal waveform, the general sampling process can be described as ∆Z = βv c (t = τ k )⋅ p k  (7)  In equation (  7 ) k P is a sampling pulse vector that spans the window that is applied to the probe tip at a particular measurement step k. For a pulse vector with m equally spaced sampling pulses we denote the vector as k P as


P k = p k,1 , p k,2 ,L, p k,m -1 , { p k,m } (8)


Here i k p , is defined as the amplitude of the i-th sampling-pulse in the vector for the k-th step. The temporal locations of the pulses will be denoted by the vector τ k as


τ k = τ k,1 ,τ k,2 ,L, τ k, m-1 , { τ k, m } (9)


so that the deflection of the probe as given by (  7 ) will be a sum of the contributions of all pulses in the vector. For the single pulse sampling process, as described previously, the vector will contain only one non-zero element that is shifted along the vector one position at a time at each sampling step k.

In this case, the recovered signal is the optimally recoverable signal under noise in the least-square sense. Also, the algorithm has no limitations on the choices of the pulse matrices. A unique solution exists as long as the inverse of the pulse matrix exists.

If we assume the sampling pulse has exactly the same amplitude, the improvement of signal-to-noise ratio is proportional to the average number of pulses in the pulse vectors.


An implementation of the above mentioned algorithm is illustrated in Figure  3 . The signal recovery process is illustrated in Figure  4 . Groups of pulses are applied at each step to the probe tip to excite the mechanical vibration of the probe tip cantilever. The amplitude of the vibration of the tip is collected for each step at the resonant frequency of the tip. When a sufficient number of measurements are made, the signal can be recovered using the inverse pulse matrix. To recover the signal fully in temporal dimension, some form of scan process may then be employed.


### Implementation


Implementation


Theoretically, we can use pulses with different amplitude to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio of a sampled EFM system. Unfortunately, no standard fast pulse or stimulus generators commercially available have the capability to generate ultra-fast, narrow pulse trains with controllable amplitudes. We have to rely on high-speed digital pulse generators to generate the sampling pulses. In this case, we can control only the "on" and "off" of a particular pulse and the elements of the pulse matrix can have value "1" or "0" only.


As illustrated in equation (  14 ), there are two problems that hinder a cost effective and efficient implementation. Firstly, we have to calculate a matrix inversion to recover the signal. This is not a problem when the length of the pulse train is very limited. However, with a pulse train length of 1024 or above for better SNR, the inverse of the pulse matrix takes a significant amount of CPU time. For real-time recovery of the signal this is a heavy burden. One solution is to store the inverse matrices of all possible pulse matrices. This solution needs a very large amount of storage space, is less flexible, and may slow down the measurement process. The second issue is that, due to the limited storage capability of commercially available high-speed digital pulse generators, a new pulse train has to be downloaded to the pulse generator at each measurement step. For a measurement with m pulses, at least m vectors have to be downloaded to the pulse generator in addition to the time for measurements. This is very time consuming and the vector download time does not improve our measurement performance. To address these two issues, we have to find a set of pulse trains that maximize not only the SNR of the system but also minimize the storage requirements, improve the computing efficiency, and shorten the vector download time simultaneously.


This appears to be a very challenging task. Fortunately, pioneers in astronomy have solved the problem for us in their quest to achieve better SNR in their measurement of spectral compositions  [22, 23, 24, 25] . The following discussions concentrate on what we need for our implementation. Please refer to  [22, 23, 24]  for further details.

Assume our pulse vector is cyclic. As illustrated in Figure  5 , we can simply download the first row of the pulse vector followed by its duplicate to the pulse generator. Since each row is a simple cyclic shift of the previous row, a simple change of the loop start/end location will generate other pulse matrix rows. Vector download can be performed at a single step at the beginning of test. Application of a cyclic matrix as our pulse matrix will minimize our storage and download requirements.


### . Cyclic pulse matrix


. Cyclic pulse matrix


There are three known algorithms to construct cyclic S-matrices: the quadratic residue construction, the construction using maximal length shift register sequences, and the twin prime construction. Each method covers a different number space. The quadratic residue construction produces S-matrices of order n that is a prime number of the form The combination of these three approaches can generate S-matrices with various orders for pulse matrix construction. Our current implementation is capable of automatically calculating the best Smatrix fit to the specified pulse train length.


A block diagram of the multi-pulse sampled EFM system is depicted in Figure  6 . The system is controlled by an IBM-PC and based on SUSS MicroTec's AFM probe  [7] . A Tektronix HFS9009 stimulus generator is used to generate the pulse vectors and to simulate a test pattern generator for some tests. The generated pulse trains pass through a pulse generator to narrow the width of sampling pulses to 240ps. A trace of the sampling pulse is shown in Figure  7 . The pulse width is 240ps with rise times of well under 100ps on both the leading and falling edges. The amplitude of the pulse is 4-5 volts.

Figure 7. Trace of the sampling pulse


Applying more pulses in a single measurement step can improve the SNR. However, since more pulses need longer acquisition time, drift and other low frequency noise become an issue. Practically, the number of pulses that can be applied in a single measurement step is also limited by the mechanical property of the cantilever of the probe tip and the length of the test vector. An operator may specify the number of pulses that is best for a particular signal measurements process.


A photograph of the system is shown in Figure  8 .


### Figure 8. The multi-pulse sampled EFM system


Figure 8. The multi-pulse sampled EFM system


The non-contact probing user interface is illustrated in Figure  9 . An operator has full control of the noncontact probe process and a set of simple tools for signal property measurements. In the screen capture, the signal pulses are 3 volts and have duration of 7ns with 14ns spacing. The duty cycle is 10240:1 and the signal SNR is approximately 8.87. 3.5 It is interesting to notice that there is a systematic source of noise that keeps the signal to noise ratio from exceeded approximately 10:1 in current setup at low duty cycles. This may be due to vibration, electronic noise or some other source of noise that is not related to the fundamental source of noise, the thermal vibration of the cantilever. At higher duty cycles the thermal noise of the cantilever begins to dominate and the SNR begins to drop.


### Temporal Resolution of the system


Temporal Resolution of the system


One of the very important performance requirements of the system is its temporal resolution. Unfortunately, due to the limitation of current setup (HFS9009), we are not able to generate a signal with very narrow pulses. Therefore, we evaluate the temporal resolution of the system by measuring the rising and falling edge of pulses instead.


Due to limitation of HFS9009 (the maximum rate is 633MHz), the minimum distance between the sampling pulses in current setup is 2.4ns. With a sampling pulse with of 240ps up to 10 scanning steps are needed to recover the signal fully in the temporal dimension. An operator may setup the scanning step to either over-scan to have better SNR or to underscan to have lower temporal resolution but shorter acquisition time. Figure  10  shows a typical result with a scan step size of 500ps and duty cycle of 2560:1. The signal pulse is 7ns with a spacing of 14ns. The amplitude of the signal is 3 volts. The system has no difficulty to resolve both the rising and the falling edge accurately. In fact, the deformation of the signal top due to signal reflection is visible in the acquired waveforms.


### Figure 10. Resolve signal edges


Figure 10. Resolve signal edges


In our experiments, the system illustrates it has a temporal resolution approaching the width of the sampling pulse.


### Stress Test


Stress Test


We have performed a set of the experiments to evaluate the performance limits of the multi-pulse sampled EFM with current setup. It is a stress test to evaluate both the stability of the system over long acquisition time and SNR characteristics on long duty cycles.


The signal and the synchronization trigger are shown in Figure  11 . The top scope trace is the pattern used to stimulate the test chip. The bottom trace is the scope trigger pulse generated by one channel of HFS9009. The trigger pulse to HFS9009 and the pattern to test chip were generated in B2 and B1 channels of a HFS 9003 respectively. The B1 channel was delayed using " lead delay" to program occurrence of B2 pulse. A lead-delay of 230 ns on B1 channel was used. The pattern was repeated every ~15 us (6250 * 2.4 ns). The top trace was programmed to be 2.5V in amplitude. Please note that the measured signal is only ~2 V after going through the transmission line in the test chip. Figure  12  shows the signal recovered by the multi-pulse sampled EFM setup. The test used 127 pulses. The Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for this is calculated to be 3.


In the experiments, the cyclic pulse vector scheme has not been implemented. The data acquisition time can be further improved by eliminate the sampling vector download time using the cyclic pulse vector scheme.


A novel approach that utilizes multiple sampling pulses to improve the SNR of pulse sampled EFM is discussed in this paper. The new approach can easily provide an order of magnitude improvement to pulse sampled EFM technology without significant increase of the complexity of the system. We have demonstrated that multi-pulse sampled EFM has the potential to bring the sampled EFM technology into a large class of practical applications in integrated circuit characterization and failure diagnostics and/or analysis that require non-invasive signal measurements with high spatial, temporal, and amplitude resolution.
