### TEM Analysis


TEM Analysis


Cross-section TEM analysis was conducted on one non contaminated and one contaminated bondpads to determine the thickness of the native Al oxide layers. The TEM samples were first prepared by Focused Ion Beam (FIB) using a FEI 200 FIB System until the sample was less than 100 nm thick. The TEM membrane was then plucked out by a glass needle and placed on a carbon supporting film on a Cu grid. TEM observations were then performed on a Philips TECNAI F20 TEM operated at 200KeV.


### Ion Chromatograph Analysis


Ion Chromatograph Analysis


Trace fluorine contamination in the packaging foam material samples was determined by Ion Chromatography (IC) technique. The 6 inch foam samples were soaked in at least 200 ml ultra-pure deionized water (DI) for 20 minutes at ambient temperature of 22 o C. Leaching was performed in a rinsed polypropylene bag with the foam sample totally immersed in the DI water. The water extracted was then analyzed by Ion Chromatography. To improve the accuracy of the results, a leach blank was prepared in each analysis process and analyzed under the same identical conditions and the blank results were subtracted from the sample's results


### AES Analysis


In wafer fab, Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) has been widely used for failure analysis. It is a commonly used surface analytical technique as it has the particular advantage of being easily applicable to the light elements such as C, N, O, F, etc. In this study, AES was used to determine F and C contamination levels on bondpads. Analyses were carried out using a VG ESCALAB 220i-XL XPS/AES machine. The conditions used are: operating vacuum at 3 x 10 -9 m Bar, electron gun beam energy at 3 keV and ion gun beam energy at 4 keV. Measurements were made on the asreceived surface of each bondpads, and sequentially after argon ion etching to depths of 50, 100 and 150 Å if necessary. These etch depths are equivalent argon ion sputter depths using a Ta 2 O 5 standard. The relative atomic concentrations (at %) were derived from the Auger survey spectra. The values were calculated by first measuring elemental peak-to-peak heights in the survey scans and then applying sensitivity factors based on standard spectra of pure elements or selected compounds:


C i = I i / (I std S i D i ) (3)


Where I i is the peak-to-peak amplitude of the element i from the test specimen, I std is the peak-topeak amplitude of the element i from the standard, S i is the relative sensitivity factor and D i is a relative scale factor between the spectra for the test specimen and standard.


### Results and Discussions


Failure analysis was done on the affected wafers. Optical visual inspection revealed discoloration with black dots on the bondpads of the affected wafers (Fig 1  , top ). However, some bondpads were     Based on the TEM results, it was concluded that the fluorine contamination caused the thicker native oxide on the "flower-like" defect area on the affected bondpad. It was hypothesized that the fluorine reacted with Al to form a complex compound, which was difficult to be cleaned away. Re-cleaning was attempted but was not successful.


### Root Cause Investigation


Root Cause Investigation


In wafer fabrication, after bondpad opening etch and clean processes, there is still a low level of fluorine and carbon contamination on normal bondpads, which do not affect bondpad bonding. Our previous Auger monitoring results from the same Fab showed that the contamination level of fluorine and carbon on the normal bondpads were about 6.5 at % (Ave) and 2.6 at % (Ave), respectively.


In order to find the root cause of fluorine contamination on bad bondpads, Auger analysis was performed on the affected wafers and in-line process wafers immediately after the etch and clean processes to check the contamination level of fluorine and carbon on bondpads. Auger results on the affected bondpad showed that the atomic concentration of the elements on surface (as received) were F: 34.69 at %, O: 11.51 at%, C: 16.71 at% and Al: 37.09 at%, respectively (Fig  6 ).


One can see that F and C on the affected bondpad were much higher than those detected on the normal bondpads from the monitoring average values. However, on the bondpad of the in-line process wafer, the concentration of fluorine and carbon were only 4.6 at% and 2.6 at%, respectively Fig 6 . F contamination was very higher (34.7 at %) on the affected bondpad, which was much higher than the monitoring average value of 6.5 at%. (  Fig 7) , which are in or below the monitoring average values. Therefore, it was hypothesized that the fluorine contamination issue was not caused by the fab process, as the in-line wafers were not affected.


After making further investigations, it was suspected that the fluorine contamination might be due to the wafer packaging foam material.


### Simulation Experiments and Results


Simulation Experiments and Results


At first, some simulation experiments were conducted immediately using the wet box testing to determine the effects of the packaging materials. The simulation results showed that if the wafers touched the foam directly without filter paper isolation, the wafers (in box C) were contaminated by higher fluorine. However, if without the foam in testing, no fluorine contamination was found on the wafers (in boxes B and D). Thus, the fluorine contamination on bondpads might be due to the packaging foam material containing traces of fluorine.


### Ion Chromatograph Analysis and Results


Ion Chromatograph Analysis and Results


To determine the presence of fluorine in the packaging foam material and variation of fluorine amount between the foams used on affected wafers VS good wafers, ion chromatography (IC) analysis technique was employed to determine the level of trace concentration of fluorine in the foam samples.


Foam samples from both packaging boxes of affected (bad) and not affected wafers (good) were analyzed by IC technique. The foam samples were soaked in DI water for 20 mins at ambient temperature. The water extracted from each sample was then analyzed by ion chromatography. The ionic evaluation results showed that fluorine amount was less than 4 ng/cm 2 for the good wafer packaging foam samples. However, on the contamination wafer foam samples, the fluorine amounts were higher than 100 ng/cm 2 , which is 25 times higher than that on the good foam samples.


Based on the IC analysis results, the fluorine contamination on bondpads was confirmed to be due to the packaging foam material.


Preventive actions that were immediately taken were: (a) changing all the bad wafer foam material to the good wafer foam material for all affected wafers packaged; (b) setting-up a specification to control the fluorine concentration in the packaging foam materials and (c) determining the fluorine concentration in the packaging foam materials using IC technique and ensuring that it must be less than the specification value (4ng/cm 2 ). The bondpad fluorine contamination problem was overcome after the preventive actions were implemented.


### Studies of Fluorine-Induced Defects on Bondpads by XPS/ESCA and TOF-SIMS Techniques


Studies of Fluorine-Induced Defects on Bondpads by XPS/ESCA and TOF-SIMS Techniques


It is well-known fact that it is difficult to obtain chemical bonding information by using the above FA tools such as SEM, EDX, TEM, Auger and IC. Therefore, in this section, further investigation of the chemical and physical nature of Al-F complex compounds using XPS/ESCA and TOF-SIMS techniques was performed. These techniques provide chemical bonding information of fluorineinduced defects.


### XPS Analysis and Results


XPS Analysis and Results


XPS/ESCA was performed on a VG ESCALAB 220i-XL microanalysis XPS system. Monochromatic Al source was used for high energy resolution analysis on bond pad. The area of analysis is 50 um diameter. An Ar+ sputter gun was operated at 3 KeV and rastered 500 x 500 um 2 for depth profiling. The sputter rate was calibrated against Ta 2 O 5 standard. Low energy charge compensation electron gun was incorporated in the analysis. XPS survey scan (Fig 8 ) showed the presence of very high concentration of F on the affected bondpad. The concentration of the elements on surface were F: 33.9 at%, O: 19.7 at%, C: 16.1 at% and Al: 30.3 at%, respectively. One can see that the XPS results are in agreement with the above Auger results from the affected bondpads. XPS depth profiling results showed that F thickness was more than 500 A. The native oxide thickness was 800 A, which was much thicker than 20-30 A on the normal bondpad (Fig  9 ). Thus, XPS results confirmed the TEM observation. 1 ) revealed that AlF 3 (45.6%) and the un-known Al compound (39.4%) were the main compositions on the affected bondpads and Al element was about 10% only. This confirms that non-stick bondpad problem was due to higher fluorine compound and low concentration of Al on the affected bondpads.


### Al Trifluoride (AlF 3 )


Al Trifluoride (AlF 3 )


AlF 3 is a well-known compound form of the Al fluorides. XPS bonding energy is at 76.3 eV. Its electronic configuration of is 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 1. Al atoms form 3 equivalent hybrid-bonding orbitals from one 3s and two 3p atomic orbitals. Therefore, Al atom is described as sp 2 hybridized by one 3s and two 3p atomic orbitals and form 3 sigma bonds that lie on the same plane and giving a trigonal structure separated by 120° degrees. However, SEM micrograph showed that the defects on the affected bondpads are the "flower-like" defect (refer to  Fig 2)  and was not a trigonal planar structure, but most like a hexagonal planar structure. Thus, it was concluded that the unknown compound is not Al Trifluoride (AlF 3 ).


### Al Hexafluoride [AlF 6 ] 3-


Al Hexafluoride [AlF 6 ] 3-


The un-known Al compound, at the chemical bonding energy position of 78.7 eV could not be confirmed in any reference books and tables  [5] [6] . Therefore, it is necessary to find what is this compound at the position of 78.7 eV. Moreover, we have understood that this finding and characterization helped us to set up a theoretical model electrochemically and made further explanation theoretically for the fluorine-induced corrosion on aluminium bondpads.


In this study, we will try to identify this un-known Al compound. After performing detail studies, we think that it is most likely a F-Al complex compound, [AlF 6 ] 3-and using TOF-SIMS analysis technique we have obtained supporting results.


Book references  [13] [14]  mentioned and showed that Al and some heavier elements are not restricted to an octet of electrons in their valence shells, and for these elements the coordination numbers can be higher than 3 or 4 such as 6 in [AlF 6 ] 3-.


In the research work, to fit the CHF 3 treated spectrum properly, an additional peak at ~ 77.75 eV chemical bonding was also added to XPS fitting process by Matsuo et al  [12] . This peak was attributed to a fluoride contribution from AlF x . Unfortunately, Matsuo et al did not show the value of the x in AlF x. Therefore, we think initially that the un-known compound also is one of AlF x compounds as its chemical bonding energy is 78.7 eV, which is near 77.75 eV. Moreover, from Fig  2,  SEM micrograph shows that the defects are not in a trigonal planar structure, but like a hexagonal planar structure.


Based on the above discussions, we strongly believe that the un-known Al compound peak in XPS fitting results is contributed by AlF x compound and x is more than 3, most likely 6, thus the un-known compound is [AlF 6 ] 3-. In chemistry, [AlF 6 ] 3-is called as a coordination complex compound and the coordination number is 6.


However, before we identify the un-known compound as [AlF 6 ] 3-, We have to answer 2 questions :  (1) . What is the probability to form this coordination complex compound of [AlF 6 ] 3-? And (2) Is [AlF 6 ] 3-a chemically stable complex compound?


In order to answer the first question, we discuss the values of E o (standard electrode and Redox potentials) shown in Table  2 [15] . If the E o values are positive, the equilibrium tends to shift to the right. However, if the E o values are negative, the equilibrium tends to shift to the left. This explains why Fe is easily oxidized compared to element Au and Cu as the E o of Fe is negative, but those of Au and Cu are positive. In Eqn  (11)  of the Table  2 , the E o is highly negative and it is -2.07. Thus the equilibrium in Eqn  (11)  favours to the left and the formation of [AlF 6 ] 3-. Therefore, we can understand that the probability to form [AlF 6 ] 3-is very high if fluorine contamination is present on Al bondpads.


Then we discuss the chemical equilibrium constants of fluorine coordination complex compound shown in Table  3  so as to answer the above second question. In Table 3  [15] , theoretically, if k value is large, the equilibrium in Eqn  (12)  tends to shift to the right. In Eqn  (12) , k value is 6.92 x 10 19 , which is extremely large. Therefore, we also can understand that it is highly probable to form [AlF 6 ] 3-as it is a stable compound chemically.


### Support Data from TOF-SIMS Analysis


Support Data from TOF-SIMS Analysis


From the above discussion, we think that the unknown peak is contributed by AlF x compounds, most likely [AlF 6 ] 3-. We have showed that it is high probable to form [AlF 6 ] 3-and it is a stable coordination complex compound. However, more evidence is necessary to make this conclusion.


To achieve this, we employed TOF-SIMS technique to get more supporting data.


### TOF-SIMS Analysis and Results


TOF-SIMS Analysis and Results


TOF-SIMS analysis was carried out on an ION-TOF SIMS IV system. A 25 KeV Ga gun was operated in both imaging and high mass resolution mode to identify the chemical species and obtain the distribution at the same time. Both positive and negative ion images were obtained for higher secondary ion yield ( TOF-SIMS analysis was performed on a normal bondpad and an affected bondpad with F contamination. The analysis area was about 27 um x 27 um, the collecting time was 100 secs and the peak calibration used F and Ga peaks for positive spectra and F and Al for negative spectra. The intensities detected from the positive and negative ions are summarized in Table  4 . To compare the difference contamination levels between a normal bondpad and an affected bondpad, the spectra of the positive ions (NH 4 ) + and [AlF 2 ] + and the spectrum of the negative ion [AlF 4 ]  -detected are shown in Figs 12-14. One can see that the positive spectra detected higher [AlF] 2+ , [AlF 2 ]  + and (NH 4 ) + on the affected bondpad and the negative spectra detected higher F -and [AlF 4 ] -which was from [AlF 6 ]  3-. From Table  4 , we also can see that the negative ions of (NH) 2-(NH 2 ) -were detected. fragment peak of [AlF 6 ] 3- . However, why did we only detect negative ion of [AlF 4 ] -, but no negative ion of [AlF 5 ]  2-was detected? This can be explained by using the stable constants K of the complex compounds listed in Table  3 . One can see that the K value of [AlF 5 ] 2-is much smaller than that of [AlF 4 ]  -. This means that [AlF 4 ] -is more stable and most of [AlF 5 ]  2-had been bombard into [AlF 4 ] - during TOF-SIMS analysis. Therefore, only negative ion of [AlF 4 ] -was detected.


### Mechanism of F-induced Corrosion


Mechanism of F-induced Corrosion


From TOF-SIMS results, one can see that besides the ion of (NH 4 ) + , the negative ions of (NH) 2-and (NH 2 ) -were also detected. We think that they were from (NH 4 ) + , which was formed from N 2 and H 2 O (moisture) in the air. This is because fluorine contamination on Al bondpads will form complex compound of [AlF 6 ] 3-. Once complex compound of [AlF 6 ] 3-forms on bondpad, it will become an electrochemical Anode and cause further electrochemical corrosion reaction. While the Cathode consists by N 2 and H 2 O (moisture) and the corrosion products will be (NH 4 ) + and OH -, which will result in further Al bondpad OH - corrosion. The details of electrochemical theory and corrosion model is studied and discussed in another paper  [16] .


Therefore, in this case, we think that the fluorine contamination on bondpad had formed [AlF 6 ] 3-on the affected bondpads. Then the complex compound of [AlF 6 ] 3-had caused further electrochemical reactions and formed a new product of (NH 4 ) + .and OH -. Finally, [AlF 6 ] 3-and (NH 4 ) + combined and formed a corrosive coordination complex compound, (NH 4 ) 3 (AlF 6 ) on the affected bondpads, while the product of OH - reacted with Al and caused further corrosion. These corrosive Al products resulted in bondpad discoloration and non-stick bondpad issue.


### Summary and Conclusion


Optical inspection confirmed bondpad discoloration with the black dots on the bondpads of the affected wafers. SEM results showed some "flower-like" defects on the affected bondpads. EDX analysis detected high fluorine contamination on the "flower-like" defects of bondpad. TEM results showed that the native oxide was only 20-30 A on a normal bondpad, but it was abnormally higher than 500 A at the "flower-like" defect area. Based on Auger analysis, wafer wet box simulation and ion chromatograph results, it is concluded that the fluorine contamination was due to wafer shipping packaging foam material.


Using XPS/ESCA analysis techniques, we not only confirmed the presence of fluorine contamination and the TEM observation of the defects, but also found an un-known Al-F compound at chemical bonding energy of 78.7 eV. After theoretical studies, we identified the un-known Al-F compound as [AlF 6 ] 3-, which was supported and proven by TOF-SIMS analysis results.   1.

Metallurgical reactions between solder bumps and under bump metallization (UBM) systems during solder reflow cycles or after reliability and thermal stresses have deterministic effects on the system performance. It has been shown the reliability performance of many commercially available UBM systems can be directly linked to its microstructure at the solder/UBM interface during and after thermal stresses. (1)  Conventionally the UBM microstructures studies using optical microscopy, X-ray diffractometry (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy with X-ray energy spectrometry (SEM/EDS) are limited in resolution power. The identification of different intermetallics relies on the contrast between different layers, which is often obscured or totally indistinguishable in optical microscopy and SEM. Furthermore, the ultra-thin intermetallic layers formed less than a few nanometers (nm) thick are often invisible to the best available SEM, resulting in wrong or misleading experimental conclusions. While the advanced packaging technology has pushed the system miniaturization, the UBM microstructure becomes more difficult or impossible to be observed and studied using SEM. New and more powerful techniques are needed. It was demonstrated that transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is the tool for such a challenging task. (2,3) The key to TEM analysis relies on the sample preparation techniques that can cut through the area of interest to produce a thin slide of sample no more than 200 nm in thickness and without introducing artifacts or microstructure changes.


### Experiments


Experiments


The basic thin film structures of the two different UBM systems and the conventional Au/Al ball bonding are summarized in Table  I . Cross section TEM (XTEM) was used to study the samples which experienced different reflow cycles (as received, 1X, 3X, and 10X) as well as samples annealed at 150 0 C for 1000 hours. One important concern is the samples are highly temperature sensitive and any prolonged exposure of the sample in temperature higher than 100 0 C will alter the microstructure that needs to be studied. As such, special care was taken to ensure the overall TEM sample preparation procedure was done at temperatures lower than 100 0 C and the ion milling time was less than 5 minutes. Liquid nitrogen cooled ion milling sample stage was tested in some cases and was found unnecessary.


Focus ion beam assisted sample thinning was found to introduce artifacts and was inappropriate in most of the cases. TEM analysis was done with FEI/Philips CM200 FEG TEM        reaction is highly sensitive to wire bond parameters, like substrate temperature, transfer speed, and even bonding force, …etc. It is suspected that during the wire bonding, a temperature gradient has built up across the Au/Al interface. On the Au side, the temperature is much higher since Au was melted to form a ball at the wire bonder head. While transferring the Au ball in contact with Al pad, which has been pre-heated to 160-200 o C before in contact with Au, Al was heated up from Au side and the reaction was pushed into Al started from the Au/Al interface with highest temperature in the very beginning. (7) As reaction continues, part of the heat was absorbed by Al pad as the Si substrate acts as a heat sink, the interface temperature decreases rapidly. Subsequent intermetallics formed under such swift temperature change and the whole reaction stopped when the temperature cooled down to below 100 o C. The reaction is summarized in Fig  13 .


Studies on the microstructure evolution of the Eutectic PbSn solder/Ni-based UBM systems and the old Au/Al ball bonding metallurgy are shown to be of critical value in understanding the package processibility and reliability issues. For Cu/Ni(V)/Al UBM system, Cu 6 Sn 5 formation provides a stable interface and prevents solder from attacking Ni(V) layer. Without Cu 6 Sn 5 , Ni(V) can be consumed easily by Sn, results in Ni 3 Sn 4 spalling and eventually leads to desoldering. (8) For Au/Ni(P) UBM system, both Ni 3 Sn 4 and Ni 3 P are formed in as reflow condition and both grew/evolved continuously during the subsequent thermal treatments. Since the electroless Ni(P) is relatively thick (usually more than 5 um), depletion of Ni(P) and subsequent desoldering is not a concern and the Au/Ni(P) is a rather robust UBM system as has been reported in our previous studies. (1,2)   It is demonstrated that a detailed study on the intermetallic formation in solder/UBM interaction is desirable and TEM is capable of providing the vital information in both process characterization and in reliability evaluation stages. In many cases, a direct correlation between the interface microstructure and the overall system reliability can be established. (1)  Such microstructure study capability using TEM is even more important when failure analysis on a specific solder bump at a specific location is needed.


On the other hand, the age-old Au/Al ball bonding was shown to be of high thermal robustness due to the formation of a thick and stable Au 4 Al intermetallic layer, which stopped subsequent diffusion and degradation of the interface. For the new Ni-based UBM systems, although the intermetallics formed are highly stable, the interactions are continuously evolving even after 1000 hours of 150 O C high temperature storage.  1 The comparison of various transient techniques can be found elsewhere. 2 Other techniques include the 3ω method, 3,4 the differential photoacoustic method, 5 and the pulsed photothermal displacement technique. 6  Additional techniques can be found in ref.  7 .


Although a variety of techniques are available for measuring thermal conductivity, many of them suffer from low accuracy, have a limited thermal conductivity range, or are timeconsuming and/or expensive to setup.


Recently, the hot disk technique, which is a transient plane source technique, has gained popularity as a tool for rapid and accurate thermal conductivity measurement. A precursor to the hot disk technique was first described by Gustafsson in 1967 as a non-steady-state method of measuring thermal conductivity of transparent liquids. 8 In the original experimental design, a thin rectangular metallic foil suspended in the liquid was heated by a constant electric current. The temperature distribution around the foil was measured optically as a function of time. From this result, the thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity of the liquid could be determined. Later, this technique, which has been called the hot strip method, has been modified so that it can


Proceedings from the 28 th International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis, 3-7 November, 2002, Phoenix, Arizona be used to measure the thermal conductivity of a wide range of materials, including materials with low electrical conductivity, 9 building materials (e.g., cement and brick powder), 10,11 stainless steel, 12 copper powder, 13 anisotropic solids (e.g., crystalline quartz), 14 and thin metallic materials (e.g., copper, aluminum, and brass). 15   The hot disk method 15-19 is based on using a metal disk as a continuous plane heat source and as a sensor to monitor the temperature increase in the metal disk. During the measurement, the sensor is sandwiched between two pieces of the sample. By supplying a constant current to the metal disk, the output heating power is nearly constant. The temperature change in the disk itself is highly dependent on the thermal transport properties of the material surrounding the sensor, and this temperature change can be accurately measured by measuring the electric resistance across the disk sensor. By monitoring the temperature increase over a short period of time (typically a few seconds) after the start of the experiment, it is possible to obtain precise information on the thermal transport properties of the material surrounding the metal disk.


In this paper, we will first discuss the theoretical background of the hot disk technique, and then we will provide examples of using this technique to measure several thermal interface materials used for electronic packaging. In addition, the measurement accuracy of this metrology will be evaluated using standard samples.


### Theory


Theory


A hot disk sensor is composed of a double spiral of nickel wire sandwiched between two thin films of Kapton™ or polyimide, as illustrated in figure  1 . During the measurement, the Kapton™ or polyimide films serve as electrical insulation.


Figure  1 . Illustration of a hot disk sensor. 17   To understand the theory behind the hot disk technique, we need to obtain the temperature profile on the sensor surface and relate this profile to the thermal transport properties of the surrounding material, which is the sample we intended to measure. For this purpose, it is very useful to start from the point source solution for the conduction of heat in an isotropic material.

### Other Considerations


Other Considerations


### Probing Depth


Probing Depth


The theoretical treatment above assumes that the heat conduction media is infinite in size. In reality, the sample size during a hot disk measurement is always finite. Therefore, it is essential that during the measurement time t, the influence of the sample boundaries on the hot disk solution is small. It can be shown 12 that one can define a quantity called probing depth, ∆p, which is the shortest distance from the edge of the sample to the edge of the sensor. If


t p κ 4 ≥ ∆ , (17)


then the effect of sample boundaries can be neglected and the hot disk solution is valid. During a hot disk measurement, this criterion is used to guide sample preparation.


### Time Correction


Time Correction


In the ideal situation, the temperature response of the sample is assumed to be instantaneous when the current to the hot disk sensor is switched on. In reality, however, there are a number of factors which could affect the temperature response time, including non-ideal electric components; the heat capacity of the sensor and insulation material (Kapton™); time delay caused by thermal resistance between the sensor and the material; and intrinsic instrument dead time. 12  For these reasons, a time correction, t c , is needed when evaluating the thermal conductivity using Equation 14:


), ( )

is the corrected characteristic time. The time correction can be obtained by least square fitting so that the average temperature increase is linearly dependent on the function D(τ c ). 12


### Contact Resistance


Contact Resistance


Contact resistance is the interfacial thermal resistance between the sample surface and the sensor. It is present in almost all measurement techniques. In the hot disk technique, the presence of insulating layers (Kapton™) adds an additional contact resistance between the material and the sensing disk. However, it was noted that the influence of contact resistance on the average temperature increase becomes a constant, ∆T, after a short period of time: 11, 12   ), ( )


( 2 / 3 c o c D aK P T T τ π τ + ∆ = ∆ ( 19


where ∆T is inversely proportional to the thermal conductivity of the insulating layer and is related to the dimensions of the insulating layer. Numerical simulations have shown that for a 25 µm thick Kapton™ insulation layer, the time needed for ∆T to become a constant is ~50 ms. Thus, this term can be easily separated in the software when


) ( c T τ ∆ vs. ) ( c D τ


is plotted using data points generated after t  >  50 ms.


### Temperature Drift


Temperature Drift


Before an actual measurement, any systematic temperature drift surrounding the hot disk sensor is monitored for 25 seconds. Any systematic temperature drift will be corrected when thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity are calculated.


### Heat Capacity


Heat Capacity


Because the hot disk sensor has its own heat capacity that can influence the temperature change of the sensor, heat capacity of the sensor itself is corrected. This process is handled by the analysis software.


In principle, it is not necessary to know a material's specific heat and density in order to calculate thermal conductivity. After the raw experimental data are collected, a linear regression is performed to obtain the optimized τ value so that a linear relationship is obtained for ) ( c T τ ∆ vs. D(τ c ). Thermal diffusivity, κ, of the material can be easily calculated when τ is known. Then, thermal conductivity, K, of the material can be obtained from the slope of the linear fit. When both κ and K are known, the volumetric specific heat, ρC, can be determined.


### Experimental


### Material


Material


Thermal transport properties, including thermal conductivity, thermal diffusivity, and specific heat of several thermal interface materials with potential applications in electronic packaging were studied using the hot disk technique and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) techniques. These materials include three thermal greases, code-named G9, G1, and S78, and two thermal gels named S56 and G-SE. They are all silicone-based polymeric materials with up to 90 wt.% of thermally conductive fillers. The specific gravity of these materials was listed in table 1. Among these materials, the thermal greases do not require any cure, while the two thermal gel materials need to be cured before hot disk and DSC measurements.


### Hot Disk Measurement


Hot Disk Measurement


### A. Sample Preparation


A. Sample Preparation


To prepare grease samples for hot disk measurement, the material is dispensed into a cylindrical plastic container. In our experiments, we found that plastic juice bottle caps can be used as sample containers. The depth and the diameter of the container are approximately 10 mm and 40 mm, respectively. During the measurement, the hot disk sensor is sandwiched between two bottle caps filled with the grease material. Due to the high viscosity of the grease material, the overflow of the material in the top container is minimal during the test.


To prepare thermal gel samples for hot disk measurement, uncured material is dispensed into a Teflon mold which has a cavity of 76 mm long, 38 mm wide, and 6 mm deep. The material is then cured at 125°C for 1 hour in a nitrogenpurged oven. The cured TIM is then cut into half so that we have two pieces of 38 mm × 38 mm × 6 mm specimens. During the measurement, the hot disk sensor is sandwiched between the two pieces of samples.


### B. Instrumentation


The hot disk sensor used in this study has a thickness of 10 µm and a radius of 3.3 mm. During our experiments, the applied output power to the sensor is 0.5 W and the typical duration of a single measurement is 2.5 to 5 seconds. The total data points collected within the duration of the measurement is 200. The effects of possible temperature drift during the measurement, thermal contact resistance between the sensor and the sample (including the thermal resistance of the Kapton™ film), instrument time delay, and the specific heat of the sensor itself are all corrected when the thermal conductivity and the thermal diffusivity of the sample are calculated. For each material, 10 measurements were performed.


### Specific Heat Measurement


Specific Heat Measurement


When performing a thermal conductivity measurement using the hot disk sensor, it is always a good idea to determine the sample's specific heat, C, and its density, ρ, in order to calculate its thermal diffusivity and thermal conductivity accurately. Specific heat can be measured using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The principle of using DSC to measure specific heat has been discussed elsewhere. 21, 22   Specific heat measurement was conducted using a Perkin-Elmer DSC7 system with sapphire single crystal as a standard because its specific heat is well known. The mass of the sapphire standard is 61.37 mg, and the typical sample mass is 60-90 mg. The thermal program used for the specific heat measurement is:


1. Isothermally held at 25°C for 5 min; 2. Ramp at 10°C/min to 100°C; 3. Isothermally held at 100°C for 3 min.


To start the specific heat measurement, a baseline heat flow curve was first measured with empty aluminum pans placed in the DSC reference cell and sample cell. Next, a sapphire standard was placed into the sample pan and the heat flow curve was measured using the same program. Finally, the heat flow curve of the real sample was measured using the same sample pan and thermal program. The specific heat of the material can then be calculated as 21, 22


C y m y m C ⋅ = , (20)


where C 1 and C 2 are specific heat of the sample and sapphire standard, respectively; m 1 and m 2 are the sample mass and the mass of the sapphire; and y 1 and y 2 are the net heat flow of the sample and the sapphire, respectively.

### Hot Disk Results


Hot Disk Results


Figure  4  plots the average temperature increase T ∆ measured by the hot disk sensor as a function of time based on a single measurement. The average temperature drift just before the measurement is negligible ( <  0.05 K). Even this small drift is corrected by the software when calculating the bulk thermal conductivity. ∆ vs. D(τ). Based on figure  5 , the thermal conductivity of this thermal gel material is calculated to be 3.51 W/m⋅K, and the corresponding thermal diffusivity is 1.65 mm 2 /sec. The time correction is t o = 0.0795 sec. The corresponding probing depth is 5.43 mm, smaller than sample thickness. Measurements were repeated 10 times and the average results are shown in table 1. The standard deviation of the thermal conductivity for the 10 measurements is only 0.01 W/m⋅K, which is rather small. This demonstrates that the measurement results are very repeatable. In addition, our results are in excellent agreement with the results provided by the material supplier, as shown in table 1.


Hot disk measurements for the other thermal interface materials were performed in the same way. For each material, 10 measurements were conducted and the thermal conductivity and thermal diffusivity results are listed in table 1. Our results showed that all measurements are highly repeatable, as indicated by the small standard deviation values for all of the materials studied. Based on the results listed in table 1, it can be seen that our results are well correlated with the supplier data.


### Accuracy of the Measurement


Accuracy of the Measurement


To verify the accuracy of the hot disk results, we used this technique to measure the thermal conductivity of a stainless steel standard (supplied by the instrument vendor) and a sample of Pyrex® glass. The thermal conductivity for the stainless steel sample is 13.5 W/m⋅K, as provided by the instrument vendor (measured using laser flash technique). For Pyrex® glass, the established literature value for thermal conductivity is 1.13 W/m⋅K. Thermal conductivity values obtained by the hot disk technique are 13.33 and 1.10 W/m⋅K for the stainless steel and Pyrex® glass, respectively. The deviations from the established values are less than 1.5% for both samples. This indicates that thermal conductivity obtained from hot disk technique is highly accurate.


In this paper, we discussed the theory of the hot disk technique, which is a transient plane source technique for rapid thermal conductivity measurement. The central part of the hot disk technique is a sensor made of a double spiral of nickel wire. During the measurement, the sensor is sandwiched between two halves of a sample. The sensor is supplied with a small, constant current and serves as a heat source as


Technology of backside probing has evolved dramatically in recent years with the introduction of two new techniques, the first is the laser voltage probing (LVP) and the second is the Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) or generally referred to as Time Resolved Light Emission Microscopy (TRLEM).


### Laser voltage probing (LVP)


Laser voltage probing (LVP)


The LVP is a novel IR probing technology (3) that provides a way to measure voltage waveforms directly from the P-N junction through the backside of the silicon substrate. Since extrinsic silicon is partially transparent to IR light, an IR laser beam at a wavelength of 1064 nm is focused through the silicon onto the P-N junction. The small optoelectronic interaction that occurs between the focused beam and the junction can be measured stroboscopically to determine the voltage variations at the internal signal node. The LVP is composed of a mode-locked laser that operates with output pulses at 100MHz repetition rate. The incident beam is reflected from the diffusion and compared to a reference beam, the modulations of the reflected beam are of the order of 10 -5 therefore considerable averaging is required in order to reproduce a waveform with a meaningful signal to noise ratio. Unlike the E-beam, the LVP system is extremely sensitive to measurement conditions and operating environment. If any of these is not optimal, it is unlikely that the signal will rise out of the noise.


### Time resolved light emission microscopy


Time resolved light emission microscopy


(TRLEM) PICA or TRLEM (4) techniques are non-invasive, passive optical methods for measuring electrical switching of CMOS transistors in integrated circuits. The technique is based on the detection and analysis of the weak light emission, which is emitted by field effect transistors during switching. This technology relies on the dramatic improvement in measurement methods for temporally resolved, extremely faint, optical signals. Since hot carrier emission is exponentially dependent on the effective gate length and the bias voltage, the detection capability, with state of the art detectors, is drastically reduced at bias voltages lower then 1.4V for 0.13um gate length. Similar to the LVP, the stimulating pattern must run in loop and 10 3 -10 5 runs are required for  > 3 SNR.


### Application of Emission Microscopy (EM) for


Application of Emission Microscopy (EM) for


functional FA Traditionally EM is applied for a small family of functional failures  (5) , which generate steady state emissions. For photon detection using a dynamically changing test vector, it is required that the time of applying failing voltage conditions be longer then the minimum detection limit. This limit with the advanced MCT detector is in the order of several mSec. If we require a clear image of the emission site one should either freeze the test conditions, as shown in figure  1 , or gate the emission acquisition to the failing vectors. The second procedure is very difficult to implement with MCT detectors since the failing period may take one or only a few clock cycles, which is too short for good signal to noise ratio unless dynamic noise subtraction hardware is used. The freezing technique was developed by Ishii et al  (2) , who named the technique: Dynamic fault isolation with Emission Microscopy (dEMS). We prefer to use the term pseudo-dynamic instead of dynamic (PDEM) since the test vector is actually frozen and not dynamic. The concept behind the PDEM technique is the creation of steady failing conditions under which constant photon emission is generated from the failing node. Photon emission is generated only if the failure is related to current consumption conditions during one or more vectors along the run. This, for example, can be due to contentions or floating gates. In order to halt the device at the desired point we must have total control over all signal transitions inside the device circuits i.e. no PLL or other independent oscillators should be active at any time and propagate internal signals independently. Full control over internal states in the device is coming from the input pins connected to the ATE. It is usually extremely difficult to halt the patterns without ATE.
 Another essential pre-condition for the PDEM technique is knowledge of the exact temporal location of the failure. This information is normally received by cross testing of the device at various conditions and patterns. The analyst must bare in mind that emission conditions may sometimes be generated in a healthy device at one point or another during normal operation, therefore it may be required to check several emission sites and to determine which one is leading to the failure.


### Case study


Case study


### Failure history


Failure history


Device showed significant yield loss at low voltage and low temperature testing conditions. The detailed analysis of voltage -frequency (Shmoo plot) and voltage -temperature relations showed that the most important factor was supply voltage level, where the proper functional operation was limited above an original design target. The failure was almost independent of frequency over the whole operational range (from nominal frequency and lower). Temperature changes had little influence on the failure voltage level, where a decrease of the ambient temperature led to an increase in the failure voltage level. Analysis on evaluation board (EVB) demonstrated that the failure appeared during access to embedded SRAM memory.


Further analysis of March LR based memory tests allowed to minimize test to single write and read operation on any memory location. The result was that, "write and read accesses at high voltage are successful", "write access at high voltage and read at low" passes and "write access at low voltage and read at high" fails.


Figure  3  -LVP measurements of the memory output during read cycle -This measurement done by the LVP misled the analysts; since the failure was not stable, while fetching from the memory it appeared as if the test was passing at 1.3V, while actually it passed only occasionally. Had the analysis continued using LVP, there would have been no chance of finding the root cause of the failure. The broken line is placed to guide the eye.


### Measurements with LVP


Measurements with LVP


A special pattern was prepared to run on ATE. In this test five addresses were consecutively written and followed by five read cycles. A section of the pattern is shown in figure  2 . The first signal that was probed with the LVP was the internal memory bi-directional failing data bus, which is common to the entire memory group. The signal transitions on the data bus were measured as good signals in all voltage conditions during the write access, which indicated that data approached the memory properly. When we tried to measure during the read cycle we discovered that a measurable signal appeared also during read at low voltage on the data bus, where it was supposed to be failing (no read). These measurements are presented in figure  3 . From these waveforms we were not able to determine weather data succeeded to be written into the memory bit-cells during the write access. This measurement appeared to be contradicting the results obtained while testing on the evaluation board.


### Failure isolation with PDEM technique


Failure isolation with PDEM technique


At this point a new approach was taken. Since we suspected that this failure might be due to some sort of contention that was aggravated at lower temperatures and voltages, the idea was to investigate this failure using the PDEM technique. The halting points are described at figure 2. From examination of the memory group buffer during emission we indeed discovered a single emission point that appears while write access is performed (in some cases also during read). The emission spot is shown in figure  4 . With the aid of CAD alignment, we were able to correlate the emission spot with a flip-flop (FF) cell in the row clock module (which generates the clock signal for the memory group).


Figure  4 -Emission image of the failure siteemission appeared only when the test was halted at the points where contention conditions were developed and the voltage was lower then 1.3V. At this voltage the feedback transistor did not allow switching of the latch (see figure  5 ).


The FF cell schematic is presented in figure  5  and the failure was further localized to the feedback inverter of the master latch of this cell. The localization allowed us to speculate that the root cause of the failure is contention between the feedback inverter, and the driver into the FF cell. This driver was designed with marginal strength that was enhanced with process variations. With logic simulations it was clear that if the master latch was not inverted the memory clock will not be generated properly. In order to verify the simulation results beyond any doubt we microprobed the clock output by growing a pad on this signal from the backside. The procedure for backside pad growth is long and delicate and could be approached when we have concrete evidence for the failure location. The probing results are presented in figure  6  for the read cycled at 1.5V and 1.3V. The measurements show that the clock behaves most of the time as expected, and fails at 1.3V, nevertheless part of the loops pass the test, and failure is arbitrary. This phenomenon is demonstrated during the read where the 2 last cycles are passing. As we increase the voltage toward the passing voltage the amount of passing cycles increases. This measurement explains the extreme difficulty in measuring with the LVP and the diminished magnitude of the pulse at 1.3V, which is averaging over passing and failing (no pulse) sampling.
