Localization of ESD damages in ICs is often a complex task, especially if one needs to detect latent or soft ESD damages that can later result in field failures. ESD damages in CMOS ICs are known to induce gate oxide degradation or punch-through, metal and/or silicon melting that partially or completely short-circuit p-n junctions, and metal fusing. Such defects can result in open or short circuits, increased leakage, decreased breakdown voltage or soft junction 1 . Emission microscopy has been commonly used to localize ESD damages in CMOS ICs. However it implies that the ESD damage does not completely short-circuit the p-n junctions or the gate oxide. It also implies that the bias voltage and the leakage current are large enough to generate significant emission.


The objective of this paper is to present the attractiveness of laser beam based techniques at precisely and non-destructively localizing ESD damage in Silicon as well as in GaAs ICs. The Thermal Laser Stimulation (TLS) technique, also known as OBIRCH 2 or TIVA 3 , has been shown to be more sensitive than Emission Microscopy at detecting such damage under low voltage and current consumption. More importantly, when used under no bias condition, it has proven to be capable of localizing ESD defects within the silicon substrate. This non-biased Thermal Laser Stimulation (NB-TLS) technique, also called SEI 3 , detects the Seebeck voltage generated upon laser heating of a thermocouple composed of molten silicon (ESD damaged silicon) and crystalline silicon. This capability is highly beneficial when it comes to localizing latent ESD damages for the following reason: under no bias there is no defect alteration.


The pulsed Optical Beam Induced Current technique 4  was also studied under no biasing condition (NB-OBIC). This technique uses a visible or a near-IR laser of energy above the silicon band-gap to generate electron-hole pairs in the silicon. Due to the different nature of the laser-matter interaction, the NB-OBIC technique proved to be complementary to the Thermal Laser Stimulation technique in several ways. In addition to allowing precise localization of ESD damaged p-n junctions, it permits one to gain insight into the ESD induced degradation.


### Thermal Laser Stimulation


Thermal Laser Stimulation


### Principles behind TLS and NB-TLS


Principles behind TLS and NB-TLS


The Thermal Laser Stimulation technique has been shown to be able to localize current related defects in the IC's metallic elements as well as in the silicon and polysilicon layers 5 . It uses a near-IR laser of energy below the silicon band-gap to generate heat in the absorbing elements of ICs. The deposited laser power, which is converted into thermal power, modifies the electrical properties of the medium, namely its resistivity, according to:


∆ρ = ρ 0 α TCR ∆T (1)


where ρ 0 is the resistivity, α TCR the resistance thermal coefficient, and ∆T the temperature variation.


When the device under test is biased, the thermally induced resistance variation is monitored through the device voltage or current consumption depending on the biasing method, as illustrated by the following equations:


∆V = ∆R I (2) ∆I = -(∆R/R 2 )V (3)


Since the heating and the resistance variation are strongly dependent on the heated structure, resistive defects such as filaments and short-circuits can be precisely located by correlating the induced current or voltage variations with the laser spot location.


Under the no bias condition, the Thermal Laser Stimulation technique makes use of the Seebeck effect to detect thermocouples 6 . When a thermocouple composed of two different materials is heated, a Seebeck voltage, based on the generation of an electromotive force by temperature gradients, is induced according to:


∆V = (Q 1 -Q 2 )∆T = Q 1-2 ∆T (4)


where Q 1 , Q 2 and Q 1-2 are respectively the thermoelectric power of each material and the relative thermoelectric power of the two materials.


This thermally induced voltage variation is detected in a straightforward manner with a low noise voltage amplifier. The polarity of the Seebeck voltage depends on the induced temperature gradient.


The non-biased Thermal Laser Stimulation (NB-TLS) technique allows, in principle, the visualization and localization of material discontinuities, which can be defect induced. These would be undetectable using the TLS technique since the Seebeck contribution is most often negligible in comparison to the current or voltage variations occurring when the device under test is biased. Another advantage of the NB-TLS technique is the very small electrical power involved, which is in the order of picoWatts. The defects, as well as the device under test, are therefore unaltered upon NB-TLS testing.


### TLS System


TLS System


The Thermal Laser Stimulation technique is implemented at the CNES on the PHEMOS-1000 emission microscope from Hamamatsu. This system integrates a confocal laser-scanning microscope that uses an infrared-laser, which can be utilized to perform TLS studies (it uses a wavelength of 1.3µm and power of 100mW). A specific voltage/current amplifier developed at the CNES, which is described elsewhere 7 , is used to pick up the weak voltage or current variations upon thermal laser stimulation. Both Emission Microscopy and Thermal Laser Stimulation tests can be performed using the same electrical setup.


The Thermal Laser Stimulation images of the power consumption variations are visualized using Hamamatsu's acquisition card and software. A precise localization of the TLS signal is obtained by superposing the TLS images on the laser-reflected images taken with the infrared laser-scanning microscope.


### Localization of ESD Defects in Silicon ICs using TLS and NB-TLS


Localization of ESD Defects in Silicon ICs using TLS and NB-TLS


### Experimental Results on ESD Protection Test Structures


It was found experimentally that ESD defects could be detected with the Thermal Laser Stimulation technique. It is illustrated here on a failed ESD protection test structure presenting a leakage current of 26µA under 5V bias. Using the TLS technique at this voltage, the defect was localized in the p-n junction of the latchup guard ring of the protection structure. Figure  1  shows the TLS image of the current induced variations as well as its superposition on the laser reflected image obtained with a 20x objective. A 200x magnification of the localized defect is shown in Figure  2 . The ESD defect is most likely a molten silicon filament causing current leakage by short circuiting the p-n junction. Upon Thermal Laser Stimulation, this filament is preferentially heated thus modifying its resistivity. The small size of the defect results in a large resistance variation, therefore allowing its detection through the current variation. Note that Emission Microscopy did not detect any emission as the p-n junction is short-circuited by the ESD induced defect.


Most interestingly, the defect could be localized without any bias applied to the protection test structure as shown in the right image of Figure  2 .


The NB-TLS signal can be explained by the presence of a thermocouple made of a vertical junction between the previously observed molten silicon filament with the crystalline silicon layer. The Thermal Laser Stimulation of the upper junction generates a temperature difference between the two materials that induces a Seebeck voltage detectable by the CNES amplifier. This hypothesis is verified on other case studies, related here in the following section, through physical analysis.


### Application to ESD Latent Defect localization in Prototype and Commercial ICs


Application to ESD Latent Defect localization in Prototype and Commercial ICs


The application of the Thermal Laser Stimulation technique to the localization of ESD latent defects is presented through several examples. As mentioned previously, the localization of such defects is a challenging task. First they are quite difficult to detect electrically since the device is still functional and the defect can be inside the device's core. In addition, latent ESD defects are invisible to optical microscopy, and conventional localization techniques such as emission microscopy cannot detect them without significantly degrading the physical defect. Nonetheless, these defects need to be precisely localized to allow for their understanding since, as will be discussed later, they will inevitably result in device field failure.


Several prototype and commercial ICs were ESD stressed according to the JEDEC standard Human Body Model (HBM) and Machine Model (MM) in order to generate latent defects. The methodology used during ESD stressing is as follows: the I(V) characteristics of several I/O protection structures were characterized. The asymptotic voltage of the I(V) curve, shown in Figure  3 , was monitored. HBM or MM stresses, generated using a commercial ESD tester, were successively applied to the I/O until a shift in the asymptotic voltage was detected. An example of I(V) characteristic obtained on an I/O after ESD stress is also shown in Figure  3 . The functionality of the protection structure is preserved. However the threshold voltage is slightly lower than before ESD stressing. Physical analysis of one of the ESD stressed devices was performed. After removing the silicon oxide by plasma etching, the silicon surface was observed using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM). In the image shown in Figure  5 , a filament short-circuiting the metallization with the substrate is observed. As could be expected, Energy Dispersive X-Ray (EDX) analysis identified silicon as well as aluminum in the defect. The presence of this molten silicon/aluminum filament explains the observed NB-TLS signal. The interface between this filament and the crystalline silicon substrate generated a non-negligible Seebeck voltage when heated by the laser.


### Example #2: HBM ESD stressed commercial IC


Example #2: HBM ESD stressed commercial IC


This second example also illustrates the ability of the NB-TLS technique to non-destructively localize several ESD damages induced in the protection structure of a commercial IC. Three successive HBM ESD stresses of 6kV were applied on one of the I/O. The obtained NB-TLS image acquired with a 50x objective on the full protection structure is shown in Figure  6 . Several sensitive points could be detected in the depletion region of the protection structure's p-n junction. In order to understand the origin of this NB-TLS signature, physical analysis of the ESD stressed protection structure was undertaken. A SEM image of the silicon surface obtained after silicon oxide removal by plasma etching is shown in Figure  7 . In this case, several holes could be observed in the Si substrate. The presence of these holes is explained by preferential etching of the ESD induced defects by the plasma due to the presence of oxygen in the silicon. Upon ESD stressing, the oxygen from the silicon oxide is introduced into the ESD molten silicon spikes. The thermocouple created by this amorphous silicon layer with the crystalline silicon substrate explains the observed NB-TLS signal. In order to obtain a shift in the voltage threshold, more than 20 consecutive HBM stresses were performed at 6kV. The ESD stressed ICs were tested using the NB-TLS technique. However, no signal was detected this time. Therefore the ICs were biased to 100mV in order to obtain a leakage current less than 100µA. Note that the normal threshold voltage of these devices is in the order of 300mV. The TLS image obtained at a 200x magnification on one of the ESD stressed prototype ICs is shown in Figure  8 . For all the ESD stressed ICs, the defect is always localized on the drain side of the GGNMOS gate contact. A SEM image obtained after removing the silicon oxide by plasma etching shows two holes at the gate and silicon substrate level (Figure  9 ). The presence of these holes is explained by the preferential etching of ESD induced polysilicon filaments. These filaments originate from the gate. They extend into the silicon substrate thus partially short-circuiting the gate to drain p-n junction. This "weak point" in the protection structure was also confirmed on several protection test structures.


### Backside Localization of ESD Defects in GaAs ICs Using TLS


Backside Localization of ESD Defects in GaAs ICs Using TLS


This case study is presented in order to illustrate the ability of the TLS technique to localize ESD defects from the backside of GaAs ICs. Several failed MMIC (Microwave Monolithic Integrated Circuit) amplifiers were characterized. An abnormal leakage current ranging from tens of microamps to hundreds of microamps was measured when the devices were submitted to the 3V operating bias. The GaAs ICs, comprised of three gold metal layers, are packaged in SOP plastic packages. Front side decapsulation was attempted but most often resulted in the loss of device functionality. The nitric and sulfuric acids used to decapsulate the plastic resin are found to attack the Benzocyclobutene (BCB) dielectric used in these GaAs ICs.


The main advantage of backside analysis in this case study is the ease of backside decapsulation as  The efficiency of Thermal Laser Stimulation to localize current related defects under low voltage is explained by the fact that the Thermal Laser Stimulation signal is proportional to the leakage current. This is not exactly the case for emission microscopy for which under a certain bias no emission occurs. To observe emission from the backside of the GaAs devices, the bias had to be increased to 10V. However it resulted in defect alteration and further device degradation. As indicated by an arrow in the emission image obtained with a 100x objective shown in Figure  12 , a molten metal path was induced upon high voltage biasing. The MESFET transistor along this molten path is not emitting since it is completely short-circuited. However the other two MESFET transistors connected to the Vdd line are emitting, one more strongly than the other, as can be expected from the TLS results. Only using the Thermal Laser Stimulation technique could the defect be localized without further degrading the device. This result


### Vdd line


Vdd line


illustrates well the negative effect of over stressing the device and the need to perform failure analysis under normal operating conditions or even under lower biases. OBIC experiments were performed with the pulsed laser test bench located at the IXL laboratory. This experimental set-up is shown in Figure  14 , described in detail elsewhere 8 , and has the following features.


The main laser source delivers picosecond pulses. Its repetition rate is adjustable using a pulse picker and its wavelength is continuously tunable from 750nm to 1080nm. The whole system is automated and allows both frontside and backside OBIC imaging of ICs. The ability to control the repetition rate with an external signal allows for using a lock-in detection scheme that permits enhancement of the signal to noise ratio as well as the performance of dynamic studies. The study presented here was performed using a laser wavelength of 800nm, which corresponds to the front side configuration. The OBIC signal is monitored using both current and lock-in amplifiers. The repetition rate is set to 40 kHz according to the relaxation time of the OBIC signal, previously measured at several points on the IC.


Figure  14 : Experimental set-up of the pulsed OBIC system.


The NB-OBIC studies are performed on the same ESD stressed protection test structure characterized previously by Thermal Laser Stimulation. The corresponding TLS and NB-TLS images were shown in Figure  1  and Figure  2 . The NB-OBIC map obtained in the area of interest using a 50x objective and a 2µm translation stage step is shown in Figure  15 . Note that a thresholding procedure, which is described below, was applied on the NB-OBIC image. The circled area in the NB-OBIC map of Figure  15  points a white region in the junction corresponding to a diminution of the OBIC signal. This p-n junction corresponds to the one where the TLS defect was located previously. In order to evaluate the spatial resolution of this weak OBIC signal, further studies were performed with a 100x objective and a translation stage step of 0.3µm. The laser beam has a spot size of 1µm when focused.


First the NB-OBIC signal obtained at the center of the full width of the failed p-n junction is characterized. As can be seen in Figure  16 , the signal alteration due to the defect is about 3% of the global optical beam induced current. The thresholding procedure applied to the NB-OBIC images is also illustrated in this figure. It consists of setting to black all the pixels above a given threshold.


The NB-OBIC image of the full p-n junction area clearly reveals an OBIC signal reduction at the TLS localized molten silicon ESD defect. This signal reduction is represented in white in Figure  17 . For comparison, the obtained TLS image of the defect is also shown in Figure  17 .


The reduction of the Optical Beam Induced Current signal can be attributed to several factors: i) reduction of the electron-hole pair generation at the defect, ii) increased recombination sites at the defect level, and iii) alteration of the electric field in the space charge region, caused by the defect. The band structure of the silicon is most likely altered upon ESD stress and no generation should occur at the molten silicon filament. However, due to the small size of the defect as compared to the laser beam spot size, this effect should not be predominant. In fact, the defect might create recombination centers that would reduce the optical beam induced currents in its vicinity. Finally, the molten silicon defect short-circuits the p-n junction. The built-in electrical field should therefore vanish in the defect area. The electron-holes pairs created by the laser beam will recombine, thus reducing further the detected OBIC signal.


The NB-OBIC technique clearly offers complementary information to that obtained with the TLS and NB-TLS techniques. However, to correctly interpret the NB-OBIC maps, more studies are needed to understand the generation/recombination characteristics of ESD damaged p-n junctions. Physical simulations are presently undergoing aimed at evaluating the influence of a molten silicon filament on the Optical Beam Induced Current.


Single Contact Optical Beam Induced Current (SCOBIC) 9 analysis was also attempted but did not yield as good results as those from the NB-OBIC technique. The p-n junctions could be identified as expected from this technique, but the ESD induced TLS NB-OBIC defect could not be revealed due to the very low currents obtained during SCOBIC. Improvements in the testing methodology are being studied in order to optimize this technique for ESD defect localization as well.


### Conclusion


In this paper two laser beam based techniques dedicated to defect localization in integrated circuits were characterized. Thermal Laser Stimulation has proven to be a reliable technique to non-destructively localize ESD damage in silicon and gallium arsenide ICs. Its application under non-biased conditions could reveal ESD molten silicon defects in the silicon substrate. ESD defects induced in the polysilicon and metal layers could also be detected under low bias voltage and low current consumption. Non-biased OBIC also proved to be a highly sensitive technique to non-destructively detect and analyze ESD induced defects inside the active areas of the silicon substrate. Both techniques provided complementary information regarding ESD degradation occurring in p-n junctions. However, further studies need to be performed in order to understand the influence of a junction defect on the optical beam induced current.


The laser beam based techniques studied here offer a good perspective when it comes to the localization of ESD induced latent defects. The Thermal Laser Stimulation technique has shown to be able to nondestructively detect such defects where conventional techniques such as emission microscopy could not. A thorough study of latent defects should therefore be undertaken rapidly knowing that these defects can result in device functionality losses during life-span.


### Introduction to Milling of Cu


Introduction to Milling of Cu


Several years ago the anticipated introduction of Cu into devices set off a flurry of activity on developing FIB milling protocols for Cu. After it became clear that thick, large grained Cu did not mill smoothly (Figure  1 ), efforts quickly turned to GAE processes. Unfortunately the most common GAE processes (chlorine, bromine and iodine-based etches) were not successful in cleanly 1 removing Cu. Moreover corrosive, electrically conductive Cu halides spontaneously formed (Figure  2 ) on exposed Cu surfaces 2 . Less common etches such as NO 2 were tried; the results were qualitatively similar 3 to those shown in Figure  2 . The failure of Cu GAE processes is attributed to the fact that Cu halides are not volatile at room temperature. Elevated temperature studies of Cl 2 and Br 2 GAE on a 250°C heated substrate (hot stage) showed that Cu halides did not volatilize at these temperatures. Moreover, at elevated temperatures, Cu halide debris formed over a wider area of Cu than at room temperature. Note: Cu halides form spontaneously (beam not required) on any Cu surfaces that have been "depassivated" by a scan with the Ga beam. Fluorine, on the other hand, does not form mounds of CuFx debris. Cu mills more smoothly in the presence of fluorine but the milling rate is inhibited relative to normal FIB milling. This fact is useful when accessing thin Cu interconnect lines under a layer of insulation using the XeF 2 GAE process.


### Milling of Thick Cu (CoppeRx™)


Milling of Thick Cu (CoppeRx™)


Following the unsuccessful attempts to develop a GAE process for Cu, a rather novel, room temperature protocol (US. Patent 6,322,672 B1) was developed which cleanly mills thick, polycrystalline Cu (Figure  3 ) without the aid of corrosive etches 4 ; this process is marketed as CoppeRx™. The fact that CoppeRx™ is selective for Cu relative to dielectric materials contributes to smooth Cu clearing with minimal over etch (normally 0.1-0.2µm) into the underlying dielectric. At this time, most CoppeRx™ studies have been done with SiO 2 based dielectrics, but not with spin-on organic materials. Note that the 10µm x 10µm box in Figure  3  was milled in 2 ¼ minutes.


### CoppeRx™ Science


CoppeRx™ Science


The principles behind the CoppeRx™ protocol for milling thick, large-grained, polycrystalline Cu are based on single crystal Cu studies. Three orientations of Cu, a face centered cubic crystal structure, differ by 3-4 X in milling rates (Table  1 ). The fastest, the (111) orientation, also has the highest packing density (91%); the slowest, (110), has the lowest (51%). This supports the theory that channeling contrast, i.e. variations in Ga ion penetration depth and variations in secondary electron emissions, are related to milling efficiency. Moreover, the (110) structure forms a Cu 3 Ga phase 5 that is extremely resistant to milling, further reducing the removal rate of this grain orientation. These single crystal studies explain why polycrystalline Cu mills unevenly; these studies also suggested approaches for polycrystalline milling that have been incorporated into CoppeRx™.


### Table 1


Table 1


Single crystal, face centered cubic Cu milling rates. The effect of heavy atoms (tungsten) on the milling rates is also presented. Milling dose = 5nC/µm 2 .


### CoppeRx™ -Step 1


Step 1 of CoppeRx™ involves milling an "egg crate" topography into polycrystalline Cu (Figure  4 ). This topography is created while flowing W(CO) 6 gas which is normally used to deposit metal structures. The Step 1 Rationale is: a. The egg crate topography inhibits the formation and propagation of the slow milling Cu 3 Ga phase. It had been noted that Cu 3 Ga forms only in (110) Cu surfaces which are perpendicular to the incident Ga beam; it did not form on sidewalls and contours that were angled, rather than perpendicular, to the Ga beam. Note: the single crystal studies were done with a 50kV Ga beam; however the CoppeRx™ protocol is also successful with a 25-30 kV Ga beam. b. Surfaces that are angled, rather than perpendicular, to the Ga beam mill faster 6 . c. W(CO) 6 creates a heavy atom surface layer (U.S. Patent Application number 20,010,053,605) that scatters incident Ga ions, thereby reducing the channeling influences on the Cu milling rate. The single crystal study, (Table  1 ), empirically established that W(CO) 6 does level the milling rates of (111), (  100 ) and (110) orientations.


Devices ranging in complexity from microprocessors to standard components are currently being offered in flip chip configuration and gaining market acceptance. Bare solder bumped silicon chips are either attached directly to the customer's board (Direct Chip Attach, DCA) or packaged in an interposing substrate such as a Flip Chip Ball Grid Array (FCBGA) depending on the application and board pitch requirements. This packaging is preferred over traditional wire bonding in almost every application due to its superior electrical performance, and inherent compact design. Coupled with its advantages, flip chip packaging also creates handling and reliability issues, which must be addressed in detail. One area of intense study is the reliability of the under bump metallurgy (UBM)  [1] .


Although there are different UBM schemes, their basic function is threefold: to form an adhesion layer to the device I/O pad, to form a solderable surface to the bump, and to create a diffusion barrier preventing solder from diffusing through the UBM to the aluminum device I/O pad. If solder were to diffuse through the barrier layer and reach a non-solderable surface such as aluminum, solder joint adhesion would be lost and failure would eventually occur  [2] .


One UBM used in the industry today, Al/Ni-V/Cu, is the subject of this paper. The UBM aluminum metallization layer is in direct contact with the device I/O pad, also composed of aluminum. The next layer is Ni-V, which is a diffusion barrier to prevent the solder from contacting the aluminum surface. The final layer, copper, prevents oxidation of Ni-V before formation of the solder bump and provides a solderable surface for the solder bump. The solder bumps discussed in this paper are 63Sn/37Pb eutectic solder and are henceforth referred to as "solder." Minimal diffusion of the Ni-V barrier layer into the solder is crucial to the solder joint reliability and must be fully characterized to ensure that the system will withstand the thermal excursions expected in a given application.


The presence of gold, even in low concentrations, will greatly expedite diffusion of the Ni in the Ni-V barrier layer  [3] . Gold enters the solder joint via the gold plated pad finish on the customer's circuit board or on the interposing substrate when the device is mounted in a FCBGA package. A concentration of 1.2 wt% gold can accelerate the Ni diffusion rate by a factor of 400 compared to the case of no gold  [3] . As the device is subjected to reflows and thermal aging, the UBM Cu diffuses into the Sn in the solder subjecting the Ni-V to Sn exposure. Continued time at elevated temperature will form Ni 3 Sn 4 intermetallic, eventually degrading the Ni-V barrier integrity. If the Ni-V is entirely consumed, failure at the interface will eventually occur  [3] . A reliable method for measuring gold concentration in the 0.1 to 1 wt% range would facilitate future characterization and development projects.


Energy dispersive x-ray microanalysis (EDS) is a common tool for metallurgical analysis based on measurement of characteristic x-ray line energy and intensity. When the electron beam from a scanning electron microscope (SEM) is used to excite the x-rays, elemental identification and concentration measurements with analysis volumes in the micrometer range are possible. Quantitative x-ray analysis is performed by comparing the x-ray peak integral of the sample to that of a known standard. If the composition of the standard is considerably different than that of the sample, then corrections to account for absorption and fluorescence must be applied. When x-rays are generated by electron beam, not only are the characteristic x-ray lines produced, but also a continuous background or bremsstrahlung spectrum results. This background must be accurately removed from the characteristic peak for accurate quantification. Due to the statistical nature of x-ray generation, there is always a natural variation in the characteristic and background integrals. The minimum detection limit for the analysis is approached when the peak integral is on the order of the natural variation of the background integral under the peak. Such was the case for Au in the Sn/Pb solder bumps in this analysis. Although many detailed statistical treatments of the EDS x-ray microanalysis measurement capability exist  [6, 7] , the authors believe that few analysts use them often citing a commonly accepted value of approximately 0.1 wt.% for heavy elements.


Unfortunately, for the case of Au in Sn/Pb solder, the EDS detection limit was found to be considerably worse. Wavelength dispersive x-ray microanalysis (WDS) is typically considered to be about 10X more sensitive than EDS, however this tool was not available.


Another analytical technique which has found widespread use for determining phase diagrams for different metal systems is Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC)  [4, 5] . This technique utilizes a closed system where a sample and reference are heated at a constant rate with the heat flow in and out of the sample and reference monitored differentially.


Sensitive melting behavior of solid solution of metals such as solders can be determined accurately. It was thought that this technique might provide the sensitivity needed for determination of very low Au concentrations (0.1 -1.0%) in a Sn/Pb eutectic solder.


The original EDS x-ray microanalysis of the solder bumps will first be described. Since this appeared inadequate to measure Au concentrations expected to be in the 0.25 -1.0 % range an experiment was devised to generate solder "standards" with known Au concentrations and determine the EDS sensitivity by analyzing these samples. When it was found that EDS was not capable of measuring Au in Pb/Sn solder in the range of interest, the sensitivity of DSC was tested using the same "standards." Once it was found that DSC could measure the range of interest, it was used successfully to measure gold concentration in the original bumps.


Solder Bump EDS SEM/EDS x-ray microanalysis for Au concentration was performed on cross-sectioned reflowed bumps expected to contain about 0.5 wt% Au in the solder. The samples were coated with a thin layer of evaporated carbon to eliminate charging. Spectra were acquired using a 10mm 2 SiLi EDS detector (133 eV resolution) with a 30 degree take off angle and 25 mm distance from the crystal to sample in a field emission SEM at 30 keV beam energy. Beam current was adjusted to produce about 2000 counts per second (cps) using the longest pulse processor time constant. Acquisitions were run for 300 sec live time with the electron beam scanning an area of about 250 um by 250 um, comprising most of the bump. Somewhat to our surprise, neither the Au L peak nor the Au M peak, after striping a similarly acquired Pb M peak, were discernable from the background. An experiment was performed to measure the EDS x-ray microanalysis minimum detection limit for Au in solder.


### Gold in Solder Standards


Gold in Solder Standards


Au in 63Sn/37Pb eutectic solder "standards" were produced by melting measured amounts (to 0.1 mg) of Au and solder in small beakers on a hot plate. The samples were covered with a watersoluble flux and agitated vigorously during melting then quenched in ice water. The beakers were broken to free the solder buttons and the flux removed by ultrasonic cleaning in a water -alcohol mix. 0, 0.11, 0.26, 0.51, 0.76, 1.02, 2.04, 3.46, 5.30, and 6.96 wt% Au in solder standards were produced. Samples for EDS and DSC experiments were cut from the button centers.


### EDS Analysis of Au in Solder Standards


EDS Analysis of Au in Solder Standards


Small pieces of each standard were encapsulated and the surface polished flat in the same manner as were the solder bumps. Carbon was applied to eliminate charging. EDS was performed using the same parameters as had been used for the solder bumps.


The standardless semiquant program resident in the EDS tool was generating erratic results so it was decided to attempt to manually generate a calibration curve by plotting the ratio of the Au / Sn peak integrals against the known Au concentrations.


Since the Au M peak is severely overlapped by the Pb M peak (figure  1 ), the Pb peak was stripped from each spectrum using a Pb spectrum from the solder acquired under the same conditions and using the vendor's stripping routine. The peak and background integrals were calculated by the EDS tool using appropriate regions of interest. Although the Au M line was severely overlapped, it had a significantly larger peak integral at 30 keV beam energy than the Au L, which was not overlapped. Calibration curves were produced by plotting Au M / Sn L, and Au L / Sn L ratios against their respective known Au concentrations to determine which curve produced the better analytical precision. Four runs were made of each standard from 1 to 7 wt% Au in solder and the results graphed. The results for the Au M peak are shown in figure  2 . No useful information could be obtained for standards with less than or equal to 0.76 wt% Au.


### DSC Analysis of Au in Solder Standards


DSC Analysis of Au in Solder Standards


The solder bumps used for analysis were manually excised with a tweezer and scalpel, under a stereomicroscope from substrates that had not been subjected to any thermal aging, but had been subjected to two short reflows.


A heat flux differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) was used for determining the eutectic melt temperatures. The cell uses a constantan disk as its primary means of transferring heat to the sample and reference platforms. Samples were encapsulated in anodized aluminum pans. The differential heat flow to the sample and reference was monitored by area thermocouples that were formed by a junction of the constantan disk and chromel wafers that covered the underside of the platforms. Chromel and alumel wires that are attached to the chromel wafers form thermocouples that directly monitor the sample temperature. Constant calorimetric sensitivity is maintained throughout the temperature range of the cell by electronic linearization of a cell calibration coefficient. The standards and the bumps were subjected to a 3°C/minute linear heating rate in a flowing N 2 ambient. The total heat flow as a function of temperature was recorded. The sample was heated from 0°C to 250°C. The sample was then cooled to 0°C at 3°C/minute and reheated to 250°C using the same conditions as the first heating. The results of the second heating were used for analysis. The sample size for the bumps and the standards was 0.1-0.2 mg.


The reproducibility of the DSC technique was found to be excellent.


Heating samples 5 times in succession resulted in a temperature measurement error of +/-0.02°C at a 95% confidence limit.


### Results / Discussion


Results / Discussion


### EDS Au in Solder Detection Limit


EDS Au in Solder Detection Limit


The EDS detection limit ultimately depends on the ability to perceive characteristic x-ray counts into a peak above the continuum background spectrum. X-ray counts into a peak depend on the elemental concentration, electron beam current, and counting time. On modern FESEMs the beam current is generally high enough that the detector counting rate limit can be approached leaving counting time as the adjustable operation parameter. A live time of 300 sec was chosen as the maximum time that an operator would wait when acquiring upwards of 10-20 spectra. A lower detection limit may be achievable if longer counting time was used.


However, a practical consideration of instrument drift and other instabilities will ultimately limit the maximum usable counting time.


Inspection of the calibration curve indicates the precision obtained is not sufficient to measure gold concentrations below 1.0 wt%, based on the spread of the experimental data points.


In the best case, neglecting all other sources of x-ray count variation other than the natural variation of x-ray emission, the standard deviation can be the described by Poisson statistics as shown in Equation 1  [7] .

where: N = average number x-ray counts in peak Using this criterion, and Equation 2, the 99% confidence interval was used to calculate the error bar on the Au M calibration curve (+/-3 standard deviation) for the 1.06 wt% Au standard, and applied to the graph in Figure  2 .

### DSC Au in Solder Detection Limit


DSC Au in Solder Detection Limit


Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measures heat flow versus time or temperature. DSC provides quantitative information about physical and chemical changes that involve absorption of heat, endothermic, or evolution of heat, exothermic, processes. As such, DSC detects phase transitions such as melting and crystallization.


The presence of Au in the Sn/Pb solder modifies its melting point  [48] . As the gold concentration increases, the solder melting point decreases. When used to monitor the change in the melting point of the solder, DSC serves as an indirect method for measuring the gold content in Sn/Pb solder. The mass of the solder bumps limited the DSC sample size to about 0.2 milligrams. This mass was matched by equally small masses of the calibration sample to minimize DSC errors due to thermal lag when comparing the samples and calibration samples. All samples were run in triplicate with an error of +/-0.1°C at a 95% confidence limit which resulted in +/-0.02 wt% range in measured Au concentration. The repeatability was +/-0.02°C at a 95% confidence limit. The resulting calibration curve shown in Figure  3 , shows good sensitivity for gold in the 0 to 1 wt % range. The DSC method was used successfully for analysis of two differently designed solder bump structures intended to vary the Au concentration.


Analysis was performed on bumps subjected to two short reflows with no thermal aging.


One design measured 0.27 wt% Au while the other measured 0.45 wt% Au. Both experimental measurements correlated with the calculated concentration based on gold thickness and solder volume.


Differential scanning calorimetry was shown to have sufficient sensitivity for measuring between 0.1 and 1 wt% gold with an error of approximately 0.02 wt% Au in eutectic tin/lead solder. This accuracy is sufficient for verifying Au content of bumps in flip chip ball grid array (FCBGA) packages during experiments designed to measure the effect of Au on the UBM reliability. The DSC analysis technique resulted in gold measurements within the expected range when applied to actual bump measurements. This compares to the SEM/EDS measurement capability which was found to be approximately +/-1.2 wt% gold resulting in unacceptably high error when measuring less than a few percent gold in eutectic tin/lead solder. The high error for the SEM/EDS is primarily due to the strong overlap of the Pb M and Au M peaks and small number of x-ray counts accumulated at the Au L line.


The Infrared Emission Microscope (IREM) has been highly successful in detecting and localizing circuit problems and defects during silicon debug, low yield analysis (LYA), and fault isolation of the Pentium ® ||| and Pentium ® 4 Microprocessors. Test vectors that activate failing mechanisms are applied to the processor by a highspeed device tester while docked to the IREM  [1] . Emissions are observed from the backside through a thinned substrate  [2] [3] . A comparison can be made between passing and failing units. An abnormal emission seen on the failing unit but not seen on the passing unit indicates that a defect is likely associated with the abnormal emission, and localization techniques such as alignment to the layout database can be used to determine the location of the defect  [4] . But what happens if no abnormal emission is seen? A new methodology presented in this paper expands the applicability of IREM to include the ability to create an accurate on-die logic map which can be used in silicon debug and fault isolation (FI) to localize the failing location in the event that no abnormal emission is observed.


Based on IREM images obtained from 0.18 µm and 0.13 µm process technology Pentium ® ||| Processors, static emissions (obtained while the clock was halted but the circuit state maintained) were observed that appeared to originate as a result of normal circuit operation. All units showed these emissions, and the emissions were observed to change depending on where the functional pattern was halted. It was hypothesized that these emissions were related to the logic state of the circuits. An investigation was made to see if a correlation existed between the emissions and the logic states of several circuit nodes.


The results showed a clear and consistent correlation between the observed emissions and the simulated logic states of the nodes being "probed". These emissions are seen on the n-and p-diffusions of inverters. If the input to the inverter is logic 0, the n-diffusion region emits. If the input to the inverter is logic 1, the p-diffusion region emits.


Since inverters are such an abundant circuit element, a probing methodology is proposed which makes use of this phenomenon. The input and output logic values of many inverters on the die can be determined by the use of this methodology. Prior logic state mapping techniques have been successfully demonstrated, such as by light-induced voltage alteration (LIVA) with a scanning optical microscope using a 1064 nm laser  [5] . The technique presented here requires no laser stimulus as it passively looks at the static infrared emissions coming from the backside of the die.


### A New IREM Methodology


A New IREM Methodology


During the course of fault isolation and silicon debug of the 0.18 µm and 0.13 µm process technology Pentium ® ||| Processors, IREM has proven itself to be a useful tool. The fault isolation and debug groups logged numerous successes using the IREM, including detection of circuit errata, marginal circuits or layout issues, and manufacturing and reliability issues. The IREM has become a central part of Intel's microprocessor fault isolation and root cause debug flow, shown in figure  1 .


In the case that IREM shows no abnormal emissions, the currently used methods for silicon debug and fault isolation on logic circuits typically involve using Laser Voltage Probing (LVP) and Probeless Fault Isolation techniques. LVP has some limitations including the ability to probe only a single point at a time, the requirement for looping the test pattern with a maximum and minimum loop length, and sometimes long through-put times for acquiring accurate waveforms. Similarly, probeless approaches require long periods of time to run simulations, capture data through scanout or array readouts, and trace schematics to determine the point of failure. The probeless approaches are also limited as only certain signals can be accessed using the design-fortestability (DFT) features, even in full-scan designs. In addition, to be effective at Probeless FI, extensive architecture and circuit knowledge is required on the part of the engineer doing the debug/FI. A new methodology has been developed which has the potential to offer, to some degree, all of these advantages. This technique uses the IREM to perform static logic state mapping by making use of the static emissions that occur due to the visible device emission of Intel's 0.13µm process.


The idea for this methodology came from IREM work done on the 0.18 µm process-based Pentium ® ||| Processor. During debug of this product, the On-Die Clock Shrink (ODCS) feature was used to stop the clock and halt the processor in specific clock states. The ODCS feature is the addition of an edge manipulation circuit in the digital portion of the clock generator. It is primarily used for activation of speedpaths by moving specific clock edges to "shrink" clock cycles and activate speedpaths. The ODCS circuitry also allows for killing individual clock cycles and for stopping the clock altogether. This latter capability was the capability that was used and is the capability upon which the static logic state mapping methodology is based.


When IREM images were obtained in these static states, it was observed that faint static emissions could be seen coming from certain devices. At the time, it was not well understood what these emissions were, so no real investigation of them was made. Also, the ODCS feature at that time could only stop the clock on the low phase, so if any potential for mapping these signals to logic states existed, it could only be applied on half of the processor states.


With the arrival of the 0.13 µm process-based Pentium ® ||| Processor, these emissions were still present, and much more intense. In addition, the new ODCS provided the ability to stop the clock on either the low or high phase. Thus, it was felt that enough potential existed for logic state mapping of these emissions that an investigation was made.


Case studies to determine if IREM static logic state imaging (LSI) was possible were formulated and carried out. The method and results of these case studies are discussed in the next section.


Out of these case studies, the methodology for performing IREM static logic state imaging was developed, and the steps for this are as follows:


1) Initial characterization is performed to determine the signal name and clock cycle that the defect or speedpath is first manifested (e.g. first scanout mismatch).


2) The device tester along with the ODCS capability of the processor (or equivalent stopclock capability) is used to halt the processor at several different clock cycles before the mismatch, while in the failing condition.


3) While the processor is halted but maintaining state, the IREM is used to capture static images of the area of the failing signal.


4) The equivalent region of the layout is overlaid onto the IREM images after appropriate scaling.


5) The overlay images are used to create an on-die logic state map, using the observed relationship between emission and logic states.


If desired, steps 2-5 can be repeated for the passing condition on a passing unit for comparison.


### Results


The first case study was performed in order to gain an understanding of the emissions that had been observed and to attempt to correlate these emissions to the logic simulation.


Buffer circuitry with large drivers was selected to make an initial correlation. These drivers had strong emissions that had been observed to change states over time, thus proving to be ideal candidates for the case study.


A logic state simulation was run to get the expected values with which to correlate the IREM images to. Core cycles were chosen in a range in which the target signals were changing values. This range of core clock cycles in logic simulation was 5605.0 (low phase) to 5607.1 (high phase).


A known good unit was used for the case study. A functional debug tester was used as the tester platform.


The ODCS feature was used to stop the clock at each cycle and each clock phase within the simulated range of core clock cycles.


On the IREM, the area of interest was found and examined by zooming in to 50X magnification. While halting in each clock state, emission images were obtained. An example image is shown in figure  2 . Each IREM image was saved to disk in the IREM digital image format. Each image takes 128 kilobytes of disk space. After the series of 6 images was obtained, the digital zoom feature of the IREM was used to zoom in on the area of interest for each image.


The die layout in the area of interest was captured and overlaid on each of the digitally zoomed emission images. This was done by manually scaling the images and using the transparency and multi-layer features in image editing software. The overlay corresponding to core cycle 5605.1 is shown in figure  3 .


From the overlaid images, it was observed that the large inverters each emitted either on the p-diffusion or on the n-diffusion. Since the simulation had already been run for these signals, the next step was to superimpose the simulated logic values of each inverter over the corresponding locations on the overlaid image. The results of this are shown in figure  4 . Based on the results of this superimposing, it was concluded that the n-diffusion region would emit if the output of the inverter was logic 1, and the p-diffusion region would emit if the output was logic 0 (i.e. emission is seen from the transistor that is not conducting). Some investigation was made to understand the device physics explanation for why the emissions are seen in this way. The physics of the emission mechanism have been modeled by a Chynoweth model of electron-hole pair generation.


The electron excess concentration is determined by the balance of avalanche generation, Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) recombination, and radiative recombination.


The current and electric field distributions were obtained through numerical simulation and the overall radiation was obtained by integrating over all the depletion regions. As the source-drain voltage is increased, an exponential increase in emission intensity is observed. As the channel lengths get narrower with successive process generations, the emission mechanism used in this technique will continue to become more observable, if the supply voltage can be kept relatively constant. The static nature of the technique makes it possible to elevate the supply voltage without overheating the unit under analysis.


From these simulations, it was determined that the emission mechanism being observed is soft avalanche breakdown, in which a high concentration of electron-hole plasma in the drain region recombines in part through indirect radiative recombination.


### Second Case Study


The IREM static logic state mapping technique was used successfully on several cases in FI and debug of the Pentium ® ||| Processor. One of these cases is included to illustrate the practical use of the technique.


One of the product qualification stress tests produced a number of units that failed functional test after stress. In this case, the probeless FI methodology was used, and the failure was isolated to a chain of CMOS inverters driving long interconnect segments. However, further isolation to which exact inverter or signal line was failing was accomplished by use of IREM static logic state imaging.


The failing clock cycle was determined by analysis of scanout and by probeless FI. A logic simulation was run to determine the expected logic states. It was found that the failing signal was supposed to toggle from 0 to 1 at that clock cycle, but instead was stuck at 0.


Next, the ODCS feature was used to halt the clock at the failing cycle and at the preceding cycle. IREM images were obtained at both clock cycles for each inverter along the chain. The layout was then overlaid on these images. Figure  5  shows the emission from one of these inverters at clock cycle 14391.0 (low phase), and figure  6  shows the same inverter at 14391.1 (high phase), the failing clock cycle. In these images, red regions are highest intensity, blue are lowest. Notice that the emission state has clearly toggled for this inverter. At 14391.0, the p-diffusion region is emitting strongly, while at 14391.1, neither the p-diffusion or the ndiffusions are emitting. This would indicate that no bias sufficient to cause emission exists across the source-drain. So while the output is expected to be at logic 1, causing emission at the n-diffusion region, if the output were stuck at zero such a situation would be expected to be observed.


To test the hypothesis that the output of the inverter is stuck at 0, IREM images were then collected at the next inverter in the chain at the same clock cycles. Again, the layout was overlaid on these images.


Figure  7  shows the emission from this inverter at cycle 14391.0, and figure  8  shows its emission at cycle 14391.1. Notice that for this inverter, no toggling was observed. We can conclude from this that the input did not toggle, and that the input signal


SRH RAD SRH e n R R J τ α ∆ ≅ + =


534 must be stuck at zero (because the inverter output emits on its n-diffusion). 1. Static logic state imaging using the IREM is possible on Intel's manufacturing processes due to the shortness of the device channels.


2. Inverters emit in their n-diffusion area if the input is logic 0, or in their p-diffusion area if the input is logic 1. This is based on correlation of the emissions to the simulated values.


3. The intensity of the emissions is proportional to the width of the gates in the inverter. For the same gate width, the n-diffusion region has much higher emission intensity than the pdiffusion region.


4. The technique can be applied to any logic device which contains an inverter, including AND gates, multiplexers, latches, and flip-flops.


Templates can be developed for each type of cell, where the inputs and/or outputs of each cell can be determined by comparison of the IREM overlay images to the templates.


The primary limitation of the technique is the sensitivity of the IREM camera array. While the sensitivity is adequate to detect emissions from medium-to-large inverters, some inverters are too small to differentiate their emissions from the background. This is especially true for the p-diffusion regions. However, by increasing integration time or temperature and moving to alternative scaling methods, even small devices have been successfully logic state imaged. The smallest inverter which was successfully logic state mapped had a PMOS device with W=3 um. Also helping to reduce this limitation will be the Next Generation IREM (NG-IREM), currently in development.


The NG-IREM is expected to increase sensitivity and improve the signal-to-noise ratio, and is expected to be critical for work on the next process technology (90 nm).


Table  1  has been compiled so that the reader can ascertain the differences between LVP probing and IREM logic state mapping. The intent is not to show which method is better, but rather to show that by having both methods available, it increases the range of problems that can be root caused.


The implications of this technique are very meaningful for both silicon debug and fault isolation. At present, if conventional IREM analysis does not produce results, LVP probing and/or Probeless FI techniques must be used.


As discussed previously, both of these techniques have their own limitations. By adding static logic state mapping capability, the IREM becomes an even more useful tool.


Several tools are currently being developed which will automate the tasks of data collection, layout overlay, and logic state mapping. When completed, these tools would greatly speed up the process, providing for up to a 10X improvement in throughput time for silicon debug, LYA, and fault isolation cases. 2 ) improved the technique and coupled an emission microscope to the tester for functional failure analysis of DRAMs and logic LSIs. Using consecutive step-by-step tester halting coupled to a sensitive emission microscope, one is able detect the failure while it occurs. We will describe a failure analysis case in which marginal design and process variations combined to create contention at certain logic states. Since the failure occurred arbitrarily, the use of the traditional LVP, that requires a stable failure, misled the analysts. Furthermore, even if we used advanced tools as PICA, which was actually designed to locate such failures, we believe that there would have been little chance of observing the failure since the failure appeared only below 1.3V where the PICA tool has diminished photon detection sensitivity. For this case the step-by-step halting technique helped to isolate the failure location after a short round of measurements. With the use of logic simulations, the root cause of the failure was clear once the failing gate was known.


The growing need for high frequency devices in the CMOS industry widened the interest in flip-chip packaging for these devices. With the transition to flip-chip assembly and multi layer interconnect, existing techniques for obtaining time resolved waveforms using E-beam probing of metal interconnects from the front side have become obsolete. Once the front side of the chip is inaccessible, electrical measurements of internal nodes can only be obtained from the backside of the die.

Milling of Thin Cu Interconnects

### GAE of Low k Dielectrics


GAE of Low k Dielectrics


Reduced line/space dimensions and increased signal speed in advanced Cu devices requires reduced capacitance in the circuits. A variety of low k (dielectric constant) dielectric materials are being used to this end, namely F and C doped CVD oxides such as Applied Materials' Black Diamond™, a Cdoped SiO 2 and spin-on organic materials such as Dow Chemical's SiLK™. GAE of Doped SiO 2

Accessing Cu through XeF 2 GAE holes in doped oxide benefits from the fact that Cu acts as an etch stop. XeF 2 forms a thin, passivating fluoride layer on the Cu surface, not the large, spontaneously growing grains that are seen with C1, Br and I based etches.

GAE of SiLK™
