Achieving this improved beam profile with the VisION™ column required a column design that emphasized a reduction in ion-ion interactions as the beam was transported within the column.


Two empirical measures of beam quality are imaging evaluations and trench profiles. Images obtained with the VisION™ column are compared to those obtained with the previous generation of FEI columns at 50 and at 30 kV. The 50 kV, Au on carbon images (Figure  5 ) were recorded at a fast scan, simulating conditions used for real time imaging during failure analyses and circuit edit functions. Signal/noise analyses showed 50% improvements in the VisION™ image. At 30 kV and a slower scan speed, improved image resolution with the VisION™ is very obvious for a Cr on quartz sample (Figure  6 ). Note that these imaging improvements are useful in the FIB repair of Cr photolithography masks.


A comparison of profiles of the trench milled with the 50kV VisION™ column and that milled with the previous generation of FEI columns (Figure  7 ) suggests that the current density is distributed more towards the center of the beam with less in the beam tails in the VisION™ column. The two trenches were done with approximately 8pA beams; each required approximately 1 hour to mill. At this time, the most noticeable advantage of the improved beam profile is the higher resolution, real time imaging which enables end-point detection on sub 0.13µm features during milling.


FIB process technologies are presented for milling Cu and low k dielectrics. An oxide with an intermediate resistivity has been formulated for use in design verification of analog and SOC designs. A more Gaussian Ga beam is proving useful (and necessary) for accessing sub 0.13µm features in advanced devices.


Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Circuit Edit (CE) technology continues to be used extensively in the debug and validation of modern multi-GHz microprocessors  [1, 2, 3] .


Critical applications include the identification of performance limiting circuits and the prototype verification of engineering change orders (ECO) prior to the costly silicon implementation. Furthermore, FIB CE technology is beginning to be used in the debug of network chips designed for the current 10Gb/s and the next generation 40Gb/s optical communication (OC) data rate standards  [4] . However, despite the increasing reliance upon FIB CE technology to validate and debug ICs operating at microwave frequencies, little attention has been directed towards understanding the high-frequency characteristics of the interconnects fabricated using FIB technology and more importantly the impact that these interconnects have on the critical timing of modern VLSI circuits. Such interconnects are routinely fabricated on the backside of locally thinned C4 packaged ICs for the purpose of reconfiguring on-die signal paths and can span distances of several hundred microns or more. * A histogram of backside interconnect lengths encountered during the debug of a leading edge microprocessor is shown below in Figure  1 . The histogram shows that circuit edit modification interconnects cover a large range, with heavy utilization for short jumpers and a diminished percentage of lines greater than 60um. Of particular concern is the relatively poor conductivity of FIB deposited metal, which can limit the use of FIB metallization in some common CE scenarios. The backside FIB interconnect introduces an additional time delay to the electrical signal propagating through it, the magnitude of which can be appreciable in modern VLSI technologies. If unaccounted for in the design of the ECO, the additional signal delay can lead to erroneous conclusions about the root cause for a system's underperformance. This is particularly true if the ECO is implemented to fix a subtle timing issue. Therefore, signal delays incurred by the backside interconnect should be minimized where possible and at a minimum should be thoroughly characterized to achieve near one-to-one matching between the CE and ECO.


### Materials and Technology


Materials and Technology


The amount of signal delay incurred by propagation through the backside interconnect is determined by the electrical properties of the interconnect as well as those of the circuit elements connected at its two terminals. One can not independently account for the signal delays of the interconnect without consideration of the circuit in which it is implemented. Since the type of circuit elements bounding the interconnect is determined by the chip design and is thus not typically within the control of the circuit edit, we begin our analysis by focusing on the electrical characteristics of an isolated interconnect and return to the more complete discussion of the circuit in following sections.


### Interconnect Fabrication


Interconnect Fabrication


Throughout this analysis, an FEI Vectra 986 Flip Chip FIB system was used in combination with a conformal dielectric deposition system to construct parallel plate transmission line interconnects on the backside of C4 packaged devices as depicted in Figure  2 . Each interconnect spans the surface of a thin film SiO 2 layer deposited on the backside of the locally thinned p-type substrate, which acts as a ground plane for the interconnect. At the two ends of the transmission line are two submicron via connections down to the copper metal layer where the signals are either generated or terminated by the CMOS circuit elements. Prior to fabricating the interconnects, the sample is prepared using a series of process steps consistent with those outlined in references 1, 2, and 3 to gain local access to the nodes of interest from the backside of the C4 packaged die.


Once the silicon has been locally thinned to within 1-3um of the active device layer, a node access hole (NAH) is etched into the remaining silicon exposing the shallow trench isolation (STI) region. At this step, the sample is coated with a thin conformal SiO 2 dielectric layer for electrical isolation of the silicon substrate. The dielectric layer thickness on the surface of the substrate typically ranges from 0.25um to 1.0um depending on the application. However, within the NAH the thickness can drop well below 100nm due to the tight lateral dimensions typically required and can be a considerable source of stray capacitance.


Access to the copper signal line beneath is accomplished by etching a via through the STI region and intermediate dielectric layers. Once the metal is exposed, a tungsten metal plug is formed by means of ion beam induced deposition of a W(CO) 6 precursor gas. The filling of the access hole completes the via fabrication step. Finally, a tungsten line connecting the two vias is deposited on top of the SiO 2 layer using direct write FIB deposition thus completing the interconnect structure.


### D.C. Electrical Characteristics


D.C. Electrical Characteristics


The electrical resistivity of FIB W deposited on planar surfaces has been thoroughly characterized and many sources of its value can be found in the literature  [7, 8] . In practice, it ranges between 150-250 µΩ-cm depending on the amounts of residual carbon, oxygen, and gallium * . For a W line having a 1um x 1um cross-sectional area the resistance-perlength would range between 1.5-2.5Ω/um accordingly. Based on precision resistance measurements and cross-sectional analysis of deep submicron high-aspect ratio vias we have concluded that FIB W resistivity does not change appreciably when deposited in such small dimension features. Furthermore, by varying the contact area between the via and the VLSI copper interconnect in special test structures, we were able to conclude that the contact resistance between the FIB deposited W and the copper interconnect was generally negligible compared to the total via resistance, which ranged between 5-20 Ω/via depending on the feature dimensions. For the dimensions used in this analysis, the resistance per via was about 10 Ω. The dielectric that insulates the W line and via from the substrate has been measured to have a resistivity of greater than 1x10 15 µohm-cm. Its low-frequency dielectric constant is comparable to that of pure SiO 2 (~3.9) although slightly reduced.


The FIB metal is deposited on top of the insulating dielectric, which coats a highly conductive p-type substrate.


This metal-insulator-semiconductor material stack forms an M-I-S capacitor, which exhibits strong voltage dependency particularly in the low voltage range. To account for the appropriate capacitance-per-length of the transmission line, one must consider the M-I-S behavior under appropriate operating conditions. To assist in the calculation of the capacitance, a MATLAB program was written to accurately simulate the capacitance-voltage relationship at both quasi-static and microwave frequency transient conditions. An example of the CV relationship for a W/SiO 2 /p-Si M-I-S capacitor with 400nm oxide thickness is shown in Figure  3 . At very low frequency (~ 1Hz) minority carrier electrons in the locally thinned substrate have time to be thermally generated and/or diffuse from highly doped n-type regions to the surface dielectricsubstrate interface in response to the applied signal. Thus, at sufficient voltage, the surface will invert its polarity and force the capacitance to its maximum C' max :


] 2 [F/m max ox t o ε ox K C' = (1)


which neglects fringing fields. For a 1um wide interconnect line with dielectric thickness ranging between 0.5-1.0um thick, the maximum capacitanceper-length would range between 7x10 -17 F/um and 3.5x10 -17 F/um. The depletion of mobile charge adjacent to the dielectric-semiconductor interface for midrange voltages reduces the effective capacitance that the signal experiences during a voltage ramp thus the use of C' max in timing analysis will undoubtedly be conservative.


### Microwave Frequency Electrical Characteristics


Microwave Frequency Electrical Characteristics


Differences between the low and high-frequency capacitance characteristics of the interconnect is determined largely by the threshold voltage of the M-I-S structure. If the threshold voltage is sufficiently large such that it is out of the range of normal device operation, then both regimes will exhibit near identical behavior as is shown in Figure  3  for voltages up to about 4V. Since the operating voltages of modern high-performance ICs are typically below 2V and the dielectric thickness used for insulation in the FIB interconnect is typically several hundred nanometers thick, the M-I-S structure will almost always operate in depletion mode where its capacitance is significantly reduced. The effective capacitance will fall somewhere between the maximum capacitance and the minimum capacitance, C' min , calculated at the maximum operating voltage. At higher frequencies, resistance increases due to the skin effect. To assist in calculating the increase in effective resistivity, we used a 2-D electromagnetic field solver tool to calculate resistance as a function of frequency for several different line dimensions. Figure  4 . shows the calculated resistance as a function of frequency up to 100GHz for 100um long lines having 1um x 1um cross-sectional area and a d.c. resistivity value of 180uOhm-cm. The simulation results indicated that the skin effect was causing the effective resistivity to appear about 25% higher than the d.c. value. of the interconnect as a function of frequency and the results are also displayed in Figure  4 . The modeling indicates that the inductive elements of the line are negligible compared to the resistance over the frequency range of interest. However, the inductive reactance is increasing at a faster rate than the resistance and is speculated to dominate the resistance component at several hundred GHz.


### Equivalent High-Frequency Electrical Model


Equivalent High-Frequency Electrical Model


In accordance with references 10 and 11, the transmission line component of the interconnect can be modeled as a distributed RC network of n discrete stages with increased number of segments leading to higher levels of accuracy. For sufficiently short interconnects, the interconnect could be adequately described as a single series resistor and capacitor to ground but for longer interconnects the error is appreciable on the order of 50% as determined in our analysis. In this analysis, 10 segments were found to exhibit sufficient accuracy for SPICE simulations. Depicted in Figure  6 , the transmission line portion has 10 discrete resistors and 11 capacitors. With exception to the end points, each resistor and capacitor in the transmission line is assigned a value equal the total resistance or capacitance of the line divided by the number of segments, in this case n=10. To ensure symmetry, the capacitance at the two ends of the interconnect were halved thus each receiving C total /2*n. Since the via has a much smaller spatial extent, we adopt a simple lumped parameter model for the two vias at the opposite ends of the transmission line. Again, to ensure symmetry, we adopt the approach of distributing the capacitance of the via, C_via at the two ends of the via resistor, R_via.


### Figure 6. Equivalent electrical model of backside interconnect. Experimental


Figure 6. Equivalent electrical model of backside interconnect. Experimental


Specially designed digital CMOS ring oscillators and supporting circuits were designed and implemented into an advanced test chip in order to facilitate the study of propagation delay in backside interconnects fabricated with FIB technology. The test chip was fabricated on Intel's 90nm 300mm wafer process technology  [12, 13]  and was assembled in an organic C4 package similar to that used in high-performance microprocessors. The primary objective of the experiment was to determine the relationship between propagation delay and the parameters of the interconnect (i.e. material properties and physical construction) as well as the bounding circuit elements. It is known that the following 4 parameters affect the change in propagation delay of the circuit as a function of interconnect line length:


r = interconnect resistance/length [Ω/um] c = interconnect capacitance/length [F/um]  R s = effective source resistance [Ω] C load = effective load capacitance [F]


A general expression describing this relationship was shown to have the functional form of Equation 2


l rC c R B Arcl load s delay ) ( 2 + + = ∆ τ [ps] (2)


where A and B are constants  [10, 11] . For relatively short interconnects the quadratic term is negligible and propagation delay exhibits a linear characteristic. To separate out the effects of the via and the transmission line, the targeted via parameters were fixed for all experiments presented in this paper.


### Propagation Delay Monitoring with Digital Ring Oscillator Test Circuits


Propagation Delay Monitoring with Digital Ring Oscillator Test Circuits


Ring oscillators (ROC's) are often implemented as delay monitoring circuits for a wide range of integrated circuit test applications  [14, 15] . In this analysis, we use specially designed ROC's to monitor the changes in propagation delay due to the insertion of a FIB fabricated interconnect between two stages. To first order, the frequency of a digital ring oscillator consisting of n stages of equal propagation delay and a backside interconnect inserted between two stages can be described by equation (  3 ), where τ p is the nominal propagation delay of each stage of the ring oscillator and τ FIB is the propagation delay due to the backside interconnect. In order to fully characterize the relationship between propagation delay and tungsten interconnect length, three types of ring oscillators were used, each having a variation in device size and fan-out scenario. The first ROC type, which we refer to as ROC#1, has for each stage a small inverter driving a fan-out of three (Figure  7a ). The second scenario, ROC#2 maintained the same inverter sizes as in ROC#1 but the fan-out was reduced to unity (Figure  7b ). Effectively, the ROC#1 and ROC#2 designs were equivalent except that ROC#1 stages were driving three times the load capacitance. In the last scenario, ROC#3, the stages are progressively sized while maintaining a fan-out of 2 at each stage (Figure  7c ). For each of these ring oscillator scenarios, the copper interconnection between the two stages was physically cut and a backside interconnect was inserted at opposite end of the cut to reconnect the two stages. A schematic representation of the insertion of a backside interconnect (thick "I" shaped line segment) between two stages of a ROC#2 type circuit is shown in Figure  8 . By physically changing the length of this interconnect with the FIB, we could measure the change in frequency of the ring oscillator as a function of the interconnect line length and circuit parameters.


Three main experiments were performed in this analysis using the ROC types described above. In Experiment I. we examined the effect of line capacitance on the additional propagation delay in a ROC#1 type circuit by changing the dielectric thickness between two equally prepared samples. The metal line dimensions of the interconnects were maintained at approximately equal values between the two data sets as depicted in Figure  9 . In Experiment II we explored the role of the load capacitance on the additional propagation delay of the circuit. To change the load capacitance without changing the source resistance we used both ROC#1 and ROC#2 configured circuits. Finally, in Experiment III we performed a series of experiments on ROC#2 and ROC#3 scenarios with the objective of determining the role that the source resistance and load capacitance has on the additional propagation delay of the circuit. For the particular stage in which the backside interconnect was inserted into ROC#3, the input device and load device widths (NMOS and PMOS) were a factor of 3.08 times and 6.15 times greater than those for the ROC#2 circuit respectively. Thus, the effective driver resistance is about 3 times smaller for ROC#3 and the load capacitance is about 6 times larger.


Before a tungsten interconnect was inserted between the two stages of the ROC the existing copper interconnect was cut using a FIB etch process and subsequently tested. Next, two vias were made at the output of the driving stage and the input of the subsequent stage. Then approximately 200 microns of tungsten interconnect was added between the two vias in a "I" shape pattern thus reviving the signal continuity between the two stages. The interconnect length was then incrementally reduced using the FIB (Figure  10a ). At each interconnect length, the frequency of the modified ROC and the control ROC were measured and the changes recorded. Following these steps a four-point probe resistance measurement * was performed on a section of the line to determine the d.c. resistance-per-length value. To facilitate these measurements, tungsten probe pads were deposited on the backside by FIB and connected to the line in a manner shown in Figure  10b . Once all electrical data was extracted from the interconnect the actual dimensions of the line, dielectric and vias were determined through precision cross sectioning with a tilt stage FIB * The 4 point method minimizes the probe resistance impact on the measurement. system (Figures  10c, 10d ).


### Data Collection Methodology


Data Collection Methodology


The outputs of each of the ROC's located on the test chip were accessible by external pins after their frequency was divided by 16. The divider block was necessary since the ROC frequencies were running in the multi-GHz range. Frequency measurements were collected using a 6 GHz digital sampling oscilloscope monitoring the output at the external pins being driven by the buffered frequency divider block. The block of ROC's located on the test chip was split into two sub-blocks, block 'A' and block 'B'. These subblocks were exact copies of each other such that for every type of ROC, there was an identical mate with an independent frequency divider block and output path. Circuit edits were performed on the ring oscillators in block 'A' while the block 'B' ring oscillators were used as control devices enabling us to account for environmental and voltage supply fluctuations between testing intervals. In order to compensate for natural thermal drift of the ROC frequency and to compensate for small differences in the operating voltage of the chip, it was necessary to determine a projected frequency (f ROCA,proj ) for ROC A as if there was no edit performed.


Then, using the actual frequency measured after the CE was performed (f ROCA,act ), equation (  4 ) could then be used to calculate the change in propagation delay (∆τ d ). The factor of 1/16 is included to account for the frequency division performed on the test chip f ROCA,proj was calculated using equation (  5 ). The subscript "before" refers to the ROC frequency prior to the CE on ROC A. The subscript "after" refers to its frequency following the CE on ROC A.


Note that this value is the total change in delay due to the interconnect, which includes the sum of the changes in the rising and failing edges as well as a small change in the subsequent inverter stage delay.


Error in the frequency measurement was accounted for by propagating the positive and negative 3-sigma frequency measurement error through equation (  6 ) for the set of conditions yielding the largest error.


### Time-Domain SPICE Modeling


Time-Domain SPICE Modeling


The most up-to-date device models for the 90nm technology were used for modeling the various ring oscillator circuits but in order to accurately model the effective drive strength of the transistors slight adjustments to the parameterized channel length were made such that the ROC frequencies matched silicon performance precisely. This ensured that the effective source resistance of the inverter stage driving the interconnect was modeled as accurately as possible. Each of the ROC scenarios were modeled with the insertion of the backside interconnect between two of the inverter segments. Changes in line length were modeled through equivalent changes in the R and C values per segment. Then, to estimate the via capacitance, the C_via parameter was swept over a range of 1-5fF.


### Experiment I. Delay vs. Line Capacitance


Experiment I. Delay vs. Line Capacitance


Additional propagation delays due to the FIB interconnect obtained in the three experiments discussed in previous sections are displayed in Figures 12-14. Figure  12 . shows the results of Experiment I performed on ROC#1 (Figure  7a ) configured circuits. The most relevant measured and calculated parameters for the two lines used in this experiment are tabulated below for reference in Table  1 . The dielectric thickness for Sample (b) is approximately 2.25 times thicker than that for Sample (a). When combined with the measured line width, w, the estimated capacitance-per-length of the line in Sample (a) was approximately 2.31 times that of the line in sample (b). Examining the two lines in Figure  12 , we see that the ratio of capacitances for the two lines is close to the ratio of the delay-perlength values obtained. This result supports the conclusion that the line capacitance for this circuit configuration dominates the propagation delay since the change in slope value closely tracks the change in the R s cl term in Equation  2 .

### Experiment II. Delay vs. Load Capacitance, Source Resistance


Experiment II. Delay vs. Load Capacitance, Source Resistance


The results of Experiment II are shown in Figure  13 . Data Set (a) and (c) were extracted from ROC's having the ROC#2 (Figure  7b ) circuit configuration and Data Set (b) was extracted from ROC#1 configured circuits (Figure  7a ). From these results we see that there is very little variation in slope between the three data sets despite an increase of the load capacitance by a factor of three in going from Data Sets (a) and (c) to Data Set (b). This further suggests that it is the propagation delay component involving the distributed line capacitance, not the line resistance, which is playing the biggest role in propagation delay for the devices with smaller drive strength or equivalently larger effective resistance. This can only be explained by accounting for the reduction in effective source resistance of the driving stage which was approximately 3 times smaller than that of ROC#2. Once again, the data supports the conclusion that the capacitance R s cl component of Equation 2 dominates the change in propagation delay for the size of devices used in this analysis. The most important feature obtained from this simulation is that increasing the load capacitance by a factor of three barely changes the slope as the results of Experiment II did show. The slopes calculated using SPICE were reasonably close to the slopes found empirically but are slightly higher than measured. This can be explained by reducing the effective distributed capacitance due to the depletion mode of the M-I-S structure which was not modeled for this case.


The next set of simulation results helps to explain all of the previous results. Here the change in propagation delay is calculated for increasing line length for the ROC#1 scenario for three different device scaling scenarios. Data Set (a) has the nominal device sizes implemented in the actual ROC#1 circuit. In Data Set (b) and (c) all of the devices have been scaled by a factor of 2 an 4 times respectively. The simulations show that the slope actually decrease, albeit at a diminishing rate, despite increasing the load capacitance by increasing amounts. This can be easily explained by modeling the driver device as an effective resistance and the load device as an effective capacitance. With a fixed fan-out ratio, scaling the device sizes by a factor of two effectively reduced the driver resistance while increasing the effective load capacitance by a similar amount. For increases in the device sizes, the R s c time constant of Equation 2 is effectively reduced  by the scaling factor but the rC load component of Equation 2 is increased by the same factor. At sufficiently large device sizes, the resistance of the line will begin to play a much more crucial role in the propagation delay of the circuit whereas the capacitance of the line will have decreasing importance.


### Implications in FIB CE Capability


Implications in FIB CE Capability


As a general rule of thumb device designers push the limits of internal device parameters to achieve about 1mA/um at the nominal operating voltage, which is on the order of 1V in today's most advanced technologies. A quick analysis can be made if we model the driver gate as a simple resistor with resistance of about 1V/1mA/um or 1KΩ-um. Furthermore, the gate capacitance-per-gate-width is roughly maintained through scaling of the equivalent oxide thickness (EOT) and is typically on the order of 2fF/um. If the device width is increased by a fixed amount ( > 1) while maintaining a constant fan-out then the effective resistance would decrease by the same amount. However, the load capacitance would increase by that amount. Thus for a fixed set of interconnect r and c parameters and the use of Equation  2 , one can construct a family of curves showing the influence that each of these elements has on propagation delay as a function of absolute device size. Figure  17  shows such a set of curves for three different backside interconnect lengths and two different fan-out conditions. Here we can clearly see that for each curve, there are two distinct operating regimes, a region where the line capacitance dominates (closest to y-axis) and the region where the line resistance dominates (towards increasing W/W 0 values). Depending on which operating regime one is performing the majority of circuit edits there will be different requirements for improving interconnect materials and/or physical construction.


To understand the future capability of FIB metallization in interconnect technology we must consider general technology scaling trends. It is well known that in order to meet the stringent demands of Moore's Law, the lateral device dimensions scale approximately 0.7x to 0.8x per process generation  [16] . Since the width of the minimum device will continue to shrink by approximately 0.7x per generation a greater emphasis must be placed on minimizing line capacitance rather than the line resistance going forward. This is because the effective source resistance of devices will get larger whereas the load capacitance will reduce. This is good news since the relatively few routing restrictions placed on the backside interconnections make it possible to reduce capacitance by simply increasing the dielectric film thickness among other means. The only remaining issue is the capacitance associated with the through-silicon vias. As shown in this analysis this capacitance can have a considerable impact on next generation VLSI circuits. The ability to maintain FIB CE capability will be tantamount upon maintaining an appropriate scaling of this capacitance.


Although the resistance for vias used today are well within an acceptable range of values, the continuous reduction in via dimensions at each process node causes via resistance to grow at a non-linear rate. The continuous reduction in lateral via dimension is a requirement for maintaining CE capability from generation to generation. Since typical device scaling occurs in both lateral dimensions at a rate of 0.7x each, this means the resistance of the via will double at each technology node assuming that the vertical portion of the via remains fixed. The impact of via resistance should be closely monitored as the technology advances.


For the first time, propagation delay measurements were made for backside FIB fabricated interconnects inserted between CMOS inverter stages of ring oscillator test structures. By varying the source resistance, the load capacitance and the line parameters, we were able to show that the resistance of the interconnect line adds negligible propagation delay to average sized inverters fabricated on 90nm technology. Rather, for small devices the capacitance of the line is the dominant source of propagation delay. For line lengths up to 200um the propagation delay was linear with a slope ranging between 0.17-0.64ps/um depending on the interconnect and circuit parameters and a 0-line length delay offset as high as 20ps due to capacitance of the two vias. Simulation results helped to gain valuable insight into the role of each of the elements involved in the propagation delay of the circuit and were able to show the validity of the distributed RC equivalent electrical model as applied to the backside interconnect.


Historically there have been many approaches to systematic defect learning. In many cases the learning approach has not been targeted at the main yield limiting mechanisms or does not enable Defect Engineering to focus and drive efforts for defect and yield improvements. Current approaches of full wafer defect analysis requires sophisticated tools like 8 or 12 inch wafer stages with stage accuracies in the 1 micron regime to travel from defect to defect as failure analysis engineering performs full wafer deprocessing with inspections at each layer. This type of approach is very inefficient, requires a lot of manpower, and provides poor feedback for defect learning since the sample size is so limited and the time delay is too long for optimum effectiveness.


Our approach to solve this problem requires an appropriate definition of the objectives of the defect analysis. In our manufacturing line, it is most desirable for the Defect Engineering group to have primary ownership of the defect related yield improvement since they inspect a high percentage of the line and need to understand which types of defects are yield killers. Enabling the Defect Engineering team to focus on the most yield relevant defects is of primary importance. Therefore, the objectives of the defect learning are: a) identify the killer defects that cause failures in our manufacturing line, b) identify defects that our defect inspection tools do not detect, and c) ultimately provide a yield related defect pareto 1,2 on a periodic basis that accurately reflects the priorities of the Yield, Defect, and Processing Engineering teams.


### Project Definition


Historically in the yield enhancement process, there have been two main mechanisms that drive improvements. The first is the feedback loop from inline inspections. While wafers are being fabricated, sample inspections are performed at critical layers. The observed defects from the inspections are classified and analyzed. Proper steps are then taken to reduce the defects that are causing the highest defectivity. This short loop corrective action can be the most valuable in improving baseline defect densities if the tools and recipes are actually observing the killer defects. In this corrective action process however, there is no way to validate that the defects being inspected are the main contributor to the actual yield at wafer test. Without this validation, corrective action efforts may not lead to the reduction in defect density that was expected.


The second mechanism that is used for yield enhancement is physical failure analysis (PFA). Root dominant failure mechanism. Corrective action can then be taken to reduce the occurrence of this mechanism. PFA has the advantage that results are from known bad die and root cause defects are known to be killer defects. However, to obtain results on the number of die that is statistically significant for baseline yield enhancement it is slow and or costly.


Both PFA and inline inspections have been used independently and have proven to be an effective way to drive baseline line yields in the past. However, as defects become less observable with traditional inline inspection tools, and PFA cycle times increase, it becomes more important that these two methods do not remain isolated and independent.


Treating these methods independently leads to inefficiencies and inaccuracies. Utilizing concepts such as memory bit mapping and logic mapping, one can streamline the yield enhancement process. When these methods are employed, validation of the effectiveness of the inline inspection process is obtained and wasted PFA on defects already found with inline inspection is avoided. Also, when PFA is needed, it provides feedback to the inline inspection tools and recipes that makes them more effective in the short loop corrective action.


Figure  4  shows a flow chart of the yield enhancement process when utilizing a logic mapping approach. While the flow chart specifically targets logic mapping, it is also applicable to memory bit mapping. The process requires the coordination of inline inspection and wafer test on targeted wafers. Following is a description of each step in the process.


• Fabrication -during the fabrication process, select wafers are targeted and inline inspection is performed at all production inline inspection layers. It is critical that these wafer receive a full suite of inline inspection to produce meaningful results after overlays are performed. • Wafer test -during wafer test, extra testing is performed on failing devices from the wafers that were targeted and received full layer inline inspections. During scan chain testing, datalogs are collected of the failing vectors up to a predetermined limit. • Logic mapping -As described above.


• Feedback -The output from the logic mapping process is then analyzed and feedback is provided to tool owners. There are actually three outputs from the logic mapping process, which are shown on the flow chart and described below.

This feedback loop can be used as a way to run experiments on the tools and recipes to improve their abilities and accurateness without ever needing PFA. As an over simplified example, targeted wafers can receive multiple inspections at a particular layer with different recipes or different tools. The recipe that generates the highest OHR would then be selected as the production recipe. Similar experiments could be run where inspections occur at different process locations than normal to see what impact inspections at this step would have. Without logic mapping and the OHR, there would not be an effective way of getting electrical verification of the inspection results.


The second hit rate is the ratio of the number of successfully diagnosed die to the number of die failing the scan test and is referred to as the diagnosable hit rate (DHR).

Hits Misses DHR Candidates

The DHR measures the ability of the scan diagnosis tool to converge on a result. This result is important in driving improvements in the ATPG diagnosis tool.


The last ratio is the number of die where a defect was found to correlate to a scan diagnosed failing net to the number of candidate die and is referred to as the total hit rate (THR).


### Hits THR OHR DHR Candidates


Hits THR OHR DHR Candidates


= × =


The THR quantifies how well the correlating defects explain the overall yield. When the THR is high, the identified killer defects accurately represent the population of defects causing the yield fallout and can be acted upon to improve the yield. When the THR is low, the defect list must be used cautiously as it does not represent the actual population of defects of the samples considered.


### Automatic Root Cause Determination and Killer


Automatic Root Cause Determination and Killer


Defect Pareto Each defect from the inline inspection that is present on a die categorized as a hit or a miss can be considered to be either a killer or non-killer defect. Defects present on this group of dies that correlate to the ATPG diagnosis can be classified as a killer, while all other defects on these die can be classified as non-killer. From this classification, it is possible to generate electrically verified kill ratios and killer defect paretos. While kill ratios and killer defect paretos are a common output of most inline inspection processes, the killer non-killer defect classification is never verified with electrical test. Without the electrical verification which logic mapping can provide, the killer defect classification can only be assumed to be correct. Therefore, the killer defect classification is an important output from the logic mapping process and has direct impact on the yield enhancement process.


### Automated Fault Localization and PFA Candidates


Automated Fault Localization and PFA Candidates


The last output from logic mapping is a set of die that have complete electrical failure analysis results that do not have an inline defect correlation. These die then become candidates for PFA. PFA is still a very critical part of the yield enhancement process, however it is used with a different intention. PFA in this case is not intended to provide direct yield enhancement, but rather is performed to explain why inline inspections did not find a correlating defect. PFA is only required when the OHR is low. For a given sample of die, a low OHR means that inline inspections did not find the majority of the defects causing the yield fallout. Although a sample size can come from many different categories, perhaps the most sensible sample set of die is by wafer. Therefore, as indicated on the flow chart, PFA is performed on wafers with an OHR that is below a given threshold. Results from the PFA are used to make adjustments to the inspection recipes and to which layers receive inspections.


The yield enhancement process using logic mapping can be summarized as follows. The primary effort behind this process is to validate and improve inline inspections. Secondarily, logic mapping outputs can be used as a killer / non-killer defect classification tool. As PFA efforts become increasingly more time consuming, it becomes more critical to coordinate the inline inspection and PFA efforts using techniques such as logic mapping.


Logic mapping was performed on 10 production wafers of a single product. The 10 wafers consisted of 2 wafers from each of 5 different lots and each wafer was representative of the baseline yield.


Measures were taken to ensure that each wafer in the experiment received a full inspection at each of the standard production inline inspection layers. The specifications for the product chosen for the experiment are listed below: Experimental results were obtained by datalogging up to 100 failing vectors at an average test time of 9.1 sec/die and using a threshold distance of 20µm to consider an inline defect as an overlay hit. The 20µm threshold was chosen based on the tolerance given for the inline inspection tool.


Table  1  summarizes the logic mapping results for the 10 wafers. The table shows the quantities for each of the logic map result categories as well as the calculated hit rates that are described above. Although devices that fail the scan chain continuity test can in principle be diagnosed, measures were not taken to do so and were thus considered nondiagnosable for these results.


### Overlay Hit Rate


Overlay Hit Rate


The results show that the success rate of finding an inline defect that correlates to a diagnosed failure ranges from 8% to 50% with an average of 31%. An OHR of 31% means that approximately one out of every three diagnosed failures can be explained by an observed inline defect. This OHR is very reasonable and is consistent with the 18% to 24% hit rate reported by Kinra et. al.  [7] . However, there is a large variation in the OHR that is somewhat unexpected. At the high end, the 50% OHR suggests that the ATPG diagnosis and the defect overlay process is accurate. Because of this, the low 8% OHR can only be explained by a lack of killer defects being found during inline inspection for this wafer. In order to make the right conclusion and ultimately improve the OHR, physical failure analysis must be performed on the dies that are considered misses when the OHR is low.


Physical FA was performed on wafer #2 from lot #4, which had a very low 7.7% OHR. Interestingly, the physical FA success was very poor as well, returning a root cause defect on only 1 out of 8 dies attempted. The poor success rate of finding the killer defects for both the inline inspection and physical FA suggests that the offending defects are likely to be fairly subtle. Figure  5  shows a SEM photograph of the defect found on the unit with successful FA. The defect was an unfilled contact, with an intact liner. This defect was not found by inline inspection because all contacts are unfilled at the time of the inspection, therefore at that inspection layer, the contact would not have looked defective. Defects such as this help to explain a low OHR, however, continued physical FA efforts are ongoing and will be needed to improve the OHR. Because the OHR is a direct measure of inline inspection capability and thus the short loop yield enhancement capability, it is perhaps the single most important result from the logic mapping process.


### Total Hit Rate and Killer Defect Analysis


Total Hit Rate and Killer Defect Analysis


Once the killer and non-killer classification of inline defects has been done via logic mapping, the data can be analyzed in any number of ways that are typical in inline inspection data analysis.


One common analysis is a pareto of the killer defects by layer. Figure  6  shows a pareto of the killer defects by layer  as classified by logic mapping for the 10 wafers. It is further broken down by the defect type classification as classified by the inline inspection tool. The vertical axis in this case is the number of failures explained by a particular layer divided by the total number of failures and represents the percentage of failure due to defects on that layer. The largest category is Metal 1 and accounts for 5.6% of the failures, while the THR for all layers combined is 13.8%. This means that if the Metal 1 defects identified here by logic mapping were eliminated, it would reduce the total failures by at least 5.6% and if all defect identified were eliminated the impact would be 13.8%. This is the most conservative analysis of this data. It is expected that the actual reduction of failures would more closely follow the OHR at 31%.


### Diagnosable Hit Rate


Diagnosable Hit Rate


The discrepancy between the OHR and the THR is due to the large population of scan failures that fall into the non-diagnosable category. The DHR of the 10 wafers is also listed in table 1 and ranges from 28% to 57% with an average of 44%. Of the 56% of the candidate dies that are not diagnosable, 95% are due to devices that fail the scan continuity test, and only 5% cannot be diagnosed by the ATPG software. In this case, a very strong conclusion can be reached that the DHR was directly impacted by the defective chain failures that were not diagnosed. To improve the DHR and thus the THR, it is necessary to include scan chain continuity failures in the diagnosis.


There are three reasons that a device will fail the scan chain continuity test.


1. Defect in the scan flip-flop or Q to SI path 2. Defect in the clock tree 3. Defect in the scan enable tree Defects present in the first category should not present any problems for logic mapping, however the probability of this event happening is much lower than the other possibilities given the relative areas for these categories. The probability that the defect is in the clock tree is highest because it consumes the largest area of these categories, however, because the tree is so highly buffered, it is unlikely that the defect will be located on the net associated with the ATPG diagnosed flip-flop. Lastly, the probability that the defect resides in the scan enable tree is again high. In this case though, the scan enable tree is not as well buffered and the net attached to the suspected flop can be quite large. Therefore, it is expected that the majority of logic mapping hits would occur on scan enable.


A preliminary experiment was carried out in which scan chain continuity fails were included in the logic mapping process for one wafer. A wafer was chosen that had a relatively high OHR for the standard ATPG fails to assure that the inline inspections had found a large population of the killer defects. The wafer chosen had an OHR of 35%, a DHR of 60% and a THR of 21%. The results of this small study show that including defective chain failures improved the DHR from 60% to 92% and the THR from 21% to 30%. The improvement to the THR means more accuracy for the killer defect analysis and suggests that it is worthwhile to include the defective chain failures in the logic mapping process. However, the OHR is significantly lower for the defective chain failures versus the standard fails. In the case of the defective chain fails, it is not a valid assumption that the logic mapping process is accurate due to the buffered clock tree. In fact, an analysis of the killer defects from the defective chain failures showed that 100% of the defects were correlated to the scan enable net. Therefore, the OHR of the defective chains is determined both by the inaccuracies in logic mapping and the missed defects from inline inspections and should not be used as a figure of merit of the inline inspection capability.


### Future Work and Conclusions


Future Work and Conclusions


A tool has been developed and implemented to perform logic mapping at LSI Logic. While the tool and its implementation are still in their infancy, promising results are being obtained. The tool has proven to be effective in generating accurate overlays for killer defect classification and providing electrical verification of inline inspection results. An average overlay success rate of 31% has been obtained and diagnosability success has been shown to be as high as 92% when scan chain continuity failures are included in the diagnosis.


Future work will include more PFA on the overlay misses. PFA on overlay misses is the primary way to improve the inline inspections. PFA needs to be performed on wafers that have both a high OHR as well as a low OHR. When the OHR is high it means the defects identified as killers by logic mapping are representative of the killer defects on the wafer. When it is low, it is expected that the dominant mechanism has not been observed inline. PFA is necessary to define the threshold between a high and low OHR. Once the threshold is determined, PFA will only be required when the OHR is below this threshold.


Other future work includes expanding logic mapping to other products. Expanding this tool to other products will provide better understanding and more validation.


Finally, as technology shrinks the defects become harder to inspect with optical inspection tools. When new inspection tools are made available, it will be imperative that logic mapping be expanded to include defects found by these tools. The learning curve on new inspection equipment will be greatly enhanced by logic mapping.


As modern, state of the art semiconductor fabrication facilities increase the amount of inline inspection and electrical test data used for defect reduction, a unified methodology for validating the accuracy and capability of the different systems used to collect, store, and analyze this data becomes increasingly necessary 1 . Such is the case for the manufacturing process used to produce AMD microprocessors. The methodology presented here enables such systems to be calibrated and cross-correlated.


### Project Overview


Project Overview


This methodology consists of creating a production lot and processing it through the manufacturing fab with defects strategically manufactured at key process steps within areas of the microprocessor's cache, see Figure  1 . The defects were artificially manufactured by editing a decommissioned reticle set from a previous product revision that still contained valid cache architecture, see Figure  2a , 2b. This ensured the artificial defects would be present on multiple die on each wafer, thus virtually eliminating the possibility that random defects would render the artificially defective test die unusable. This methodology allowed several of our manufacturing defect reduction systems to be audited using a single correlation lot. The systems audited and correlated included reticle scan tools, inline defect scan tools, electrical/bitmap test programs, defect navigation software, and wafer level failure analysis tools. A reticle defect in a high volume manufacturing fab can cause a tremendous risk to yield loss in a short period.


Reticle integrity must be monitored frequently to reduce such a risk. The reticle scan tool audited was a KLA SL300HR STARlight Review tool, which successfully identified every reticle edit made, albeit it was slightly aided, by the residual effects of the FIB, which remained on the reticle glass after editing. See Figure  3 . A standard KLA inspection tool was used for inline inspections at final inspect (FI). One wafer, "golden wafer", containing the artificial defects was kept at each layer. This golden wafer allowed inspection recipe calibrations to be performed by measuring an inspection recipe's sensitivity, accuracy, and throughput against a known defect type and size. This provided consistent and repeatable killer defect data to more closely quantify the trade off between defect inspection recipe sensitivity, nuisance counts, and throughput, a common dilemma associated with defect inspection tools.


Electrical test was performed using a Teradyne tester with a test program revision matching the revision of the decommissioned reticles. Furthermore, the latest revision of the bitmap portion of the test program was employed.


Only one artificial defect was not properly reported by the test program.


State of the art microprocessors containing multiple large memory arrays pose a tremendous challenge to test program developers. It is often difficult to accurately detect and report bitmap failure locations due to the logical to physical address scrambling employed and the "mirroring" of sub caches by layout designers. A high level of confidence in bitmap data is critical to the success of physical failure analysis and rapid isolation of a defect's root cause. This methodology provides a comprehensive way of validating the accuracy and integrity of the bitmap data.


Wafer level failure analysis tools range from state of the art software to perform virtual stripback analysis 2 , by correlating inline defect data with bitmap test results, to traditional physical stripback and inspection. The traditional physical stripback and inspection was the tool audited by this methodology. This consisted primarily of the inspection stations navigation system. However, indirectly, the failure analysis technicians ability to stripback the wafer and identify the failure mechanism was also quantified.

### Correlation Results


Correlation Results


Table  B  shows the summary of the correlation between systems. Surprisingly, only sixty eight percent (68%) of the artificial defects successfully printed on the wafer. The remaining 32% did not print due to the large exposure/develop margin in photolithography for those layers, highlighting an unexpected find. Almost half (46%) of the defects that successfully printed were not found by the production inline scans. This finding prompted development of improved inline scan recipes with higher sensitivities targeted at planar defects (extra pattern defects).


Significantly better, the bitmap test program was able to capture seventy seven percent (77%) of the defects. Two (2) of the three (3) defects not reported by the bitmap test program were later confirmed to have passed due to redundancy in the layout, improving the effective hit rate of the bitmap program to 92%. The remaining escape was an LI to LI short placed in the periphery circuitry outside the cache.


Finally, physical stripback capability was assessed via two failure analysis technicians working independently. Technician "A" was able to locate 80% of the defects, while technician "B" found 70% of the defects. Even though they accounted for 100% of the artificial defects together, stripback recipes were improved. Utilization of an FEI820 SEM for Contact 1 and Metal 1 inspections also led to defect detection improvements and minimized the differences in hit rates between the two technicians.
