### Learning Opportunities


Learning Opportunities


This methodology allowed systematic correlation of several of our manufacturing defect reduction systems using a single correlation lot. Specifically, the KLA SL300HR StarLight inspection system was able to successfully identify all defects placed on the reticles. While some inline defect scan recipes did not find all of the defects, this highlighted the delicate balance between sensitivity/throughput and generated discussions on inspection strategies for planar, partial height, and surface defects. Subsequently, the sensitivity of the Contact 1 and Metal 1 inspection recipes was increased.


Also demonstrated was the importance of verifying the accuracy of bitmap defect locations across all available sub-caches and multiple rows/cols.


The exercise above demonstrates a comprehensive, repeatable, and efficient method for correlating physical defect inspection and navigation systems with electrical bitmap data through the fabrication of artificial defects. The value of this methodology was not only measured in terms of defect detection capability improvements across multiple systems, but also in its ability to assess the accuracy of the defect locations reported by these systems against a defect's true physical location. Every opportunity to verify this data should be taken prior to starting high volume production and time-consuming yield improvement efforts.


The goal of failure analysis (FA) is to provide rapid and accurate data on yield limiting defects in order to drive yield improvement. The first step in FA, fault site isolation, has traditionally started after end of line (EOL) test. The completed circuit enables a number of different techniques to be used. A major limitation of EOL FA is the length of time between the introduction of the defect and completion of FA. Before FA may even start, the remaining fabrication steps must be completed. For front-end defects, this may take a month. Once started, FA can take several days to weeks to complete. Generally many process layers must be removed before the defect can be found. The time required for FA is typically longer for an open circuit due to the necessity of unique equipment and techniques for defect isolation 1 . Open or high resistive circuit faults are becoming predominant as feature size and power supply voltages for new technology continue to trend downward.


This paper describes how inspection scanning electron microscopy (SEM) technology with passive voltage contrast capability and focused ion beam (FIB) cross section analysis may be used to greatly accelerate the process of locating and characterizing front end yield limiting defects on product wafers. Recent advances in inspection SEM technology now make in-line, large area passive voltage contrast (PVC) inspection possible. The ability of inspection SEM technology to non-destructively inspect wafers inline allows yield-limiting defects to be detected soon after they are created. Often these failure modes are due to buried defectivity. Root cause FA may immediately be applied to representative failures to determine the failure mechanism so that improvement efforts may proceed promptly.


The ability to inspect large areas provides a second major advantage over EOL FA, very large numbers of failures are captured. This enables an extremely accurate pareto of the failure modes affecting a particular module to be generated for each lot. The pareto of failure modes is used to concentrate attention on the major yield limiters as well as for split experiment evaluation. With EOL FA, typically only a small sample of failures is analyzed.


Inspection SEM technology is now used along with special test structures, which mimic the back end processing of product wafers, to rapidly resolve back end defect issues 2-3 .


In certain situations however, product itself may be effectively inspected using inline PVC. This is preferable because test structures consume area, and defectivity captured using the test structures does not necessarily represent that affecting product. Liang et al. describes using in-line PVC inspection to capture systematic front-end defectivity 4 . Inspection tool capability at the time of this paper limited the area that could be inspected and therefore the scope to just select systematic defectivity. Our work is distinctly different in that the focus is random defectivity, which requires large area inspection.


A case study is presented in this paper, which illustrates how in-line PVC inspection and FIB cross sectional analysis in combination may be used to rapidly resolve front-end buried defect issues in a self-aligned (enhanced) static random access memory (ESRAM) process. In addition to describing the process of localizing and characterizing this defectivity, partition and split experiments to identify the root cause of the defectivity and prove in solutions are also discussed. Incorporation of large blocks of ESRAM is advantageous for many new chip designs. To maximize the amount of memory on these chips, Agere like many other manufacturers has developed a self-aligned contact (SAC) process module, which greatly increases the memory density. In Background section, the apparatus and software used for this work along with the SAC process module are described. The case study is presented in the Results section.


### Background


### Apparatus and Software


Apparatus and Software


A KLA -Tencor eS20XP inspection SEM operating at 600eV was utilized for the PVC inspections. This tool is able to inspect more than one billion windows per hour. Both opens and shorts are detectable by the use of PVC. In general, this technique utilizes a scanning electron microscope (SEM) operating at less than 2.5keV to induce a bias within the IC. The bias of the IC is observed as a change in contrast. For the application of ESRAM, knowledge of the bias state in terms of a forward-bias/reverse-bias diode gives rise to the nature of the fail, i.e. whether the fail is an open or a short defect 4-6 . Other in-line inspections were conducted using a KLA -Tencor 2138 (KLA) and a KLA-Tencor AIT2 (AIT2). A pixel size of 0.39um was used for the KLA and a 7um spot size was used for the AIT2.


Select defects were cross-sectioned using a FEI 800 FIB operating at 30kV. The defect map capabilities of this tool allowed these defects to be located very quickly. For an extended period this tool was not available and instead an alternate FIB was used. Due to the limited coordinate accuracy of this second FIB tool and its inability to take whole wafers, defects were first located using a review SEM in the analytical lab. Burn marks and detailed navigation notes were utilized to relocate these defects on the FIB. Once cross sectioned, the sample was prepared for scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM) analysis.


Correlation of the failures detected with PVC with EOL yield was performed using Klarity TM QDB Defect, a KLA-Tencor data analysis package. In addition to images of overlaid wafer maps, this package provides kill ratios 7,8 and estimates of yield impact for each failure mode. The kill ratio for a particular defect type is an estimate of the increased chance of a die failing given the presence of that defect type. The yield impact is estimated by multiplying the kill ratio by the ratio of die with this defect type to total die. Correlation of the PVC failures with KLA and AIT inspection data was performed using KLA -Tencor's Klarity TM Defect. The data was downloaded into Microsoft Excel and JMP for split analysis and to generate customized plots.


### Self-aligned Contact Process Module


Self-aligned Contact Process Module


The self-aligned contact process module utilizes an additional contact mask to create self-aligned drain and source contacts (also referred to as windows). The gate stack and spacers are covered with a nitride layer. The interlayer dielectric is deposited over this layer. The source and drain contacts may overlap with the gate as shown in Fig.  1 . The effective spacing of the source and drain contacts to the gate is predefined by the spacers, hence the label selfaligned contact. Two separate etches are used to create the drain and source contacts. The first etch stops on the nitride. The second etch removes the nitride layer. After completion of the contact etch steps, a barrier of Ti/TiN is deposited and the contacts are then filled with W. The PVC inspection of the ESRAM follows a W CMP step. These contacts are sometimes referred to as window 1 t (w1t). A SEM micrograph of a defect free block of memory and the corresponding design file is shown in Fig.  2 . At an acceleration voltage of 600eV, those contacts which electrically contact the substrate appear bright, while floating contacts appear dark. In Fig.  2 , only the w1t's in the ntub have a ground path and therefore are bright. The contacts to poly-silicon appear dark due to the isolation of poly-silicon from the substrate by gate oxide. Also, the source/drain contacts in the p-tub region have a dark contrast due to the N+ source/drain implant; the contact develops a positive potential and the N+ to P tub junction becomes reverse-biased. In the N tub region, the source/drain implant is P+. The P+ to N tub region becomes forward-biased providing a path to the substrate.
 Most of the defect types causing the failures affecting the SAC module are not visible with SEM, optical, or laser-based inspection or review tools, and therefore are termed non-visual defects. Therefore FA is necessary to diagnose the root cause.


In-line PVC inspection and FA are being applied to a high running memory chip manufactured with Agere's 0.2um technology. This chip contains 2 megabits of ESRAM. Typically 30% of the die on 5 to 8 wafers are inspected per lot; for split experiments additional wafers are inspected. The ESRAM for this chip is affected by multiple failure modes as shown in Fig.  3 . These failures include "columns of window shorts", clusters of window opens", single window opens", "missing windows", "W puddles" and "w1t to poly shorts". This pareto for lot 48104 is very typical. Images of each of these failure modes are shown in Fig 4 . Comparison with the reference image in Fig.  2  shows the anomalous nature of each of these images. With the exception of the "W puddles" and "missing windows", the defects causing these failures are nonvisual.


A plot of the kill ratio and yield impact for each of these failure types is shown in Fig.  5 . The kill ratio for "column of window shorts" is approximately zero indicating this defect type does not impact yield. Four of the five other failure modes have kill ratios of 1, indicating every defect correlated with a dead chip. For the 0.8 kill ratio for the "missing windows" almost all the defects correlated with dead chips. The density and yield impact of window opens are scaled by two since only opens on half of the windows, those in the N-tub, can be detected. The "single open windows" and "clusters of open windows" are the dominant killer defect types. Figure  6  shows their spatial patterns. Only the regions shown in white, 40% of the wafer, were inspected. These defects appear as boxes on the wafer maps since images were captured for each. Figure  7  shows the strong correlation between the defectivity captured by the eS20 and the wafer probe map. Finding this etch stop condition was a surprise. Inline PVC inspection is also being applied to the ESRAM module for Agere's 0.14u technology.


Recent FMA results revealed a particulate problem as shown in Fig.  9 . A particle separates the thin-ox region from the window. This particle was under the nitride layer. The first SAC etch stopped on the nitride layer as planned. The second SAC etch removed the nitride. Since the nitride layer rested on the particle and not on the thin-ox, the window failed to contact the thin-ox. A cross section for a "w1t to poly short" is shown in Fig.  11 . This image shows a spike of W extending through the spacer to contact both the WSi and polysilicon. A discontinuity between the thin-ox and field oxide is present which may be the cause of this failure. The second window to poly is also shorted to ground, but it's not certain how from the image. The remaining spacer appears quite thin on all the other w1t's that were cross-sectioned; most likely the shorting occurred through this spacer. The w1t etch time or conditions could be adjusted to increase this margin. Since the number of "w1t to poly shorts" was very low on recent lots, such experiments are not currently a priority. Previously such experiments were conducted using the results of a post W cmp eS20 inspection as the metric. This data will not be presented here due to space limitations.


Figure  11 : Cross section of a "w1t to poly short".


### Extensions


Extensions


In this paper, the benefits of applying PVC inspection complemented by in-line cross-section analysis to product wafers for baseline yield improvement were presented. This work is extendable in various directions. The SAC module and the contact process level in general are an ideal application of this technique. To effectively inspect using PVC, the process level of interest must contain interspersed grounded and floating structures. The first, second and third metal levels and second and third window levels of ESRAM also meet this criterion, although their density is not as great as for window 1. Test structures, which are more tightly packed, in certain situations are a better option. This technique is also useful for excursion monitoring. The eS20XP is capable of inspecting and reviewing approximately a wafer per hour. Currently the review step with manual classification takes two thirds of this time. The review could be conducted on a review SEM, a much less expensive tool, allowing a three-wafer sample from each lot to be inspected in an hour.


In-line PVC inspection combined with standard FIB cross section techniques enable real time fault site isolation, and therefore may be used to greatly accelerate the yield ramp of certain process modules which lend themselves to voltage contrast inspection. The merits and limitations of this approach are summarized in Table  1 . The principal advantages are speed and volume of data. Yield limiting defectivity is captured in-line immediately after the completion of the process module rather than at EOL. The majority of defectivity in very large areas is captured providing a great deal of detail about each lot. Once the root cause of a failure mechanism is determined, in-line PVC may be used to provide an in-line metric for evaluating process improvement DOEs. This approach allows experiments to be completed much more quickly and efficiently than through the use of probe and EOL FA results.


Project Definition


As mentioned in the Introduction, prior methods relied on full wafer deprocessing, optical/SEM inspections at each layer, and analysis of all defects. This resulted in vague, inconclusive results and failure analysis success rates were poor. In addition, detailed analysis of many low incidence defect mechanisms was not value added in determining the primary defect related yield detractors and required a large amount of engineering resources. Therefore, a Targeted Defect Analysis Project was launched to improve the yield, efficiently use resources, and calibrate the defect reduction program. The analysis priorities defined by this project were to 1) understand what defects are present and how they are yield relevant, 2) understand which defects cannot be detected by defect inspection tools, 3) determine which defects require further analysis and focusdefects which cannot be resolved by inspection or classification, and 4) increase the volume of samples analyzed to improve the defect statistics.


### Methodology


Methodology


This section of the paper defines the methodology of the project from start to finish. This includes the wafer selection criteria, wafer review and defect correlation, pareto generation, line partitioning, and classification.


### Wafer Selection Criteria


Wafer Selection Criteria


To properly select wafers for a defect reduction program, an effective wafer selection methodology must be implemented. The first step in this process is to clearly define and understand different product yields. In general, product yields may be grouped into different classes depending on the failing test groups. Specifically, in the case of Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) testing, three different yields may be clearly defined. These yields are categorized as follows: 1) DC yield, 2) basic functional yield (SCN), and 3) soft fail test yield. Of these three yield groups, typically only the DC and SCN yields are affected by inline manufacturing induced defects. As a result, the wafer selection criteria will be restricted only to wafers meeting a yield criteria defined by a combination yield comprised of basic functional and DC yields.


The final step in the wafer selection process is to define a yield improvement objective. Since yield loss in the tail of a yield distribution is typically driven by systematic causes, the focus of the defect oriented yield improvement is to move the peak of the yield distribution higher (figure  1 ). Therefore, analysis wafers were chosen from a sample around the peak of the yield distribution, with the assumption that any known systematic issues did not affect the selected wafers. The sample size was further restricted to a group of randomly selected lots reviewed by the defect reduction team at all inspection steps throughout the fabrication process (baseline wafers). Inline defects identified were classified, reviewed, and imaged with the intent of creating a data set to be used for defect to yield correlation.


### Wafer Review and Defect Correlation


Wafer Review and Defect Correlation


Once the lot has been probed, compressed bit fail maps are generated for all wafers and die tested. Die that fail the DC and SCN tests are selected for detailed review. Die that fail for systematic reasons are eliminated from the analysis. This increases the probability that only die which fail due to defectivity are used in the analysis.


To facilitate the classification accuracy, an uncompressed bit map is generated for the baseline wafers. The bit map for each die in the analysis is compared to a map of the defects that were detected with the SEM review for that die (figure  2 ). A manual correlation is established between the defect map and bit map to correlate inline observed defects to the bitmap image. The within die defects are compared to the bit map to determine if the electrical signature in the bit map correlates to the defect. If the bit map fail and a defect overlay, and the process layer of the defect can explain the physical fail, then the fail and defect are determined to correlate. The defect map in figure  2  shows a defect in the same location as the fail. Defect maps are colorized to define the different inline inspection layers (not shown in this illustration).


Following this analysis the die are binned into one of three categories: defect explains, bitmap explains, and bitmap does not explain. The first category, defect explains (DE), is for die where the physical fail signature and the defect map correlate as seen in figure  2 . For each correlating die, an assessment is made to identify the responsible process layer. If the electrical bit map signature explains the failure, but not the defect map, the die is classified into the bitmap explains category (BFE).


Based on product/layout and technology knowledge, the


### Pareto Generation


Pareto Generation


After all of the selected die have been analyzed, the data is added to a defect correlation database. This process is repeated until a statistically valid sample size is generated. Three distinct paretos are generated, one for each of the three categories discussed in the previous section. These paretos show the success rate of the defect inspection and the percentage of failing die which could not be explained by either a defect or the bit map (details will shown in the Results section of the manuscript).


To determine the layer producing the most "killer" defects, two of the three paretos were used. The first pareto includes all the die in the DE category. This pareto shows the number of failing die per process layer, and is used to identify which process layer is responsible for the largest portion of the defect driven yield loss. The second pareto summarizes the BFE category, and shows the number of die attributed to each probable process layer. Therefore, it may also be used to highlight a weakness at inline defect inspection of the corresponding layer , and may result in an algorithm modification or sensitivity adjustment of the defect inspection tools. If the first and second paretos point to the same inline layers, the SEM review is deemed accurate enough, and the DE pareto can be used to drive yield improvement focus.


The third pareto shows the electrical classification of the BDE fails.


### Partitioning


Partitioning


Once a statistical sample size of failing die is collected, data analysis by means of pareto charts is used to identify the process(es) with the highest yield relevance. In many cases, the specific process area generating the defects is not obvious. Therefore, once a segment of the process line is identified as problematic, the defect reduction's inspection and review tools can be utilized to pinpoint the specific process areas that are creating the yield detracting defects through line partitioning. By performing defect inspections before and after each process stage, and comparing this data to the bitmaps, as explained above, the specific process(es) which have the greatest yield impact can be identified.


### Classifying the Defect Cause


Classifying the Defect Cause


The partitioning results not only showed the specific process that producing the most defects, but also provided the necessary information to identify the root process cause of the defects seen on the baseline wafers. The SEM images from the partitioning wafers were assigned to the partitioned process layer and compared to the SEM images gathered from the standard baseline analysis. This enabled the baseline images to be reassigned to a more specific process step as compared to the earlier classifications. Once all of the die from the partitioning were reanalyzed, a new pareto was generated. This pareto allowed the group to accurately prioritize the problem areas of the line.


This cycle of partitioning and reclassification is continued until a specific process step(s) can be identified as the greatest cause of yield detracting defects.


As the processes of interest become clear, it is useful to adjust sampling methodologies to focus resources where they will have the most impact. For example, once the partitioning data pinpointed a certain process, it is then useful to increase the SEM review level at this stage in order to give concise feedback to the process area regarding defect types. As a result, the defect reduction and process engineers can identify the root cause and run experiments or take actions to eliminate the issue.


### Results and Analysis


As discussed in the Pareto Generation section, the first pareto (figure  3 ) generated was the overall analysis classification. The second pareto generated was the DE analysis classification (figure  4 ). Defect inspections layers are shown in process order on the x axis of the graph and are defined as: deep trench (DT), active area (AA), gate conductor (GC), metal zero (M0), metal one (M1), contact two (C2), and metal two (M2); whereas, the y axis describes the relative percentage of DE defects observed at each layer. The results showed that the majority of the killer defects were concentrated in latter stages (M1, C2, M2) of the manufacturing process. The third pareto (figure  5 ) generated was of the most probable defect layer for die with an electrical bit map signature not correlated to the defect map. In this case, product, layout, and process knowledge were used to assign the electrical bit map signature to an inline manufacturing process segment. The largest bar in this pareto consists of failed die with special bitmap signatures, but with no assignable process layer (BMO). The remaining majority of defects classified fell under the upper metal layers (C2/M2). Since the data in this pareto is well correlated to the information presented in the DE pareto, it was determined that the existing defect inspection program was properly calibrated. Some of the reasons for these defects not being observed by the inspection tools were dielectric fails between M2 and M1 and areas where the periphery circuits were excluded from the inline inspection. Investigation into the BMO category, depicted in figure  5 , revealed that the majority of die classified in the BFE analysis classification had a common electrical bit map signature defined as a catastrophic four-megabit memory array failure (4Meg block fail). Extensive data and physical failure analysis was required to solve the 4Meg block failure issue.


Liquid crystal hotspot analysis and emission microscopy were employed to localize the defect, but no significant information could be gleaned from these methods. As a result, detailed circuit layout review coupled with layer by layer deprocessing and cross-sections were used to isolate the fail. Crosssections in the suspect area showed that certain isolated gate lines were much wider than expected, resulting in a substantial loss of alignment margin, and thus a high probability of contact to GC shorts, see figure  6 . Once the root cause of the contact to gate failure mechanism was determined, the BFE pareto was modified to reflect the finding (figure  7 ). In the case of 4Meg block fails, the failure mechanism identified was non-defect related, so adjustments to the BFE The final and most difficult classification was for die with no inline defect or bit map electrical signature (BDE). The first step required to understand these fails was to break them down by the respective probe electrical signature. The classification results are shown in figure  8 . A large portion of the die in the BDE category was classified as power up failures -die unable to reach nominal product voltage settings after the application of a DC voltage source. These die were investigated in depth to determine the root cause failure mechanism. Extensive hot spot and physical analysis provided an indication that failure cause was related to M1/C2 dielectric failures resulting in shorts between M1 and M2 power busses.


These preliminary results prompted a detailed product current analysis to properly characterize the failed die. Results of this evaluation revealed a characteristic signature, for the power up fails, defined by high GC current with little to no additional current or voltage swing on the transistor data line (bitline). This analysis allowed for an accurate assessment of the volume data to determine what percentage of BDE power up fails could be explained by the different groups detailed in figure  9 . Results of the volume analysis showed that the majority of the power up fails were characterized by high GC current (star symbol * in figure  9  graph), and therefore were placed in the GC to GND category. This classification is consistent with the physical analysis findings indicating an M1 (GC) to M2 (GND) short. The other data points (diamonds in figure  9 ) were representative of systematic wafer edge fails for the current fail category in the analysis. As a result, it was concluded that a large percentage of BDE's were also failing due to defectivity in the upper metal layers of the process, and that only 12% of the die in the power up fail category were not assigned to a specific process layer. Additionally, it was determined that the BDE power fails were just a severe version of other M1 to M2 shorts observed in DE and BFE classifications. experiments focused on the upper metal layers were initiated. Several iterations of partitioning and enhanced classification were run to identify the process layer(s) producing "killer" defect. These experimental results, along with the enhanced classification of the baseline wafers pointed more closely to a specific process layer, as shown in figure  10 . The final results of the targeted focus on the upper metal layers showed that 47% of the "killer" defects were due to M1/M2 deposition, 36% due to C2 dielectric deposition, and 17% due to M1/M2 etch processes.


As a final check, all data gathered was integrated to make an overall assessment of the success of the project, and to determine if any further focus was required. Over 50% of all analyzed fails could be attributed to the upper metal layers (M1, C2/M2). This was followed by 9% and 8% fails assigned to the M0 and GC layers, respectively. In the course of analysis, a systematic 4M Blk failure (10% of all affected die) was uncovered and corrective actions were initiated for this classification group. A total of 19%, consisting of BM0 and BDE fails, was not assigned to a process layer, as further classification would have required extensive resource re-allocation.


Results of the targeted defect reduction program for the 140nm product investigated were applied to products with similar design rules, with the exception of the M0 bucket (DE, BFE, and BDE). In this case, a different product design scheme made the related 140nm product very sensitive to M0 defectivity. Therefore, product specific activities were initiated to target this particular group of defects.


### Automation: Yield to Defect Pareto


Automation: Yield to Defect Pareto


To monitor the manufacturing volume, an automatic defect to yield correlation 1 was used to create a pareto of yield loss per layer. Yield loss was assigned only when a positive overlay hit could be established between the defect and bit map data, see figure  11 . Information obtained from the automatic yield to defect pareto is compared to data gathered from the targeted defect reduction program. If discrepancies are found, adjustments are made realign the results.


Results of volume analysis further strengthened the conclusion that the majority of the defect driven yield loss was due to particles in the upper metal layers. Based on our Targeted Defect Analysis, the successful overlay fails (DE) were representative of the overall defect related fails. This yield loss per layer can then be used on a volume basis to drive prioritization of activities from a defect standpoint. Defect Engineering, working with Process Engineering, can take ownership of the defect related yield loss and allow Yield Engineering to focus on systematic or product issues.


### Discussion and Conclusions


Three objectives of the project were defined and successfully completed. First, yield relevant defects were understood, and about 82% of the defects could be explained by successful defect to compressed bitmap overlay or matching electrical signatures. Failures that did not have compressed bitmap to defect overlay were analyzed and the results showed that the pareto of the successful overlay fails was representative of all fails. Further, yield relevant defects for other products with different layer sensitivities (due to design and chip size considerations) could be identified and prioritized. Second, in the case of our 140nm technology, our defect inspection program was found to be well calibrated based on the capabilities of the defect inspection tools and manufacturing considerations. Third, a well-correlated defect to compressed bitmap program based on volume data was defined such that Defect and Process Engineering Teams could be identified to focus on the main defect induced yield detractors. It was important to have this good correlation on a volume basis to prioritize resources for experiments and analysis geared towards defect reduction. Experiments, tool modifications, and revisions in tool process procedures are currently ongoing to improve the overall yield of the 140nm products and are expected to be a three to six month project.


### Pareto of Partitioning and Enhanced Classification Die


Pareto of Partitioning and Enhanced Classification Die


Smaller device sizes and increased design complexity and integration are making it harder for traditional failure analysis (FA) techniques to effectively drive baseline yields in the semiconductor fabrication industry.


Traditional FA techniques such as mechanical probing, front side emission microscopy and Liquid Crystal have given way to back side emission microscopy, SQUID microscopy, LIVA, TIVA and PICA  [1] . These new techniques while powerful and necessary have the drawback of increased FA cycle times due to increased sample preparation. To effectively drive baseline defect densities, root cause must be determined on a statistically significant number of samples in a timely fashion. To this end, more software-based FA tools will need to be implemented in the manufacturing process for automatic root cause determination of the failures.


Memory bitmapping is one such software-based tool that has proven effective in supplementing traditional physical FA  [2] . In this technique, data is collected on the failing test vectors and translated into physical coordinates for failing memory cells. When data collection is implemented in the production test environment, a negligible amount of added test time can provide real time fault localization, leaving in general only construction analysis to be performed to find root cause. Alleviating the need to perform emission microscopy, electrical probing or liquid crystal analysis, can have a dramatic impact on FA throughput and cycle times.


Overlaying and correlating bitmap results to inline defect inspection data can result in the automatic root cause determination of some failures without the need for any physical FA  [3] . This is important in prioritizing failures that need physical FA as well as providing feedback to the inline inspection process as to the effectiveness of the tools.


Advances in scan chain testing and diagnosis have made it possible to extend the memory bitmapping concept to the core logic. Commercially available scan-based diagnosis tools are available that diagnose failing vector information and produce a list of potential defective nodes in the core logic. Like memory bitmapping this tool can provide fault localization and alleviate much of the time consuming physical FA steps. In order to take full advantage of these fault localization abilities and effectively drive baseline yields, these electrical FA results need to be correlated to the inline defect inspection data. Logic mapping is the process of correlating the polygons of the physical layout associated with the suspected defective nodes in the core logic with the inline defect inspection data.


While it is important to see memory bitmapping and logic mapping as companions in electrical FA, there will be circumstances where one technique is preferred over the other. In the specific case of ASICs, logic mapping will prove to be preferred when memory area on the device is small. Also, in general core logic will be susceptible to a wider class of defects than memories due to the larger number of physical layers used and the less structured, more diverse layout conditions. This paper will present the early results of implementing logic mapping as part of the ASIC manufacturing flow at LSI Logic. The following section will present the details of the logic mapping process including design and data collection requirements and other considerations. Section 3 will focus on the baseline yield enhancement flow using logic mapping. Section 4 will present the results from five wafer lots of one product. Section 5 will present future work and conclusions.


### Scan-Based ATPG Diagnosis and Logic Mapping Details


Scan-Based ATPG Diagnosis and Logic Mapping Details


Before logic mapping can be implemented, there are certain requirements that must be completed during the design cycle. First, the design must incorporate The other requirement for logic mapping is that all needed design files must be archived at the end of the design process and made available to the manufacturing support community. These files include those necessary for the ATPG diagnosis, the physical design database and any cross reference files that are needed to translate gate level net names used by the ATPG diagnosis to layout database net names. Special care must be taken to produce a layout database that can be used for the purpose of referencing physical coordinate information by net name. In the simplest form this might be an enhanced GDS file.


The logic mapping software was created in house and consisted of the modules that are shown in the flow chart in figure  2 . The boxes that are shaded gray represent commercially available tools. The logic mapping modules are broken down in the following way:


• Transform scan failing datalogs into datalogs that are useable by the ATPG diagnostic software  • Extract the inline defect coordinate and size information from the inline defect database • For each observed inline defect, calculate the distance from the defect to the nearest polygon. Each inline inspected layer has an associated layer in the layout. Only polygons from the associated layer as well as one layer above and below are considered during the distance calculation. The distance is measured from nearest edges, not centers. Defects are considered to be rectangles with a center coordinate and x and y extents. A decision is deferred until reporting time whether a defect is within the critical distance to be considered a killer defect. This allows the killer distance threshold to be adjusted without having to re-run the overlay process. • Load the overlay and scan diagnosis results into a database. Also load the killer / non-killer defect classification back into the inline defect database.


Figure  3  shows a typical overlay result from the logic mapping tool.


Figure  3a  shows the layout representation of the die, the extracted defects, and the polygons associated with the net that was identified by the ATPG diagnosis. Figure  3b  and 3c  show a close up of the net where an observed inline defect was found to correlate. Figure  3d  shows the defect and only those polygons that are considered for the overlay. In this case, the overlay distance between the defect and the nearest polygon is about 4µm. The discrepancy between the observed defect location and the actual defect location is due to the tolerance of the inline inspection tool, which is about 20µm. Figure  3e  shows the inline inspection photo of the defect.


### Baseline Yield Enhancement using Logic Mapping


Baseline Yield Enhancement using Logic Mapping


The shrinking of transistor sizes has continued to allow for increased densities, greater performance, and ultimately lower cost per memory bit and/or function for a given die size. With the scaling of transistor dimensions, sub-threshold leakage increases in a predictable manner due to equally scaled, lower threshold voltages as indicated in Figure  1  below  [1] . However the combination of sub-0.35 um gate lengths, sub-micron transistor widths, and current STI processes has greatly increased the density and severity of silicon mechanical stress-induced and defect-related leakage mechanisms in non-optimized processes  [2] .


### Silicon "Pipes"


Silicon "Pipes"


The particular failure mechanism of this study involves transistor channel "pipe" formations, which are similar in nature to diffusion enhancing defects  [3] . In essence, silicon lattice defects can generate localized, diffusion-enhanced regions of a dopant species so as to produce an inadvertently doped path (or "pipe") along the effective span of the defect. Depending on their effective size, as well as if the defects are in the same direction as the transistor channel length, such diffusion enhanced "pipes" can adversely affect the performance of the transistor by counter-doping a narrow, source-to-drain pathway within the channel.


The "pipes" discussed in this paper exclusively involve N-channel silicon micro-twinning near the STI/active interface and contribute only to subthreshold channel leakage, rather than junction leakage from dislocations. N-channel devices appear to be uniquely affected as related to the larger arsenic atoms used for creating the source/drain (S/D) regions. These larger atoms add more stress to a typically already strained lattice and represent the exclusive difference between affected N+ transistors and identically formed, boron implanted P+ transistors, which do not exhibit this sub-threshold leakage mechanism.


If the formation of these silicon defects is in a direction parallel to the transistor length, then S/D and/or lightly doped drain (LDD) implant species can inadvertently diffuse along the silicon defect. This form of defect-enhanced diffusion generates an undesired N-type doped path within the channel, ultimately decreasing the L eff , while providing a


Proceedings from the 28 th International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis, 3-7 November, 2002, Phoenix, Arizona much lower Vt in the channel within the narrow "pipe" formation region.


### Transistor "Pipe" Electrical Characteristics


Transistor "Pipe" Electrical Characteristics


Device testing of the isolated, failing transistors solely indicates channel leakage as responsible for generating the emission sites. Graphs of nominal versus failing transistor performance can be seen in the plot of Figure  2    Measurements of numerous failing, N-channel transistor sub-threshold leakage sites, determined leakage levels varying from 0.5 to 5 uA, for nominally applied supply voltages (V gate = 0V). A typical leakage value for an identical, unaffected transistor with a 0 V gate level is ~16 pA. The drain voltage is a constant 4 Volts for each measurement. Thus, these "pipes" produce a sub-threshold leakage, which can typically be "shut off" given the application of a sufficiently negative gate value. Nominal Vt's (defined in this case as the gate voltage required to achieve 1 uA of drain current) for these transistors are typically near 0.7 Volts and should be the same for all three devices.


Whereas the nominally performing device turns off very well as the gate voltage is lowered below 0.7 Volts, the marginally affected and grossly affected devices do not. They both require a greater negative gate voltage to achieve a "nominal" Id off measurement. The variation in sub-threshold leakages associated with the two failing curves is due to increased respective transistor "pipe" sizes for the marginally failing (0.5 -1 uA) versus grossly failing devices (5+ uA).


### Effects of STI on Pipe Formation


Effects of STI on Pipe Formation


Although similar studies have been performed which involve examination of mechanical stress induced dislocations near the STI interface  [4] , these types of one-dimensional silicon defects were associated with contributing to junction leakage, rather than the subthreshold transistor leakage mechanism discussed in this paper. However, the general STI process flow does incorporate a variety of contributing factors with respect to mechanical stress and strain, all of which contribute to the deformational, twodimensional micro-twinning seen in the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) photo of Figure  3 . This photo represents a cross-section of a known affected transistor in a direction perpendicular to its length and depicts the edge of the STI/channel interface with a polycrystalline film above the gate oxide. The trench oxide is to the right, with the channel silicon to the left. Note the angular set of micro-twins near the STI corner. Figure  4  illustrates the structure of a Face-centered-cubic (FCC) twin band  [5] . The twin plane is perpendicular to the plane of the main drawing and the twin axis lies within it.


Figures  5, 6 , and 7 illustrate the various forces associated with the thermal mismatch in strain between the isolation dielectric and the silicon substrate, the intrinsic stress of the nitride mask, and volume expansion-induced stress of the side-wall oxidation  [2] .


All forces provide a compressive lateral stress in the isolated silicon active area, which is additive in determining the final channel stress. The resulting strain within a particular point in the silicon is also heavily influenced by transistor width, length, implant species, and position to a STI corner.


Furthermore, the highest magnitude of compressive stress is typically found at the top of the silicon (i.e., just below the polycrystalline gate). Although these    forces are identical for similarly-sized P-channel devices, N-Channel transistors are almost exclusively affected with the micro-twinning failure mechanism due to the added stress in the lattice from the very large arsenic atoms, which are almost solely used for the latest generation N-type CMOS transistors. Thus, it is worth noting that identically shaped and sized Pchannel transistors do not indicate this type of channel "pipe" leakage mechanism.


### Overview of "Pipe" Induced Failure Mechanism


Overview of "Pipe" Induced Failure Mechanism


Due to the relatively low levels of current associated with this type of minimal transistor leakage (typically less than 2 uA per site), the failure mode generated from the transistor "pipe" failure mechanism was excessive standby current, rather than any sort of functional anomaly. Despite the fact that all affected transistors could still easily maintain their desired logic states, certain customer product requirements constrained the maximum standby current to less than 10 uA. Therefore, if any die contained more than five or six such failure sites, the die would exceed maximum standby current levels and fail standby testing. Yields were adversely affected by 10 -20% due to this failure mechanism.


### Emission Microscopy Results


Emission Microscopy Results


Emission microscopy was extremely helpful in locating these defects, not only due to the very low level of excessive current draw (greatly limiting the methods available for use in low-level leakages), but also because this failure mechanism allowed for exceptional emission generation related to electrons flowing through the transistor "pipe". Figure  8  below is a photo of one such emission site, for a magnification of 2000x. The emission photograph in Figure  8  was produced by means of biasing the substrate, source and gate at 0V, with the drain at 4V. For most failing transistors, this set-up produced approximately 0.5 -2 uA of excessive standby leakage.


### Defect Formation Sensitive to Layout


Defect Formation Sensitive to Layout


The vast majority of failure sites were traced to a very repeatable transistor layout. Figure  9  illustrates such a N-channel device, which is approximately 4 um wide and 0.35 um long. Although a significant portion of the N-channels for this particular chip have identical feature sizes, it is typically only the device surrounded on three sides by the STI process which is most sensitive to the formation of the microtwin defects. However, some minimum length transistors with widths less than 1 um were also affected on a repeated basis but are not discussed in detail in this paper.


The location of the leakage-generating channel defects, for the layout discussed above, is always on the same side of the transistor (left side as viewed in Figure  9 ). It is this same side of the transistor which contains a slight jog in the active at the STI interface.


Although both corners theoretically contain nearly identical stresses, the placement of the channel closer to the active/STI jog on the left side predisposes the channel to a slightly greater probability of a silicon defect. It is believed that this difference makes this layout more susceptible to defect generation due to the increased lateral compressive STI stress at this corner. The proximity of the jog in the poly gate to the STI interface is also a possible factor in increasing the probability of a defect formation.


### Conventional Decoration Etch Limitations


Conventional Decoration Etch Limitations


One-dimensional silicon dislocations/defects will typically form etch pits in the silicon when exposed to optimized selective wet silicon decoration etches (e.g., Wright, Sirtl, and Polysilicon etches, or any variety of junction stains). Failure mechanism confirmation involving silicon leakage paths is thus fairly straightforward, with proper preparation and wet etching of the known failing locations.


However, one of the more challenging aspects of the presented channel "pipe" sub-threshold leakage mechanism is that it is formed from a two dimensional silicon micro-twin (see Figure  3 ), rather than a pure dislocation or group of dislocations. The micro-twin defect mechanism does not consistently etch preferentially with respect to pure crystalline silicon when exposed to wet silicon decoration etches, and when it does, it never produces a defect in the channel (the actual location of the electrical leakage). TEM has been the only means able to locate the defect's true position as it relates to the generation of channel leakage.


Despite the fact that silicon decoration etches (Wright and Sirtl) rarely decorate out any noticeable channel defect for this specific failure mechanism, a very small percentage of the transistors containing the grossest of sub-threshold leakage levels (i.e., greater than 5+ uA/site) were able to produce defects along the STI edge as seen in Figure  10 . The below sample was prepared by removing all layers above the silicon (including the polysilicon gate), prior to decoration etch exposure, so as to make possible the subsequent decoration of any channel defect. Thus, for the typical 0.5 -2 uA defects, TEM is required to determine the actual appearance of these defects, and TEM is absolutely necessary to determine the exact locations of these defects as they affect the device.


Figure  11  is a top-down photograph representing the location and thickness of the actual TEM sample that produced Figure  3 .


### Experimental Results


The probability of "pipe" formation appears to be strictly based on the additive stresses within the silicon. If these stresses are sufficient to generate a micro-twin defect within the channel, and it becomes inadvertently doped, then sub-threshold channel leakage results. Obviously, there is a minimum stress necessary to generate such a defect.


The stress in a corner region such as in Figure  10  is obviously the greatest due to the additive lattice stress from both directions. Although the micro-twin most likely initiates near the edge, the length can vary significantly based on total lattice stress. Thus, if a nearby transistor channel intersects a sufficiently large twin, the defect can generate a sub-threshold leakage within the channel. This overall stress has been seen, through experimental results, to be related to the STI process, crystal orientation, nitride and pad oxide film thickness, transistor size in both width and length dimensions, implant species, dopant amounts, and subsequent anneals, to name a few.


The device layout also appears to be a factor, as certain transistors are repeatedly affected, with proximity of the channel to STI corners/edges and jogs a common denominator. Other transistors affected were short, minimum width devices. Thus, proximity of the transistor with respect to STI corners, and overall transistor width (or STI to STI spacing) appear to be the predominant contributing factors with regard to layout-induced stress. However, process modifications, rather than design changes, were exclusively addressed in this experimental study.


The following experimental results were obtained with the goal of reducing overall standby current levels. To achieve this goal, bin categories were developed to monitor the actual degree of standby leakage for each die. Acceptable levels of standby current draw are typically less than 15 uA, depending on the customer for a given device. Thus, the degree of success in any of the following experiments was measured by the relative increase in the percentage of die (% die) for the lowest standby current bin categories. This metric holds for Figures  12 13 14 . For each experiment, the predominant failure mechanism responsible for excessive standby current was traced to defect-induced, sub-threshold "pipe" leakage.


### STI Fill Oxide Densification and Pad


STI Fill Oxide Densification and Pad


Oxide/Nitride Film Thickness


The graph in Figure  12  indicates reductions in the amount of higher standby leakage levels, and respective increases in the number of die categorized for the lower leakage levels (fewer defects), for variations in the STI processing. Specifically, the 'no densification, modified N-Well drive' of the STI fill oxide and 'no densification followed by an anneal' processes provided for the best reduction in standby current levels, while the 'standard densification' process produced the greatest number of higher standby current devices.


Densification of the STI oxide produces additional compressive stress in the active silicon regions, especially at the STI/active corners, and obviously contributes to silicon channel defect formation. Thus, no densification, followed by an anneal, gives an approximate 5% improvement in the die yield for the lowest standby current bin.


Pad oxide and Nitride thickness variations prior to the STI process also appear to have a very noticeable effect on the overall stress within the silicon, especially when coupled with previously mentioned STI densification experiments. Figure  13  illustrates that thinner pad oxide and thicker blocking Nitride within the STI module definitely increase the stress in the silicon channel, while the opposite decreases the channel stress. An overlapping densification experiment was also performed in this study, with repeated results of better yield following no densification of the trench fill oxide. Thus, dramatic differences in standby current yield (up to 30% for the lowest current bin) can be achieved with changes only to the densification and pad oxide/blocking nitride thickness processing.


### N+ Arsenic Dose Reduction


N+ Arsenic Dose Reduction


Because the N+ arsenic S/D implant represents a significant increase in lattice strain (larger implant species), dose experiments were performed. These experiments indicated that the reduction of the arsenic dose (by half) definitely reduces the stress in the channel (see Figure  14 ), and ultimately reduces the excessive standby current failure occurrence by half. Thus, pronounced differences in yield (~20 %) are produced through the modulation of the N+ arsenic dose. Implant energy was not chosen as a variable based on previous work, which indicated it was not influential in generating lattice strain following proper anneals  [2] .


### STI Trench Depth


STI Trench Depth


Figure  15  represents experimental data with respect to variations from nominal in trench isolation depth. Deeper STI trench formation is seen to significantly increase the stress in the channel regions and subsequently produces a dramatic yield loss for increased standby current, while shallower trench formation decreases the number of failures associated with high standby leakage levels. Overall variations in yield, due to the split, range 25 percentage points, or nearly a five-fold increase in the failure rate from the shallowest trench process to the deepest.


### Crystal Orientation and Transistor Size


Crystal Orientation and Transistor Size


The silicon lattice micro-twinning occurs along a crystal plane within the  < 100 >  silicon. Since the transistors and polycrystalline gates are also oriented along this family of planes, orthogonal crystalline "surface" defects can run in a direction normal to the transistor polysilicon gate width. However, if the affected transistors are oriented with a 45 degree shift to the  < 100 >  silicon (C-flat starting material), then the size of the defect must increase in length with respect to the lattice if it is to generate the same failing condition.


This shift in transistor orientation also appears to change the stress imposed upon the active/STI sidewalls, thereby somewhat decreasing the overall occurrence of the micro-twinning defects. However, use of the C-flat material also alters certain transistor parameters, which may be unacceptable for a given design. In the past, standby current failures have been seen to be reduced by as much as 90% with the use of C-flat wafers, when the predominant failure mechanism has been known to be related to defectinduced, sub-threshold leakage.


A slight over-sizing of the polycrystalline gate critical dimension (~0.01 -0.02 um increase in length) has also been seen to generate a slight positive influence in lowering the susceptibility of the devices to channel defects of a given size. Within this experiment, general short channel behavior was known not to be an issue based on failure analysis efforts, which located transistor leakages to specific sites, as opposed to a generic, broad-based punchthrough mechanism.


It should be noted that additional, previous studies of silicon stress reduction involve rapid thermal oxidation (RTO) processing of the gate oxide in an H 2 O environment  [4] . Due to equipment limitations, this study was not performed.


### Summary and Conclusions


A number of factors have been listed which have been seen to contribute to increased mechanical stresses within advanced technologies incorporating STI processing. The combined effect of these compressive stresses, with the larger species of arsenic N+ implant, is responsible for the formation of the silicon lattice deformational twinning, thereby generating a form of diffusion enhanced defect, or "pipe," ultimately providing for substantially smaller transistor L eff 's. In sufficient quantity, these defects can substantially increase the device standby current levels to unacceptably higher values, thereby adversely affecting yields.


With the proper stress-induced, micro-twinning failure mechanism identified as the culprit, the responsible processing parameters were selected for modification, and altered so as to significantly reduce the occurrence of this defect mechanism. The four greatest influences producing this failure mechanism were found to involve implant dose, STI fill oxide densification, STI trench depth, and pad oxide/nitride film thickness variations. Finally, the optimization of these process parameters allowed for a consistent yield increase of 5 -10%, with respect to the Nchannel "pipe" sub-threshold leakage failure mechanism.


Recent economic conditions and ongoing cost pressures are driving a need for Failure Analysis organizations to justify their role and highlight their contribution in today's rapidly evolving and changing low cost PC environment. In addition, quality and product performance expectations are becoming increasingly more challenging, requiring a highly engaged analytical role that is driving timely problem resolution and the support of ongoing continuous improvement efforts. The challenge facing Failure Analysis organizations is to establish a framework, processes, and techniques in order to meet these requirements. Further compounding this challenge are the multiple levels of integration required by the final product [Figure  1 .] as well as the drive to outsource assembly and manufacturing services. All of these factors must be considered as part of the overall solution and require the need for an effective integrated Failure Analysis Model.

## 5. Test Support Engagement in FA Framework


5. Test Support Engagement in FA Framework


Failure Symptom to Failure Analysis The "initial" failure symptom seen at a PC or systemlevel by the user must be isolated and associated to the affected sub-system (i.e. Hard Drive, Memory Module, Power Supply, Motherboard, etc.) with subsequent analysis required based on the subsystem specific Failure Symptom to drive the isolation of the next level of analysis. In the case of a Motherboard, this could be anything from the PCB to digital and/or analog circuitry. This can lead to individual sub-system functionality analysis and potentially the analysis of silicon. This hierarchy of analysis needs to be performed without the destruction of the failure signature in order to facilitate the next level of analysis.


## Timely Failure Analysis


Timely Failure Analysis


The compression of the product life cycle brings a criticality to the usability of failure analysis information. Actionable information is information that is statistically valid and comprehensive enough to drive effective process, component, or design changes. Achieving this validity in the shortest possible timeframe becomes critical to allow the information to be usable and acted upon. This timeframe needs to consider improvement implementation on the next product generation as well as the improvement interception on current product performance.


## Failure Analysis Steps


Failure Analysis Steps


The traditional role of Failure Analysis groups consists of two main steps: Fault Isolation and Failure Analysis (FI/FA). Fault Isolation is focused on defect localization and usually involves electrical diagnostic techniques, while Failure Analysis involves physical and/or material analysis that establishes a failure mechanism, hence supporting failure root cause. These steps are usually sequential, and in the past were generally performed by the same FA group or organization. The drive to improve timeliness of information requires that steps be reconsidered as to how and when they are preformed. This problem is being solved through the development of the integrated Failure Analysis Team and the integration of failure analysis requirements into the Product Test solution. In addition, intelligent selection methods are being utilized to focus Failure Analysis on the areas that provide the most significant return to the business hence data systems and tools must deliver failure signature information to the solution providers as quickly as possible.


## Product Testing, FA Engagement and Fault Isolation


Product Testing, FA Engagement and Fault Isolation


The inclusion of Product Test as a part of the fault isolation process is changing the role of product test development groups to deliver solutions that not only validate the product quality, but also provide analytical direction. This is achieved by enhancing product test algorithms to output granular failure information that is utilized as the first step in the analysis process. This requirement is driving the need for a closer partnership between the Failure Analysis and the Test Development groups and the development of Design for Test (DFT) rules that enable the analytical factor to be supported. Effective characterization and sorting during the test process as well as careful evaluation of the data stream can support the isolation of significant events from random noise allowing the majority of the Fault Isolation activities to be completed even before the FA group have received the failed unit.


## Root Cause Analysis


Root Cause Analysis


The need to perform detailed root cause analysis is well embraced by Failure Analysis groups today. The move from "what" is defective to "why" has been embedded in the FA way of thinking that supports design, engineering and material groups in the process of problem and issue resolution. Time constraints and failure opportunities are now challenging FA groups to look deeper into why something failed, to identification of what "triggered" the failure event in the first place. To address this challenge, failure analysis must take on the role of Failure Investigation. As in any investigative work, hypothesis development and testing becomes the key tools utilized in support of root cause analysis.


## Failure Investigation


Failure Investigation


To support this approach, FA groups need to replicate the conditions at the time of failure and establish the critical parameters that were in existence at that time. This requires an assessment of the user's environment and details of the user's and product technical support's action. Based on this information, a defined Design of Experiments (DOE) can be developed that duplicates the failure event and supplies the necessary clue to what triggered the failure. Utilizing "Fault Injection" techniques, the engineering, design, or material group can apply the appropriate containment and long-term solution approach. This expansion of the Failure Analysis group's role has yielded significant improvement in both timeliness and effectiveness of the solution. This approach has enabled the implementation of solutions that have resulted in significant improvement within the current product cycle in addition to next generation product improvements.
