Figure 6. Hypothesis Testing and FI impact on Cost


## Destructive Vs Non Destructive Analysis


Techniques Advancement in analytical capabilities has created several approaches that can be followed in support of the analysis of a failure. The probability of having several common failure opportunities is low requiring a systematic structured analytical approach [Figure  7 ]. The need to maintain the failure signature for as long as possible requires the utilization of analytical tools   8 ] can be used as a first step in electrical failure isolation. It is a very effective non-destructive method for quickly isolating fault locations of resistive failures. IR thermal detection systems can produce a thermal profile of an entire motherboard or sub-assembly at one time.


Applying image subtraction techniques to resulting profiles allows quick comparison of test assemblies against "golden" units isolating suspect areas for further, more in-depth analysis. This approach can be taken a step further in cases where thermal failure signatures are well understood. IR Thermal Imaging can provide confirmation of a suspected failure mechanism potentially eliminating the need for further analysis. The utilization of these techniques to identify root cause and develop actionable data allows the corrective action team(s) to respond in a timely and effective manner. The development of Corrective Action and the implementation of a solution complete the cycle and deliver the result that was identified as part of the FA Framework [Figure  11 ].


## Cost Factor


Cost Factor


The implications of the bottom line and the ongoing cost pressures in the PC environment are driving the Personal Computing Business to investigate all aspects of the business model in the hunt for cost savings. Warranty costs are viewed as a prime source of cost savings opportunities even in the existing environment of continuously increasing quality and service expectations by customers. Warranty cost reduction is achieved most effectively through the utilization of an integrated failure analysis model [Figure  11 ]. 13 ].


## Cost Saving Opportunities


Cost Saving Opportunities


## Summary


Through the establishment of an Integrated Failure Analysis framework and the utilization of unique processes and techniques, critical focus can be applied to a very dynamic and cost driven business in a fashion that has significant Value Add and impact to the bottom line. The need for emphasis on "Timely Actionable Information" is apparent and requires Failure Analysis Groups to step outside the traditional boundaries and engage in areas of Product Test, Intelligent Failure Selection, Failure Investigation and Root Cause Analysis to enable resolution of failure trends in a timely and effective manner that maximizes the rate of cost saving realization. The application of Non-Destructive Analytical techniques to maintain the Failure Signature, and the engagement of Product Test Development Groups, to aid in early Fault Isolation, are critical factors to making this approach successful.


Generational Improvements and Defect Rate reduction results are confirming the Value Add this approach is bringing to the Personal Computing Business and is an example of how intrinsic and valuable FA groups are becoming as they step beyond the traditional FI/FA role.


The role of Failure Analysis groups has changed in response to the dynamic and increasing cost pressures of the Personal Computing business. Failure Analysis groups must establish integrated frameworks and working models that support increased effectiveness and responsiveness with the primary goal of delivering data and information that is timely and actionable and can quickly be used to drive issues to resolution. Results have shown that utilization of Product Test solutions for failure selection and early fault isolation allows issue resolution to impact current and future generation products and by so doing support the realization of cost avoidance opportunities.


The emergence of a variety of system level interface devices from a number of silicon vendors has provided designers with the flexibility to extend to system level the boundary-scan test capability already implemented within their design architecture in support of manufacturing board test strategy. This system level test architecture can be utilised to provide either enhanced diagnostic capability or a more flexible test capability as detailed below.


• Provide single-point access to multiple scan chains in support of a partitioned diagnostic capability or for optimizing in-system configuration of cPLD and FPGA devices.


• Support a board-to-board interconnect test strategy which will diagnose backplane interconnect test failures to edge connector pin level.


• Accommodate system checkout prior to shipment to customers including verification of firmware objects.


• Accommodate the upgrade of firmware objects within a field environment.


• Provide a single point access capability in support of environmental stress testing and accurate diagnostics.


## Topologies and Supporting Devices


Topologies and Supporting Devices


The selection of boundary-scan system level architecture for routing the test access port (TAP) signals is extremely important as it will dictate which system level access devices are selected and the respective implementation requirements. There are 3 major TAP routing strategies 1 that can be adopted, 'RING', 'STAR' and 'MULTI-DROP'.


## Multi-Drop Architecture


Multi-Drop Architecture


The most popular system level routing strategy adopted by the industry is MULTI-DROP. In this scheme, the five primary IEEE Std. 1149.1 test access signals TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO and TRST are connected in parallel to all backplane slots within the system configuration. Each of the slots within this multi-drop configuration will have a unique slot address consisting of six/seven address lines providing up to 64/128 unique addresses which will be hard-wired within the backplane architecture. Figure .1. Each of the boards within the system configuration is accessed by broadcasting its backplane slot unique address via the primary TDI signal line. The board located in the slot corresponding to the broadcast address will wake-up and allow access to selected local scan chains (LSC's) via the system device access protocol.


## Supporting Devices


Supporting Devices


Demand for a boundary-scan system level test capability has resulted in the development of a variety of supporting devices as depicted by the table, Figure  2   Lattice Semiconductor also provides the LSC BSCAN-1 and LSC BSCAN-2 as IP, provided that the target device is a Lattice Semiconductor part in which case the core function will be hard-coded into that device and sold as a pre-programmed part.


The primary function of all the devices defined in the table is to provide access from a primary boundaryscan bus to specific local scan chains (LSC's) selected via the system level device protocol as depicted in Figure  3 . This is a particularly useful feature when partitioning board designs in support of the in-system programming of flash memory devices. Under these circumstances the number and length of vectors shifted around the boundary-scan chain on the board should be kept to an absolute minimum in order to optimize the flash programming cycle time.


In this situation the boundary-scan device that has direct access to the flash address, data and control signal nets will be located in its own LSC, and this LSC will only be selected during the flash programming phase, whereas all the LSC's would be selected for board level interconnect testing.


This test partitioning feature can also be utilised when conducting board-to-board interconnect testing within a backplane environment. In this test scenario it is highly likely that only a few devices will provide the I/O access to the board edge connector, subsequently it is only necessary to shift test vectors to the devices responsible for providing the stimulus and capturing the respective responses.


In this instance the devices that access the board-toboard interconnect signal nets will be located in their respective local scan chains.


## Architectural Decisions


Architectural Decisions


It is important that the correct system level interface device is selected that supports your system test access and configuration requirements.


These key features can be categorized as:-


• How many local scan ports are required?


• Can the device be accessed within a multidrop configuration? • Can the system level devices be cascaded to provide access to multiple scan chains?


• Is there a requirement to perform board-toboard interconnect testing?


• Is there provision to access proprietary boundary-scan test controller signals?


• Can I access multi-vendor in-system configurable devices using the vendor specific proprietary tool suite?


• Can I read back the identification and version code of boards located within addressed backplane slots?


## How Many Local Scan Ports?


How Many Local Scan Ports?


Depending on the board level architecture it will be necessary to consider how many LSC's can be accessed by the system level interface device. The minimum is three; however, there are variants from Firecron and National Semiconductor that support in excess of six LSC's


## Does the System Level Interface Device Support


Does the System Level Interface Device Support


Multidrop Access?


If the system level backplane architecture has been designed for multi-drop access, it is imperative that the selected system level access device supports multi-drop addressing as shown in Figure  4 .


## Figure 4: Multidrop Access


Figure 4: Multidrop Access


Can System Level Devices be Cascaded?


It may be necessary to cascade multiple system level devices as shown for the Board 2 configuration in Figure  4 . This is extremely important when the selected device will only support a maximum of three LSC's. In this instance multiple system level devices will be cascaded to provide access to the requisite number of local scan chains. However, this will necessitate the placement of multiple devices on the board resulting in overhead in real-estate. This problem can be resolved by cascading IP cores into a single piece of silicon as identified in Figure  2 .


## Is There a Requirement to Perform Board-to-Board Interconnect Testing?


Is There a Requirement to Perform Board-to-Board Interconnect Testing?


In order to support board-to-board interconnect testing it will be necessary to PARK all selected unparked local scan ports (LSP's The system level interface device must be able to route this signal through to the appropriate local scan chain as shown in Figure  5 . It may be necessary to access cPLD or FPGA devices located in local scan chains, directly using vendor specific JTAG programming or emulation tools.


It is unlikely that this will be possible if a system level interface device is located between the primary JTAG port and the LSC's, because the vendor specific programming/emulation tools do not support the protocols necessary for communicating with these devices.


Under these circumstances a generic pass-through capability is required which can either be selected by the appropriate binary combination on specific control lines in conjunction with a pass through enable signal as shown in Figure  6 , or in the case of the STA111, by shifting the TRANSPARENTn instruction into the bridge device instruction register (where n is the selected LSP).


As the bridge device state machine moves into the Run-Test-Idle (RTI) state, all the LSP signals will follow the primary backplane signals, such that the bridge becomes transparent. Depending upon the system level architecture it may be necessary that after establishing a board is present in a unique backplane slot location, to have the capability to read back the identity and version of the board residing in that slot. This is particularly important within a system architecture where any board type can be located within any of the slots, which means that the board type and version must be established before the appropriate test vectors can be broadcast to that slot address 2 .


## Additional Features


Additional Features


A number of the system level interface devices have additional features, such as LSP_ACTIVE or BRIDGE_SELECT signal pins which are asserted once the device is selected. This feature can be utilised to control device specific boundary-scan enable pins or disable some glue logic, so that boundary-scan tests can be executed successfully.


## Embedded Vector Delivery


Embedded Vector Delivery


All the discussions so far have focused on implementing a board level architecture that will support a system level test strategy which utilises an external controller to provide the vector delivery to boards residing in backplane slots addressed by a broadcast address as shown in Figure  7 . The following discussion will address the different backplane architectures that are commonly implemented to support embedded vector delivery. These are as follows:-


• Passive Backplane -Local Test Bus Master • Passive Backplane -System Test Bus Master • Active Backplane • Passive Backplane -BIST Sequencer


## Passive Backplane -Local Test Bus Master


Passive Backplane -Local Test Bus Master


In this configuration each plug-in module (board) has its own Test Bus Master (TBM) as shown in Figure  8 , which has full access via the System Level Interface device to all the local scan chains.


The boundary-scan test vectors will be stored locally in flash memory and will be accessed via the TBM under control of the on-board processor.


Hence, each plug-in module is independently and concurrently performing a self test. Inter-board interconnect testing is possible but all TBM's must be synchronized or one board within the backplane configuration must become the Master. In this configuration one module in the backplane is the system Master and all the other modules become Slaves to the system master as shown in Figure  9 .


The boundary-scan tests vectors for testing the slave modules individually or for performing board-toboard interconnect tests are broadcast serially across the primary JTAG bus under the control of the system Test Bus Master.


## Active Backplane


Active Backplane


In this configuration the backplane becomes active with the Test Bus Master, microprocessor and embedded test vectors located on the backplane.


This allows the TBM master controller to be isolated from all the plug-in modules, allowing a full multidrop architecture to be implemented.


## Plug-in Module


Plug-in Module


Figure  9 : Active Backplane


## Passive Backplane -BIST Sequencer


Passive Backplane -BIST Sequencer


The limitation with the System TBM and Active Backplane architectures is that test vectors must be shifted serially from the TBM across the primary JTAG bus to the relevant slave modules within the backplane configuration.


This could amount to an excessive amount of data, particularly if the test vectors are performing full module interconnect tests or the in-system configuration of cPLD's or FPGA devices.


If the relevant test vectors were stored and executed locally as described for the Local TBM configuration, the amount of data broadcast across the primary JTAG bus is limited.


Because of these limitations and the requirement to be able to execute locally stored test vectors sequentially without the overhead of the on-board processor, which will free-up the processor to perform other operations. Firecron Ltd in conjunction with Motorola NSS developed a BIST Sequencer 1 which has been implemented within Motorola's 3G Base Station designs.


This device has no intelligence but acts as a sequencer for shifting test vectors to and from the local scan chains as selected by the local system interface device as shown in Figure  10 .


## SIFT Scanner System


SIFT Scanner System


The concept began with the author back in 1986 by placing a pinhole in aluminum foil to reduce the illumination spot size on a B+L optical microscope on a probe station and manually rastering the spot over the device under functional test. 2 A looping test pattern went into failure as the spot was scanned over the defect. This technique was also used parametrically with a curve tracer to localize and confirm the defects during the stripback process.


The SIFT scanner does not use traditional laser scanning microscope optics and is actually quite straightforward in construction. DUT scan area can be microns to 12" or more, allowing whole boards, packages and die to be analyzed since the scanners are stepper-based rather than internal optics based. Field of view limitations of objectives on LSM (Laser Scan Microscope) based equipment are eliminated with SIFT. Data output is to a PC via multiple RS232 channels and contains data from the scan for X, Y, and multi-channel data for each step in the scan. This data is coordinate data but can also be displayed photographically in .raw format using Adobe photoshop at present. Channel data consists of pass/fail signals from the tester as well as analog information. The scan and step is user defined based on spot size.


The system can be based on either a motorized probe station or microscope stand for test head applications. Unlike LSMs, SIFT uses a stationary beam and moves either the stage or the microscope head in a raster scan pattern. Figure  1  is a block diagram of the apparatus. A microscope and stage are equipped with stepper motors to control the X, Y, and Z motion of the scan. Obviously servo motors or similar linear positioning devices can be used in place of stepper motors. Z control is necessary to control the spot size of the stimulus by either focus or proximity control of the source. Laser based SIFT uses a laser attached to the top camera port of the microscope and can be any wavelength compatible with the selected optics. The selected objective, aperture, and focus control spot size, in this case.


CO2 lasers can be mounted in place of the microscope and raster scanned over large areas for thermal SIFT. The stimulus can also be introduced over the DUT with the raster applied to the stage. This method of SIFT can be thought of in the same way a probe is positioned over a DUT by moving the stage. The microcontroller is based on a Microchip Inc. PIC17C756 and runs over 1500 lines of C code to handle all the required functions.


The microcontroller handles X-Y-Z positioning, stimulus, and communicates with the tester. Communication can be synchronous, where the microcontroller will step only after receiving pass/fail from the tester or handshake with the tester, for multi-loop platforms. In this paper, the synchronous mode is used to demonstrate interfacing to the tester without any electrical connections via phototransistors. It should be apparent that direct connection means are also possible.


## Stimulus Methods


Stimulus Methods


## Optical Beam Induced Current


Optical Beam Induced Current


The setup to obtain an OBIC (Optical Beam Induced Current) image using SIFT will allow a comparison and facilitate an explanation of the scanner. Traditional OBIC uses a LSM and a current detection amplifier to sense and display photocurrents induced by the laser. 3 SIFT is implemented by either using the current detection amplifier or by interfacing a curve tracer to the analog signal input of the microcontroller. The curve tracer X and Y internal amp signals are wired to the microcontroller, allowing the curve tracer to handle the scaling while the X and Y outputs supply .5V/division signals. The curve tracer spot positioning serves to set the offset to the microcontroller. The advantages of this method hinge on being able to monitor I-V relationships rather than only constant voltage or constant current methods.


The overlay image or photograph also needs to be obtained. One method is to scale an optical image or layout to the scanned image since the scanned image has exact coordinates for the scan compatible with layout information. The other method is to create the image by sampling the reflected light from the laser during the scan in a similar manner as the LSM. The laser source is a 670nm laser diode, which is focused to the diffraction limit (smallest spot size), for the scan. The detector is a phototransistor linked to the microcontroller with an adjustable gain. The 30 frames/second CCD camera and LCD monitor allow navigation as well as the ability to serve as a photodetector port.


The user may insert the photodetector in the microscope path in place of an eyepiece or similar port for reflected light sampling or the photodetector could be affixed to the LCD screen associated with the CCD image. This method works so well that it is the preferred method. A settle time of 40 msec is used at each sample location for the LCD display-based detection. Although this may seem slow compared to traditional OBIC techniques, most applications have significant capacitance, especially decoupling at Vdd. Control of the scan sample rate is important based on the device parameters for settle time. Figure  2  is an OBIC image obtained with the curve trace interface and the photodetector affixed to the screen. The microcontroller runs the scan based on input parameters. The step is set to 3 um, which means that the microcontroller will stop every 3 um and sample the OBIC signal and reflected laser signal simultaneously. The scan area is determined by simply setting the origin and navigating with the joystick +X and +Y to define the scan area. The display shows how large, in pixels, the photo will be as well as the pixel size in microns. Upon initiation, the scanner will raster scan until coordinate 0,0 is reached. The resulting data files can be viewed in CSV (Comma Separated Values for a Spreadsheet) or raw (photoshop) formats depending on the preference. The spot size for the stimulus can be different than the spot size for the background image, unlike an LSM system. An active circuit useful for supplying constant current type performance with constant voltage control is described in figure  3 . 10 The circuit consists of a voltage controlled constant current source, which is used to drive a constant current across the DUT. The resulting voltage drop across the DUT is buffered at J2 and supplied to a lowpass filter. The lowpass filter supplies the DC value of the DUT bias to a summing circuit which adds the negative desired set-point of the DUT (Compliance voltage set-point) to the actual measured DUT bias. The result is multiplied by -2.7 and used to control the dependent current source such that Vcc is maintained on the DUT. The signal at J2 is also supplied to a high gain active filter for detection of the ONS (Oxide Noise Signature) signal. The ONS signal is monitored during a SIFT scan to identify minute shifts in operation during a scan.


## RF Stimulus


RF Stimulus


RF SIFT uses an RF probe tip to either inject or receive RF energy over the DUT. This technique is useful for board, package, and die level to trace circuit paths carrying the characteristic frequency.


Opens can be identified assuming the capacitive coupling across the open is not dominant. Spatial resolution and signal strength are impacted by proximity of the DUT to the source as well as tip geometry. Frequency is selected based on the amount of capacitive coupling desired between the tip and source. The tip is normally the sensor with the trace biased at the desired RF frequency. As with any electric field based method, the conductor of interest must not be shielded. Figure  4  is a scan taken of a 70 um copper trace in Kapton tape on an inkjet cartridge. The highlighted area is the active trace with a 100KHz signal present. This technique is comparable to CIVA, however, CIVA requires an e-beam whereas this method works in air and allows both positive and negative charge to be imposed locally for identifying floating nodes and circuit paths.


## Thermal Stimulus


Thermal Stimulus


Thermal stimulus is useful for localizing ohmic shorts or intermittent connections as well as timing related failures. Ohmic ESD or Vdd failures are candidates for this technique. Thermal methods of SIFT scanning can be based on the following:


1. Scanning hot probe tip.


2. Laser at appropriate wavelength.


3. Magnetic Induction.


Parametric issues surrounding thermal management need to be understood so that appropriate power levels can be chosen for both frontside as well as backside analysis. A simple way to determine the required energy is to look at a diode to substrate on the device under test. Generically, the substrate diode associated with a given input pin is a known temperature sensor. . Figure  5 . Typical diode forward drop versus temperature relationships for 3 current drive levels.


Whereas the forward voltage may vary process to process, the ∆V can still be used to measure temperature excursions as shown in equation 1.


∆V/2.0E-3 ≅ ∆T @0.1mA


(1) ∆V/1.6E-3 ≅ ∆T @1mA ∆V/1.5E-3 ≅ ∆T @2mA ∆V = Change in diode forward voltage ∆T = Celsius change in temperature


The next parameter to evaluate is the thermal propagation in silicon for frontside and backside. For frontside, the excursion in temperature is fairly small, on the order of 5 to 10 degrees, as shown in Figure  6 . Note the small fast waves are the on-off pulses of the laser and the general slope downward represents general die heating. Since the substrate is tied to a copper paddle, the general die heating is reliant on the paddle, which is floating. The temperature gradient is only 4 to 5 degrees Centigrade due to the thermal conduction of the die and paddle. Figure  6 . Thermal excursion with a pulsed IR laser on the frontside of silicon. Signal is inverted. Scale is Horz: 2 seconds/div, Vert: 5 0 C/div.


For the backside, a die was thinned to 30 um remaining silicon thickness and evaluated. Note the rapid ramp and gradient now better than 100 0 C. Since the silicon is thin and has greatly reduced volume there is much less lateral heat spread. Figure  7 . Thermal excursion with a pulsed IR laser on the backside of silicon. 30um thickness. Signal is inverted. Scale is Horz: 1 second/div,Vert:100 0 C/div.


## Thermal Stimulus using CW lasers


Thermal Stimulus using CW lasers


Normally for thermal stimulus with a laser, wavelengths outside the indirect bandgap of silicon are required, such as 1.3 um, to avoid generation of photocurrents. 11 It is difficult to get the power necessary in a large spot to heat significantly at this wavelength due to numerous factors such as laser power limitations. The silicon doesn't heat at this wavelength. The primary heating is accomplished from absorption of the laser energy by the metal, which typically scatters a significant amount of the radiation. As reported by Cole, the temperature gradient at metal is roughly 1 0 C/mW with typical heating of the metal up to around 30 0 C with a 1.3 um laser. 11 Temperature excursion of the related silicon will be typically less than 1 0 C, inadequate for silicon based thermal analyses.


Functional SIFT needs to be able to scan a large spot with sufficient energy to create thermal gradients in the silicon as well as metal. The scan area and laser spot size are successively reduced, based on results, so the math doesn't become a problem. If the tester can loop every 100 msec and the spot size is 1 um across a small die such as 2mmX2mm it will take 400000 seconds (4.6 days) to complete 1 scan. SIFT allows for variable spot sizes and step values to allow quick reduction of the scan area to minutes. SIFT also needs to create a significant temperature gradient in order to differentiate functional timing failures.


Ordinarily, shorter wavelength lasers generate too much photocurrent to be useful thermally. Several laser wavelengths of importance, due to their ability to generate higher power, are: 532nm, 808nm, 940nm, and 1064nm. All of these wavelengths will generate photocurrents unless they are masked from the die. This is accomplished by applying high temperature flat black paint to the die surface by spray, brush or spin deposition. The 532nm laser does not need to be masked when used backside due to the absorption of the laser by the silicon substrate. Carbon sputtering can also be used backside or frontside if the connections are passivated first. A 5 watt 808nm laser was chosen to locally heat the surface with around 1 to 2 watts depending on spot size and desired heating. No photocurrents are generated, as shown in figures 8 and 9, due to the opaque layer.


## High Frequency Magnetic Induction


High Frequency Magnetic Induction


By scanning a miniature induction coil over the device, as shown in figure  10 , package level shorts can be mapped. The spatial resolution is currently limited to about 2 mm based on the frequency used (10-20 MHz). Magnetic induction couples and directly heats the conductors embedded in a package due to formed eddy currents within the IC. The device can be operated during the scan and multilayer devices are well suited for induction based on coupling. The power supply was developed for this application, as commercial units cannot operate at these high frequencies. Parametric shifts of the diode in the corner of figure  11  are monitored during the scan by the microcontroller in relation to the coordinates. Induction also allows monitoring of phase based on coupling to the conductors. Imaging is possible due to phase/frequency relationships during the scan. Future work is intended at higher frequencies to address these possibilities but is beyond the scope of this paper.


## Functional SIFT


Functional SIFT


Now that the foundations have been laid, the pieces of the puzzle come together as functional SIFT. Functional SIFT is based on pass/fail test criteria that can be complete vector tests including parametrics or subsets as appropriate. The setup involves a quick interface to a tester display with photosensors, such as shown in figure  12 , or direct wiring to the tester. The photosensors are attached to the LCD screen with double stick tape at the appropriate locations on the screen. The clear advantage to this method is that the tester can be of any type allowing multiple links to the SIFT scanner without any tester modification.


The simplest method is to monitor the pass-fail light bar on a tester and strobe the SIFT through full test loops. This allows the die to be fully tested at each stimulus coordinate controlled by the SIFT scanner. In the case of figure  12 , two sensors are used. The sensor labeled D is the data sensor, which looks for a change in data after sensor S transitions from low to high (strobe). After a strobe, the scanner will move to the next coordinate in the scan. It may sound complicated, but it actually boils down to looping the test program, (even if it was written by someone who left the company years ago) setting the spot size and intensity to trigger the failure and running the scan. Obviously, the sensors can monitor presence or absence of numeric data or pass fail flags on the screen as needed. Multiple sensors can be used to overlay several data parameters at the same time. Future work will involve direct connection to the tester video interface.


Figure  12 . View of the screen on a tester with 2 sensors affixed. The sensor labeled D is the data sensor, which looks for a change in data after sensor S transitions from low to high (strobe).


A die scan over the entire die using a 670nm laser was performed to identify a faulty Y decoder causing several SRAM columns to fail. Light sensitivity of the die was noted. SIFT was used linked to the tester with the laser spot set to .5mm and the scanner set to .4mm to allow overlap of the 2.9X5.1mm die. The scan size in pixels, with plenty of die overlap, was 9X14 equating to 126 test loops to complete the die scan. The loop was 1 second requiring 126 seconds to scan the entire die. Although images are being provided to show the location, the scanner actually gives exacting coordinates for each sample point. In this case, 126 coordinates were output with associated sensor readings. This allows for linking to CAD layout. Figures  14  and 15  are reduced area scans where the spot was also scaled down. Each scan took  < 5 minutes to complete.


A new method of complete failure analysis has been presented which now allows multiple beam based stimulus to be linked to any tester or parametric analyzer. The problem of insufficient laser power and insufficient thermal gradients to analyze functional failures has been overcome with backside preparation as well as mask methods. 100 0 C temperature gradients are now routine, allowing timing sensitive failures to be localized as well as a host of failure mechanisms. SIFT techniques have been shown for both traditional laser based techniques as well as new methods. Comparative disturb between reference and failing or threshold dependent failures is now possible. Variable spot size allows faster scans and uniform stimulus of larger blocks on an IC for timing/thermal analyses. Stimulus includes thermal, high frequency magnetic induction, OBIC and RF injection using a scanning probe tip. Since the data is based on coordinate information, it can be converted to the traditional photo form or analyzed for maxima and minima based on coordinates for x and y in spreadsheet form as well as CAD overlays. Scan size is virtually unlimited. Scan speed is limited both by stepper speed and loop test time.


Given the fast pace of the computer manufacturing industry along with resource limitations due to the current economic climate, delivering effective system and motherboard failure analysis in a useful time-frame has become a challenge. The timeliness of failure analysis information has become a key element of its value. In addition to short life-cycles and resource constraints, adding to this challenge is the reduced form factor of the motherboard, the increased population density of components, and in-house test equipment that is quickly becoming less effective in isolating certain common active and passive component failures.


The opportunity primarily lies in reducing the time it takes between identifying a verified failed system or sub-system and finding the root cause of the failure event. It becomes even more relevant in the fast pace of the computer industry where large quantities of motherboards are manufactured in a short period of time, coupled to an extremely short shelf life. This necessitates quick failure identification and corrective action in order for failure analysis to have a positive impact.


The time to Root Cause Failure Analysis (RCFA) must therefore be reduced, which increases the importance and demand for new tools and techniques that provide rapid, nondestructive failure analysis.


Motherboard failures in computers can be divided into the following categories relative to passive components, integrated circuits, and other related functions:


• Logic failures (for example, digital processing) • Signal analog failures (for example, audio, voltage regulator policing circuits) • Power analog failures (for example, voltage regulators or direct current to direct current (DC-DC) regulators integrated onto the motherboard)


Equipment used for isolation of digital-and analog-related failures are readily available to rapidly zoom into a failed logic or analog circuit to isolate the suspect component. However, this is not always the case with resistive failures or shorts on a motherboard. Isolating these types of failures are extremely challenging without inadvertently destroying the evidence due to a large number of circuits that utilize many components connected to the same node.


A common failure mode occurs when components fail resistively, between V cc and ground. These resistive failures can be characterized as high or low impedance failures; for example, a cracked printed circuit board (PCB) trace would exhibit itself as a high resistance failure while a leaky capacitor would exhibit itself as a low impedance failure. A simple ohmmeter is unable to locate a low resistance component failure when parallel components are associated with the same node, and all components will measure a low resistance defect. Test equipment using Time Domain Reflectrometry (TDR) or milli-ohm meter techniques have become less effective in isolating the shorted or resistive component. This is due to the high population density and reduced form factor of the motherboards. It is more likely than not to find multiple components connected to the same node in a one-centimeter radius. In addition, false results could result from adjacent components connected to the same node but with unequal trace lengths. Collectively, these deficiencies make TDR and milli-ohm meter techniques less effective on today's high-density products than on less complex and lower density circuit board designs of the past.


A process of elimination could be implemented, removing suspect parts or cutting traces where possible. However, it is an undesirable and destructive method to isolate the failed component or defect.


Evidence may be destroyed in the process, and therefore the final root cause failure analysis results could be distorted. All the above processes may be time consuming.


To overcome these problems, a cost effective test setup was developed which uses an infrared (IR) camera based thermography system to identify failures that may otherwise be time consuming to isolate. A suitable wavelength IR camera was chosen for our needs. The camera detector frequency range was within the IR spectrum. Other primary factors in our choice included characteristics such as feature set, image quality, and equipment cost. This paper does not cover RCFA but rather presents techniques useful in the failure discovery process. In order to use the IR thermography system to its full potential, all aspects of IR thermal imaging had to be understood.


Our research revealed the following: the blackbody is an object that absorbs all radiation at any frequency. According to Kirchoff's law  [1] , an object that absorbs all radiation at any frequency is equally capable of radiating all the absorbed radiation. If the blackbody reaches about 525°C, the radiated frequency increases to the visible portion of the spectrum and the object is perceived as red  [2]  by the human eye. Planck's law  [3]  describes the spectral distribution of radiation from a blackbody. 1 Where, W λb = the blackbody spectral emittance at wavelength λ c = 3 × 10 8 meter per second (velocity of light) h = 6.6 × 10 -34 Joule second (Planck's constant) k = 1.4 × 10 -23 joule per Kelvin (Boltzmann's constant) T = absolute temperature of a blackbody in Kelvin λ = wavelength of the electromagnetic wave in meters Plotting any particular Planck curve shows that the higher the temperature, the higher the frequency, hence the shorter the wavelength (the frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional). If you differentiate Planck's law with respect to λ (wave length), you would end up with Wien's displacement law  [4] . 2 Where, λ max = maximum wavelength in meters T = absolute temperature of a blackbody in Kelvin Wien's law shows mathematically that colors relate to temperatures. Therefore the frequency of a color is equal to the wavelength calculated for λ max .


      = T mK T µ λ 2898 max ………..Equation


To characterize the total radiance of a blackbody, you need to integrate Planck's formula from λ = 0 to λ = ∞. This transforms Planck's law to the Stefan-Boltzmann equation  [5] , where σ = 5.7 ×  3 Where, W b = total radiant emittance of a blackbody σ = 5.7 × 10 -8 Watts per meter square (Stefan-Boltzmann constant) T = absolute temperature of a blackbody in Kelvin This mathematical explanation only relates to a blackbody.


10 -8       2 m Watt .       = 2 4 m Watt T W b σ ….…………..Equation


However, in practice, as a complication, not all objects represent blackbodies and should therefore be characterized as non-blackbody emitters. The emissivity of a non-blackbody object can be characterized by its spectral emissivity (ε λ ). The spectral emissivity is defined as the ratio between the spectral radiation from a nonblackbody divided by the spectral radiation from a perfect blackbody. 4 Where, ε λ = spectral emissivity of an object W λo = spectral radiant power from an object W λb = spectral radiant power from a blackbody   1 ) can be generated using equation 4. The emissivity of an object can be determined through the following steps. First, attach a thermocouple to the object to measure the actual temperature of the object. Second, use the IR thermography system to measure the perceived temperature of the object. Third, using equation 4, ε λ can be calculated using the measured temperature and the temperature displayed by the IR system. Once ε λ is known for this particular object, the correct absolute temperature (W λo ) for the object can be calculated.


When thermal comparisons between an exemplar and suspect circuit board are used to identify a possible failure, absolute temperature measurements may not be important. Therefore it is important to take different precautions. In many cases, the test environment may introduce ambient reflected IR into the thermal image, which could originate from the room, operator, other adjacent objects and also the heat generated by the camera case and heat emitted through the camera lens.


## IR Camera


IR Camera


The IR spectrum covers electromagnetic wavelengths from 0.75µm to 15µm. As the electromagnetic wavelength decreases to below 0.75µm, the heat that is generated becomes visible to the human eye  [7] . This effect is typically reached when the object becomes visibly red and is related to temperatures above 525°C. In contrast, the temperature requirements at the failure analysis (FA) laboratory normally range between 0°C and 200°C requiring a tool capable of imaging longer wavelengths. The decision was made to choose an IR system with an uncooled focal plane array (FPA), operating in the intermediate to far infrared spectrum, which is typically between 6µm to 15µm. Due to cost considerations, a camera with a detector resolution of 160 × 120 pixels was chosen. The spectral range of the detector was between 7.5µm and 13µm with a built-in atmospheric filter compensating for distance, atmospheric temperature, and humidity.


The camera accuracy was calibrated by the manufacturer at ±2% of the measurement range and the thermal sensitivity, typically 0.1°C at 30°C  [8] .


The system setup was placed in an enclosure to thermally isolate the IR camera and object from external environmental interferences. The controlling computer, power supplies, and other heat generating equipment were mounted outside the IR camera enclosure.


## Case Studies


Case Studies


The remainder of this paper focuses on the experience gained from nine different case studies.


In the case studies, the IR thermography system was used to both measure relative temperatures as well as absolute temperatures of components.


Relative temperature characterization of a circuit board allowed the FA engineer to rapidly and nondestructively isolate and identify a defective component, manufacturing defect or defective site on a high component density computer motherboard.


Absolute temperature measurements allowed the engineer to rapidly and in real time record the temperature of known suspect components. The IR thermography system was used in various failure investigations in order to test the limits of the acquired system as well as developing test procedures to identify various failures. The following nine types of failures were investigated:


• Overdriven components.


• Finding end of life (EOL) but still functional components. The nine investigated failure modes were delineated into two subsets, relative temperature comparison measurements and absolute temperature measurements. In both subsets, the same test vectors were used in the same environment and registration to insure consistent results.


## Absolute Temperature Characterization of Known Objects


Absolute Temperature Characterization of Known Objects


Absolute temperature measurements were used to determine the precise temperature of the components.


Temperatures from selected components were measured and compared to functionally similar designs or exemplar circuit boards. Temperature calibration of the setup was essential.


The emissivity of the objects had to be determined and the necessary adjustments in the IR thermography system software had to be made to ensure that the correct temperature of the object was reported. Once the setup was complete, measurements of the suspect objects could then be performed at a rapid pace. A case study on overdriven components was the only study performed related to absolute temperature characterization.


## Overdriven components


Overdriven components


Temperatures from selected components within specific circuits were measured and compared in order to determine if the components were overdriven causing them to operate at a temperature that may compromise their reliability.


Figure  1  shows how the thermal system software can be used to measure component temperatures. In the case of absolute temperature measurements, the emissivity of the component must be determined and factored into the IR thermography system measurement for accurate temperature results.


An exemplar circuit board component can be thermally characterized to establish the normal operating temperature under a specified load and environmental conditions.


These thermal characteristics can then be compared to the result obtained from the circuit board under investigation to see if the parts operate at a higher temperature and therefore are more stressed. If the temperature difference was significant, a flag was set for further investigation.


Subsequent measurements could be performed at a rapid pace with a calibrated IR thermography system. This allowed the FA engineer to save time screening for failures during the investigation.


Figure  1  The thermal image from a three-phase CPU voltage regulator high side three FETs. The three FETs of interest were marked and calibrated, using the IR thermography system software to display the absolute component temperature.


## Relative Temperature Characterization of Known Objects


Relative Temperature Characterization of Known Objects


Relative temperature comparisons were performed utilizing an exemplar thermal image and comparing it to a suspect image in order to highlight components or locations that appeared either hotter or colder. Three distinct techniques were developed:


• If the failure node was not known, image subtraction between an exemplar and suspect circuit board was performed to highlight the suspect areas. • If the failure node was known and the components relating to the node known, image subtraction was not necessary. • When screening for known suspect component in known locations but on various nodes, the components could be marked in a thermal image template and easily monitored and compared to the exemplar circuit board. Depending on the number of components and nodes, image subtraction may or may not be necessary.


The following types of failures were used in case studies using the IR thermography system and relative temperature measurements:


Finding EOL but still functional components An End-Of-Life (EOL) component is a component that no longer performs to specification but has not caused a functional failure of the circuit. However, there are circumstances that may cause the component to reach premature EOL. The causes may relate to external factors not related to the quality of the component.


The hypothesis was that an EOL component might exhibit some form of thermal image that may be detected by the thermography system before the component self-destructed or failed. One real success that was achieved in identifying EOL components was in the case of aluminum electrolytic capacitors with halogencontaminated electrolyte. The hotter operating temperature of the part as a result of higher internal leakage current could easily be identified.


A template was generated, with the suspect component location marked in the thermal image. The temperatures of all the parallel aluminum electrolytic capacitors on the exemplar circuit board were characterized after the circuit board was powered for 10 minutes (see Figure  2 ).


The suspect circuit boards were mounted in the same fixture to ensure consistent registration. They were powered for 10 minutes before the temperature measurements were taken. When a capacitor was identified with a higher relative temperature, it was removed for further analysis. In Figure  3 , the black circle marked B shows the increased heating signature of a capacitor that reached premature EOL.


The cause of the failure was ionic contamination, degrading the oxide dielectric in the capacitor, causing increased leakage current and subsequent internal heating. In this case, a deviation of more than 3°C was investigated. The deviation trigger point can be obtained from thermally characterizing more than one exemplar circuit board, calculating the mean and recording maximum and minimum temperatures of the known parts.


Due to the relative temperature profile comparison capability afforded by the IR thermography system, absolute and accurate temperature measurements were not necessary.


Boards could be screened at 10-minute intervals, and only the suspect parts were sent for further RCFA. Correctly specified components with quality defects This type of defect exhibits itself as either high resistance or low resistance between the V cc and ground. The IR thermography system was most valuable and most effective in cases where the failed component was connected in parallel with similar or different components and the failed component failed for low resistance between V cc and ground. Isolation of this type of failure, without the IR thermography system, was extremely difficult without becoming destructive.


## A B 635


A B 635


In this case study, the failure node was known and therefore image subtraction was not necessary due to the low number of associated components. Stimulating the suspect node with a small amount of current isolated the failed component. Initial current flow was carefully limited to 10 milli-ampere and incremented until the failing component exhibited itself (see Figure  4 ). The component was identified and the testing immediately halted to preserve the sample integrity.


## Incorrect component placement


Incorrect component placement


This failure mode can be characterized as components populated incorrectly on the circuit board. It may lead to an event where the component may internally heat when the circuit board was powered, for example, polarized capacitors (tantalum or aluminum electrolytic) populated with reversed polarity.


However, the absence of a thermal signature or identification of a cold spot was also a valuable indicator and a good example of this nature can be seen in Figure  5 .


The under driven component or cold spot in the thermal image is identified by arrow A and the overdrive or hot spot is identified by arrow B.


What became evident in this case was that identifying a failed component or failure location did not always relate to the hotter component or the hotter location but also to the absence of heat or cold spot. In this case, FET A was not heating up. FET A was incorrectly populated on the circuit board and therefore never switched ON. It should be noted that FET B was in parallel to FET A, providing parallel paths to support the high current demands of the circuit. Since FET A was always OFF, all the current now flowed through FET B. The end result was a cold spot at FET A and an abnormally hot spot at FET B.


## Internal V cc to ground low resistance integrated circuits (IC) failures


Internal V cc to ground low resistance integrated circuits (IC) failures


Integrated circuit failures can also be identified by their thermal signature. A typical observed failure mode was an abnormal increase in temperature when a device was powered. The observed failure mode was typically caused by extensive damage to the die, due to some failure induced event, resulting in an internal V cc to ground low resistance failure. The current through the low internal resistance caused the device to heat abnormally.


In order to get further granularity in establishing trends and setting failure analysis priorities, the location of the failure on the die (black box in Figure  6 , indicates the location of the die) was documented using the camera macro lens (see Figure  6 ). This method allows identification of the location and profiling of the fault on the die without requiring any physical de-capsulation, thus reducing the risk of contaminating, or losing, any failure evidence.


VLSI device RCFA was not performed in-house and characterization of the failure location on the die did not assist in the initial RCFA. However, root cause trends can be established that can later be correlated back to the thermal failure signature, potentially eliminating the need for RCFA of samples exhibiting the same thermal signature.


PCB defects resulting in power to ground failures These types of failure were all associated with low resistance defects between V cc and ground.


A classic case where the IR thermography system proved to be invaluable was a 3.3V cc power plane low resistance short to ground on a motherboard. The possible causes for this failure were numerous since 3.3V cc power was supplied to most of the circuitry. Trouble shooting all the possible causes of the failure would have been time intensive, trying to isolate nodes and components in an attempt to zoom to the failure location and/or component.


The motherboards were mounted on tempans with securing screws. Removing the screws could clear the fault, indicating possible stress relief of internal power planes or vias. The failure area was rapidly identified using the IR thermography system. Figure  7  shows the thermal image after current was injected into the 3.3V cc power circuit. The IR thermography system highlighted (see Figure  7 , area inside the black circle) the failure location, resulting in identification of the mounting screw that caused the failure.


During assembly, the mounting screw was not installed perpendicular to the motherboard surface, but at an angle. The washer was integrated into the screw head and responsible for cutting into the PCB through the V cc layer, shorting the 3.3V cc to ground.


## Soldering defects resulting in lead-opens or solder-bridges Soldering defects typically result in either an


Soldering defects resulting in lead-opens or solder-bridges Soldering defects typically result in either an


electrically open circuit, where solder flow was not established, or in an electrical short due to a solder bridge between two or more nodes. Solder cracks can also be induced into a good solder joint by mechanical stress. Solder bridges in motherboards were commonly seen in small pitch surface mounted components, when the solder bridges two or more adjacent pins and creates an electrical short.


Typically components with solder defects relating to output driver circuits or power supply pins cause the component to generate more heat which may generate a detectable thermal signature. The same applies to a cold joint where less heat may be generated. This type of failure mode was not always successfully detected by the IR thermography system because of a lack of an identifiable thermal signature. These failures modes could only be detected if the solder open or solder bridge resulted in a hot spot or cold spot, flagging the node for further investigation.


## Copper trace manufacturing defects (opens)


Copper trace manufacturing defects (opens)


or stress induced cracks Cracks in copper traces could be mechanically induced or the result from manufacturing process defects.


Under normal operating conditions, data and signal traces on a motherboard do not have a thermal signature due to their low current densities. The same is true for power planes. Detecting trace opens on multi-layer circuit boards were further complicated by shadowing of power planes and multiple other traces.


It soon became apparent that the IR thermography system did not provide an advantage above the continuity tester, a multimeter or TDR system for detecting copper trace open circuits on a PCB.


## General Thermographic Lessons Learned


General Thermographic Lessons Learned


Various obstacles were encountered and various test procedures were developed during the nine failures investigated.


The following is a summary of the phenomena that were encountered, and the procedures that were developed to improve test results:


## Low resistance defect testing methodology


Low resistance defect testing methodology


A generic test procedure for low resistance V cc to ground component failures was developed and was adjusted depending on the failure investigation and components involved. For example, in the case of a suspected low resistance short, the testing was initially started with a low current, such as 10mA (milli-Ampere), and was incremented until a thermal signature was observed. The starting current will depend on the circuit board or node to be analyzed and the component associated with the failure. User experience will dictate what is a reasonable starting current for effective results. The following generalized procedure was used:


• Install the camera on a vertical axis to get a birds-eye view of the circuit board or suspect components. • Install the IR thermography system in an environment free from external heat reflections. • Position the circuit board or suspect components below the camera at a slight angle to eliminate any false heat reflections. Ensure repeatable registration of the circuit board. • Set the temperature sensitivity scale at ± 2°C above and below ambient temperature, as indicated by the thermography camera. In the case of other measurements, the temperature scale can be initially set at 50°C above ambient and adjusted accordingly to get the best possible results. • Focus the camera on the circuit board or components of interests and begin the thermal acquisition. • In the case of a specific suspect circuit, an external power supply can be connected to the suspect circuit and the current slowly increased in 10mA increments (the initial starting point current setting should be based on the tester discretion -rather start at a too low current setting than risking destroying the defective part with a too high current setting). If a component emits abnormal internal heating, identify it and terminate the test.


## Graphic image subtraction


Graphic image subtraction


In order to achieve consistent results and highlight the differences between an exemplar circuit board and a suspect circuit board, graphic software was used. The software was used to highlight the inconsistencies between the exemplar and the circuit board being investigated. These inconsistencies can then be further investigated.


Two graphic manipulation approaches were evaluated:


• The first method used an exemplar versus suspect thermal image overlay feature: The suspect image was inverted, projected over the exemplar image, and the transparency set at about 50%. This technique was successful and the image in Figure  7  was generated using this technique. However, the technique was cumbersome due to the image manipulation and associated time required.


• Image subtraction was the second technique that was evaluated. A reference image was produced using an exemplar circuit board. This reference image was then subtracted from the investigated circuit board thermal image; effectively removing the most unwanted reflection induced hot spots while highlighting inconsistencies for further investigation. If the IR reflections to be removed were located in the area of investigation, care was taken to minimize the reflections prior to subtraction. The image in Figure  8  was subtracted from an exemplar image under the same test parameters and once image subtraction was completed, the image in Figure  9  was the result.


In order to achieve effective thermal image subtraction the following needs to be taken into consideration:


• Randomized ambient room reflected IR.


• Operator randomized reflected IR.


• Image registration error.


• Camera induced induced reflected IR.


The image subtraction technique proved very effective.


The added advantage of the subtraction technique was simplicity of use, which related to huge timesavings in generating the final thermal image. Image subtraction also provides a method to eliminate unwanted common reflected artifacts from the final thermal image.


## Emissivity


Emissivity


Figure  10  demonstrates the emissivity of materials and how it affects the absolute temperature readings using an IR thermography system. The thermal image in Figure  10  shows a copper trace that was heated with current. Arrow A and arrow B point to the same trace. However, the thermal image indicates two different temperatures for this trace.


The conformal coating was left intact at arrow A (see Figure  10 ) and removed from the copper trace, exposing the copper, at arrow B (see Figure  10 ). The perceived temperature difference between arrow A and arrow B illustrates the difference in emissivity for copper and conformal coating paint and how easily misleading temperature readings could be obtained. It is therefore important, should absolute temperature measurements be required, to calibrate the software so that the temperature reading takes emissivity into account resulting in an accurate measurement.


Establishing the emissivity correction factor for different materials can be accomplished by recording the temperature of the suspect  The calculated emissivity factor can then be used to re-calibrate the spot temperature in the software for future measurements.


## Registration and temperature scale


Registration and temperature scale


When any relative thermal images are compared, it is important to ensure that the registration of the test circuit board and the exemplar circuit board match so that image subtraction will effectively eliminate any common irrelevant hot spots.


To prevent any false results, the temperature scale for both images must be the same.


From the testing performed with the IR thermography system, the following could be concluded:


• The associated savings in time using the thermography system easily justified the cost of the system. In addition, the system allowed more effective identification of desired failure modes for further analysis ultimately reducing the time to root cause of an identified issue.


• The IR thermography system was successfully applied to identify and locate components with internally resistive failure modes exhibiting an identifiable thermal image. It was also effective in identifying and locating power plane related resistive failures.


• The IR thermography system was very effective in large volume screening for known failure conditions. It eliminated the uncertainty of selecting valid samples within a date code range of suspected defects. The sample quality and confidence level was dramatically improved; focusing the RCFA effort on verified defective components.


• The thermography system was less effective in identifying solder defects and broken/defective traces due to the absence of consistent thermal signatures.


• When absolute values were measured, the emissivity of the investigated object became important. The proper emissivity correction had to be applied to ensure accurate temperature measurements with an IR thermography system. Absolute temperature measurements on objects consisting of multiple different materials were not viable due to the multiple emissivity corrections that had to be made.


• A disadvantage of the thermography system profile was the low resolution of the detector, 160 × 120 pixels. It was challenging to identify small components when a large circuit board was thermally imaged.


• The thermal camera needed to be housed in an enclosure to prevent any thermal influences distorting the thermal image. The user should be aware that heat reflected from the IR camera, if not accounted for, may distort temperature measurement results, especially on aluminum surfaces like electrolytic capacitors.


• Graphic image software assisted in identifying possible defective areas that needed further investigation by highlighting these areas. Image overlay was rather cumbersome compared to image subtraction.


Dynamic hot-electron emission using time resolved photon counting has the potential to address the long-term failure analysis and debug requirements of the semiconductor industry's advanced devices 1-4 . Challenges for measuring dynamic emission include imaging and detection of progressively smaller devices and signals, reduced operating voltages, and higher power consumption. The key benefits of dynamic emission are its noninvasiveness and compatibility with new materials and processes such as silicon on insulator (SOI).


This paper identifies the key system parameters and components that are required to scale and keep pace with the industry's requirements. It also addresses the scalability of dynamic emission with the semiconductor advanced device roadmap.


## Time-resolved emission measurement overview


Time-resolved emission measurement overview


Figure  1  shows a conceptual diagram of a dynamic emission system. The basic technique of timeresolved emission for device analysis has been presented in other publications 3 .


NIR photon emission from a CMOS IC occurs when current flows in the presence of a high electric field. When a transistor is in saturation, hot carriers can emit photons through interactions with lattice phonons or impurities. In CMOS devices, transistors go into saturation briefly during switching events, thus photon emission is synchronous with transistor switching times.


The signal is produced by accumulating detected photons are stamping them in time relative to the start of a test loop. The time-resolved photons are then typically displayed as a histogram.


The noise in the signal comes from background events in the detector, also known as dark counts, and from the statistics of the photon arrivals from the switching transistor, also known as the signal counts. The dark and signal counts are indistinguishable electronically.


A typical signal is shown in Figure  2 . The signal is generally a peak which gradually rises from the dark counts of the detector.


It is important, then, to understand the limitations to determining that a switching event has occurred. We first explain the criteria for event detection. Event detection is suitable for tracking signal propagation and looking for logic or other faults in which timing is not critical. We then discuss conditions for event timing. The goal of event timing is to determine accurately when a switching event has occurred, usually for speed path analysis. For the sake of simplicity we assume that the emission is a Gaussian function of time and that the background noise is Poissonian, or randomly spaced.


Another use of a dynamic emission system is to identify faults by studying the emission as a general function of time 5 . We will not treat such applications in this paper because they do not lend themselves to general analysis. However, they may be significant for failure analysis applications.

## Silicon substrate absorption,


Silicon substrate absorption,


) (E Si α Silicon absorbs light through intra-band and interband transitions. At photon energies below the silicon bandgap energy, the intra-band transitions are very strong. The inter-band transitions are considerably weaker, and go to zero for undoped silicon.


The silicon substrate should be anti-reflection coated to reduce the reflection loss at the silicon-to-air interface. Alternately, an immersion objective can be used. An immersion objective will simultaneously increase the collection solid angle Ω and further increase the overall system quantum efficiency.


## Transmission of system optics,


Transmission of system optics,


) (E optics α Reflection losses should be minimized by applying optical coatings to all interface surfaces. A typical optical train may involve 12 or more surfaces. In addition, if the photons are fiber-coupled into a detector there may be additional loss. The S-25 detector, used in the Mepsicron II, and Si single-photon avalanche detectors (SPADs) have good quantum efficiency at high energies, but very poor quantum efficiency at the typical photons energies present in dynamic emission. The S-1 detector overlaps well with the photon spectrum, but has a very low overall quantum efficiency. Newer detectors, such as InGaAs APD detectors, have promising quantum efficiencies but are technically challenging to operate as single-photon detectors.

## Dark count


Dark count


The dark count rate dark R is a measure of the thermal event rate that is observed in total darkness. Because the dark count rate has a thermal origin, it can often be reduced through cooling of the detector. Detectors with better IR sensitivity tend to have larger dark count. As we shall show, dark count is an important parameter in overall system performance.


## Jitter


Jitter


The jitter of the detector jitter t ∆ is a measure of the uncertainty in the detection time of a single photon.


A photon-counting detector converts an incident photon into an electrical signal that can be resolved in time. The process of converting a single photon into an electrical pulse entails processes that fluctuate in time. Thus, a photon arriving exactly at some time interval would appear to be smeared out in time by the jitter in the detector system.


There are three important timing concepts

## Event detection considerations


Event detection considerations


During data acquisition, the dynamic emission system accumulates events from device photon emission and from dark counts (noise) generated by the detector. The noise events will have random fluctuations spread over the entire time window of interest, while the signal events, which occur synchronously with the acquisition loop, will be bunched around the CMOS switching times. The goal of this section is to describe a methodology for determining how to distinguish between the signal and the noise.


## Overcoming the noise


Overcoming the noise


To simplify the calculation we choose a bin width equal to the width of the transition. There is a chance that the binning will split the peak, but this can be avoided by adjusting the phase of the peaks to maximize the height of the peak of interest.


The background photons will be randomly distributed with Poissonian statistics in the time bins in the time window. In order to be certain that a peak with amplitude th n is due to a switching event, th n must be statistically significant compared to the fluctuation in the background signal.


Consider a transistor that switches once per loop. As the acquisition proceeds, dark counts will accumulate, but eventually a signal peak will rise above the noise.


The probability of detecting n counts in a bin with a mean of λ counts per bin is given by a Poisson ) , ( ) (  (11)  This is also equal to the probability that the signal is not caused by noise. As we increase the number of bins is becomes more likely that the event is caused by noise. Increasing th n increases the probability than any bin with more photons than th n is not caused by dark counts.

## Technology trends and implications for dynamic emission systems


Technology trends and implications for dynamic emission systems


## Device scaling


Device scaling


The probability sig R that a transistor will emit a photon during an event depends on the hot electron distribution within the channel and the current. The hot electron distribution in turn depends on the electric fields within the channel.


For short channel devices the electric field distribution must be treated as a two-dimensional function. Simulation of the hot electron distribution requires detailed two-dimensional semiconductor modeling 9-11 . Tsang et al. have shown that Coulomb interactions can produce an additional hot electron tail, which is absent from a treatment without Coulomb interactions 2 . However, the photon emission is still dominated by photons with energy below 1.1 eV. Although the details of the hotelectron-to-photon conversion mechanism remain unclear, it is certain that the vast majority of emitted photons will be in the NIR (below 1.0 um).


Device scaling typically attempts to maintain a constant electric field in the channel, so the emission should remain approximately constant. However, the capacitive load (and hence the total charge sourced or sunk) is reducing while the saturation current is increasing.


Experimentally, Rusu et al. have shown that the device emission


) (E R FET


decreases approximately 2x with each device generation from 0.25 um to 0.13 um 7 while the shape of the emission curve is approximately unchanged. For long loop lengths, sensitive detectors, and high dark count rates, we typically operate in the dark-count-limited regime.

2. Increase the transistor width FET
