3. Increase the operating voltage. The emission is exponential in voltage 7 . However, often the failure condition occurs at specific voltages, and for many situations this is not possible.


4. Thin the substrate to reduce the silicon absorption. For NIR sensitive detectors the improvement by device thinning is not very large.


We see from the above that it is generally difficult for the end user to compensate for decreasing emission strengths. The responsibility for maintaining the acquisition time thus falls mostly on the dynamic emission system designer.


## SOI Technology


SOI Technology


The device layer in SOI technology is separated from the silicon substrate by an insulating layer. There are two basic flavors for SOI devices, fully and partially depleted SOI.


Partially-depleted SOI has a thicker body region which should produce emission similar to that of bulk silicon devices. The substrate of SOI devices is often more lightly doped than bulk, causing less freecarrier absorption than more heavily doped silicon.


Fully-depleted SOI has a very shallow channel region. The electric field distributions resemble those of long-channel devices. The impact of fullydepleted SOI on the dynamic emission signal is not clear.


Benefits of SOI:


1. The substrate doping is generally lower, resulting in smaller substrate absorption for the same substrate thickness.


2. The substrate can be completely etched (using the insulating layer as a silicon etch stop) or polished away, as long as sufficient heat sinking is be provided to keep the part operational. Removing the silicon allows photons with energy above the band gap to be detected.


Challenges of SOI 1. The oxide-silicon interface will create reflections and light loss.


2. The emission signal may be difficult to interpret in some circuits because of the floating body effects.


We have outlined the important system considerations for dynamic photon emission. In the final presentation we will include data from specific detector systems and devices to illustrate these points.


The basic concepts of time-resolved hot-electron photon emission for probing of integrated circuits have already been presented  [1, 2] . Time-resolved photon emission has been shown to be useful in analyzing clock skews and timing-related defects in flip-chip devices  [3] [4] [5] . However, the PICA (Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis) system originally demonstrated in  [2]  and used in subsequent applications suffers from a very inefficient photoncounting detector. In practice, time-resolved photon emission using the S-25 Quantar detector cannot be used at long loop lengths (typically  > 10 µs) because the S-25 photocathode used in PICA has very low quantum efficiency at wavelengths longer than 1 µm.


This low quantum efficiency creates unrealistically long acquisition times for most debug applications.


The only way to reduce the acquisition time, when using the PICA system, is to keep the loop length well under 1 µs.


Short loops are not practical for many failure-analysis and debug applications. Timing defects and clock skew can usually be stimulated with short-looplength tests ( < < 10 µs) because the device's state does not have to be reset each loop. Logic failures that create scan failures, however, require much longer loop lengths because scan chains must be re-loaded with each loop. A scan chain with 1000 latches, shifting at 20 MHz, requires a loop length of at least 50 µs to load the chain. Such a long loop would be nearly impossible to probe with PICA.


Laser voltage probing (LVP)  [9] , another flip-chip waveform acquisition tool, is capable of probing scan failures with long loop lengths. Unfortunately, LVP is not capable of probing SOI devices  [6] .


In this paper, we use a near-infrared (NIR) optimized time-resolved emission system to demonstrate that even with long loop lengths time-resolved photon emission can be extremely useful for defect localization. Specifically, we will show how timeresolved photon emission was used to solve two different issues that caused scan fails on silicon-oninsulator (SOI) devices, and briefly discuss interpretation of the optical waveforms.


## Time Resolved Photon Emission System Description


Time Resolved Photon Emission System Description


The time-resolved photon emission systems used at Motorola is the EmiScope ® I developed and manufactured by Optonics, Inc. in Mountain View, CA. Figure  1  shows the key components of the EmiScope I. The primary elements of the system are an infra-red microscope for navigation through the backside of the DUT, a high-speed proprietary photon detector system for collecting the arrival times of photons emitted by the DUT, an XYZ highresolution mechanical stage for positioning the inverted column imaging and collection system on the DUT, and a vibration-isolation table to reduce the transfer of floor vibrations to the system. The system is controlled by a separate electronics rack and a computer with a GUI for navigation and timing data analysis. path is switched to allow direct collection of the photons emitted by the DUT. A tester or other function generator stimulates the DUT. The proprietary photon counting detection system and electronics records the arrival times of the emitted photons relative to a trigger signal, usually provided by the tester.


The system has been optimized for detecting nearinfrared (NIR) photons with wavelengths between 1 -1.6 µm. Figure  2  shows the quantum efficiency of the detector as a function of energy. The typical photon emission spectrum has been published elsewhere  [7] . We calculated the filtering effect of 100 µm of silicon with ~1.2e19 p-doping and have


shown the transmitted spectrum as a dashed line. The quantum efficiency of the NIR-optimized detector is in the tens of percent and overlaps very well with the emitted spectrum, as can be seen in the figure. The cutoff in the emission at 0.82 eV is caused by a filter in the optical path of the detector used to take the data. The photon emission data is taken from  [7] .


PICA (Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis) requires long acquisition times because the effective quantum efficiency (QE) of the PICA (S-25) detector is very poor in the near infrared.


Error! Reference source not found.Figure  3  shows the quantum efficiency of the PICA (S-25) detector as a function of energy. The expected photon spectrum is shown as a dashed line. Although the QE of the PICA detector is good below 900 nm, it falls off rapidly at longer wavelengths. The effective QE of the PICA system is very low because the overlap of the quantum efficiency with the photon spectrum transmitted through silicon is very poor. Absorption through the silicon substrate filters the wavelengths shorter than ~1µm, this limiting PICA for flip-chip applications. The PICA system has the feature of being able to resolve photons in both position and time, but the acquisition times are measured in tens of hours for loop lengths of only few microseconds. In contrast, the EmiScope I acquisition times are measured in minutes, even for loops lengths in excess of 50 µs. As with all photon-collection systems, the EmiScope I is completely non-invasive because it detects photons which are naturally emitted by the device.

### 3.2 Chip area


In order to study the area dependence of the silicon etch rate, the silicon samples to be etched were cut into pieces with the area of 0.25 cm 2 , 1 cm 2 , 2.25 cm 2 , 4 cm 2 and 9 cm 2 . We found a strong area dependence for small chip area and a weak area dependence for large chip area, shown in the Figure  3 . After studying the area dependence of the silicon etch rate, we used silicon chips with 1 cm 2 for the following experiments. Etch characteristics are often dependent on plasma parameters including pressure, ion energy and plasma density. Chamber pressure can change plasma conditions including the mean free path and the collision frequency, which cause ion energy and plasma density to change. In this paper, we have studied the pressure dependence of silicon etching characteristics including etch rate and surface roughness. Keeping other process parameters constant, the chamber pressure was varied from 30 mTorr to 250 mTorr. We found the silicon etch rate increases with increasing pressure at low pressure while decreases with increasing pressure at high pressure. At pressure of 150 mTorr, maximum silicon etch rate was achieved. Although anisotropic etching can be achieved by operating at low chamber pressure to minimize ion scatting and lateral etching, RIE process with a lower pressure results in a more rough silicon surface shown in Figure  5 . Figure  5  (a), (b) and (c) correspond to the pressure of 30, 100 and 200 mTorr respectively. The roughness would be attributed to non-uniform reactivity of surface, i.e. the reactant adsorption, surface reaction or product desorption. The other reason is that as the chamber pressure is lowered, the vertical etch rate increases and then the surface roughness increases  [4] .


### 3.4 RIE power


3.4 RIE power


Moreover, the impacts of RIE power on the etch rate of silicon, surface roughness have also been evaluated.


There is a strong RIE dependence of silicon etch rate. We found, with the increase of the RIE power, the increase of the silicon etch rate has a saturation effect. We also found the surface becomes rougher with the increase of the RIE power. The reason would be that high power conditions cause high self-bias potentials, then increase of the ion bombardment energy  [4, 5] . Moreover, as the RIE power increases, the potential for surface damage increases. In consideration of etch rate, surface roughness and surface damage, we choose RIE power of 200 Watts.

3.5 ICP Power

The DUT is thinned (to 100 µm or thinner) and polished. Broadband near infrared anti-reflection coating also improves image quality and acquisition time.


The dark count of the EmiScope I detector is approximately 10,000 counts per second (cps). Although this is higher than the PICA (Super S-25) detector, the much larger quantum efficiency allows for fast acquisition times and keeps the noise to a controllable level, as we shall show in the data. Note, however, that the detector used to acquire the data in this paper was an older technology detector with a dark count of approximately 88,000 cps.


The timing jitter in the photon detection system is 80 ps, which corresponds to a system bandwidth of 4.0 GHz. The S-25 detector used on PICA has an impulse response greater than 100ps. Lower jitter also contributes to shorter acquisition times.


## Interpretation of Optical Waveforms


Interpretation of Optical Waveforms


The optical waveform from a time-resolved photon emission system is not a direct representation of the more well-known voltage waveform. Photon emission takes place when the transistor draws current. For CMOS devices, this translates into a photon pulse as the device switches. The correlation in timing between the current and photon pulses has been demonstrated elsewhere  [7] . Interpretation of the optical waveforms and correlating these to voltage waveforms and switching events can be challenging. Qualitative rules-of-thumb are useful for failure analysts and designers using the waveforms.


Rule #1. The waveform from a transistor in a CMOS logic gate is a representation of switching at the output of that gate.


The time-resolved photon emission signal comes from transistors. The traditional micro-probed signal comes from nets. Rule #1 bridges the two viewpoints. Time-resolved photon emission cannot detect changes on the input of a CMOS gate, if the output of the gate does not change. Only the transistor that causes the output of a CMOS gate to switch value will generate a signal.


A NOR gate is shown in Figure  4 . At time=0, both inputs are low, so the output is high. First, "In1" transitions high, creating an emission signal at transistor 1 as the output transitions low. Later, "In2" transitions high. Transistor 2 does not generate an emission signal, because the output does not changeit stays low. As discussed in  [8] , peak emission during switching occurs when the instantaneous values of V DS and V GS satisfy the following equation at high values of V DS .


V GS = V DS /2 (1)


In CMOS gates, this condition is achieved for the PMOS transistors on the rising edge of the output, and for the NMOS transistors on the falling edge of the output.


In Figure  5  the optical waveform acquired simultaneously from both the PMOS and NMOS of an inverter is shown, along with the equivalent logical waveform. The rising edge signal from the PMOS is easily recognized, because its amplitude is much smaller  [2] . In  [8] , the possibility of emission from the NMOS during the rising edge (and the PMOS, during the falling edge) of the output is discussed, for unloaded CMOS gates. Capacitive loading at the output of the gate, however, reduces that emission significantly, because the value of V DS at which Equation 1 is satisfied is decreased. We have seen rising-edge NMOS emission on lightly-loaded gates.


Rule #3. Non-CMOS structures, such as transmission gates, in which current flows but there is not a high lateral electric field in the channel, may not generate any photon emission.


To understand if emission will be present, the transient response of the circuit should be simulated. To a first order, emission can be detected if Equation  1 is satisfied for a high value of V DS at some time during the response.


## Rule #4. Emission detected by static detectors such as MCT cameras is visible in a time-resolved detection system as a possibly time-dependent increased background level.


First applied in  [4] , this feature of time-resolved systems gives the analyst much more analog information than LVP. While probing through logic, an increased background level is strong evidence that the defect is within a couple levels of logic. The time-dependence of the increased background level can be used to relate the defect to neighboring signals.


## Rule #5.


Rule #5.


A signal, from a CMOS gate, that exhibits a time-dependent high background level is more likely due to a defect on the inputs than on the output of the gate.


Equation 1 gives the condition for peak emission, but transistors also emit (weakly) over much of the saturation region. As a demonstration, the saturation condition in the simple square-law transistor model occurs when


V DS  >  V GS -V T (2)


The transistors in a non-switching CMOS gate not biased in the saturation region -V DS and V GS are either at the power supply voltage V DD or at 0V. Unless voltages above V DD are present on the chip, it is almost impossible for a defect to cause V DS or V GS to become greater than V DD or less than 0V.


Consider the NMOS of an inverter. A defect at the output will only affect the V DS . If the input to the inverter is low, V GS is 0V and no positive value of V DS will allow current flow and emission from the transistor. However, when V GS is V DD , weak emission may be present if Equation 2 is satisfied.


V DS  >  V DD -V T (3)


Equation 3 implies that V DS must be within V T of V DD , a very small voltage range for emission. In addition, typical threshold voltages will not allow Equation 1 to be satisfied. A defect at the output of a gate will cause very weak emission, if at all.


Consider a defect at the input of the inverter (or at a previous logic level).


The defect affects the transistors' V GS , biasing the input of the inverter at some value between 0V and V DD. In  [8] , the dependence of emission on the input voltage to an inverter is shown. Detectable emission is present for almost half the input voltage range. Because the range is wide, and because Equation 1 has a chance of being satisfied, a defect at the input of a gate is more likely to create emission than if the defect is at the output of the gate.


## Rule #6. A device with short L eff transistors may exhibit voltage-like optical waveforms.


Rule #6. A device with short L eff transistors may exhibit voltage-like optical waveforms.


A fab process, optimized for speed, may create transistors with very short effective gate lengths that exhibit subthreshold leakage currents. As shown in Figure  6 , the subthreshold leakage current can create a voltagelike waveform. A short L eff NMOS transistor in an inverter will exhibit emission when the output is high, but not when the output is low.


## Case Study 1


Case Study 1


Several SOI devices failing customer stress were submitted for analysis. One of the failing devices was probed on the Emiscope while exercising it with the failing scan test, with a loop length of approximately 60 µs. The power supply voltage was 1.8 V.


A partial schematic of the probed area is shown in Figure  7  and the optical waveforms that revealed the location of the defect are shown in Figure  8 . In the optical waveforms, the signals from both the PMOS and NMOS of each inverter are shown. A good, negative pulse at "A" induces a positive pulse at "B" and "C". However, at "D", the pulse is distorted, with a high background level.


A comparison of the background noise in waveforms at "C" and "D" is shown in Figure  9 .


In the indicated region, waveform "C" exhibits the noise due to the detector's dark count -in this particular detector, 88,000 cps. Waveform D has a much higher background count at 534 kcps. The significant emission from the transistors at D indicates that they are in saturation. Rule 5 suggests that the defect is likely to be at the input of the inverter that creates "D".


In fact, as shown in Figure  10 , the cause of the failure was an anomaly at the base of VIA1 at the output of "C" (and the input of "D"). The optical waveforms shown in Figure  8  were obtained from relatively wide transistors, so the acquisition times were very short ( <  2 minutes). During the same analysis, however, inverters with near-minimum width transistors were probed. An example of one of these is shown in Figure  11 . In this waveform, only the narrow NMOS (W=1µm) was probed. A distinct signal was visible after an acquisition of 311 seconds.


## Case Study 2


Case Study 2


Several devices manufactured in Motorola's HIP6SOI process were failing the same scan tests after 168 hours and 504 hours of burn-in, and were submitted for analysis. One of the failing devices was probed on the Emiscope while exercising it with the failing scan test, with a loop length of approximately 60µs. The power supply voltage of the device was 1.8V.


The optical waveforms that revealed the location of the defect are shown in Figure  12 , and a partial schematic of the probed area is shown in Figure  13 . Each of these waveforms required less than 5 minutes of acquisition to achieve the excellent S/N illustrated. A typical waveform is "B", acquired from the 0.98µm-wide NMOS of the inverter at B. The acquisition time of this signal was 182 seconds. Because of the short acquisition time, the analyst was able to easily probe many different gates to isolate the failure. Figure  13  shows only part of a 16:1 mux. In the output stage of the mux, a NAND gate acts as either a keeper or as a weak pull-up, depending on the state of the "test_" signal. In scan mode, "test_" is low, so the NAND acts as a weak pull-up. Naturally, this pull-up will create contention when a selected "din" is high. This contention is not a failing state; it is expected.


The output, "C", of the mux, is captured into a scan latch when the "c1_clock" pulses late in the waveforms shown in Figure  12 . At the time of the "c1_clock" pulse, the signal at "C" has a high background level (100 kcps) on a good device. However, on the failing device, the signal at "C" has a low background level of 86 kpcs, the dark rate of the detector.


Two signals in contention will cause any NMOS or PMOS they drive to saturate, and hence, create emission that can be detected with a time-resolved photon emission system. The low level of emission on the failing device at "C" indicates that the NAND gate pull-up is not in contention with the signal driven through the mux, as it should be. The waveform at "B" on the failing device indicates a falling edge that selects the correct output of the mux. The waveform at "A" indicates a falling edge to the inverted data that should be in contention with the NAND gate.


The conclusion from the optical waveform evidence was that an open must exist between "A" and the NAND gate. As shown in Figure  14 , an open metal line was discovered in the SEM. Further investigation revealed that incorrect burn-in code allowed several select lines on the mux to be simultaneously activated. This condition created high currents at the NAND gate output, which caused electromigration.

## Experiment description


Experiment description


The circuit under test is composed of two sections containing 64 ring oscillators (ROs) each (see Fig.  1 ). The ROs differ in the number of stages, gate type (inverters or NANDs), dimension (W/L ratio) and capacitance load (C L ). The logic circuit is composed of minimum size transistors (L=0.18µm) and is located between the two RO sections. The logic is designed to control all the latches that enable/disable each individual chain separately (see Fig.  1 ). Three different power supplies are available for the logic and each RO section. An external enable pin, LT, is provided in order to globally disable (LT=1) all the ROs independently from the logical status scanned in. Optical inspection of the IC was based on a high quantum efficiency CCD mounted on a standard probe station as shown in Fig.  2 . The chip was electrically biased through a probe card connected to Keithley 2400 source meters, in order to accurately monitor power consumption. Since diced chips were not available during the test, the luminescence emission was collected from the front-side of the wafer, which was possible thanks to the limited number of metal levels (three) screening the circuit emission.


## Optical inspection of high I DDQ


Optical inspection of high I DDQ


The optical inspection of the chip using a IR CCD camera was initially performed in order to identify the cause of the high quiescence current (   of the two RO sections, while they both absorb a comparable amount of current. Moreover CCD timeintegrated acquisitions (see Fig.  3 ) show a very uniform emission pattern over the entire IC, thus excluding other design problems (e.g., unintentional short-circuits between V DD and ground) and showing that all ROs emit light even while they are not running.


The comparison of static luminescence acquired from high and low V t transistors, present on the same chip, demonstrated that only the latter emit a significant amount of NIR light. In particular, transistors with minimum channel length are much brighter than the others (see Fig.  4 ). The high I DDQ current is due to the global transistor leakage caused by the low threshold process.


## Application of leakage luminescence


After successfully completing the previous task, the leakage related luminescence was also used to probe different electrical properties of the IC, such as supply voltage fluctuations. It is very important to monitor such variations because they affect many features of the IC, e.g. propagation delays and skews, as well as providing useful information regarding digital noise. Thanks to its exponential dependence on the applied voltage  [4] , the luminescence intensity can be effectively used as a very sensitive probe of supply voltage distribution. Although the standard PICA technique can be used to evaluate voltage variations, the development of a method based only on time-integrated images, obtained by means of a high quantum efficiency CCD, permits a reduction in acquisition time. This technique is to be used when dynamic information is not strictly needed. the measurement. In the latter case (b) the luminescence is instead caused only by leakage current. Fig.  5  shows that the emission intensity is much fainter when most of the ROs are enabled (a), although the absorbed current is significantly larger as shown in Fig.  6 . This is in clear contradiction with measurements of prior technologies demonstrating that the emission of switching transitions is significantly higher than the emission caused by leakage current. In fact, both the device current and the electrical field are larger when the MOSFET is conducting in saturation, unless the supply voltage is significantly reduced by the increased current absorption. Such a hypothesis is also confirmed by the emission intensity of the control logic (see left block in Fig.  5 ) that does not change significantly when one enables and disables the RO sections since it does not share the same power grid.


## Estimation of supply voltage drop


Estimation of supply voltage drop


As optical emission from leakage current depends only on applied voltage, it can be used as an effective electro-optical transducer for testing. In order to estimate the resistance of the power grid of the IC, we took a series of short time-integrated acquisitions at different voltages with all the ROs disabled. As discussed in previous paragraphs, the emission is nevertheless sustained by leakage current and the corresponding curve (squares) is shown in Fig 7 . By scanning in a specific sequence in the logic control latches, we enabled most of, but not all, the ROs and measured the emission intensity coming from a reference RO that was kept disabled (triangle). Theoretically, the two curves should superimpose exactly because they correspond to the same device in the same operating condition (i.e. disabled).


However, a significant reduction of the intensity is observed when most of the subcircuits are working. Such an effect can be directly attributed to the voltage drop on the power grid of the IC, caused by the large absorption of current by running ROs. Since we know that the two curves should superimpose in the absence of voltage variations, it is possible to set up the following equation for correcting the voltage drop:

## Identification of working ROs


Identification of working ROs


The PICA technique is able to study precisely the oscillation characteristics of ROs, by using a Mepsicron photo-multiplier tube capable of measuring the photon arrival time and the spatial position. However, such a detector has very poor quantum efficiency for detecting NIR photons, thus leading to significantly longer acquisition times as compared to a CCD. For testing purpose, it is not always important to be able to exploit all the features of the dynamic signal, but rather simply identify working subcircuits. In the following, we will show that, by using the CCD time-integrated images of the IC, one can determine which ROs are functional.


If the leakage current of the transistors in the ROs not running were less intense, the issue would be commonplace since only switching gates would emit light and they would be immediately pinpointed by a CCD acquisition. However, given the high leakage in this technology, there are two methods for determining which RO is running: direct RO observation or indirect latch observation. In a running RO, the signal propagates along the loop, turning on the gates in rapid succession. Therefore, when a time-integrated image of the circuit is acquired, all the gates were enabled for the same time, i.e. every gate emits the same amount of light on average (see rows denoted by ON in Fig.  9 ). On the contrary, when a latch disables a RO, logic states are frozen along the chain in an alternation of opposite voltage levels. In an inverter gate, with the input at V DD or ground, the leaking transistor is the one with elevated drain voltage (V DS ≈V DD ) and low gate voltage (V GS  < V t ). Therefore, when the RO is not running, the leaky transistors show as alternating nand p-FETs. However, p-FETs emit much less light than n-FETs because the hole effective mass is significantly larger than that of the electron. Therefore, the NIR image of the circuit shows a series of light spots representing every second n-FETs (see rows denoted by OFF in Fig.  9 ). When direct access to the ROs is not available, e.g. if they are covered by too many metal lines and the backside option is not feasible, it is still possible to identify which of the ROs were running by analyzing the emission intensity coming from the latches that actually enable/disable the ROs. There should be NIR emission only when the transistor is switching.


In the high leakage conditions of the IC under test, the luminescence related to switching transitions is still more intense than the emission due to the leakage, when circuit supply voltage drop due to the higher current absorption is corrected. Therefore, higher peaks are observed as corresponding to the working gates shown in Fig.  10 . The same figure also


In this paper the optical testing of a low power test chip has been discussed. By means of luminescence measurements it was possible to identify three inverter chains with floating inputs, allowing external noise to couple in and turn on the first stages of the chain. This problem can account for significant power consumption the source of which would have been impossible to discover without optical inspection. However, we proved that an intense and diffuse light emanates from all the low V t transistors with minimum channel length, leading to transistor leakage being the actual cause of the high quiescence current of the circuit. Time-integrated acquisitions of optical emission from leakage current were also exploited in order to calculate the voltage drop on the power grid of the circuit, allowing for the estimation of the actual value of the locally supplied voltage in the critical regions of complex circuits. Moreover, light emission was used to identify the working ROs notwithstanding the high leakage conditions.


## Characterization of Reactive Ion Etching of Silicon Substrate


Characterization of Reactive Ion Etching of Silicon Substrate


for Backside Failure Mode Analysis Huixian Wu, James Cargo Agere Systems, IC Quality Organization, Product Analysis Lab Room: 30U-217DJ, 555 Union Blvd., Allentown, PA 18109, USA Phone: 610-712-5998, Email: hwu7@agere.com


Abstract: With technology scaling down to sub 0.16um and metalization exceeding 7 levels, the development of reproducible backside silicon sample preparation techniques becomes increasingly important to accurately localize defects. Bulk silicon thinning is a critical step in the backside sample preparation process. This paper will discuss two different ways for silicon thinning: reactive ion etching (RIE) alone, and RIE in conjunction with mechanical milling. In addition, the characterization and optimization of the RIE process for backside silicon thinning will be discussed in this paper. We have found mechanical milling works well for many package types; however, we have had difficulty reproducibly thinning certain package types such as very small die or packages where the wire bonds are in the plane of the silicon die and are in very close proximity to the edge of the die. In these cases, we have found that reactive ion etching (RIE) can be used successfully. We have also found that for package types where mechanical milling works, the combination of mechanical milling and reactive ion etching process is a useful technique for accurately controlling the final thickness of the silicon. This technique combines the speed of mechanically milling and the advantage of RIE process to accurately control the etch rate and etch process in the final stages of thinning the silicon die.


## 1. Introduction


1. Introduction


Conventional front side site identification of defects has become less and less effective as technology scales down to sub-quarter microns, and the number of metallic layers in ICs increase. Electrical defect localization in new package types such as flip chip or lead-on-chip can only be carried out from the backside of the die. So the development of backside sample preparation for site identification of defects is increasingly important for new technology and new package types. Depending on the package type involved backside sample preparation can require many of the following steps: heat sink removal, ceramic package removal, de-capsulation, copper paddle removal, die attach removal, silicon substrate thinning and final polishing. A critical step in backside sample preparation is the silicon substrate thinning. In many cases the silicon die needs to be thinned to 100 um or less to allow IR light to pass through the die while keeping the device still electrically functional.


There are several techniques available for the backside sample preparation such as mechanical milling, mechanical polishing, wet chemical, and plasma etching. The preferred thinning method chosen is dependent upon the package configuration. Typically mechanical polishing is chosen for flip-chip; however, this technique does not work with package types such as BGAs, TQFPs, etc.; where in order to keep the DUT electrically intact, a cavity must be generated in the backside of the die and then the die thinned from within that cavity. We have found mechanical milling works well for many package types; however, we have had difficulty reproducibly thinning certain package types such as very small die or packages where the wire bonds are in the plane of the silicon die and are in very close proximity to the edge of the die. In these cases, we have found that reactive ion etching (RIE) alone, and RIE in conjunction with mechanical milling can be used successfully for silicon thinning.


## 2 Experiments


2 Experiments


Several removal techniques such as mechanical milling, wet chemical etching and reactive ion etching can be used for silicon thinning in backside sample preparation process. The concerns for wet chemical etching are over etch as well as the difficulty in accurately controlling the etching rate and etching process. Mechanical milling has the potential of mechanical and thermal stress as well as wire damage problems in certain package types. The concerns for reactive ion etching of silicon include: by-product residue, surface roughness, plasma damage and low etching rate. In order for a RIE recipe to be useful for backside silicon thinning it should result in a clean surface, low surface roughness and a high etch rate.


We conducted the following experiments in order to optimize the parameters used in RIE for backside silicon thinning. A Hypervision Chip-Unzip system was used for mechanical milling in this study. In addition, a Trion Phantom RIE system was used for etching silicon die with fluorine-based plasmas (SF 6 /O 2 ). This system incorporates two power systems: ICP and RIE. The former one uses an Inductively Coupled Plasma source and the latter one uses a traditional RF plasma source. RIE utilizes both the chemical and physical components of an etch mechanism to achieve anisotropic profiles, fast etch rates and dimensional control. RIE plasma is typically generated by applying radio frequency (RF) power of 13.56 MHz between two parallel electrodes in a reactive gas. Etching silicon with a plasma containing SF 6 is a highly chemical process, and then the etching process is fast and isotropic. We chose SF 6 as one reactive gas because it is well known as a good silicon etcher. The other gas we used was oxygen. The addition of oxygen produces a chemically un-reactive layer at the etch site, known as an etch inhibitor  [1, 2] . The inhibitor reduces chemical etching while increasing ion assisted etching, which results in a reduction in the lateral etch rate and thus an increase in the anisotropy nature of the etch profile  [1, 2, 3] . Highly anisotropic etching can also be achieved by the use of Argon-added plasmas due to the high physical reaction. In this work, we have characterized and optimized the RIE process parameters, which are chamber pressure, RIE power, ICP power, chip area, gas flow rate and gas ratio.


## 3. Characterization of RIE Process for Backside Silicon Thinning


3. Characterization of RIE Process for Backside Silicon Thinning


Silicon RIE recipes, with high etch rate, minimum surface damage and redeposition, need to be developed and characterized for backside silicon thinning. The characterization of the RIE process is a challenge because the RIE process is complex and there are many process parameters that should be characterized. This characterization work is also very critical to optimize the RIE process parameters for obtaining maximum silicon etch rate for backside silicon thinning. Unfortunately, there is not much work reported on these issues. In this work, we have also studied the dependence of the silicon etch rate on the RIE process parameters. In addition to etch rates, surface roughness can be very important for silicon etch as well as the resulting backside failure analysis. The impacts of these RIE process parameters on the etch rate of silicon and surface roughness have also been evaluated.


### 3.1 Oxygen flow


Firstly, we have studied the effects of various O 2 flow rates on both the silicon etch rate and on the surface roughness. During the experiments, the flow rate of SF 6 was kept constant at 45 sccm and the O 2 flow rate ranged from 0 sccm to 45 sccm. Process pressure was set at 100 mTorr. The ICP power was set at 350 Watts and the RIE power was set at 200 Watts. Figure  1  shows that the O 2 gases flow has an impact on the silicon etch rate. The silicon etch rate increases with increasing O 2 gas flow at low O 2 gas flow. However, the silicon etch rate decreases with increasing O 2 gas flow at high O 2 gas flow. This can be explained as follows: RIE process with a low O 2 gas flow results in a very rough surface caused by the redeposition of byproducts which inhibit the further etching process and decrease the etch rate. With the increase of O 2 , there is more oxygen to react with the byproduct deposited on the surface and this has an effect of cleaning the silicon surface and thus increases the etch rate. The RIE process using a very high O 2 gas flow results in a competition between the SF 6 and the O 2 coming in contact with the silicon surface, which decreases the reaction rate of SF 6 with silicon. Oxyge n Flow (sccm ) Etch Rate (um/min)


### Figure 1 Oxygen flow dependence of etch rate


### 4.1Small die


4.1Small die


We have found that very small dies are not easily thinned using mechanical milling techniques due to the milling bit size. In these cases, RIE works as an alternative, providing accurate removal with minimal damage to the surrounding package. The process requires a cavity to be opened above the die either by mechanical or chemical means. Then RIE is used to thin the Silicon to the required thick ness.


### 4.2 RIE thinning where milling causes wire damage


4.2 RIE thinning where milling causes wire damage


Certain IC packages contain wire geometries, which are more susceptible to wire damage problems during the mechanical milling process of thinning the silicon. Problems can occur in packages where the wire bonds are in the plane of the silicon needing removal and are in very close proximity to the edge of the die. Figure  12  shows an example of a package cross section, where the wire bond on the left has the potential for wire bond damage, since it is the plane of material to be removed (red box). The wire bond on the right is below the plane of silicon to be removed and therefore has less chance of damage. RIE can be used as a successful replacement for the mechanical removal of silicon in the thinning process.


## 5. Case Study


Firstly an X ray image of the device was taken to get the dimensions of the die and paddle in order to set up a cavity size for de-capsulation. Cross section analysis was also carried out to find the depth between paddle and backside of the die, paddle thickness and die thickness. A SEM image of the cross section of a device can be taken and the depth can be measured in the SEM analysis.


The molding compound package material, copper paddle and die attach were removed by mechanical milling using a crosscut mill. Then a flycut diamond milling tool was used for silicon thinning in the Chip-Unzip machine. Finally, the silicon surface needs to be polished to decrease the surface roughness and minimize the light distortion in PEM analysis. The sample was sent for IR imaging. The IR image shown in Figure  15  (a) is not clear because the thickness of the die is not thin enough. The sample was sent to RIE for 8 minutes and an IR image was taken again.


## 5. Conclusion


For the RIE process of silicon removal, we have studied the oxygen flow, pressure, chip area, ICP power and RIE power dependence of etch rate and characterized and optimized these RIE process parameters. The impacts of the oxygen flow, chamber pressure and RIE power on the silicon surface roughness have also been evaluated. The rough surface would be attributed to non-uniform reactivity of surface, i.e. the reactant adsorption, surface reaction or product desorption. By-products or re-deposition will also cause the rough surface. We also found the surface becomes rougher with the increase of the power. The reason would be that high power conditions cause high self-bias potentials, then increase of the ion bombardment energy. Moreover, as the power increases, the potential for damage to surface increases. Finally, we optimized the RIE process parameters and achieved recipes of silicon etch with a useful etch rate (5 um/min), no plasma damage, and uniform and smooth surfaces.


Backside silicon thinning is a critical step in backside failure analysis sample preparation. Mechanical milling works well for the backside preparation of large packages and large dies especially with regards to the preparation time and process reliability. Nevertheless, we have found that reactive ion etching can be used for small die, and package types which result in wire damage problems due to mechanical milling accuracy. In addition, RIE can be also be used for the final silicon thinning after mechanical milling of the bulk silicon to achieve more precise control of the thickness of remaining silicon.


When an open or short is found on a flip-chip device the challenge becomes deciding from the available tools the best method to isolate the failure cause.


The decision is often dependent on the number of available devices exhibiting the same failure mode. If only one device exists the analyst must do everything possible with non-destructive tools to isolate the failure site. This would include the use of C-SAM, X-ray, TDR, etc. Once the failure site has been narrowed a decision must then be made as to the type of destructive analysis tool that will be used to proceed further. These can include crosssectioning, parallel lapping, wet and dry deprocessing, etc.


In the case where there are many of the same type of failure, one may sacrifice some samples to shorten the cycle time of the overall analysis.


What is being presented here is an addition to the analysts' destructive physical analysis (DPA) tool set. The idea is to selectively remove sections of the die or the printed circuit board (PCB) to expose the under-fill and solder bumps. This makes it possible to isolate other nodes that can be directly tested to further isolate the cause of the failure.


The basic operation for selective area milling will be presented. Two examples using this technique will also be presented.


## Milling


Milling


Until recently, the primary milling tools have been in the form of sophisticated CNC machines 1 and as simple as a Dremel tool. The primary use has been for backside sample preparation or to improve device decapsulation 2 . By using a new tool that can be manually adjusted as to depth and opening dimensions it is possible to visually determine where the tool has milled. With a large variety of milling and grinding tips it is possible to stop within the passivation of the die or to stop in the last layer of copper of the PCB. Due to variations in die and PCB thickness this becomes somewhat impractical for a CNC machine.


## New Milling Tool


New Milling Tool


The tool used in the following examples is the Automated Selective Area Polisher (ASAP) from Ultra Tec. This tool was primarily developed to do backside sample preparation, but observing that the manual vertical adjustment could be controlled with a significant degree of precision the tool is now also used to selectively remove mold compounds, die, etc. The vertical adjustment dial indicates it's smallest divisions to be 5 microns. This sounds a bit coarse, but with practice and good observation skills this can be much smaller. The ASAP is also designed such that the sample is mounted to a table that oscillates in the X and Y directions. The table travel is manually adjustable such that openings from 1mm to greater than 30mm can be obtained. The sample holder allows for easy removal for inspection under a microscope. The table also has a tilt adjustment so that minor variations in planarity can be corrected.


## Silicon Removal Procedure


Silicon Removal Procedure


It is important to have an estimate of the silicon thickness. This can be obtained several ways including cross-section, process specification, micrometer measurement, etc. An estimate of the under-fill thickness would also help, but it is not mandatory.


Once an area is determined for removal (based on other analysis tools) the milling tool is centered over the area and the table is adjusted to the dimensions to be removed. A coarse diamond tool is used for bulk silicon removal. Several drops of water are used for lubrication and to prevent silicon dust. The table is set in motion and the grinding tool is lowered on to the sample. The speed of silicon removal is at the users discretion. Fifty-micron steps have been found to work without damage to the die. When roughly 50 microns of the die is left, the fine diamond tool is used to proceed to the desired interface. A mark is placed in the bottom of the milling hole such that one can observe when the new tool contacts the surface at the bottom of the hole. Again water is used for lubricant, allowing visual observation of the area being milled. From here to the desired interface, small increments are made with frequent changes of water so that the surface being ground can be observed. To prevent damage to the under-fill and solder bumps, the grinding should stop as soon as metal traces become visible. At this point, an inspection under an optical microscope can verify the status of the grind. If more material needs to be removed, the steps above can be repeated, with care to highlight the bottom surface of the hole so that initial contact can be visually confirmed.


To expose the solder bumps and under-fill, standard wet or dry de-processing tools can be used.


## PCB Removal Procedure


PCB Removal Procedure


For a glass/epoxy based PCB, a tungsten carbide milling tool is available that works very well at removing the copper layers of the PCB. The coarse diamond tool will also work on most boards, but if a copper layer is too dense (ground plane) or too thick, the tool can get packed with copper and stop grinding.


For a ceramic-based PCB, the only usable tool is the coarse diamond. The ceramic between copper layers works well to clean the tool after each copper section is removed. The procedure for milling a ceramic PCB is basically the same as described for a silicon die except a smaller grinding step size ( < 25 microns) should be used and the stopping point should be the top layer of copper.


The procedure for milling a glass/epoxy based PCB uses mineral oil as the lubricant and to trap the debris, while allowing clear visibility of the milling surface. The area to be exposed is estimated using data from other sources. The center of the area to be exposed is marked on the sample and the dimensions to be removed are made to the table travel. Several drops of mineral oil are placed on the sample. The table and the milling tool are turned on. Both speeds are set to a moderate setting. The milling tool is lowered until contact is observed. To make sure the milling tool cuts through the layers and does not splinter the PCB, it is recommended that increments of 25 microns or less be used. As the mineral oil fills with copper and glass fiber debris it needs to be removed and replaced on a regular basis. Cotton swabs work very well to remove the dirty oil. Plots of each PCB layer can help determine how close the milling tool is to the under-fill. With practice it is possible to stop in the copper layer just under the solder bumps and under-fill. The mineral oil is removable with acetone or alcohol.


## Limitations


This technique requires a high degree of observation skills using both sight and hearing. It also requires a good deal of patience, but with practice sample preparation can take less than 45 minutes.


## Case History 1


A new flip-chip die and package were being evaluated and the initial yield was low due to continuity failures. The device was built on a sixlayer laminate PCB. The failing continuity path was traced using layer plots. From the tracing, it was possible to access the path from the solder ball to the top of the PCB by removing the top layer of solder mask with an Exact-o knife. This allowed the path to be checked from solder ball to top trace. When this was micro-probed, the path showed no open. This eliminated the solder ball, several traces, four microvias and a plated thru hole as the source of the open. The remaining possible causes for an open are under the die and include the solder bump interfaces (die and PCB), two copper traces and two micro-vias. Both C-SAM and X-ray were used to inspect the remaining area, but no failure cause was observed. Because multiple samples were available, it was decided to mill away the die and check the interfaces as material was removed. When the die was removed to the solder bump the path could be checked between it and the previously exposed trace. This path still showed to be open. One of these traces is at layer two of the PCB. To access that trace, a new milling tool was used and the sample was repositioned to allow the PCB layer above it to be removed. The cut was made between the micro-vias so each could be checked separately. Both micro-vias were checked and the one under the die was found to be open. This was confirmed with a cross-section of the micro-via showing that the micro-via was poorly formed during board manufacture.


## Case History 2


Case History 2


A high-density flip-chip device experiencing low yield due to pin-to-pin shorts is the next example for using this tool. The device was built using a thirteenlayer ceramic PCB. Only two devices with three failure sites were provided for analysis. The PCB was traced to map the solder bumps associated with the failing solder balls. In each case, adjacent solder bumps were found. The hypothesis was that some type of defect had occurred within the under-fill and had caused the solder bumps to be shorted. Both C-SAM and X-ray were used to evaluate the area associated with the solder bumps, but no obvious defects were observed. This was particularly true of the X-ray, where the density of the copper layers in the PCB obscured the space between solder bumps. The first site was ground down to the inter-metal layers of the die. 10:1 HF was used to remove the oxide layers and the aluminum traces. A plasma etch was used to remove the nitride. The under-bump metal of the adjacent solder bumps was probed and confirmed a short still existed. This eliminated the die as a possible source for the short. To expose the solder bumps, under-fill was dissolved using Uresolve from Dynaloy. The sample was given an ultra-sonic clean as a final step. The exposed solder bumps and PCB showed no signs of defects. Probing the adjacent solder bumps revealed that the short was now gone. This confirmed that the short was within the under-fill, but had been removed by the stripping process. Another sample was selected and the die was again removed as described above. Again the solder bumps were probed and the short was confirmed. More care was taken removing the under-fill. In this case, a polyimide plasma etch recipe was used, taking off small layers each time. After each etch step, the sample was simply rinsed to remove the remaining glass fill. With care, a metal bridge between solder bumps was exposed. The protrusions were found to be very fragile and could not hold up to the action of the ultra-sonic clean.

## Cross-section view


Cross-section view


In conclusion, it has been shown that precision milling can be effectively used to assist in identifying the failure cause on flip-chip devices. Without this tool, more time consuming tools are often required to investigate a possible failure site.


Barrier properties have been proved to affect the performance of the extensively used Cu interconnect. [1] [2] [3]  Barrier coverage and via profile observation have become an important task for the improvement of Cu technology. The employment of TEM is necessary to study the barrier profile because of the small via and thin barrier.


TEM images provide two-dimensional information through projection of a thin slice of the specimen. The thickness of the TEM sample ranges from several hundred to several thousand Å. Normally, thinner specimens provide better contrast because of decreased inelastic scattering. Inelastic scattering causes focus difficulty. Ideally, if we are able to thin slice the center of the via, the measurement of the barrier thickness should be straightforward because the barrier interface is almost planar. However, while the size of the via is only several hundred nm, a typical TEM sample slice will enclose a significant portion of the via. The curvature of the cylindrical or cone shaped via might result in blurred image at the interface.


TEM image contrast comes from the scattering difference in different materials or crystal structures. [4]  The resulting images are formed from the "transmitted" electrons which can be collected in the detector or camera. If the via barrier is embedded in the matrix of a significantly lighter element (such as a carbon filled, Ta/TaN lined via surrounded by oxide), the barrier materials in the electron path will then contribute more significantly to the intensity change by assuming no diffraction contrast from orientation differences. Figure  1  shows the relationship between the electron beam path and the via. If the TEM sample thickness is t 1 , then the barrier will contribute to the intensity change from point a to c. The barrier thickness might be measured from a to c due to blurring of the curved interface. The barrier thickness measurement will then be speculated to depend on the TEM sample thickness t 1 . The precision of the TEM cross-section is also a big concern. The corresponding intensity change in the TEM image was plotted at the bottom of figure  1 . It is clear from the plot that the correct barrier thickness should be measured from point a to b while point b is the location where the largest intensity change happens. Therefore, as long as the TEM sample contains the center of the via, i.e. point a and b, then the thickness of the barrier is able to be measured correctly and the measurement should be independent of the sample thickness. Because a thinner TEM sample has less background and less inelastic scattering, the interface (point b) of the barrier is well defined in the thin specimen for thickness measurement. When the interface is not clear, especially for thicker samples, the intensity plot will help to define the correct thickness. If the TEM sample only covers less then half of the via, then the barrier thickness cannot be determined from the intensity profile.


In conclusion, the rule of thumb for TEM sample preparation of the via is "thin and containing via center". This rule is actually easy to follow for a small via because most portions of the via, including the via center, will be embedded in the TEM specimen. The next task will be to find ways to routinely prepare useful TEM samples. One approach is to use an automatic cutting program such as FEI AutoTEM wizard. Routine sample preparation using AutoTEM wizard will be introduced in this paper.


Bear in mind, the FIB process usually produces a thicker damage layer than the mechanical polishing/ion-mill process. On the other hand, the mechanical polishing / ion-mill process requires the involvement of a highly skilled person. Comparisons of these two commonly used techniques will be discussed.


For via observation, conventional TEM bright field imaging is widely employed for small feature analysis. The increasing use of other techniques for imaging thin TEM specimens are also discussed. Examples of different imaging techniques will be discussed. Other potential tools worth exploring in the future will be included.


## TEM sample preparation


TEM sample preparation


## TEM sample preparation by FIB


TEM sample preparation by FIB


TEM sample preparation is known to be time consuming and labor intensive. The dual beam FIB has been widely used in semiconductor industry. With FIB lift-out technique, a thin foil is cut out from the bulk wafer. The thin foil is then lifted out and attached to a carbon film. Because the lift-out technique usually does not require mechanical polishing at all, it dramatically improves the sample preparation cycle time. When the feature of interest is small, continuous human monitoring increases the cycle time, depending on the user experience. The initiation of an automation program is useful in reducing the human attendance during FIB process and in improving the FIB utilization efficiency.


The basic procedure of automatic cutting with FEI AutoTEM wizard is described as follows:


1. Start the AutoTEM wizard. 2. Mark the area of interest with crosses. 3. The wizard program finishes the script for sample location. 4. Use AutoFIB or RunScript to run the script file using image recognition of the fiducial marks. 5. After completion of the script, if no further fine tuning is required, the thin foil is cut off and processed as a normal lift out sample.


Steps 1 and 2 are the most important steps because the accuracy of the subsequent FIB milling will depend on the accuracy of the mark position. Figure  2 (a) shows a high magnification picture of the AUTOTEM mark. Once the marks have been precisely made, it takes only 1.5 hrs with our current settings to finish the milling (step3-4). In addition to the recognition of the mark pattern, sample bending and non-calibrated final thickness may result in the loss of the area of interest. After the program has been set up correctly for the particular FIB machine to be used, precise marking of the device is critical. As long as the marking is done correctly, the subsequent FIB cutting of the small 0.1µm via does not required a highly skilled individual.


Because the automation program does not require ebeam monitoring during FIB cutting as is needed during manual milling, the e-beam damage during sample preparation is reduced. The automatic cutting also produces a TEM foil with a much more uniform thickness than the manually cut wedge shaped specimen because the automatically prepared specimen is tilted back and forth automatically during the milling to correct the milling profile.


Using AutoTEM to routinely examine the via profile is feasible as long as the mark can be made correctly. It can be seen from figure  2 (a) that the size of the mark is very close to the size of a small via. The accuracy of the mark position is uncertain for a small feature. Sometimes, in order to cover the entire FIB cutting area in the same frame, the image magnification will be too low to mill a precise mark. Difficulty in precision marking adds significant time to the sample preparation.


## TEM sample preparation by mechanical polishing


TEM sample preparation by mechanical polishing


Although FIB has been proven to be a very useful tool for small via cutting, the 100-400 Å damage layer reported to be found on the surface of a FIBed Si specimen is still a concern for barrier observation  [5] . A polished sample was made to compare the difference. We found that both the hand polished sample and the FIB prepared sample produced images of similar quality. Sample polishing of a small via with barrier only becomes very difficult even for an experienced and skilled person. FIB, therefore, is the best choice for preparing a TEM specimen of small vias.


## TEM imaging techniques


TEM imaging techniques


AutoTEM has proven to be a useful tool for routine small via TEM sample preparation. TEM bright field imaging is an excellent choice for revealing the barrier profile of a barrier-only via while chemical imaging methods such as STEM ADF, x-ray mapping and energy filtered imaging are better choices for imaging Cu filled vias. The techniques we mentioned are useful to derive the twodimensional barrier information. Two-dimensional data may not provide enough information on barrier roughness and uniformity in three dimensions. TEM tomography promises to deliver detailed information of the barrier profile in 3-dimensions. [5]


In wafer fabrication, gate oxide integrity plays an important role in the reliability and yield of IC chips. With the continuous scaling of advanced ULSI CMOS technologies into the deep sub-micron regime, ultra-thin gate oxide is indispensable and its integrity and reliability is therefore of major concern for ULSI devices. Defects on the gate oxide may ultimately lead to gate oxide breakdown, punch through, QBD failure, etc. Thus, it is necessary to etch away the polysilicon and expose the gate oxide in order to check the integrity of the gate oxide and analyze physical defects within the gate/tunnel oxide.


A good poly etchant is thus extremely important in the failure analysis field. The poly etchant must be equipped with the following essential features: (a). The possibility of over-etching the gate oxide must be minimized in order to preserve the gate/tunnel oxide for defect analysis. (b). The etch time must be reasonable. (c). The result must be reliable, consistent and repeatable to all levels of users ranging from technicians to engineers with minimum de-processing skills. (d). The recipe must be easy to prepare using commercially available chemicals.


Three different chemical solutions are currently used in wafer fabrication failure analysis to remove the poly and expose the underlying gate/tunnel oxide. They are 6:6:1 (Acetic Acid/HNO 3 /HF), NaOH and Choline. In this paper, we will discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each of these three chemicals. We will also introduce a new chemical etchant, HB91, for removing poly and exposing the gate/tunnel oxide for identification of oxide related defects in wafer fabrication


## NaOH (Sodium Hydroxide)


NaOH (Sodium Hydroxide)


Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) has widely been used for poly removal to expose the ultra-thin gate /tunnel oxide. Theoretically, NaOH has a very good selectivity in removing the poly with respect to the oxide. It will not attack the underlying oxide thus, preserving any existing gate/tunnel oxide defects and allowing reliable measurement of the tunnel window.


After performing experiments, our optimized NaOH etching procedure for a completed wafer from a  For example, Figure  1  shows an N Channel bulk 16X structure after delayering to gate oxide using the NaOH procedure. One can see that a defect was found on the gate oxide layer. Figures  2  and 3  show a QBD tunnel window structure after delayering to tunnel oxide. We can easily measure the size of tunnel window to identify the QBD failure. However, the NaOH etchant was found to be unsuitable for large polysilicon with tungsten silicide (WSi x ) or cobalt silicide (CoSi x ). After delayering, dummy holes were introduced on the poly surface. Numerous dummy holes were observed on the large capacitor structures in the electrical test (ET) structures used to monitor the gate-oxide integrity (GOI) or the charge to breakdown (QBD) value in the EEPROM device.


One possible way to solve the problem was to remove the CoSi x or WSi x on the polysilicon surface before proceeding with the NaOH etchant. For local thin poly such as that found in the SRAM cell area for 0.13um or 0.18um devices, the sample was placed in the Reactive Ion Etchant (RIE) for surface bombardment after etching to the poly surface with the ILD layer partially intact. This induced plenty of dummy holes on the CoSi x or WSi x surface and facilitated the NaOH poly etch as the chemical could seep through the holes and attack the polysilicon. However, for large capacitor structures as mentioned earlier, such a method was often not feasible. Due to the large surface area, the dummy holes created by the RIE bombardment of the polysilicon surface did not provide sufficient NaOH seepage through the silicide to etch the underlying poly and successfully expose the gate/tunnel oxide.


Fig.  4  Optical photograph showing poly exposed on a capacitor structure using the HF deprocessing procedure. For example, our experimental results as shown in Figures  4  and 5  revealed that the polysilicon with WSi x was not etched away although many dummy holes were introduced on the tungsten silicide poly surface after 20 mins of NaOH etch.


From the above discussion, we understand that the main disadvantage of the NaOH etch is that it is difficult to etch poly with a CoSi x or WSi x silicide on the surface. In addition, it is necessary to heat the NaOH solution to 50 o C during the etch. In other words, constant monitoring of the temperature of the NaOH solution is required.


From our experiments, we also understand that KOH is another chemical, which may use to remove the poly layer. However, it is not recommended for use in exposing the gate/tunnel oxide as we found that the life of the solution is only about 15 minutes, and 15 minutes is shorter than the etch time needed. But KOH is a good solution for residual silicon oxide test on aluminum bondpads.

Choline OH: H 2 O


Recently, as reported in ISTFA2001, Choline OH was used to remove poly and to expose the gate oxide. As mentioned in the paper, it was a relatively safe etch to handle and store. Its slow etch makes it very reliable, repeatable and controllable  [1] . However, the slow etch rate at low temperatures also limits the use of the etch for rapid failure analysis. In other words, a constant high temperature of approximately 150-200 0 C was required for rapid polysilicon etch as shown in the table below  [1] .


Combining these results leads to the conclusion that when the variance of both healthy and faulty devices is reduced a threshold limit is potentially easier to set and identification of the outliers on a wafer or in a lot is also easier. Finally, this formulation of the residual and residual variance provides a means to compare ∆I DDQ and the outlier removal techniques reported in the literature 1, 3-6 . Figure  3a  is an example of a test measurement M shifted by a constant. The residual and, the original distribution as well, have the typical long, broad tail that makes identifying outliers in the distribution difficult. In this case, the constant shifted the mean too far (ie the mean is negative) and the variance is unchanged. This is because a constant estimate can not reduce the residual variance. Figure  3b  is the result of a shift using an estimate based on a local model. The mean is shifted near zero and variance of both the healthy and faulty distributions are reduced (the peaks narrow). The residual plot distinctly shows healthy and faulty distributions and the limits to separate them is easier to identify.


## Local Model Selection


Local Model Selection


Schemes to select the input and compute the estimate must be developed to reliably estimate a measurement with a local model. For SPP, the local model input is a modified version of the nearest neighbor selection. A neighbor is defined by the distance between its center point and the center of the unit of interest. For SPP, the Euclidean distances are calculated from one die to all other die on the wafer. A die's nearest neighbors are the four die immediately to North, South, East and West that are separated by unit distance (d = 1). The next four die surrounding a die at its compass corners NW, NE, SW and, SW are located slightly farther away (d = √  2) and so on.


For cases where the variation across the wafer is smooth the nearest four or eight die neighborhood produces reliable estimates 1, 3 .


Calculating the estimate has to be robust to messy data where some data values are in error from measurement noise or completely missing. For SPP and I DDQ data, the median value of the measurements of neighborhood was found to work well because it is easy to compute and less sensitive to outliers and missing data than the neighborhood mean. The median of a list of 2N + 1 values is obtained after sorting the list from smallest to largest. The median is the N + 1 value in the sorted list and represents the value where 50% of the data is smaller and 50% of the data is larger. Since the median is one of the original values it is robust (tolerant) to up to nearly N outliers in the original data.


For SPP, the selection of the neighborhood is as important as the computation. The robustness of the combination of median filter and neighborhood needs to be tested. This is done by computing the estimate using a single neighbor selected at random from the original neighborhood. In this case, the median estimate is the value of the selected neighbor. A second estimate is computed by adding a second randomly selected neighbor to the first. Now, the estimate is the av erage of the two, random neighbors. A third estimate is computed by including a third neighbor and so on to generate a sequence of estimates based on the order the neighbors were chosen. By starting with a different first neighbor this series of estimates can be repeated. The convergence and stability of the series of estimates is a measure of the estimate sensitivity (and the residual sensitivity) to the choice of the original neighborhood.


Figure  4  plots the estimate as function of the number and weight of the neighbors. The x-axis is a configuration index that represents the number and weight of the neighbors as the sequence is generated as described above. Neighbors not included in the median estimate have a weight of zero, that is they are ignored for that configuration. The estimate labeled "Regular NNR" shows a series of decreasing steps for increasing configuration number. Each step corresponds to adding one die to the set of included neighbors. To demonstrate the idea the worst estimate from the neighborhood was purposely chosen as the initial configuration so that each addition decreased the median estimate. In general, that would not be the case as seen in the other traces labeled "1st Optimization" and "2nd Optimization" where the initial configuration was chosen randomly. As shown in Figure  4  the configuration (number and weight of neighbors) has a considerable effect on the initial estimate. However, after optimization and as different configurations are explored and neighbors weighted the final point estimates settle. Regardless of the initial configurations each reaches a similar best estimate. This is an encouraging result as it builds confidence that a globally, optimized configuration can be found from the data that defines the best neighborhood for computing estimates. It was observed that for I DDQ data the nearest neighbor annulus is not always the optimal input neighborhood 2 . This generally occurs when the smooth process variation is combined with a systematic effect. A typical example of a systematic effect is the variation as a result of a stepper.
 Under these circumstances, a checkerboard effect is imposed (convolved with) the smooth pattern which can shift the best-estimate die away from physically adjacent die to die that have the same position within the stepper field. Even in this case a stable neighborhood pattern can be identified using the techniques outlined here.


Unlike skew-lot calibration methods, SPP is responsive to each data set. The ability of SPP to identify a neighborhood for a wide variety of processing outcomes is what is meant by a data-driven estimate and residual. For deep-submicron test analysis, the SPP estimate has several desirable properties. SPP neighborhood identification can adapt to systematic and smooth patterns seen in deep-submicron technologies. The estimate is the output of a kind of lowpass, smoothing filter and captures wafer-level processing patterns. The estimates are formulated to be robust to messy-data such as missing data or outliers. No special processing is required for either missing data or outliers. These properties are enhanced by computing the SPP residual. For random processing noise and no defects, the mean of the residual is zero. In practice, residuals have been close to zero. For any SPP estimate, the residual variance is less than the original measurement variance. As a result the spatial patterns in the residual are removed that can obscure die outliers or generate unwanted chip testing fallout. The spatial connection between adjacent die has been known and used in IC production for many years. Stapper's 7 defect clustering, followed more recently by Singh 8 and Riordan 9 established the advantage of screening chips based on Pass/Fail results of their neighboring die. Passing die in low yield areas are suspect and are treated differently during assembly or burn-in. SPP is the first to apply these spatial relationships to continuous-value measurements.


## I DDQ Testing


Figure  5  demonstrates SPP's key benefit of reducing residual variance and shifting the mean close to zero. The I DDQ data in Figure  5  represents a production lot with approximately 5,000 chips. As expected, the ĨDDQ residual mean near zero. The reduced variance of the residual is also clearly evident. For this example, the ĨDDQ variance is one-half the value for the original measurements.


Statistical post-processing improves the separation of healthy and faulty die and makes the limit setting easier. Howev er, the issue remains where to set the limit 10 . Testing chips with two-parameters such as I DDQ or F MAX to die temperature has provided excellent contrast between intrinsic leakage and defectbased leakage 11 . The motivation for and outcome of two-parameter screening is similar to SPP. A chip is screened when compared to other chips in the population its I DDQ or F MAX responds inconsistently to different temperatures. SPP can be combined with the two-parameter idea to yield a screen that accounts for the chip location as well as the intrinsic dependence of the transistors on temperature or V DD . It is equally clear from Figure  6  that they hav e overlapping I DDQ distributions. The use of delay as second parameter provides some welcome separation of the three lots. Unfortunately, the outliers of one lot are still obscured by the adjacent lots. A single limit on the I DDQ distributions can not be confidently applied to all three lots. The faster die in the • distribution have some isolated outliers that a single limit around 34 (dotted line in Figure  6 ) would fail. Other • delay-I DDQ distribution outliers are buried and just visible at the lowest I DDQ level of the distribution (see arrow). A final view of the three data lots is shown in Figure  8  where the histograms of the original I DDQ data and the residuals are plotted together. The original I DDQ histograms have separate peaks and long, overlapping tails. For example the tail is within the • distribu- tion. This is what prevents using a single threshold with different lots. The residual histograms centered around zero in Figure  8  show the significant variance reduction from SPP local modeling. The residual distributions have very similar characteristics easing limit setting. Table  1  summarizes burn-in results for fourteen lots. After I DDQ SPP, an average of 2% of the chips that passed all tests were rebinned as fails (coded as Bin15). The Bin15 along with a sample of the remaining Bin1 die were submitted to burn-in, approximately 2,900 chips. The failure rate for the chips in Bin15 was fifty times the rate of the final chips in Bin1. The failure rate ranged from 0% for very small lot samples to as much as 26%. This is an excellent return for an admittedly high 2% kill ratio. For ASICs the corresponding improvement in DPM and EFR is a counter-balance for the high over kill ratio. Reducing a parts SPP kill ratio is a central topic for ongoing research.
