### Figure 4: Metrics to Calculate Scores


Figure 4: Metrics to Calculate Scores


Score matching method is based on the hypothesis that the closer the fault site to the actual defect site, the better match between the tester unload data and the simulated unload data. We use the same matching calculation method as proposed in  [10] . The calculation of the score is based on the metrics of intersections, mis-predictions, and the non-predictions, these are also shown in Figure  4 . Intersection is the count of failures observed on the tester and also by the simulation. Vector-wise intersection is the count of test patterns for which the simulation results are exactly the same as the tester outputs for that test pattern. Vector-wise intersection is the strongest indication that the candidate scan cell has the defect. The misprediction is the count of the failures observed by the simulator but not on the tester. The non-prediction is the count of failures observed on the tester but not by the simulator. The score of each candidate scan cell consists of the accumulated values for vector-wise intersections, intersections, non-intersections and mis-predictions for all the ATPG test patterns with vector-wise intersection as the strongest metric and mis-prediction as the weakest metric. Stuck-at faults, transition faults and hold time faults are dealt with identically while calculating the scores. Note that the matching algorithm in  [7]  calculates scores based on the intersection, mis-prediction and non-prediction, it doesn't consider the vector-wise intersection while we use vector-wise intersection as the strongest metric  [10] . In  [7] , the mis-prediction and non-prediction are given the same priority to calculate scores while we believe the non-prediction is a stronger metric than mis-prediction and hence it is given higher priority than mis-prediction.


## 5. Experimental Results


5. Experimental Results


Experiments were performed on several products with multiple scan chains. We use simulation results and silicon data to show the effectiveness of the proposed scan chain fault diagnosis procedure for a single scan chain fault.


### 5.1 Simulation Results


5.1 Simulation Results


Simulation experiments were conducted on a chipset design with 54 scan chains. The maximum scan chain length is 410. First we evaluate the technique to identify the upper and lower bounds of the candidate list. The number of scan cells between the upper and lower bounds (also called the size of the candidate list) is used as the metric of our evaluation. One hundred modified ATPG test patterns are applied to each scan chain. We consider a fault in each scan cell. Based on the logic simulation results of the modified ATPG test patterns, we calculate the lower and upper bounds of the candidate list for the fault in each scan cell. Different fault models are used in this experiment. The typical distributions of candidate list sizes for stuck-at-1 are shown in Figure  5 . From Figure  5  we can see that for 135 scan cells the size of the candidate list is one. This means that for 32.9% of the total scan cells in a scan chain, the technique to determine the upper and lower bounds can identify the exact defective scan cell if the defect behaves as a stuck-at-1 fault. For more than 80% of the total scan cells, the size of the candidate list is less than or equal to five. These results show that Step 2 of the proposed procedure can effectively reduce the number of candidate scan cells. Note that these results are derived only by logic simulation of one hundred modified ATPG test patterns, which generally executes in a few minutes. However, from Figure  5 , it can be seen that there are some scan cells (about 20% of the total scan cells) that have a candidate list of size six or larger. This tells us that further improvement of the diagnosis resolution using Step 3 to reduce the size of the candidate list is necessary.


The typical distributions of candidate list sizes for slow-tofall faults are shown in Figure  6 . While comparing with the results shown in Figure  5 , the sizes of the candidate list for transition faults are larger than those for stuck-at faults. This can be explained by the fact that specific values of two consecutive scan cells are required to determine an upper bound or lower bound for transition faults. This is a stricter condition than that required for stuck-at fault that only requires a single scan cell value to determine an upper bound or lower bound. For transition faults, we also observed that for about 40% of the scan cells, the sizes of the candidate lists are less than or equal to five.


The typical distribution of candidate list sizes for hold-time faults are shown in Figure  7 . When comparing with the candidate list sizes distribution for transition faults, more scan cells have candidate lists consisting one scan cell. Actually, for hold time faults, there are about 35% of scan cells have a candidate list consisting of only one scan cell. This result should be expected. The reason is that even though the values of two consecutive scan cells are required to determine an upper bound or lower bound for hold time faults, this requirement is much looser than those for transition faults because any value transition (0 to 1 or 1 to 0) in the two consecutive scan cells can be used to calculate the boundary of candidate list for hold time faults. We also observed that some scan cells have a large candidate list which tells us that further improvement of the diagnostic resolution is necessary. To improve the diagnostic resolution, we used the matching algorithm to rank the candidate scan cells. In this step, we used one hundred ATPG test patterns to simulate each candidate scan cell. In this experiment, we studied some cases where larger sizes of candidate lists were obtained in the last step. The results are shown in   2 , we can see that after score and ranking, the number of candidate scan cells can be reduced dramatically, and in most cases, the number of scan cells with the highest score is one or two. As shown in Figure  8 , for about 95% of the simulated scan chain defects the candidates contain 1 to 5 scan cells, while only 5% of the defects have six or more candidate scan cells. This shows that the score and ranking step is very effective to further reduce the number of candidate scan cells and hence improve the final diagnosis resolution. It is reasonable to believe that better diagnosis resolution can be derived if more test patterns are applied for score and ranking.


### Table 2: Experimental Results for Score and Ranking


Table 2: Experimental Results for Score and Ranking


We also ran our program on another product with 78 scan chains. The longest scan chain has 1542 scan cells. Two hundred ATPG test patterns are modified with all-0 or all-1 load values for 6 scan chains. Our simulation results show that the range determination program can identify the exact location of stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1 fault on any scan cell.


### 5.2 Silicon Defect Data


5.2 Silicon Defect Data


Experimental results on silicon defects of four products are reported in this section. Table  3  lists the the specifications of the three products, i.e. the total number of gates(#Gates), the number of scan chains (#Chains), the total number of scan cells (#ScanCells) and the maximum scan chain length (ChainLength). We list the scan chain failure diagnosis results for units of designs A, B, C and D in Tables 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. For each unit of designs A, a defect was injected to a prespecified location of a scan chain using focused ion beam (FIB). Different chains are selected for the 9 units. The locations of the defects are given under the column "Cell Index". The types of the injected defects are given under the column "Defect Type". As shown in Table  4 , units 1, 2 and 3 are injected with scan data stuck-at-0 defect, units 4, 5 and 6 are injected with scan data stuck-at-1 defect, units 7 and 8 are injected with open defects and unit 9 with clock line stuck-at-0 defect.


We applied three chain test patterns to the 9 FIB injected units. The tester failures are analyzed and the fault types determined by our program are listed under column "Type Identified". For unit 1 through unit 6 which have stuck-at-0 fault or stuck-at-1 fault, our program correctly determined the defective scan chains and their fault types. Unit 7, which has an open defect in scan data line, behaves as a stuck-at-0 fault, while unit 8, which also has an open defect, behaves as SA1 fault. Our program failed to identify the fault type for unit 9 which has a clock line stuck-at-0 defect. Further study of the tester failures shows that the clock line SA0 defect behaves as a multiple-chain defect and doesn't match any of the fault models described in Section 3.


To determine the range of the candidate scan cells, we modified 100 logic test ATPG test patterns and applied them to the FIB injected units. The resulting numbers of candidate scan cells are listed under column "Range". For four units, units 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7, there is only one scan cell in the candidate list and they are the exact locations of the defects. This shows the effectiveness of the proposed technique to determine the range of the candidate scan cells. However, there are still several units that have more than one scan cells in the candidate list. Unit 1 has 35 candidate scan cells, unit 3 has 11 candidates, unit 8 has 2 candidates and unit 9 has 29 candidates. For unit 9, we could not finish the fault simulation step because of fault modeling problem. However, as an enhancement in the future, the combination of simple fault models may be used to calculate scores for the candidate cells  [9] . For the other three units, we applied two hundred original ATPG test patterns, and used matching algorithm to calculate the scores for the candidate units and finally ranked them. For all the three units, the real defect positions are included in the scan cells with the highest rank and the final number of candidate scan cells have been reduced. The last column in Table  4  gives the number of scan cells with the highest rank. It can be seen that after ranking, unit 3 and unit 8 have one candidate scan cell, which is the real defect position. Unit 1 has 15 candidates that cannot be differentiated. However, if more test patterns were applied to this unit, better diagnosis results should be derived.


For design B, we used the original production test patterns without any modification. As we stated earlier, by using the original production test patterns, we can remove the interaction between the diagnosis program by collecting tester failures only once at the very beginning. It saves the overall turn around time for the diagnosis program to generate the final results with the cost of losing resolution in the range determination step. We used FIB to inject SA0 or SA1 defects to different units. As shown in Table  5 , the second column reports the type of defects for each unit. The third column gives the fault type determined in step 1. It can be seen that our technique successfully determined the defect type for all the four units. The fourth column gives the number of candidate scan cells after the range determination. In step 2, all these four units have multiple scan cells as candidates and the real defective scan cells are included as candidates for all the four units. Even though we could not find the exact the defective scan cell for these units in step 2, the numbers of candidates are already much less than the total number of scan cells in the scan chain. The reduced number of candidates significantly reduces the time for score and ranking process. The last column reports the number of scan cells with the highest matching score after we run the score and matching algorithm on the candidate scan cells. It can be seen that for all these four units, the final numbers of candidates are very small and should be very helpful for physical fault isolation. By comparing the results for units of design A and design B, we can see that better diagnostic resolution can be achieved with modified ATPG test patterns.
5.0 Experimental Results


This algorithm was applied to the data obtained from 200 SPICE simulations of the 30,000 by 30,000 unit region of the PPG referred to as Q9 in Figure  3 . A three dimensional error map plotting the prediction error against the (x,y) coordinate of the inserted defect (modeled using a current source) is shown in Figure  17 . The prediction error is computed as the directed distance between the predicted location and the actual location of the defect. The average and worst case prediction errors are 215 and 650 units, respectively.


The size of the simulation model for the entire PPG shown in Figure  3  made it impossible to perform SPICE simulations on it. Instead, the PPG was simulated using a specialized power grid simulation engine called ALSIM. The prediction error map from 500 ALSIM simulations is shown in Figure  18 . The average and worst case prediction errors are 410 and 1,340 units, respectively. The increase in Predicted location prediction error is largely due to the more significant anomalies in the grid's structure over the larger region defined by the entire PPG.


### 6.0 Conclusions


6.0 Conclusions


The weaknesses of our previously derived resistance-based Quiescent Signal Analysis model are addressed in a new current-ratio-based technique. Calibration transistors are proposed to reduce the adverse effects of probe card resistance variations on the prediction accuracy of the new QSA technique. The calibration transistor data is also used to account for power grid resistance variations from one region to the next and asymmetrical or irregular arrangements in the positions of the power supply pads.


The current ratio contours derived through SPICE simulations of a commercial power grid are shown to be well approximated by "families" of hyperbola curves. An analytical framework is derived that allows the measured I DDQ data to be translated to physical (x,y) layout coordinates, that represent the position of the defect.


Although the analytical model that we present in this work accounts for tester environment variables such as probe card resistance variations, the simulation data was derived from a simpler model. For example, the probe card resistance was held constant at 1Ω at every supply pad, 20mA was used for defect currents, and leakage currents were not included. As pointed out, current ratios are naturally robust to variations in defect current and the calibration transistors in combination with regression analysis are expected to be effective in dealing with leakages. Simulation experiments are currently underway to verify these hypotheses.


The last issue that remains to be explored is the effectiveness of this technique on other types of grid topologies. For significantly irregular grids, we expect a lookup-table approach to be more accurate than the hyperbola-based technique. We are investigating the use of power grid simulators such as ALSIM as a means of making this type of approach practical.


Logic fault diagnosis or fault isolation is the process of analyzing failure logic portions of an integrated circuit to isolate the cause of failure to enable design or fabrication process modification to avoid similar failures. Scan design has been used widely as a design for testability methodology to improve the testability and facilitate the diagnosis of VLSI circuits. In a typical scan design, the area occupied by the logic associated with the scan chains (including the scan cells) ranges from 10%-30% of the total area of the circuit. As a consequence, about 10%-30% of defects that impact logic cause the scan chain to fail. A functional scan chain is critical to the testing and diagnosis of other parts of the circuit, hence it is necessary to find the fault location in a faulty scan chain and finally find the root cause of the failure.


Scan chain fault diagnosis is the process of identifying the defective scan cell in a scan chain. Several methods have been proposed to diagnose scan chain failures. They can be classified into two categories. In the first category, hardware modification beyond the basic scan design is necessary through special scan cell design or additional circuitry. These special designs are then used to facilitate the scan chain diagnosis process. Schafer proposed a new shift register design to connect the output of each scan cell to another scan cell such that its value can be observed by the other scan chain in diagnosis mode  [1] . Edirisooriya uses a global diagnosis signal and XOR gates between the adjacent scan cells to improve the stuck-at fault diagnosis along the scan chain  [2] . A set/reset circuitry is proposed by Nayaranan to enhance the stuck-at fault diagnosibility of the scan chain  [3] . The techniques of flipping scan flip-flops and setting/resetting scan flip-flops are used by Wu to identify the defective scan cell  [4] . The techniques in this category introduce area overhead and performance penalty, which may not be acceptable.


The other category of scan chain fault diagnosis techniques does not need any modification in addition to the basic scan design. Sequential ATPG techniques or special algorithms are designed to isolate the defective scan cell. Kundu proposed the use of sequential ATPG techniques to set the scan cells to specific values and the diagnosis information is collected during the unload of the scan cells  [5] . Because of the complexity of the sequential ATPG techniques, this method is very time-consuming and may be infeasible. Instead of using ATPG techniques, Cheney proposed to use random test pattern simulation  [6] . This method is very time efficient while the resolution largely depends on the randomly generated test patterns. Fault simulation and matching algorithm are used to find the best possible faulty scan cell  [7] . However, the number of suspect scan cells that need to be considered could be very large for a long scan chain making this method time consuming and adversely affect the resolution. IDDQ testing was proposed for scan chain fault diagnosis by loading special test patterns to the scan chain and observing the quiescent current after each shift  [8] . This method is effective in diagnosing stuck-at faults, but its application to transition faults is very limited. Further, this method requires the circuit to be IDDQ testable.


In this paper, we propose an algorithmic method to diagnose a circuit with a scan chain defect. Three steps are implemented in the proposed scan chain diagnosis procedure. In the first step, we use special chain test patterns, which only contain scan pattern load and unload operations, to determine both the faulty scan chain (we assume there is more than one scan chain in the circuit under test) and the fault type of the faulty scan chain. In the second step, we use a modified ATPG test pattern set to identify the range of the suspect scan cells. In this step, we restrict the location of the faulty scan cell both from the scan chain input and from the scan chain output. This can significantly reduce the number of scan cells to be considered and in many cases this step may even provide the exact location of the scan cell with the defect. In the last step, we use ATPG test patterns to simulate faults in the suspect scan cells. By comparing the simulation responses and the observed faulty circuit responses from the tester, each suspect scan cell is given a score. An earlier version of this work has been reported in  [9] . In this paper we focus on the application aspect of this technique and provide more application results we obtained recently.


The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, definitions used in this paper are provided. In Section 3, we discuss the fault model handled by the proposed procedure. Section 4 describes the proposed scan chain fault diagnosis procedure for a single scan chain fault. Experimental results are provided in Section 5. Section 6 concludes the paper.


## 2. Definitions


We use SCI to denote the scan data input pin of a scan chain, and SCO to denote the scan data output pin of a scan chain. The length of a scan chain is the total number of scan cells in the scan chain. Each scan cell in a scan chain is given an index. The cell connected to SCO is numbered 0 and numbers incremented up to the SCI. In this paper, the scan cell with index n is referred to as scan cell n (S n ). For a list of consecutive scan cells in a scan chain, the scan cell with the highest index is called the upper bound, and the scan cell with the lowest index is called the lower bound. The scan cells between the SCI and the scan input pin of a scan cell are called the upstream cells of this scan cell, while the scan cells between the SCO and the scan input pin of a scan cell are called the downstream cells of this scan cell. Note that from this definition, the downstream cells of a scan cell include the scan cell itself. During scan shift, data flows from upstream cells to downstream cells. For example, a scan chain of length 6 is shown in Figure  1 . The index of each scan cell is also shown in this figure. Scan cells 4 and 5 are upstream cells of scan cell 3 while scan cells 0, 1, 2, and 3 are downstream cells of scan cell 3. For a list of scan cells that consist scan cells 1, 2, 3 and 4, the lower bound of this list is scan cell 1 and the upper bound is scan cell 4.


If the number of inversion gates between the scan input pin of scan cell S c and the SCO is even, then scan cell S c has positive polarity. Otherwise, S c has negative polarity. In many cases the scan cell itself may have an inverter inside it, thus the scan input pin and the scan output pin of the scan cell may have different polarities. We define the polarity of the scan input pin of the scan cell as the polarity of the scan cell. For example, in Figure  1 , scan cells 0, 1, 4 and 5 have positive polarities and scan cells 2 and 3 have negative polarities.


In this paper, for a given load pattern or unload pattern, the right most bit is the value of scan cell 0. For example, after loading pattern 111000 to the scan chain shown in Figure  1 , the values of scan cells from 5 to 0 are 110100.


## 3. Fault Models


Both stuck-at fault models and timing related fault models have been proposed for scan chain fault diagnosis in previous works  [4] [7] . Our method targets similar fault models.


Stuck-at faults: Stuck-at-0 and Stuck-at-1 faults are the classical fault models used for logic testing and diagnosis. Stuck-at behavior may occur when a scan chain is bridged to the ground or power, when the clock signal to some scan cells stays stuck-off, or when a scan chain is open. When a SA0 or SA1 behavior occurs on a chain, the scan unload data will be a string of zeros or ones, depending on the polarity of the defect site and the stuck-at value. If the defective scan cell has positive polarity, the scan output string has the same value as the stuck-at value while if the defective scan cell has negative polarity, the scan output string has the complementary value of the stuck-at value. For example, in the scan chain shown in Figure  1 , a stuck-at-0 fault at the scan input pin of scan cell 0, which has positive polarity, results in the unload values to be a string of 0s at SCO. A stuck-at-0 fault at the scan input pin of scan cell 2, which has negative polarity, results in the unload values to be a string of 1s at SCO.


Transition faults: This fault model covers defects that cause scan cells to exhibit timing problems in transitioning from 0 to 1 or vice versa. As described in  [7] , the result could be any of the following four conditions: slow-to-rise, slow-tofall, fast-to-rise, fast-to-fall. For example, consider a defect at a positive polarity site. Suppose the fault free circuit unload pattern is 001100110011 and the defect behaves as a slow-torise fault, the observed unload values are 00100010001X (where X depends on the initial value of the faulty cell). If the defect behaves as a slow-to-fall fault, the observed output values are 011101110111. If the defect behaves as a fast-to-rise Hold time faults: If the clock to the scan latches stays ON, the function of the scan latch is the same as a buffer  [7] , or if there are large clock skews  [4] , the expected output values come out one clock cycle earlier. For example, suppose the expected unload values are 00110011. However, if there is a hold time fault in the scan chain, the observed output values are X0011001, where X depends on the next load value.


## 4 Scan Chain Fault Diagnosis Procedure


4 Scan Chain Fault Diagnosis Procedure


The detailed description of the proposed scan chain fault diagnosis procedure for a single scan chain fault is presented in this section. Figure  2  shows the block diagram of the proposed procedure. The procedure takes the circuit description and its scan chain design as the inputs. We also assume that logic ATPG test patterns are available for the circuit under test. The output of the procedure is a list of candidate scan cells in the decreasing order of the probability.


## Experimental Set Up


Experimental Set Up


An Optonics EmiScope I system used to collect the TRE data in this paper. This system was functionally equivalent to that presented by Bruce et al. 6 except for the detector. Instead of a silicon-based avalanche photo-diode (APD), the current system used a nearinfrared optimized InGaAs-based APD developed by Optonics. As seen in the data below this APD has good timing response, with a transit time spread of about 100 ps, moderate dark count rates, and a high enough quantum efficiency to enable fast acquisition times. Like the system in Bruce et al. 6 , this system had a variable aperture for defining from which transistors emission was collected. The system also had upward facing optics, allowing it to be docked to a tester. An IMS Vanguard tester was used in the current study. For the cases where a single element TRE signal is compared to an LVP waveform, a Schlumberger IDS-2500 system was used to collect the LVP data.


All the TRE and LVP data presented here were collected from a microprocessor fabricated using 0.13 µm process technology 9 and mounted in a flipchip package. The samples were prepared by manually thinning and polishing the silicon to a thickness of about 100 µm and applying an antireflection coating. A transparent heat spreader of the type described in Eiles et al. 10 was also used during the measurements. As in Bruce et al. 6


## TRE Data Analysis Method


TRE Data Analysis Method


Several examples of TRE signals are shown in the figures in the results section below. Except where noted, the signals have been smoothed using a boxcar filter with a bandwidth of 15 GHz, for ease of viewing the signals in a small format. However, the analysis of the data to determine the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the emission peaks, the number of signal photons in a peak, and the number of dark counts was performed on the raw data, data that are not smoothed. For comparison, one figure showing raw data is included (Figure  2(c) ).


The FWHM of a peak was determined by fitting a Gaussian to the peak. The method of Lo et al. 5 was then used to calculate the timing precision achieved during that acquisition: the timing precision of the peak is equal to its FWHM divided by its signal-tonoise ratio (SNR), where SNR was defined as:


noise signal signal n n n SNR + = / , (1)


where n signal was the number of signal photons within the FWHM region of a peak, while n noise was the number of dark counts within this region. In the present study, n noise and n signal were found in the following way. The sum of n noise and n signal is equal to the total number of counts within the FWHM of a peak. The number of dark counts or n noise alone was found by selecting a region equal in width to the FWHM in a section of the data with no peak. This region was made representative of the average dark counts by first selecting a much wider region with no peak and measuring the dark count rate. The number of dark counts was then measured in a region with this same dark count rate but equal in width to the FWHM.

## Results from LVP and TRE Comparison


Results from LVP and TRE Comparison


In this section LVP waveforms and TRE signals collected from the same device are presented. This example was chosen as a representative case of microprocessor speedpath debug, in which a design engineer wants to learn with good timing precision when particular transitions occur.


The device examined was a latch. The n-channel transistor gate width was 2 µm and the device had 4 legs, while the p-channel transistor gate width was 3 µm, with 4 legs. Only the p-channel transistor was probed with LVP, while the TRE emissions were collected simultaneously from both the n-and p-channel transistors. A tester loop length of 109 µs and a Vcc of 1.42 V were used. Figure  5  shows the LVP waveforms, while Figure  6  shows the TRE signals.


In both cases, a pattern with a missing clock was first run in order to locate in time the expected transition of the device. This is the top waveform or signal in Figures  5  and 6 . The lower waveform or signal is that from the suspect device.


The LVP waveforms were acquired for approximately 2 to 3 minutes, fairly typical for LVP acquisition times 5 . Note that the LVP waveform from the device is inverted as can occur under some conditions, including improper focus 5 . For TRE, the missing clock signal took under 2 minutes to acquire, while the acquisition from the suspect device took 3 minutes. The timing precision achieved on the device signal was about ± 9 ps for this acquisition time.


## Long Tester Loop Length Results


Long Tester Loop Length Results


A final example is presented here of a signal that was collected using TRE that could not be acquired with LVP. In LVP, the mode-locked probing laser must be synchronized with the tester loop length. Empirically the synchronization becomes more difficult and eventually fails for very long tester loop lengths. This may be due to the effect of tester clock stability on synchronization 5 , with any instability having a cumulatively larger impact at longer loop lengths. In this case a 2.1 ms loop length could not be used with LVP, but did work with TRE. Again, the device examined was a latch. Figure  7  shows the TRE signal after an acquisition time of 1 hour, with a Vcc of 1.4 V. This was long enough to yield a timing precision of about ± 25 ps. If better timing precision were required, the data could be collected for longer. To demonstrate, this signal was acquired in 1-hour intervals for up to 14 hours. In this case, to reach a timing precision of ± 10 ps took an acquisition time of about 12 hours. The 12-hour acquisition is also shown in Figure  7 .


## Time Response


Time Response


The time response of a single element TRE system sets a limit on the device transitions that can be resolved in time in a single acquisition. It also affects the accuracy with which time delay between events observed in separate acquisitions can be determined. Bruce et al. 6 have already demonstrated that delay times less than the system time response can be measured, showing an example of a measured delay time of about 160 ps on their system which had a 262 ps time response.


As also discussed by Bruce et al. 6 , the overall measured time response is found from the FWHM of the detected peaks, and will be made up of contributions from the jitter of the system electronics, the time response of the detector, and the time response of the device under test. In the present study, the system electronics jitter was measured at just under 20 ps. The detector response was not separately measured but was expected to be in the 100 to 110 ps range. Taking the minimum FWHM of 105 ps presented above and neglecting the device, one can infer a time response of about 103 ps for the detector. Therefore as was the case in Bruce et al. 6  the detector was the determining factor, and the overall time response of the current system can be estimated at 105 ps.


Based on the results presented above several observations about the utility of the single element TRE method and its advantages and disadvantages relative to LVP can be made. These results show that time resolved emission measurements can now be made using tester loop lengths typical of microprocessor debug without resorting to very long acquisitions times, as would be required to do the same measurements with PICA 5 . In some cases the acquisition times are even comparable to LVP on the same device.


Several advantages of single element TRE relative to LVP are also apparent. Since the TRE method can accommodate long tester loop lengths, it can be used to examine microprocessor debug cases not currently accessible with LVP. For cases where excellent timing precision is essential, the TRE data acquisition time can be extended to achieve the desired result, including sub ± 10 ps precision. The single element TRE method can also take advantage of collecting emissions from a larger area on large devices and thus reducing acquisition time, while the probing area in LVP remains fixed by its spot size 5 . This can also be a disadvantage for TRE when examining small devices, as is discussed below.


Among the disadvantages of TRE relative to LVP are that TRE yields a signal of emission peaks, rather than a waveform resembling the voltage waveform. While the LVP waveform can sometimes be inverted relative to the voltage waveform, this is only thought to be a minor disadvantage to an experienced user of LVP. Also since the time resolved emissions are lower for p-channel transistors than n-channel and for smaller area devices, acquisition times for TRE on some devices are currently still longer than those for LVP in these cases. However, while not demonstrated here, despite longer acquisition times, TRE may eventually be more useful for probing small devices than LVP if LVP invasiveness becomes an issue 5 .


The data presented here demonstrate that single element time resolved emission tools could be used for practical microprocessor circuit diagnostics, in many cases without sacrificing the conveniently short acquisition times of laser voltage probing. Compared to previously reported single element TRE data, those reported here showed emission from both nand p-channel devices from the current 0.13 µm process generation silicon, with tester loop lengths useful in typical microprocessor circuit diagnostics. Good timing precision was also still maintained, including a demonstration of sub ± 10 ps precision. Acquiring data from the same device using both the TRE and LVP methods produced comparable results with similar acquisition times. The TRE method was also shown to be applicable to microprocessor diagnostic cases with very long tester loop lengths that are not possible with LVP.


In recent years, optical beams have been used for IC fault isolation through different techniques, such as OBIC  [1] , OBIRCH  [2] , LIVA  [3] , TIVA  [4] , RIL  [5]  and laser probing  [6] . In some cases, the laser can be very invasive and can dramatically alter the transistor's performance, sometimes damaging the device permanently. During analysis of advanced microprocessors, the authors have observed functional changes, which were a direct result of laser influence. Furthermore, there were cases where the devices failed to function and were severely damaged (Figure  1 ). There is a need to understand how the optical beams affect the transistor performance and potentially damage a device. In this study, the authors used flip chip SOI test chips as the main test vehicle with 1340 nm and 1064 nm wavelength lasers being used for stimulus. These laser wavelengths are commonly used in advanced backside failure analysis techniques. Since the lasers operate in the near infrared spectral region, there are inherent thermal effects on the device. Based on semiconductor physics, the localized temperature change would affect the transistor channel resistivity and thus its performance  [7] .


Theoretically, the resistivity of a semiconductor material can be related to temperature as follows ρ=(nqµ) -1 ≈ e (Ef-Ei)/KT T -5/2  (1)  where n (electron concentration) and µ (electron mobility) are a function of temperature. It has been previously shown that thermal stimulus increases lattice and impurity scattering mechanisms and thereby reduces the movement of drifting charge carriers through the crystal lattice. This disruption of lattice periodicity effectively reduces mobility  [8] .

## Transistor Characterization


Transistor Characterization


The influence of external temperature on transistor drive strength is shown in Figure  8 . At low gate bias, drive strength increases with temperature due to the thermal generation of minority carriers within the channel region, however at higher gate bias, the reduction in mobility within the channel dominates. These phenomena can be explained by the following equations: Drive current, I ds , in the saturation region can be expressed as I ds = (µε ox /2t ox )*(W/L)*(V gs -V t ) 2  (8)


Since both µ and V t are function of temperature, the relative temperature coefficient α s can be written as α s = (1/I ds )(δI ds /δT) = µ -1 (δµ/δT) + 2(V gs -V t ) -1 (-δV t /δT) (9)


If we take δV t /δT=-.57 (from Figure  3 ) and µ ≈ T -n  [7]  where n is about 1-1.5, then α s = -nT -1 + 2(V gs -V t ) -1 *0.57 (10)  Generally speaking, when V gs is much greater than V t , the first term in equation (  10 ) dominates the second term. In this case α s is negative, and therefore the drive strength will decrease with temperature. Conversely, the drive strength will increase with temperature as V gs approaches V t.

## Damage Threshold


Damage Threshold


Figure  11  illustrates typical I-V transistor curves before and after being exposed to too much incident laser power. The arrows denote the transistor characteristics after permanent damage has been induced. Electrical characterization, in these cases showed shorts between the gate, source and drain.


Work has also been performed on advanced microprocessors where laser intrusion has been shown to alter circuit performance  [12]  or cause permanent damage to the devices under study during backside analysis.


As laser based fault isolation techniques become a mainstream portion of an analyst's tool kit, the lasers impact on transistor must be better understood. The authors have shown that laser intrusion can significantly affect transistor and circuit behavior to the point of catastrophic failure. Although laser intrusion induces temperature changes, such as decreased transistor channel mobility and V t , these effects alone are not enough to explain the observed damage phenomena. The authors have conjectured that locally induced stress within the transistor structure may be responsible.


LVP and TRPE techniques such as picosecond imaging circuit analysis (PICA) are used to measure timing signals from the internal nodes of CMOS ICs (see  [1]  and references therein for an overview of these techniques). These tools have played a key role in the development of current generation ICs such as microprocessors by helping designers debug their prototype devices  [2] [3] [4] [5] . However, improvements in the performance of these tools are necessary to allow them to keep pace with the design debug requirements of future ICs. These ICs can be SOI based, run at multi-GHz clock speeds, contain hundreds of millions of transistors, be built with 90 nm or smaller geometries, and have 1 ≤


## DD V


Volt  [6] .


For TRPE based probing of CMOS ICs, the major challenge is developing new detectors capable of compensating for the expected decrease in photon emission rates as V dd and/or gate loading is reduced  [7, 8]  while simultaneously meeting the higher bandwidth requirements of future devices. Detectors based on Si avalanche photodiodes (APD) or Gen III photocathodes are rapidly losing their usefulness for the most demanding applications because of their low quantum efficiency (QE) in the near-infrared (NIR) range of interest and/or their high jitter (which limits their bandwidth). InGaAs-APD based detectors have high QE in the NIR, but currently suffer from high timing jitter and high dark-count rates. They must also be operated in a gated mode and have minimum useable loop length restrictions  [9] . New singlephoton-counting detectors with simultaneously high QE, low jitter, and low dark-count rates are needed. For LVP, the challenge is to find ways to maintain high signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) as IC geometries shrink and the overlap between the laser beam probe and the transistor diffusions is reduced  [1] . In the past, SNR was maintained or even improved by the introduction of phase-sensitive detection  [16] , and, more recently, liquid immersion lens technology  [17] . Both techniques work by increasing detected signal levels. Currently, there is no obvious way to further improve signal strength, outside of the use of solid-immersion lenses which have limited general usefulness  [18] . However, SNR can still be improved by reducing the baseline noise level of the system.


The dominant source of noise in LVP is device vibration, especially when the system is docked to an ATE test head. A dual-laser scheme was developed to minimize the effects of this noise  [19] , but its effectiveness is reduced because of non-linear effects in silicon  [20] . The new time-differential LVP (TD-LVP) scheme presented is designed to overcome this limitation, allowing true shot-noise limited performance and the reliable extraction of weak (≈100 ppm) signals. Besides improving system sensitivity, this scheme is also expected to improve the ease-of-use of LVP by reducing its sensitivity to focus, beam placement, and sample drift.


## Time-Resolved Photon emission


Time-Resolved Photon emission


## SSPD Setup and Operation


SSPD Setup and Operation


The active region of SSPD consists of a 3 to 10 nm thick, 100 to 200 nm wide stripe of superconducting NbN on a sapphire substrate (Figure  1 ). The stripe is fabricated into a serpentine pattern occupying a region up to ≈10 µm x 10 µm to improve optical coupling onto the detector. Recent improvements to SSPD include increasing the fill factor of the NbN stripes to improve its DE. (Note: DE of SSPD is determined by dividing the measured signal-count rate by the number of photons incident on the ≈10 µm x 10 µm area of the detector. The  < 100% fill factor of the NbN stripe results in a DE that is less than the intrinsic QE of the NbN stripe. )


A schematic of the current detector setup is shown in Figure  2 . SSPD is cooled to ≈3 K by a closed-cycle, liquid-helium cryocooler. It is completely enclosed by a 40K cold shield to eliminate thermal background radiation from its surroundings. Signal photons are delivered to SSPD using a fiber optic cable. The output end (e.g., SSPD side) of the fiber is in thermal contact with the cold shield. Nearly 100% cold-stop efficiency is achieved in this way. A 1 to 1.5 µm band-pass filter is used to further reduce background radiation coupled in through the fiber.


The filter is needed because SSPD is sensitive to light with wavelength from  < 400 nm to  > 2.5 µm  [11] . Setup used to characterize SSPD and make TRPE measurements. The cryostat is evacuated to  < 10 -6 torr. Photons from the DUT are coupled to the detector using a cooled fiber optic cable and cooled optics. A 1.0 µm to 1.5 µm bandpass filter is used to further reduce background counts. A constant current source provides the bias for the detector.


Voltage pulses generated by absorbed photons are coupled out with an RF bias-T and amplified. A comparator is used to trigger the timing electronics.


SSPD operates via the mechanism of current-assisted hot-spot formation, as illustrated in Figure  3 . The detector is cooled to well below the ≈10.5 K superconducting transition temperature of the thin NbN stripe. A voltage-limited current source is used to bias the stripe near its critical current, c I , using an RF bias-T. The bias current is typically set to be  > 90% of c I . (Note: exceeding c I causes the superconductor's critical current density, c j , to be exceeded in the stripe. When this occurs, the superconductivity in the stripe breaks down and the stripe becomes resistive.) When the NbN stripe absorbs a photon (Figure  3a ), a hot electron is produced that collides with and breaks apart Cooper pairs in the stripe. This process cascades rapidly, resulting in the formation of a small resistive hot-spot (Figure  3b ) that, by itself, is not large enough to span the entire width of the NbN stripe. The superconducting current is shunted around the hot spot, causing current crowding in the remaining superconducting regions. c j is then exceeded in these regions (Figure  3c ) resulting in the creation of a transverse resistive segment that is in series with the rest of the superconducting stripe (Figure  3d ). This sudden change (within 10's of ps) in series resistance creates a voltage pulse across the ends of the stripe. RF amplifiers with a total gain of ≈50 dB and a 2 GHz (-3db) cut-off frequency are used to amplify this pulse. A comparator is used to trigger the timing electronics.


The detection efficiency of the system as a whole depends on how well the output of the fiber optic cable is coupled to the active area of SSPD. Coupling the output of a standard 50 µm core-diameter, 0.2 numerical aperture (NA), graded-index multi-mode fiber to the 10 µm x 10 µm detector requires diffraction limited optics and a solid immersion lens (5x demagnification, SSPD-side NA = 1). Obtaining diffraction limited performance of the optics when they are under vacuum and cooled to 40K is not possible with the existing system. As a result, the system detection efficiency (SDE) is currently less than the DE by ≈10x. To recover system sensitivity, an improved in-situ alignment mechanism is being implemented and custom, small core-diameter multimode fiber is being tested. Using smaller core fiber reduces the requirements on the coupling optics. For example, by decreasing the core diameter to 25 µm, the demagnification and the SSPD-side NA required of the coupling optics can be reduced by 2x. These two modifications to the system are expected to allow the full SSPD DE to be achieved at the system level.

However, when it is not convenient to have tester interactions, by using the production test patterns without any modification, the proposed technique can still generate manageable results.
