## 6. Conclusions


In this paper, we described a scan chain fault diagnosis procedure. The scan chain fault diagnosis is performed in three steps. The first step uses chain test patterns to determine the faulty chain and the fault type in the faulty chain. The second step uses special test patterns to identify the range of the suspect scan cells. Unlike previously proposed methods that restrict the faulty scan cell only from the scan chain output side, our method restricts the faulty scan cell from both the scan chain output side and the scan chain input side. Hence the number of suspect scan cells is reduced significantly in this step. The final step further improves the diagnosis resolution by ranking the suspect scan cells in the range calculated in the last step. The proposed technique can handle stuck-at faults, transition faults, and hold time faults. The experimental results show that for most failing chips, the number of candidate scan cells can be reduced to several scan cells. By using the modified production test patterns, the proposed technique can find the exact defective scan cells for most of the failing chips.


Optical probing tools and techniques have been critical for backside circuit diagnostics on flip-chip packaged microprocessors 1-3 . These tools provide the means of determining directly whether individual transistors are operating, and more importantly make available timing information on the devices. A relatively recent introduction to commercially available optical probing tools is those methods that analyze the time resolved emissions from the circuits, such as Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) 4 . Such tools are of interest at least in part because, unlike the laser voltage probing (LVP) method 5 , they are non-invasive, an advantage that may become more and more important as smaller nodes are analyzed. While imaging methods like PICA are useful for some types of diagnostics 4 , time resolved emission (TRE) techniques using highly sensitive single element detectors are more analogous in application to the LVP method currently in use and offer the prospect of faster acquisition times than PICA for common diagnostic needs.


Single element TRE results have previously been presented 6-8 . Bruce et al. 6 demonstrated a system with moderate time response, ~260 ps, but with a detector quantum efficiency high enough to detect emissions from both n-channel and p-channel devices on 0.25 µm process silicon running at about 2.5 V Vcc. Emissions from p-channel transistors are typically lower than n-channel, with Bruce et al. 6  reporting about a factor of 10 lower, and hence a more sensitive detector is needed to collect these emissions. Tester loop length and acquisition time were not reported. On the other hand, Somani et al. 7  showed excellent time response,  <  75 ps, but the detector quantum efficiency was low, so that data acquisition on only n-channel devices took 30 minutes for 0.13 µm silicon running at 1.3 V with a test pattern loop length of 100 ns. The results in the current paper improve upon these previous results, showing the first single element TRE data collected from 0.13 µm process silicon using tester loop lengths, and in many cases acquisition times, comparable to laser voltage probing. Further results are presented that compare TRE signals to LVP waveforms from the same device. This includes an example of a single element TRE application that could not be performed with LVP, a case with a long tester loop length greater than 2 ms. Some advantages and disadvantages of the TRE and LVP methods are also briefly discussed.


## Single Element TRE


Single Element TRE


For TRPE measurements from ICs, emission from the device-under-test (DUT) is collected using a high NA objective lens, as shown in Figure  4 . The center of the field-of-view of the lens is mapped to the input end of the fiber using relay optics. A selectable-area aperture (SAA) is located at an intermediate image plane to allow emission from regions outside the desired probing area to be excluded from collection by the fiber. The SAA consists of 4 individually position-able blades.


For imaging and navigation, a laser scanning microscope (LSM) is used. The center of the LSM image is aligned to the fiber. The LSM port also allows the incorporation of laser based techniques such as TD-LVP, TIVA and/or LIVA. A secondary imaging port is available for a PICA, CCD, or MCT camera. A 3-position mirror is used to switch modes between SSPD, LSM-based, and PICA/CCD/MCT acquisitions.


## SSPD Characterization


SSPD Characterization


The jitter of SSPD was characterized using a 7 ps pulse width, 1064 nm wavelength mode-locked laser as the light source. The laser's output was attenuated until there were, statistically,  < < 1 photon per pulse. The output of SSPD was used to trigger a 20 GHz digital sampling oscilloscope. The 100 MHz clock from the laser, which is synchronized to the laser's output pulses, was used as the signal to the oscilloscope. Figure  5  shows the jitter in the measured laser clock edge, which gives the jitter of SSPD. From this figure, the upper limit for SSPD jitter is 33 ps (FWHM) for the 4 µm x 4 µm detector used. The jitter contribution from the detection electronics was determined to be 15 ps while the pulse width and jitter of the laser source were negligible. Subtracting the jitter of the electronics gives an ultimate SSPD jitter of ≈ 30 ps. Overall jitter for 10 µm x 10 µm detectors using the same detection electronics is slightly worse (≈40 ps) due to a slight increase in amplitude noise of their output pulses. Changes in the detection electronics are underway to compensate for this extra noise. Figure  6  shows a plot of SDE and dark-count rate as a function of bias current through the NbN stripe for a 10 µm x 10 µm SSPD. A calibrated, 1300 nm wavelength, fiber coupled LED was used as the light source. The nominal DE of this SSPD is 5% at 1300 nm. SDE is calculated by dividing the signal-count rate by the number of 1300 nm photons input into the fiber optic cable delivering light to SSPD. The signal-count rate is calculated by subtracting the dark-count rate from the total count rate. As discussed above, presently, SDE  < DE because of imperfect optical coupling between the fiber output and the 10 µm x 10 µm active area of SSPD.


As shown in Figure  6 , SDE tends to saturate as the bias current is increased. The dark-count rate, on the other hand, increases exponentially until the maximum count rate of the detection electronics is reached. These properties of SSPD means that for high bias currents, small changes in the current have a dramatic effect on the dark-count rate but only a minimal effect on the SDE. For example, increasing the bias current from 28 µA to 30 µA improves SDE by ≈50% (from ≈0.2% SDE to ≈0.3% SDE) but increases the dark-count rate by over 3 orders of magnitude. (Note, however, that even at 30 µA bias, the dark-count rate is still only ≈2000 s -1 .) Figure  7  is a plot of SDE as a function of wavelength for the same 10 µm x 10 µm SSPD. For this measurement, the bias current was fixed at 29 µA.


The corresponding dark-count rate was  < 20 s -1 . The light source was a tungsten-halogen lamp. A monochromator was used to select the wavelength. The output from the monochromator was attenuated using banks of calibrated neutral-density filters.


The curve fit to the data in Figure  7  shows that SDE varies with wavelength according to the exponential relation: . As expected, the form of this behavior is consistent with that reported for the DE of large area SSPDs  [11] . (Note: The value of k , and, hence, the drop-off in DE with wavelength, is smaller than the reported value due to a new detector fabrication process.) From this plot, SDE is found to be  > 0.4% at 1300 nm and drops to  < 0.3% at 1500 nm. The SDE at 1300 nm determined from this measurement is in good agreement with the data shown in Figure  6 .


Currently, the maximum DE of 10 µm x 10 µm SSPDs is ≈ 5% at 1300 nm. This is limited by the line-width non-uniformity of the long NbN meander (see Figure  1  and  [10] ). For 4 µm x 4 µm detectors, DEs of ≈10% have recently been achieved. With further process characterization and improvements in the e-beam lithography step used to pattern the NbN meander, achieving 10% DE on the larger detectors will be possible. Ultimately, DEs as high as 20% should be achievable  [10] . Corresponding dark-count rate was  < 20 s -1 (see Figure  6 ). Roll off at wavelengths  < 1000 nm and  > 1500 nm is due to the action of the bandpass filter (see Figure  2 ). Fit to the data points inside the bandpass region is indicated by the solid line.


## SSPD TRPE Results


SSPD TRPE Results


A SSPD TRPE histogram from a 0.13 µm geometry nFET biased at 1.3 V is shown in Figure  8 . The test pattern was a 100 MHz square wave. The loop length was 10 µs and the total acquisition time was 10 minutes. As can be seen in Figure  8B ), SSPD allows data to be acquired over the full test pattern loop length during a single measurement. Raw data is always acquired using the minimum histogram bin width of 2.5 ps allowed by the electronics. For display and analysis (real-time or post-processing) the data can be re-sorted using larger bin sizes if desired.


Figure  8A ) and 8C) show 100 ns time slices extracted from the complete data set shown in Figure  8B ) at the locations indicated by the dashed arrows. As expected, emission peaks spaced every 10 ns are clearly visible in A) and C). Note the low dark/background noise level,  < < 1 count per bin on average, between switching events in 8A) and 8C). No background subtraction, smoothing, or filtering was performed on this data.


Figure  9  shows the emission peak from a single nFET switching event, taken from another TRPE acquisition. The cause of the relatively broad peak width (compared to the ≈40 ps minimum overall jitter of the 10 µm x 10 µm SSPD and detection electronics used) has been determined to be due, in part, to a mis-set trigger level of the detection electronics' comparator. The timing electronics and the DUT stimulus are other possible sources of excess jitter. Somewhat surprisingly, chromatic jitter in the fiber due to the broadband emission from the DUT does not appear to be the limiting factor at this time. This source of jitter was tested for in two ways: First, by using long pass filters to reduce the spectral range of the detected photons, and second, by using a longer fiber to increase the chromatic dispersion. No effects on the histogram pulse width were observed in either test. These TRPE measurements demonstrate some of the unique capabilities of SSPD. First, the low dark/background-count rate keeps the recorded data volume low. Second, the absence of afterpulsing problems such as exist for InGaAs-APDs  [9, 21] , means that SSPD operation need not be gated. This allows data to be acquired over the full test pattern loop during a single acquisition. With an InGaAs-APD, photons emitted during switching events outside the short gating period are missed. To obtain the full data shown in Figure  8B ), for example, an InGaAs-APD using a 100ns long gating time would require 100 separate acquisitions and take 100 times longer. Third, the absence of gating restrictions for SSPD means that there is no loss of acquisition efficiency when using short test loops. For example, an InGaAs-APD with a recovery time of 10 µs would have its acquisition efficiency reduced by 10 times when acquiring data using a 1 µs long test loop. SSPD will operate at full efficiency at essentially any loop length (up to the hardware-limited maximum of ≈650 µs), and has been tested using loops shorter than 10 ns.


## SSPD TRPE Performance Scaling


SSPD TRPE Performance Scaling


As , where TTS t ∆ is the jitter of the detector, is the probability of detecting a dark-count within the signal peak per switching event. SNR is the signalto-noise ratio required of the measurement, which depends on the timing accuracy needed and the detector jitter  [1] .


For a low dark-count rate detector like SSPD,   (6)  for both detectors. By virtual of its lower dark count rate, SSPD with half the SDE would provide the same performance as the InGaAs-APD under the stated conditions. (Note, it is assumed that SDE ≈ DE ≈ QE for an InGaAs-APD because of its 100% fill factor and larger active area.) However, if the photon emission rate drops by 3 times (which might happen when measuring 0.13 µm geometry pFET emission, or 90 nm geometry nFET emission) then ph gate S w decreases by the same factor and, again from Equation (1), SSPD would be twice as fast as the InGaAs-APD. If the photon emission rate drops by 10x (which might happen for 90 nm geometry pFETs) SSPD will be  > 5x faster.


Figure  10 , a plot of Equation (  1 ) for the two detectors, shows this graphically. The axes were normalized to the expected values for a 0.13 µm geometry nFET biased at 1.3 V. This plot clearly shows that as photon emission rates decrease, the performance of an optimized SSPD will scale better than the InGaAs-APD will. (normalized to the values expected for a 0.13 µm geometry nFET biased at 1.3 V). See text for details.


To make up for increasing acquisition times due to decreasing emission rates, the test pattern loop length could be decreased (where possible) if SSPD is used. Since acquisition times are proportional to loop length ( loop T ), a 10x shorter loop will compensate for a 10x reduction in emission rate with SSPD. For an InGaAs-APD, which has a minimum useable loop length restriction, it is not possible to reduce loop T beyond the minimum allowed without loss of efficiency.


Improving DE of SSPD to compensate for decreasing emission rates will also be possible. DEs of 20%, or more, are ultimately achievable  [10] . As mentioned above, achieving higher DEs for SSPD is primarily a matter of improving the line-width uniformity of the NbN stripes. Since DE is, for the most part, independent of dark-count rate and jitter for SSPD, it will be possible to increase DE without degrading these other properties. For InGaAs-APDs, on the other hand, it will be difficult to significantly increase QE without seriously degrading its dark-count rate because of their exponential relationship. [21] .


## Time-Differential Laser Voltage Probing


Time-Differential Laser Voltage Probing


Noise Rejection in LVP


The major challenge with LVP is extracting the relatively weak (≈100 to 1000 parts-per-million, ppm) signal modulations from the large (≈100,000 to 200,000 ppm) background noise generated by DUT vibrations  [16, 19] . Lock-in techniques can not be used because they require that the DUT stimulus be chopped, which is not generally possible for complicated ICs. Instead, a two-laser probing scheme was developed to reduce the impact of this noise.


This scheme works as follows: Within each loop, a 150 ns long reference pulse, generated by chopping the output of a continuous wave laser (CWL), samples the DUT at a fixed time, relative to the start of the test pattern. During the same loop, a 35 ps wide probe pulse, generated by a mode-locked laser (MLL), samples the DUT at a variable time. Both laser pulses track the slow reflectivity changes caused by DUT vibrations, but only the MLL pulse tracks the fast changes caused by the DUT signal.


Taking the ratio of MLL to CWL pulses each loop reduces the effects of vibrational noise by ≈20-30x.


The lasers used for LVP have 1.17 eV photon energy, slightly higher than the silicon band gap energy of 1.12 eV. As a result, significant numbers of electron-hole pairs are generated in a very short time by the MLL pulse in the reverse biased junction being probed. These charge carriers generate a relatively large photo-current pulse that can affect device operation. Despite this electrical perturbation, accurate LVP waveforms can be acquired by using equivalent time sampling.


In equivalent time sampling, the DUT test pattern must be made to repeat continuously. At the end of each loop of the test pattern, the DUT is reset to its electrical state at the start of the loop and any electrical disturbances are terminated. This means that each measurement made by the mode-locked laser is on an undisturbed signal. Since the modelocked laser makes its measurement within 35 ps, the measurement is valid because it is made before the DUT voltage can change significantly.


Accurate LVP measurements require that there be no significant perturbation to the circuit caused by the CWL pulse. The device state is not reset after the 759 CWL measurement so any disturbance that it causes could, under certain circumstances, propagate in the DUT and affect the MLL measurement. The photocurrent generated by the CWL pulse has been measured and is  < 1 µA for the duration of its 150 ns pulse. For most logic circuits, this level of photocurrent has not been a serious problem.


Further improvements to LVP waveform SNR can be achieved by improving vibrational noise rejection. The level of rejection possible using the dual-laser scheme is limited by non-linear refractive index effects in silicon  [22] . The high peak power in the MLL pulse (≈150 MW/cm 2 ) is  > 4000x larger than that for the CWL pulse. This difference results in a small, but significant, difference in how the two laser pulses respond to DUT vibrations. Replacing the CWL with a second MLL to eliminate the peak power differences is not practical because of the possible effects of the electrical perturbation that would be caused by a MLL pulse (and because of the added expense!).


## TD-LVP Scheme


TD-LVP Scheme


To overcome the limitations in LVP noise rejection imposed by the Si non-linearities, a time-differential probing scheme is being investigated. The simplest implementation of this scheme is shown in Figure  11 .


A single MLL pulse is split in two using a polarizing beam splitter (PBS1) to form the reference (r) and probe (p) pulses. An optical delay arm is used to time shift the probe pulse with respect to the reference pulse by a small, fixed, amount, t ∆ (≈ laser pulse width). The two pulses are then spatially recombined using a second polarizing beam splitter (PBS2). Both pulses are focused into the active region of the DUT. After retro-reflection from the DUT, the return pulses are diverted from the incident beam path using a fixed-ratio beam splitter (50/50BS). The reflected probe and reference pulses are then spatially separated using a third polarizing beam splitter (PBS3) and detected individually. Their signals are subtracted from each other to generate the TD-LVP signal.


Figure  12  is a timing diagram illustrating how a TD-LVP waveform is generated. DUT signal variations occurring within the time t ∆ , at time delay D t (Figure  12a , b) cause the reflected signal amplitudes of the probe and reference beams to differ (Figure  12c ). This difference is measured at different points in the DUT test pattern by varying D t . (As in the standard dual-laser scheme, this is done by phase shifting the laser output with respect to the DUT stimulus  [19] .) The TD-LVP waveform (Figure  12d ) is generated by plotting the measured reflectivity differences as a function of D t . In principle, this scheme will be able to achieve nearly perfect vibrational noise cancellation. Since the probe and reference pulses have equal peak powers, differences due to non-linear refractive index effects in Si are eliminated. As an added benefit, laser noise is cancelled automatically because the probe and reference pulses are derived from the same MLL pulse. With properly designed electronics, the limiting noise is expected to be the shot noise in the laser pulses.


Assuming 10 µW of reflected power in each beam, the combined shot noise of the two pulses will be  < 2000 ppm (rms). After 100 waveform averages, with 40 samples per pixel, a 9-point running average, and 500 pixels per waveform (typical conditions for LVP acquisitions) the rms noise level will be reduced to 10 ppm. This should make it possible to acquire 100 ppm signals in a few minutes, even for 100 µs long loops.


## TD-LVP Bench Measurement


TD-LVP Bench Measurement


A test-bench measurement, using the optical layout schematically shown in Figure  11 , was made as a proof-of-principle demonstration of the TD-LVP scheme. The results are shown in Figure  13 . For this measurement, the DUT was driven with a 100 MHz square wave. A 35 ps pulse width laser was used, and the probe and reference beams were separated in time by 200 ps. (Smaller delays could not be generated using the simple scheme implemented.) The reflected probe and reference signals were simultaneously acquired, then digitally subtracted to generate the difference signal. While not a true test of the noise rejection capability of this technique, it nevertheless demonstrates the TD-LVP principle of operation.


## Summary and Conclusions


A new superconducting single-photon detector, SSPD, for time-resolved photon emission measurements was presented. Recent changes in the SSPD fabrication process have resulted in a  > 100x increase in DE for large area detectors. Presented results demonstrate its unique properties of high DE in the NIR, low jitter, and low dark/background count rates. In addition, it does not suffer from the afterpulsing problems that can limit the usefulness of InGaAs-APD based detectors. An, as yet, unexploited property of SSPD is its wide spectral sensitivity range, which extends from  < 400 nm to  > 2500 nm. TRPE measurements of emission from a 0.13 µm geometry nFET biased at 1.3 V demonstrate SSPD's advantages. These include its ability to collect data over the complete test pattern loop, at full resolution, during a single acquisition, and its ability to run essentially any loop length at full efficiency.


A 10x improvement in SSPD system DE (to ≈5%) is expected shortly. This will be achieved through improvements in the in-situ alignment mechanism of the fiber-to-SSPD coupling optics and through the use of custom, small core-diameter, fiber optic cable. Calculations show that this level of SDE, combined with the low dark/background-count rate, would enable SSPD to match or exceed the performance of an InGaAs-APD with 10% QE. Ultimate DEs (and SDEs) as high as 20% should be possible without degrading SSPD's timing resolution or low darkcount rate. Improvements in the system jitter (to  < 50 ps) are also expected shortly through improvements in the acquisition electronics. An ultimate system jitter of ≈30 ps is possible because of the inherently low jitter of SSPD.


A new time-differential acquisition scheme for LVP, TD-LVP, was also presented. This scheme is designed to improve the vibrational noise rejection of LVP and will lead to improved ease-of-use and increased measurement sensitivity. 100 ppm signals are expected to be measure-able, reliably and consistently. A proof-of-concept demonstration of the scheme was given. A prototype is being built to more fully demonstrate its potential. This prototype will incorporate a  < 10 ps pulse width MLL and will allow pulse separations as small as 10 ps. It is designed to detect amplitude as well as phase modulations. With phase sensing, it may be possible to detect charge density modulations with TD-LVP using a non-invasive laser wavelength ( 1110 ≥ λ nm)  [23] . A major goal of this project is to build a system that can be retrofitted to existing LVP systems and can be incorporated into (IDS-PICA based) TRPE systems (see Figure  4 ).


Both SSPD and TD-LVP are expected to extend the usefulness of the TRPE and LVP techniques to next generation ICs which will have smaller geometries, run at higher clock speeds, and operate at lower voltages. These ICs may be based on CMOS (bulk or SOI) or bipolar (Si or SiGe) technologies. Since each technique has advantages and disadvantages (see  [1]  for a more complete discussion) a single platform, such as the IDS-PICA system, that can be Introduction Among the wide array of possible failure mechanisms in IC's, breakdown of the gate oxide is and has been the dominant one for CMOS IC's  [1] . The root cause of such a problem can be varied  [2, 3] , and its origins may be related to raw materials and processing, or testing and handling  [4, 5] . It is very important therefore, in identifying the root cause, to discern the exact nature and morphology of the defect site. To date, few published works have dealt with localization, imaging and analysis techniques for this smallest of defect types.


Indirect or decorative methods such as wet chemical etches require very accurate control of etch parameters, and even so the results are often unsatisfactory. Even for very well controlled etching, results often only show a hole in the gate oxide, exaggerated by the etching process, and thus real root cause is difficult to establish. What we show in this study is that direct observation with transmission electron microscopy is necessary in order to establish real root cause.


## Approaching the Defect


Approaching the Defect


When gate oxide breaks-down, the poly gate will directly short to the silicon substrate. This may or may not cause a logical, functional failure. However, it will cause increased leakage current from the gate to substrate. This characteristic provides us with the opportunity to search for the defect location.


Failing SRAM and USB devices were selected for our experiments.


An extremely useful diagnostic technique for RAM devices is the ability to take current (I CC ) measurements for various states of the memory array  [6] . In this manner, the source of excess current can be localized to an individual cell. Photon emission microscopy can then be applied to image this current and further localize it within the cell  [7] . It is a non-destructive technique which in some instances can also discriminate between a forward or reverse biased pn junction, a transistor in saturation, latchup, or gate oxide breakdown. The shape of the "hot spot" can also provide information about the defect. The linear shape of the hot spots in Figure  1  indicates that the defect is long poly related. Another observation is that the defect must be on the poly layer, or a lower layer, according to the principles of photon emission (ohmic paths do not in general emit light in this range). In this way, the hot spot provides an initial three dimensional locale of the defect location.


However, the resolution of the optical microscope is not precise enough for further localization. Higher resolution equipment, such as Secondary Electron Microscope (SEM) or Focused Ion Beam (FIB), is needed for further localization of the defect.


At this point another charge-related imaging technique can be utilized. Conductor nodes which are isolated from the substrate (such as polysilicon lines which have been disconnected from their driver circuitry), will charge when imaged with a charged beam such as electron or ion beams. In contrast, if a leakage path, such as one created by a gate-oxide defect, exists, the same node will be able to discharge the beam current to the substrate. These two scenarios lead to differences in the number of secondary electrons detected, and thus readily imaged as "dark" versus "bright" nodes in a SEM or FIB. This effect is known as passive voltage contrast (PVC).


Figure  3  shows an in-situ FIB cross section of the device imaged in figure  1  above. The FIB cut was formed in such a way that the wordline drivers have been severed from the polysilicon wordlines, which should now be isolated from any junctions to the substrate. The offending wordline can clearly be seen -it appears bright, in contrast to all its neighbors which are floating and therefore dark. Note that the FIB cut was performed at a comfortable distance from the suspected defect site, and is thus non-destructive to the area of interest. At this point, an electrical path between wordline poly and substrate has been established.


Another sample preparation technique for using PVC is shown in figure  4 . Here, the sample has been mechanically polished in a top-down manner (parallel lapping), in order to remove all interconnect metalization layers. What remain are the contact plugs and the poly transistors. Contrast differences are clear in the SEM image -contacts to substrate diffusions appear bright, while those to polysilicon gates appear dark. All except one of them, indicating that this gate is leaking to the substrate. Bearing in mind that there is still nitride and other insulator passivation on top of the poly gates, this technique is also non-destructive to the defect. This enables high resolution TEM observation of the defect site. In some instances where the gate is a large capacitor, however, Electron Beam Induced Current (EBIC) should also be used  [8] . EBIC is a non-destructive technique with resolution comparable to the SEM. The technique has been used for finding crystal defects  [4, 8] .


Figure  5  is a SEM image showing the structure of the USB device after parallel lapping down to the contact and poly layers. A probe needle in the lower left corner touches one of the poly silicon lines. Figure  6  shows the EBIC hot spots at the upper left side of the image.


## Final TEM analysis -results  &  discussion


Final TEM analysis -results  &  discussion


Up to this point defect sites have been localized, but the precise nature of the defect remains unknown. TEM analysis is the final step to gain this knowledge.


TEM sample preparation can be broadly categorized into plane-view (PTEM) and xsectional (XTEM), according to the sample viewing angle.


Combining a large viewing area and high resolution, PTEM can be used for defect searching and final observation. The first image reveals a particle on the silicon substrate and the damage that particle caused. The particle and the damaged area show different contrast. Comparing this image with the XTEM image in Figure  10 , it can be seen that the PTEM in this instance is better able to determine the size and shape of the defect. The XTEM, on the other hand, gives us a better perspective on its exact position relative to the field oxide edge. This type of defect is due to Kooi oxide, and is a silicon-nitride residue on the silicon substrate  [8] .


The second PTEM image shows two gate oxide pinholes. Keeping in mind that bright contrast in the TEM means low atomic density, the bright spot at the center of each pinhole indicates a "hollow" core, and the dark ring indicates the damaged substrate and poly. Examining the image closely, in actuality we observe two concentric rings. In the XTEM image we will learn that one ring demonstrates the damaged area in substrate and the other indicates the damage are in poly. Again, the large area view of the PTEM approach is useful for such multidefects cases such as gate oxide damage resulting from ESD events.


Figure  9  shows a crystal originated pit (COP). These are imperfections in the silicon crystal, and may result not only in yield but also reliability failures, as the inferior quality gateoxide locally breaks down over time.


The TEM fringe patterns can be interpreted as thickness contours. In this image, the H-shaped fringes delineate the active areas. A nodule like defect can be seen at the edge of the gate. The polysilicon gates and nitride spacer profiles can also be observed as light "shadows" in the image, while the high density tungsten plugs are entirely opaque and thus readily discernible. In Figure  10 , the particle is on the silicon substrate. Figure  11  shows the gate oxide pinholes. The sample was parallel lapped and the defect was located with EBIC (figures 5 and 6).


Because the sample has to be lapped down to the poly layer to allow for a probe needle to touch it, this sample has very thin poly layer. In this image we can see the damage on silicon substrate but not in poly.


With the XTEM approach in figure  13 , the poly was preserved, and the damage on both poly and substrate can clearly be seen, corresponding to the dark rings in the PTEM image.


Such a combination of an initial PTEM to localize the defect, followed by an XTEM through the defect, can be thought of as a type of "three-dimensional" TEM, recently discussed in the literature  [10][11] . It solves the problem having to guess at the defect position during XTEM, but comes at a price -working with an already very thin sample, which must now be thinned along the other dimension.


The FIB has been used to prepare such samples  [9] . However, the beam damage that the FIB can induce often results in poor TEM contrast. Mechanical polishing of the PTEM sample to form an XTEM sample solves this problem, but requires exceptional skill. Figure  13  is such a manually prepared sample. The XTEM in figure  12  clearly shows that the pits in the silicon pre-existed the gate-oxidation process -gate-oxide has clearly formed along the walls of the pit. Furthermore, the area is confined to the gate-oxide and substrate, not affecting the overlying polysilicon. These observations further support the conclusion of COPs as the root cause of failure.


The above results indicate three failure mechanisms resulting in gate-oxide breakdown.


Each of them has distinct root cause. One is residue-related and attributable to processing; one is starting material related and attributable to crystal defect (COPs); the last is test and handling related and comes about as a result of ESD damage. While traditional chemical etching and decoration approaches would have concluded "gate-oxide defect," the underlying real root cause would not have been clearly identified, as it was using the above described techniques.


Detailed TEM analysis is necessary for identifying underlying root cause for gate-oxide related defects, thus enabling process improvements to eliminate such causes.


During first silicon evaluation it was found that the charge pump voltage on this device was not reaching the appropriate operating value. The Charge Pump and its associated circuitry was suspect. Potential areas to investigate included (1) circuit design problems; (2) layout errors; (3) design rule violations and (4) fab processing problems.


Voltage on the pump line can be measured or applied externally via a special IO pad when switch S1 is turned on. The pump line can also be tri-state when all three circuits are disabled. The purpose of the pump line is to drive isolation transistors across the entire chip. The correct charge pump voltage was designed to be 4.2 volts. Several wafers were sorted in order to determine if there was a wafer map pattern associated with the failures. The charge pump voltages were recorded with respect to their die location. Most of the die would not deliver the correct voltage, but a few die on the edge of some wafers did pass. The failing voltages were all found to be less than 2.2 volts.


## Fault Localization


Fault Localization


Several techniques were used to isolate the fault.


## Electrical Characterization


Electrical Characterization


It was found that with C1 or C2 enabled, the charge pump voltage was lower than expected (refer to Figures  2  and 3 ). The tri-state current of the pump line was found to be higher than normal with C1, C2 and C3 turned off (refer to Figure  4 ). The IV curve appeared normal when C3 was enabled (refer to Figure  5 ). Figures  2  and 4  suggest that Vsv is having an unwanted affect. The charge pump voltage should be independent of Vsv when C1 is on and both C2 and C3 are off. When C1, C2, and C3 are turned off and the pump line is driven externally, a tri-stated current should be recorded. Figure  4  shows that substantially higher current is found on a bad die. Additionally, when C2 is on and the other two circuits are off, the pump line should closely follow Vsv once Vsv is approximately 4 volts. Figure  3  shows that the pump line on a bad die is not able to follow Vsv correctly. These IV curves in figure  2 , 3, 4 suggest that on a bad die the pump line has a fault path to ground that is controlled by Vsv.


The results shown in figure  5  suggest that C3 operates correctly, but they do not rule out possible shorts to ground when C3 is turned off.


## FIB Isolation


FIB Isolation


An FIB was used to isolate circuits C1 and C2. The electrical signatures of each circuit were analyzed. It was found that the charge pump in C1 operated normally when it was isolated from the rest of the chip. The Vsv circuitry in C2 also operated normally when isolated.


C3 is not possible to be physically isolated completely since it is located in many places across the chip as illustrated in figure  1 .


## Front Side Photoemission and Liquid Crystal


Front Side Photoemission and Liquid Crystal


Both front side photoemission and liquid crystal analysis were attempted. Both techniques failed to localize the fault. Seven layers of metal obscured any photoemission sites. Liquid Crystal was not able to isolate the failure.


## Backside Photoemission


Backside Photoemission


Backside photoemission proved more successful. The wafer was thinned to a thickness of 300um. Emission spots were detected successfully (refer to Figure  6 ) when C1, C2, and C3 were turned off and the pump line was driven externally.


Multiple photoemission spots were detected on each die. All of the photoemission spots were located in the center of the die along a single column. It was found that a single repeating circuit was causing all of the photoemission spots. The photoemission spot was found on transistor N1 as seen in figure  7 . The devices were failing because the charge pump voltage did not reach the correct level. But conspicuously absent from the schematic was the pump line.


## Failure Mode Analysis


Failure Mode Analysis


## Modeling the Fault


Modeling the Fault


To confirm that the photoemission spot was related to the failure, INV was alternately driven "High" and "Low" to see if there was any impact on the pump line voltage. The charge pump (C1) was enabled for this experiment. The device continued to fail with the output of INV driven low. However, with the output of INV driven high, the device passed.


Figure  8  shows the IV curves of this experiment. It indicates that a short exists between node n3 and the pump line. The failure is modeled as in figure  9 .


## Verification and Fault Location Physical Isolation


Verification and Fault Location Physical Isolation


Because the measured results agreed with the model, the layout was consulted to find the location where the pump line was shorting to node n3. It was found that another transistor (labeled N3), whose gate was controlled by the pump line, was located near N2 (refer to Figure  11 ). Although there was no direct connection between the pump line and node n3 in the layout, they were drawn close together in both the metal 1 and gate poly layers. Minimal design rules were used for both of these layers in this location (refer to Figure  11 ).


## Discussion and Conclusion


Discussion and Conclusion


Three different poly layouts are found in this area. Figure  14  illustrates the case where two hammerhead poly gates face each other. Figure  15  illustrates the case where one hammerhead poly is present. Figure  16  shows the case where hammerhead poly is not used. All three cases use minimal design rules. It is found that the poly short only exists in case 1 as seen in figure  14 . The demanding requirements of transferring a reticle pattern to the wafer in deep sub-micron technology, with complex optical extensions such as OPC, demands that each type of reticle feature take into account the details of the wafer fab exposure and the process conditions  [2] . The 'hammerhead design approach' is a technique that is well known for effectively compensating for line shortening  [3] . In this case it has the unwanted affect of creating a short in an area where minimal design rules are used.


The problem has been resolved by optimizing the exposure and focus at the gate poly lithography step.


The development of 3G cellular systems (2) continues to increase circuit complexity for mixed signal ICs, and in turn the potential for development problems.


Both of these present a challenge for meeting timely market windows.


To compound matters, the demands for shorter cycle-time and reduced costs add to the problem. One of the design challenges includes optimizing power consumption to preserve battery life. Often this requires partitioning specific circuit functions at different voltage levels, which creates the need for dedicated power and ground pins as opposed to having a common supply. Another challenge involves techniques for turning off idle circuits to conserve battery life within the mobile handset.


We present the results of failure analysis during the development of an advanced 3G cellular phone integrated circuit. This multi-mode integrated circuit is intended to support the needs of the GSM/EDGE standards (3) in quadruple band 800 / 900 / 1800 / 1900 MHz mobile telephone products. This integrated circuit will aid in the reduction of parts count in the handset by eliminating the need for the IF SAW filter. In addition, the IC will improve fading performance, and the receiver's signal to noise ratio as compared to today's GSM products. This case study focuses on the excess leakage current detected on the analog receiver supply pins during the battery save mode of operation. Experiments were unable to detect a photon emission signature since the leakage was of a resistive type from VCC to ground. Due to the low level of the leakage current there was insufficient power dissipation to obtain any thermal signatures using infrared emission (4) or liquid crystal (5) analysis. After it was determined that these techniques would not be helpful to identify the fault site(s), a series of Focus Ion Beam (FIB) (6) edit operations followed by voltage drop measurements were completed. This method helped to uncover a process spacing violation which went undetected by the design rule checks (DRC) of the library database.


## Description


Description


The BBAF_VCC  &  BBAF_GND are the analog receiver supply and ground pins to the analog receiver section of the IC. The leakage problem is observed during battery save mode, when the current measured from this supply exceeds the tester upper limit of 10 uA, as detailed in the IC specification. The test limit was raised to 200 uA in order to characterize the failures and to see the interaction of this leakage on the circuit functionality. Figure  1  shows data for 50 parts from one wafer tested over temperature. The left plot is a frequency histogram for BBAF_VCC at room temperature. The right hand plot is for parts tested at 105°C, Figure  1 , BBAF_VCC at high temperature, shows that the leakage is not greatly affected by temperature and that the variation appears to be part-to-part across the wafer. This implies the leakage is not junction related. The analog receiver section consists of five circuit blocks in cascade, all supplied by the BBAF supply pins. Figure  2  shows a simple diagram of the receiver. During the design phase, the top level simulations of the entire receiver predicted a total BBAF_VCC current of ~2uA flowing into the PMA block during battery save, with all other blocks reporting ~0uA.


## FIGURE 2 -BBAF supply connections


FIGURE 2 -BBAF supply connections


Figure  3  shows the location of the circuits that are powered by the BBAF_VCC and BBAF_GND pins, which makes up approximately one-third the area of the IC. Several high leakage parts (~150uA) were decapped and verified to have the same initial leakage current before performing experiments.


## FIGURE 3 -Circuit blocks powered by BBAF_VCC and BBAF_GND pins


FIGURE 3 -Circuit blocks powered by BBAF_VCC and BBAF_GND pins


There was good correlation between the leakage measured on the ATE and the engineering IC evaluation board. Use of the evaluation board helped to duplicate the failure in the FA lab. The IC was designed to power up in the battery save mode and did not require additional programming to put the IC into the desired state. The lack of a photon emission signature, lead us to thinking of an alternate means for isolating the cause of the leakage.


## Debug


Debug


The leakage current was measured by connecting an amp-meter in series with the BBAF_VCC pin, and powering up the IC / evaluation board. To verify that the leakage is confined to only the circuits on the analog receive supply, the BBAF_GND pin was also measured and found to be returning the expected current, rather than finding an alternate return path through the substrate and/or another circuit ground. Since the magnitude of the current is on the order of several hundred micro amps (selected parts), the use of a precision voltage meter enabled us to perform a series of voltage drop experiments. FIB pads were deposited to contact the supply metal with sufficient resistance from the BBAF_VCC pad metal to each major section of the receiver. We were then able to calculate an approximate current using the voltage drop and a calculated trace resistance based on the process sheet resistance for metal layers (I=V/R). Figure  4  shows the BBAF to PMA supply metal runner and the location of the FIB pads 1 and 2 which revealed ~1.5uA of current, which agreed with simulation, and eliminated this section as being a cause of the leakage.


The major metal lines to the IFA and Filter section reside just below the BBAF supply pads and did not provide sufficient trace resistance for an accurate voltage drop measurement. The next FIB edit involved the AAF filter section. Figure  5  shows pad locations 1 and 3, which are the main supply traces leading to the AAF section. The voltage drop measured along this trace revealed greater than 95% of the overall leakage for the given part, which lead us to the AAF circuits as the major cause of leakage. Since the supply trace leading to pad 5 contained several PMOS device connections, a cut was made which separated the comparators and the DAC circuits as depicted in figure  7 . While monitoring the current from the BBAF supply, a micro-probe with a second amp-meter allowed us to reconnect the supply to the DAC circuit. Test results led us to the DAC circuit as the major cause of leakage current. After a series of additional cuts and pads, we narrowed down the leakage to a branch within the DAC circuit, which is connected from VCC to ground. Figure  8  depicts the final experiments where the DAC ground metal was split and reconnected to verify that the return path for the leakage is returning through this path. It would be ideal to be able to perform all experiments on the same part while tracking down the source of the leakage. However it is difficult to avoid damage caused during the debug by FIB edits and micro probing.


## Cause of Leakage


Cause of Leakage


The suspected branch of the DAC circuit is shown in figure  9 , along with a portion of its layout. The exact mechanism of the leakage was not known at this point but the device M51 was thought to be pulling current from VCC and completing a path to ground through device M275. The use of the device, M275, is a common circuit technique for turning off NPN devices by pulling the base input to ground using an NMOS as a switch. The NMOS device, M51, is used to reduce the base current error for the BJT mirror containing multiple base inputs. A final FIB edit experiment involved cutting away device M51 and reconnecting the circuit as annotated on figure  9 . After powering up the circuit, all the leakage current had gone away. Further investigation into the layout of the device identified a design rule violation that was not checked by the DRC code of the library. The leakage was diagnosed to be of a resistive type from VCC to ground.


In this case study we show the use of advanced failure analysis tools to identify fault locations and verify designs in mixed mode RF BiCMOS circuits. Proper use of these tools reduces cycle times, saves expensive retooling costs and cuts time to market.

The diagram in Figure  1  illustrates the primary circuits that are involved, as well as the connections between them. The charge pump drives a signal referred to as the pump line. The pump line can be selectively driven to ground, a voltage near Vsv-a reference voltage, or the charge pump voltage using three main circuits. The three main circuits have been labeled C1, C2, and C3. Only one circuit can be enabled at a time. C1 represents the charge pump circuitry and allows the pump line to be connected to the charge pump. C2 represents the circuit that allows the pump line to follow Vsv. Circuit C3 allows the pump line to be connected to ground.

|Abstract|

|The FIB deposited, 2 x 10 6 µohm•cm material is|
|---|

|formed by combining W(CO) 6 and TMCTS, in the FIB deposition process. EDX and Auger qualitatively|

|indicate the presence of Si, O, Ga, C and W; these|

|elements are uniformly distributed throughout the|

|film. Quantitative elemental compositions are being|

|determined. FIB secondary electron imaging|

|indicates that the film is single phase. The Current-|

|Voltage curve is linear over a ±10 volt range. The|

|properties of the material are unchanged after 4|

|weeks at room temperature and after passing|

|18µamps DC for 24 hours.|

|like SiLK™. H 2 O GAE enhances the removal of SiLK™ approximately 7x relative to|

|normal FIB milling. XeF 2 GAE enhances SiLK™ removal; the enhancement is 4-5x. XeF 2 GAE proves useful if one is clearing successive layers of organic|

|and oxide dielectrics. H 2 O, on the other hand, will actually inhibit oxide removal relative to normal FIB|

|milling.|

|Presently there are FIB deposition processes for|

|conductive metals and insulating materials. For|

|example, W(CO) 6 is a precursor for FIB deposited W metal which has a resistivity of approximately|

|150µhm•cm. TMCTS (the siloxane, tetramethylcyclo-|

|tetrasiloxane) combined with O 2 is a precursor for FIB deposited SiO 2 that has a resistivity of 1-2 x 10 15 µohm• cm. Neither material is suitable for fabricating|

|kilo ohm to mega ohm structures needed in activities|

|like the FIB-assisted design verification of high-|

|speed analog circuits.|

|scan based testing. Insertion of scan chains in the|
|---|

|design facilitates, among other things, better|

|testability and diagnosability by breaking the|

|sequential logic into smaller blocks of combinational|

|logic. Figure 1 shows a simple block diagram of a|

|scan chain implementation. PI and PO are the|

|primary input and output respectively. D flip-flops|

|are slightly modified to include a shift mode or scan|

|mode, which constitutes a scan flip-flop. The D, Q,|

|and CLK are the standard input, output and clock|

|signals respectively. SI is the scan input and SE is|

|the scan enable. When SE is asserted, the flip-flop is|

|in shift mode and the state present at SI is propagated|

|to Q on the clock event. In this mode, test vectors are|

|shifted in and test results are shifted out. When SE is|

|not asserted, the flip-flip operates as a standard d-flop|

|and the value on D is propagated to Q on clock,|

|which captures the test result. ATPG (Automatic test|

|pattern generation) patterns are generated which|

|target faults in the combinational logic. Because the|

|ATPG process is deterministic and each targeted fault|

## Microwave Frequency Signal Propagation in Backside Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Fabricated Interconnects


Microwave Frequency Signal Propagation in Backside Focused Ion Beam (FIB) Fabricated Interconnects


Jeremy A. Rowlette, Michael DiBattista, Seth Fortuna, Richard H. Livengood Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, CA


We present for the first time the results of a comprehensive study of the increase in propagation delay of multi-GHz digital signals due to backside FIB fabricated interconnects. Signal propagation delays were measured in 90nm CMOS technology circuits as a function of interconnect material properties and physical dimensions. We compare the empirical results of this study to SPICE calculations, which were based on an equivalent circuit element model of the interconnect. We show that the empirical data obtained in these experiments supports the validity of the equivalent electrical model for the frequency range typically encountered in modern microprocessor debug. Based on the results or our analysis, we comment on the future capability of backside FIB circuit edit (CE) interconnection technology as it pertains to the debug of flip-chip packaged IC's operating at multi-GHz frequency. This paper examines the factors and conditions that must be considered when assessing the FA scope and role, and its establishment as a critical value add requirement to maintain quality leadership and product performance expectations. The need for "Timely Actionable Information" becomes essential as part of the FA approach and a necessity to remain effective and competitive. This paper defines an approach by which this can be accomplished in the dynamic and high speed PC environment where product life cycles are consistently shrinking and the need for analytical techniques that yield "high confidence" answers quickly are becoming necessary.


The changing conditions of the PC environment are driving the PC Failure Analysis groups to respond and adapt by establishing an Integrated Failure Analysis framework. This framework may span multiple organizations or companies and must deliver proactive information in a timely manner throughout the product life cycle (PLC). The information is proactive in the sense that FA is now identifying issues and prioritizing which of those to analyze, versus the historical model of waiting for a request by another organization.

Boundary-Scan's Next Plateau: Testing and In-System


Configuration at the System Level


Hot-carrier luminescence emission is used to diagnose the cause of excess quiescence current, I DDQ , in a low power circuit implemented in CMOS 7SF technology. We found by optical inspection of the chip that the high I DDQ is related to the low threshold, V t , device process and in particular to transistors with minimum channel length (0.18µm).


In this paper we will also show that it is possible to gain knowledge regarding the operating conditions of the IC from the analysis of optical emission due to leakage current, aside from simply locating defects and failures. In particular, we will show how it is possible to calculate the voltage drop across the circuit power grid from time-integrated acquisitions of leakage luminescence.


## Methodology for TEM Analysis of Barrier Profiles


Methodology for TEM Analysis of Barrier Profiles


Tan-Chen Lee, Jui-Yen Huang, Li-Chien


In failure analysis of wafer fabrication, currently, three different types of chemical methods including 6:6:1 (Acetic Acid/HNO 3 /HF), NaOH and Choline are used in removing polysilicon (poly) layer and exposing the gate/tunnel oxide underneath. However, usage is limited due to their disadvantages. For example, 6:6:1 is a relatively fast etchant, but it is difficult to control the etch time and keep the oxide layer intact. Also, while using NaOH to remove poly and expose the silicon oxide, the solution needs to be heated. It is also difficult to etch a poly layer with a WSi x or a CoSi x silicide using NaOH. In this paper, we will discuss these 3 etchants in terms of their advantages and disadvantages. We will then introduce a new poly etchant, called HB91. HB91 is useful for removing poly to expose the gate/tunnel oxide for identification of related defects. HB91 is actually a mixture of two chemicals namely nitric acid (HNO 3 ) and buffer oxide etchant (BOE) in a 9:1 ratio. The experimental results show that it is highly selective in poly removal with respect to the gate/tunnel oxide and is a suitable poly etchant especially for removing polysilicon with/without WSi x and CoSi x in the large capacitor structure. Application results of this poly etchant (HB91) will be presented.

## A New Technique for Scan Chain Failure Diagnosis


A New Technique for Scan Chain Failure Diagnosis


In this paper, we present a scan chain fault diagnosis procedure. The diagnosis for a single scan chain failure is performed in three steps. The first step uses special chain test patterns to determine both the faulty chain and the fault type in the faulty chain. The second step uses a novel procedure to generate special test patterns to identify the suspect scan cell within a range of scan cells. Unlike previously proposed methods that restrict the location of the faulty scan cell only from the scan chain output side, our method restricts the location of the faulty scan cell from both the scan chain output side and the scan chain input side. Hence the number of suspect scan cells is reduced significantly in this step. The final step further improves the diagnostic resolution by ranking the suspect scan cells inside this range. The proposed technique handles both stuck-at and timing failures (transition faults and hold time faults). The experimental results based on simulation and silicon units for several products show the effectiveness of the proposed method.


## Hardware  &  Test Structures


Hardware  &  Test Structures


The SEMICAPS, Inc. 1005 system (Figure  2 ) was utilized to provide the laser (1340, 1064 nm) source for the study  [9] . The system provides a spot size of approximately 1um where the laser can either be used in raster or in point mode. The tool has a maximum unfiltered power through the 100X objective of approximately 100mW.


Experiments were conducted at varying degrees of incident power. A Temptronics Model TP04000A ThermoStream was used to baseline the transistor V t change versus temperature and family I-V curves versus temperature. Test structures manufactured in an advanced 0.13um SOI process were used to examine the laserinduced effects. Transistors were tested before and after backside polishing to verify that no handling damage had taken place.


## Experiments


The experiments were designed to determine the temperature and transistor drive variations resulting from increased laser power. Ultimately, results from these experiments would contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms that lead up to the catastrophic failure of a device.


## Temperature Measurements


Temperature Measurements


Figure  3  shows the transistor V t response as a function of ThermoStream temperature. The V t shift with respect to temperature was calculated to be approximately -0.57mV/°C. The following figures (Figures  4 5 6 ) show the V t response from identical transistors resulting from laser influence. Incident laser power was varied for both lasers. Figure  7  illustrates the laser induced equivalent temperature, which was extrapolated from the -0.57mV/°C threshold voltage (V t ) shift. The authors did not use the results from 1064 nm laser intrusion in the temperature calculations since induced electron-hole pairs also affect V t . At the full laser power (112mW), this translates to an equivalent temperature above 500 °C. If this were truly the induced temperature, the laser would cause severe device damage since the melting point of the Silicon doped aluminum alloy is in the same temperature range. The decrease in V t caused by the laser is most likely a result of contributions from both thermal energy as well as stress from localized heat.


## Next-Generation


Next-Generation


In recent years, there have been many advances in the equipment and techniques used to isolate faults. There are many options available to the failure analyst. The available techniques fall into the categories of electrical, photonic, thermal and electron/ion beam  [1] . Each technique has its advantages and its limitations. In this paper, we introduce a case of successful failure analysis using a combination of several fault localization techniques on a 0.15um CMOS device with seven layers of metal. It includes electrical failure mode characterization, front side photoemission, backside photoemission, Focused Ion Beam (FIB), Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and liquid crystal.


Electrical characterization along with backside photoemission proved most useful in this case as a poly short problem was found to be causing a charge pump failure. A specific type of layout, often referred to as a hammerhead layout, and the use of Optical Proximity Correction (OPC) contributed to the poly level shorts.
